events.title: CNN boss Mark Thompson is staying on in the David Ellison era. Read his memo to staffers.
events.summary: Mark Thompson will continue to lead CNN at Skydance, David Ellison's new media company. Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for Warner Bros. Discovery CNN CEO Mark Thompson will remain in charge as David Ellison's Skydance buys Warner Bros. Discovery. The news giant will share common ownership with CBS News, which Ellison shook up by hiring Bari Weiss. Read Thompson's full memo to CNN employees. Mark Thompson isn't going anywhere. David Ellison is keeping CNN's top executive in place as Paramount buys Warner Bros. Discovery, the news giant's parent company. The merger will put CNN and CBS News under one corporate roof. Thompson, who's led CNN since October 2023, told staffers on Monday that he's staying at the network. His title will be chairman and editor-in-chief. "I'm convinced that from David Ellison on down, Paramount Skydance leadership really does believe in news alongside entertainment as a top strategic opportunity for our new company," Thompson said in a memo obtained by Business Insider. Thompson told employees he has "real confidence" that Ellison will "understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for." The future of CNN — and particularly its editorial independence —was a hot political topic ahead of the $110 billion mega-merger of Paramount and WBD. Critics were concerned Ellison and his father, Larry — the Oracle billionaire and longtime Trump ally — could bend the operation to be more favorable to the president. Ellison has broadly denied that he's interested in making such changes to CNN. As part of the settlement of an antitrust lawsuit brought by 12 states, Paramount will create an independent editorial board to monitor editorial principles at both CNN and CBS News. It will report to the combined entity's corporate board through its chief compliance officer. Thompson said that leadership at Ellison's new-look media giant had "seen our digital strategy and are as excited about it as we are." CNN's top boss previously told staffers not to assume that the network would combine with CBS News after Paramount completed the WBD deal. "Don't jump to conclusions that we become one with CBS News," CNN CEO Mark Thompson had told staffers at a September town hall, a person familiar with the meeting said. Ellison shook up CBS News by hiring Bari Weiss as the network's top editor last October. Weiss, a former New York Times opinion editor who hadn't previously worked in TV news, has critiqued the mainstream media and is known for her anti-woke views. She has faced accusations of editorial interference and political bias from former CBS News employees, which she has denied. Otherwise, Paramount CEO David Ellison hasn't said much about how CNN and CBS News will operate under common ownership. The media mogul has expressed interest in building a "scaled news service," though he hasn't publicly given specifics. Besides CNN and CBS News, the combined company will house assets including two major movie studios, HBO, HBO Max, Paramount+, Pluto TV , and a slew of cable TV channels. Paramount said it expects the deal to close on Tuesday. Read Thompson's full memo to CNN employees below: Dear All, As you know, Paramount Skydance will close its deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery tomorrow, and CNN will have new owners. Later today, the company is announcing the anticipated leadership lineup of the company which is now called Skydance. You'll see my name on the list as Chairman and Editor-in-Chief of CNN. I'm writing to you now to explain what that means. The specifics of how CNN will plug into and operate in the new company have yet to be finalized — hardly surprising given that serious discussions could only begin after Paramount's anti-trust settlement a few days ago. So I can't answer every question today. Nonetheless there are a few important things I can say: First, I'm convinced that from David Ellison on down, Paramount Skydance leadership really does believe in news alongside entertainment as a top strategic opportunity for our new company. They've seen our digital strategy and are as excited about it as we are. And second, having now spoken to them at length on the topic, I have real confidence that they both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for. That's why I will be leading CNN into this new chapter as it becomes one of Skydance's suite of major media assets and global brands, and leading it as an independent Editor-in-Chief with the same responsibilities and prerogatives that I have now. I know many of you have had trepidations about this moment. That's understandable — indeed, as I've hinted before, I've had the odd moment or two myself! But I want to say that on the eve of the acquisition of CNN by Paramount Skydance, I find myself in a very positive frame of mind. I really do believe we'll be working alongside a team who don't just have real vision and real energy, but real values as well. We'll make sure that everyone gets details of how to watch the actual launch of the company tomorrow. More to come, and all the best, Mark Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Treasury yields rise to start the week; traders look ahead to Fed minutes
events.summary: U.S. Treasury yields rebounded on Monday following their sharp sell-off last week as investors digested new economic data and notes from the Federal Reserve's September meeting. The benchmark 10-year Treasury up about 2 basis points to 5.296%. The 30-year Treasury bond was also 3 basis points higher at 5.661%. The yield on the 2-year Treasury fell 1 basis point to 4.814%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. Investors have grappled with a bond market selloff over the past few weeks, while a lackluster monthly jobs report on Friday helped to bring yields down and alleviated concerns about another rate hike. Traders are now pricing in a nearly 82% chance of the Fed keeping rates unchanged at its next meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool . On the economic data front, the Institute for Supply Management's services activity report is due Monday, while investors will be looking ahead to the minutes from the central bank's September meeting on Wednesday. "The highly unsettled bond market makes the incoming US data and Fed communication particularly relevant," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note. "So the minutes will be worth watching for how the broader Committee is framing the current tightening cycle and for its discussion of the neutral rate, where estimates shifted higher in the September SEP."

events.title: Crude oil prices and refinery margins generally increased throughout the third quarter
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: Bloomberg L.P. Note: 3Q26=third quarter of 2026 Petroleum markets in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26) were characterized by increasing prices for crude oil and petroleum products amid persistent conflict in the Middle East. Crude oil prices Crude oil prices steadily climbed in 3Q26 as markets adjusted to renewed military strikes in the Middle East. The front-month futures price of a barrel of Brent crude oil began the quarter at $72 per barrel (b) on July 1, the lowest since February 26, two days before the start of the war. The low prices at the start of the quarter reflected increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz in June following the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). Following the resumption of military strikes on July 7 , crude oil prices increased, with the futures price passing $100/b on July 23 and then trading between $79/b and $98/b until September 8. Daily price volatility in this period generally reflected: Market responses to public statements by U.S., Iranian, and other regional leaders on military plans and the likelihood of a peace deal Flows and disruptions to flows through the Strait of Hormuz Other supply risks and disruptions, such as attacks on oil export infrastructure in Russia Crude oil futures prices passed $100/b again on September 9 following an escalation of military action against energy infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia, including: U.S. and Iranian attacks on crude oil tankers U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports Attacks on pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline Attacks on Saudi Arabian oil tankers around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait Ukraine’s drone attacks on Novorossiysk , one of Russia’s major oil terminals on the Black Sea Prices also increased because some of the measures that had helped to mitigate the price effects of reduced global supplies earlier in the year began to unwind. Since April, reduced crude oil imports to China lowered global oil demand, absorbing some of the shock of reduced supply from the Middle East. In 3Q26, China continued to import far less crude oil than it did before the war. However, China’s 3Q26 crude oil imports were up from May and June, adding some demand back into the market. Additionally, releases from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve slowed significantly in September, limiting additional sources of supply as the disruption has continued. The futures price for Brent crude oil peaked on September 15 at $109/b while spot prices reached as high as $132/b around the same time. Like in April, disruptions of supply— particularly out of Saudi Arabia —put more pressure on Brent crude oil spot prices as buyers struggled to find short-term supply amid the escalating military action. Crude oil prices averaged around $104/b in the final two weeks of the quarter as markets balanced peace discussions with the possibility of a wider scale war. Refinery margins Like in the previous quarter, U.S. refineries ran at unseasonally high levels in 3Q26 with utilization averaging 95%, processing the most crude oil for the third quarter since 2019, when refining capacity was 4% higher. High refinery inputs reflected strong margins for transportation fuels. Motor gasoline , distillate , and jet fuel crack spreads —measures of the refinery margins for these fuels—were all elevated. The quarterly average gasoline crack spread more than doubled the year-ago level despite declining in the second half of the quarter, and the distillate and jet fuel crack spreads almost tripled their year-ago levels as a result of tight global supply. Data source: Bloomberg L.P. Note: The crack spreads reflect the New York Harbor spot prices for RBOB, ultra-low sulfur diesel, and jet fuel minus the Dated Brent spot price. 3Q26=third quarter of 2026 Crack spreads were highest for distillate fuel oil and second highest for jet fuel because the disrupted refining activities in Russia, China, and the Middle East supplied large shares of these fuels to global markets. U.S. distillate fuel supplies have become tight because of high exports to markets in short supply, as well as higher costs for importing regions, such as the U.S. East Coast. As of the week ending September 25, U.S. distillate fuel inventories were 13% below the five-year (2021–2025) average while U.S. gasoline inventories and jet fuel inventories were 7% below and 3% above their five-year averages, respectively. events.title: Scoop: Trump's top national security aides meet secretly at Camp David on Iran, Yemen
events.summary: President Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, three U.S. officials told Axios. Why it matters: The highly unusual meeting was not announced by the Trump administration. The last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the officials said. Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. "Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East. The White House declined to comment. Driving the news: With negotiations stalled, President Trump is considering resuming major combat operations in Iran. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said on Thursday. At the same time, Trump is being asked to join Saudi Arabia's planned offensive against the Houthis in Yemen. The Saudis are urging the president to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. Trump has been leaning against it, but U.S. officials say he could change his mind. What he's saying: On Friday afternoon, while his advisers were at Camp David, Trump was asked by reporters what his next move on Iran will be. "If I told you, you would have a major story," he said. "But you will see. It is working out very well. Iran is not doing well."

events.title: I increased my income from $22K to $180K before a layoff. Taking a pay cut in my next role felt like a step backward.
events.summary: Elianor Williamson went from making $22,000 to $180,000 in a decade. Then a layoff and job search made her feel like she's taken a step backward. Courtesy of Elianor Williamson; BI Elianor Williamson is a 36-year-old living in Seattle. Business Insider has verified Williamson's income and employment history with documentation. The following as-told-to essay has been edited for length and clarity. I went to school for wine. My major was originally education, but while studying abroad for a year in Ireland, I took a class on global food and beverage, and loved it. I switched majors to global wine studies — a little bit of the marketing world and a lot of the wine world. I was drawn to it because it seemed like a fun, cool, shiny, interesting career path. Salary wasn't really discussed in my two years of studying; looking back now, that was disappointing. After graduating from Central Washington University in June 2013, I worked in the wine industry for about half a year at a tasting room, pouring wine for people and helping at events. I was broke and didn't feel I could make any money in that space. I wanted to start a corporate career. Here's my salary journey since then. Event coordinator, $22,000 Later in 2013, I found a nonprofit in my area that was hiring for an event coordinator role for wine-related events, like fundraisers where we'd auction off wine for donations. My offer was around $22,000, my first salary. I was thrilled; before, I'd been paid hourly. I had an office that I went into every day. I did that for about a year, and I realized there was a sort of ceiling on salary for nonprofit work. Salary Journeys is Business Insider's first-person series following real people and their real paychecks — how they built their income, what it means for their lives, and what they learned along the way. If you're willing to share how your salary has changed over time, please fill out this Google Form . Marketing manager, $45,000 A friend of a friend worked at a marketing agency, which I knew nothing about, but he got me an interview. I was offered a role as a marketing manager in 2015, and they asked what I was looking for from a salary perspective. I'd read all these articles about not being the first one to share a number , so I was like, "Well, it's going to have to be a lot more than what I'm making now," which wasn't helpful, because I hadn't told them what I was making. We went back and forth, and finally I asked for between $40,000 and $45,000. They came back and offered me $45,000. Again, I was thrilled with that. I moved out and got my own big girl apartment with a roommate . Program manager, $61,000 I was at that marketing agency for three years, during which I had three different titles, and one promotion in 2016. I was promoted to a program manager, and my salary at that point was around $61,000. In April 2018, I was like, "I actually kind of might hate this. I don't know what I want to do with my life." So, I quit with nothing lined up . Everyone in my life thought I was insane, but I just needed time to figure things out. Contract project manager, $40 an hour (annualized around $83,200) for a six-month contract I was unemployed, job searching, and applying to things. It only took six weeks for me to get an offer for a 6-month contract project manager role at Zillow , project managing content that would be shared at a big event for real estate agents. I was paid $40 an hour, or about $83,200 annually. Project manager, $90,000 When my contract was ending, I wanted to convert to full-time, so I pushed and worked with my manager to make it happen. In November 2018, I was converted to a full-time employee at Zillow with the same title — project manager. However, they bumped up my salary to $90,000, and I also got some stock options and other full-time benefits. Because the equity we got as employees vested over a period of four years, I don't really consider that a huge incentive or part of my income, because I wasn't able to take advantage of that. Campaign manager, $101,000 A year later, there was a reorganization, and my title changed. I moved to a different team as a campaign manager, and my salary bumped up to $101,000. This was a huge milestone for me because I was finally making six digits , which I'd been wanting to hit for a while. I was so excited and celebrated with my husband. I did that for two years. Senior project manager, $135,000 In 2022, there was another reorg within Zillow, and I got a promotion to senior project manager. My salary was $135,000. The environment at Zillow had changed under new leadership, so I decided to look for something else. Senior program manager, $150,000 Later that year, a former colleague got me an interview at a real estate tech startup called OJO. Once I got the offer and was negotiating my salary , she also encouraged me to ask for more money —so I did. I was a senior program manager with a salary of $150,000. I also got a $10,000 signing bonus, which was great. I did that for a year. Senior program manager and operations manager, $180,000 OJO was acquired by the Royal Bank of Canada in 2023 and rebranded as Houseful. I made a lateral move to be a senior program and operations manager. Six months later, I was making $155,000, plus a 20% annual cash bonus, which I'd never had before. It was huge. That year, my total compensation was over $180,000, which was absolutely mind-blowing to me. I was ecstatic. In March 2025, I was impacted by layoffs . I was unemployed for about five months and collected unemployment. It was a super stressful time. I started a TikTok account, where I shared my experience of job searching and interviewing hardships, and the mental energy it requires to keep going. Global brand operations manager $145,000 In August 2025, I started as a global brand operations manager at Starbucks. I was originally offered a salary of $131,500. I was terrified to negotiate; I was desperate for a job and would've 1000% accepted it at that salary. But I knew I'd be disappointed; I know my worth and what my work experience warrants in the market. After researching the best ways to negotiate , I emailed them back three different options I was comfortable with. I gave a combination of more PTO, a higher salary, a higher bonus, or a bigger signing bonus. I ended up accepting an offer of $145,000 with a 10% annual bonus and stock. Although I'm technically making $10,000 less in salary than what I was making before, the gap is significantly bigger if you consider my previous full compensation of $180,000. I'd love to get back to that. I think it'll probably take a couple of years. It's been hard to feel like I took a huge step backward , but I'm grateful to work at Starbucks. I love the brand, and it's a great fit for me right now. It's hybrid, and I love going to the office and seeing people. events.summary: There's a simple reason the Nasdaq-100 Index closed at new records Friday: The world's biggest company notched its first record since May. Nvidia , which accounts for 13% of the Nasdaq and 8% of the S&P 500 Index , added 1.3% Friday, ending seven weeks of sideways trading surrounding a high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump and corporate executives leading what Trump calls "super intelligence." The rally puts the value of Jensen Huang's semiconductor business at just under $5.7 trillion, and based on the price of options trading at Nvidia, it will likely cross the $6 trillion threshold by the end of this month. It should be a comforting notion for equity bulls. Currently, there is about a 50% chance Nvidia will reach a $6 trillion valuation between now and the end of this month, and a 13% chance it happens this week, according to market-maker pricing of deltas on Nvidia options expiring this week and Oct. 30, which measure the sensitivity of options pricing relative to moves in the stock. The odds it happens between now and Dec. 18 is about 67%. They're also implying about a 1-in-16 chance Nvidia could hit $7 trillion by Nov. 20. Based on the current share count, Nvidia would need to touch $248 to cross the milestone. "Nvidia's buyback announcement was a bright spot," Ben Emons, managing director at Highline Asset Management, wrote in a note to clients last week. "The buyback is not just a payout but a capital-allocation event that asserts confidence in long-run AI demand." It's important to note when using deltas to gauge a range of possibilities that the same size move in the opposite direction is also just as likely. While that's largely the case for Nvidia, some of the stock's call options are currently trading with a higher implied volatility than the equivalent puts, Barchart data shows. Such "call skew" is a sign that traders have a bias toward hedging for a rally.

events.title: Solar market set for Africa boom, says report
events.summary: Sub-Saharan Africa’s off-grid solar market is due to expand by 450% by 2035, with more than 35% of installations projected to be in Nigeria, according to a new report by global research firm Wood Mackenzie. Across the continent, persistent failures in national grids and growing populations have already created an off-grid “ shadow ” fuel market, predominantly led by diesel generators. However, the recent rise in fuel prices due to the Iran war, alongside the removal of subsidies in Nigeria and a significant drop in solar panel prices in recent decades, are driving the shift to solar. Outside Nigeria, Kenya, and DR Congo are also projected to be major solar power hubs. For more of the continent to reap the benefits of solar power, however, blended funding models and consistent rural electrification policies will be needed to help bridge the power gap, the report warned. — Paige Bruton

events.title: My partner and I always thought we agreed on money. Then, we moved in together.
events.summary: My partner and I agree on a lot when it comes to finances, but we don't always want to spend our money on the same things. Santiago Barraza Lopez When my partner and I started dating, we had similar incomes and opinions on how to split expenses . Once we moved in together, though, we realized we wanted our money to go toward different things. We came up with a plan that helped us, and accepted that sometimes, we'd just have to compromise. I was born and raised in Mexico, but I spent most of my financially independent adult life in New York and London. Living abroad made me second-guess a lot of the norms related to money and dating that I'd long internalized — for instance, the expectation that in a heterosexual relationship, men should just pay for everything. For years, though, I was single, so I never had to decide how I'd actually split finances with another person. Things changed when I entered a serious relationship. Funny enough, my partner's background is remarkably similar to mine: She is also Mexican and has built much of her adult life abroad. Given our similarities, I was curious to see how we'd approach money as a couple. We seemed pretty in sync until we decided to move in together When we decided to move in together, some of our differences were amplified. Santiago Barraza Lopez At first, we set an expectation that we'd go 50/50 on things like date nights and groceries. We had similar salaries, neither of us expected the other to fund our lifestyle, and dividing shared expenses down the middle felt like the simplest solution. This system felt like a breath of fresh air after growing up with the idea that men should always pay for everything. Then, several months into our relationship, we decided to move in together. Suddenly, we had to agree on how much of our monthly income we were comfortable putting toward rent. She wanted to find a slightly more expensive place in a better location, with more space — a home we genuinely loved. I, on the other hand, felt like we could find a more affordable spot and save money for things like flights and nice dinners . The conversation made me realize: Our main difference isn't how much we earn, or even how much we spend, but what we want our money to do for us. Once we found a place and moved in together, the same tension started appearing everywhere. What feels worthwhile to me can feel unnecessary to her, and vice versa I like to spend money on travel and experiences, but my partner would rather spend it on improving our day-to-day lifestyle. Santiago Barraza Lopez I am much quicker to spend on travel and experiences. Paying for a flight somewhere new, a weekend away, video games, or even Pokémon cards can make perfect sense to me. I tend to judge a purchase by the enjoyment or experience I expect to get from it. My partner is more willing to spend on her well-being: our home, clothes, cleaning, and things that make everyday life nicer. For her, anything that would improve our apartment is obviously something worth buying. I can look at the same thing and wonder whether we need it at all. I am sure she has had exactly the same reaction to some of my purchases. This has caused friction, because our equal-split system started to feel unfair when one of us had to pay for something we didn't want. Even when it came to things we both enjoy, such as eating dinner together, she would rather buy ingredients to cook our meal at home , whereas I'd rather splurge on going to an upscale Italian restaurant. We are not a classic saver-and-spender couple. We are both willing to spend. We just have different ideas about what deserves our money. With time, we stopped trying to make every expense perfectly equal Creating a joint bank account, having a lot of conversations, and staying flexible helped us. Santiago Barraza Lopez Eventually, we began thinking about our finances in categories. There are things we need, things I care about, things she cares about, and things we genuinely enjoy together. Seeing our spending this way made it easier to separate shared decisions from personal preferences. We created a joint savings account , which gives us a place to put money toward some goals that belong to both of us — like theater tickets or a new TV — as well as expenses like rent. With our separate accounts, we each pay for our own priorities, like plane tickets for me and house plants for her. As our circumstances evolved, we also moved beyond a rigid 50/50 split and began dividing shared costs proportionally according to income. However, we try to still be flexible and not keep score. For example, I don't drink. If we order wine at dinner , I could insist that we exclude it from my half of the bill, since technically, that might be more precise. I do not think a relationship works if every amount has to be allocated perfectly, though. Sometimes I contribute toward something she enjoys, and she does the same for me. Compromise is part of the point, and love is the center of everything. We still don't agree on every purchase, and I don't think we need to. What matters is knowing what belongs to me, what belongs to her, and what we want badly enough to build together. Our next shared project is already waiting: a dog. events.title: Cerebras stock pops 9% after Sam Altman calls the chipmaker a 'close partner'
events.summary: Cerebras stock rose on Monday, rebounding from last week's decline. It comes after OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman reassured investors of the partnership between the two companies. OpenAI said last week it would power its latest AI models with Nvidia's GPUs rather than Cerebras' chips. Cerebras stock climbed 9% on Monday, rebounding from last week's decline, after OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman reassured investors that the firm is a "close partner." The AI hardware firm, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in a monster IPO in May, saw its stock plummet 20% to its lowest price last week after it was revealed that OpenAI would power its "Ultrafast" mode for GPT-6.1 Sol with Nvidia's graphics processing units instead of Cerebras' chips. "There is some speculation about our partnership with Cerebras," Altman said in a post on X on Friday. "Cerebras is a close partner, and we have a deep engagement pushing on the frontiers of speed." The company's stock rose almost 3% in extended trading on Friday following Altman's comments. Cerebras has seen its market cap plunge since its May debut and is now valued at about $43 billion, down from $95 billion. Cerebras, a Nvidia competitor, sells large computer chips and AI systems that are designed to run AI models faster than traditional GPUs. It claimed that its flagship product, the Wafer Scale Engine 3, runs faster than Nvidia's GPU. Cerebras signed a $10 billion deal with OpenAI in January to supply it with 750 megawatts of computing power through 2028. Citi analysts said that their view of Cerebras' revenue outlook between 2026 and 2028 remains "unchanged." "We believe frontier-AI labs' latest models would initially roll out on internal chips before running on third-party or Cerebras cloud, so it's too early to read much into it," they said in a note on Friday morning. "We believe the stock's ability to outperform is increasingly tied to evidence that gross margins are stabilizing. Any further delay in the gross margin trough would likely weigh on sentiment, particularly given Cerebras' premium valuation," they added. events.title: Budding food scrap pickup services across the US want your coffee grounds and eggshells
events.summary: Composting leftover coffee grounds, eggshells and carrot tops is a way to reduce the amount of food waste that goes into landfills, where it produces the potent greenhouse gas methane DETROIT -- Every Monday, Ricky Blanding drives his Ford Ranger pickup truck around Detroit along a carefully planned route. Blanding hops in and out of the truck, grabbing buckets of food scraps from porches and restaurants, piling those scraps into bins in the truck bed and driving them to a composting site. Blanding is the CEO of Scrap Soils, one of the many budding food waste collection services across the country helping to divert food from landfills and make composting more accessible. It's especially important for those who can't compost at home, who live in cities without municipal curbside pickup or who can't get to a drop-off location. Composting leftover coffee grounds, eggshells, carrot tops and more reduces the amount of food that goes into dumps where it produces the potent greenhouse gas methane. It also ultimately helps create healthy soil for gardeners and urban farmers. Experts say companies like Scrap Soils are an important part of cleaning up the broader food ecosystem. Emily Cassidy, research associate at climate solutions nonprofit Project Drawdown, said composting offers the dual benefits of reducing landfill methane emissions and, once the composting process is complete, returning nutrients to soil. “Because methane has such a big impact on the climate in a short amount of time, the more we can reduce methane, it is like pulling the emergency brake on climate change,” Cassidy said. Beyond mitigating climate change, composting can also improve local food production, she said. “That’s a way that we can see that we’re benefiting the environment, because we’re taking food and then replenishing the ground with those nutrients,” she said. Blanding, a 34-year-old native Detroiter, co-launched Scrap Soils in 2020 to play a local part in solving a statewide food waste problem that mirrors what's happening around the globe . Food waste is a huge source of methane in Michigan landfills, estimates say, and accounts for millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions in the state. In Detroit, more than 70 homes and businesses are signed up for Scrap Soils’ weekly pickups. It's an easier way to compost than making space in one's backyard or driving to a city drop-off site. Home pickups start at $15 per month, while businesses pay $60 per month or more, depending on volume. One of those commercial customers is The Grand Porter restaurant in the Southwest neighborhood of Detroit. “We go through a lot of eggs, so mostly egg scraps, eggshells and the cardboard. We put all of our bread scraps, stale bread scraps, in here,” said Lou Hammer, the restaurant's executive chef, pointing to a large bin with bags of food waste inside. “Some tomato tops, some avocado skins. Probably a few other things in there, too.” “It doesn’t take any extra effort,” she said of the pickup service. “This was going to go in a bag anyway. It’s just going to go in a green bag instead.” After completing his nine-hour, more than 100-mile (160-kilometer) weekly route, Blanding drops off the waste at Scrap Soils' partner, Sanctuary Farms in Detroit. There, everything from apple cores to rotted pumpkins to corn husks is composted into a rich soil additive that's available for purchase. “Food waste has not only become the problem,” Blanding said, “but it’s also the solution to so many issues in climate change.” The company ultimately plans to purchase a larger truck, as well as its own property and equipment for composting. It's fundraising to meet a matching grant through the state. Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials US Marine arrested on suspicion of murder after 'brutal and heinous' death in Japan District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' That hasn't been without challenges. As Blanding seeks to grow, he's come up against skepticism that a small team with limited resources can make a big impact. Companies like Scrap Soils also face challenges ranging from gaining visibility to getting people to actually sign up and commit. At the same time, emphasizing what can and cannot be composted, and how to do it correctly — such as removing produce stickers before putting a peel in the bucket — is key to its success, too. “The role of a hauler is very important, and education around composting is also very important,” Blanding said. “Being able to continue to get more engagement and more partnership, those things go far in helping us to expand this tiny effort into something that actually can scale,” he added. Despite hurdles, other independent composting programs and companies are expanding. Examples include the Denver Compost Collective , Nashville’s Compost Co. and Compost Now , which operates in Atlanta and the North Carolina cities of Raleigh, Durham and Asheville.

events.title: Half of new accounts at private banks in Singapore industry group opened in a month: ABS
events.summary: AI and digital tools were deployed during onboarding to eliminate excessive processes. SINGAPORE – Nearly half of all new accounts opened at member banks of the Private Banking Industry Group (PBIG) were opened within a month, amid an industry push to reduce account-opening times , said the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS). These account openings, which were completed from June to August 2026, were part of PBIG’s target to reduce the median account-opening time to within one month by end-2026, ABS said in a statement on Oct 5. Gillian Tan, assistant managing director (development and international) of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and co-chair of PBIG, said: “The progress made in shortening account-opening times is a strong signal of the industry’s commitment to meet clients’ needs and strengthen Singapore’s competitiveness as a trusted and efficient wealth management centre.” Observers previously noted that private bank onboarding time is a sticking point, with the broader onboarding process taking three to 12 months, particularly for complex cases. MAS and PBIG set up an Account Opening Working Group in mid-2025 to tackle this issue, and most member banks have reduced their account-opening times since end-2025, said ABS. The association said that this was done by deploying artificial intelligence and digital tools in onboarding processes, adopting more risk-proportionate approaches to source-of-wealth due diligence and removing excessive processes. Shee Tse Koon, group executive and group head of consumer banking and wealth management at DBS and co-chair of PBIG, said that as PBIG continues to work towards its target, it will still prioritise risk-management standards equally with the client experience. “This strengthens Singapore’s standing as a wealth management hub, anchored on stability, trust and sound risk management, while staying nimble to innovate and improve,” he added. “Trust is something we build together, and we will keep at it.” THE BUSINESS TIMES ABS/Association of Banks in Singapore

events.title: US supreme court to hear big oil’s bid to block climate damage lawsuits
events.summary: Court starts new term hearing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state level The US supreme court begins its new nine-month term hearing arguments Monday in a high-stakes case in which big oil companies are attempting to strike a fatal blow against lawsuits that seek to hold them accountable for the climate crisis. In Suncor Energy versus the County Commissioners of Boulder County , local officials in Boulder are suing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil in state court to force the companies to share a portion of the costs that climate change has imposed on local taxpayers. However, Exxon and Canada-based Suncor are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing Boulder’s climate change lawsuit. If the supreme court justices side with Boulder or decide that the case is not in their jurisdiction, then it would continue in state court. But if the fossil fuel industry convinces the justices, the decision could apply not only to the Boulder case, but also to dozens of other climate cases brought by state and local governments around the US. “The hope of the industry side is that this is going to be the death blow,” said Dennis Fan, the founder and director of the Appellate Litigation Clinic at Columbia Law School who wrote an amicus brief in the case. “The industry is going for the home run, they’re going for the grand slam. They’re thinking, ‘if we win this argument, there will never, ever be climate change litigation again.’” Boulder officials filed a lawsuit in Colorado court in 2018 arguing that Exxon and Suncor concealed and misrepresented to the public what they knew about the damage that burning fossil fuels would do to the climate, and that they should pay for the resulting costs of disasters. Initially, the firms sought to have the case moved to federal court. Then when the Colorado supreme court allowed Boulder’s case to make its way toward trial in state court, Exxon and Suncor appealed that ruling up to the supreme court arguing it should be dismissed on grounds of federal preemption.. Typically, cases must be decided by lower courts before reaching the supreme court, but the justices agreed to hear this case while the state case is ongoing. “That’s an incredibly weird thing to have happen,” Fan said. The supreme court will consider whether it has proper jurisdiction to hear Boulder’s case right now, and whether federal law preempts Boulder’s case from being heard in state court. Congress has the power to pass federal laws that invalidate state laws, but the question is whether there are any federal laws that invalidate state climate cases. “They’ve had a little bit of difficulty identifying exactly what that source of federal law is,” Fan said. For instance, the fossil fuel companies claim that the federal Clean Air Act pre-empts Boulder’s case from state court, even though the law specifies that “air pollution control at its source is the primary responsibility of states and local governments”. So the fossil fuel companies in their brief claimed that supreme court decisions from a century ago suggested that federal courts have power to hear environmental cases, even without federal laws on the books, and that these decisions created a “federal common law” governing environmental lawsuits across state lines. They asserted that this federal common law is still in effect and exists in the “structure of the Constitution” even though the federal Clean Air Act has since declared states have primary jurisdiction over local air pollution. The supreme court has not historically agreed with the argument the oil companies are making, Fan said. He pointed to the tobacco and opioid companies that previously faced state public nuisance cases. “For decades, the tobacco industry tried to get the supreme court and other courts to stop state court litigation from happening against the tobacco industry, and they failed every single time,” he said. As recently as April, the supreme court decided in Hencely v Fluor Corp that “there is no federal pre-emption [in isolation] without a constitutional text or a federal statute to assert it”. Climate advocates and wildfire survivors were planning a rally Monday morning outside the supreme court in Washington DC. Daryl McCool, an artist who lost her home when the 2021 Marshall fire destroyed her neighborhood in Boulder county, Colorado, is not involved in the case but planned to attend the rally. The fire was fueled by record warmth and extreme drought that scientists found were intensified by climate change. The fire caused damage estimated at more than $2bn , and a recent report estimated that climate change could cost Colorado up to $37bn by 2050. “The case itself is meaningful because it affects every single human, every single creature, it affects everyone that is on this earth,” McCool said. “At this point in time, we’re seeing [these companies] … they’re not willing to change, and so they need to be held accountable.

We ranked the 16 actors who portrayed the teens of Forks (and La Push) based on success, with factors including, but not limited to, quality and quantity of projects, social media followings, other business ventures outside entertainment, and general presence in pop culture today. The UK-based tabletop games retailer and manufacturer of the globally popular Warhammer figures said that under the fixed-term contract, the heroic individual would take overall responsibility for its global IT and customer technology capability, and report to the Chief Operating Officer. “The role has a broad remit spanning our core technology estate, information security, major systems change and the technology behind our customer-facing digital platforms, including warhammer.com,” the job ad said , although sadly it closed for applications over the weekend. “We need someone who can understand what Games Workshop needs now, anticipate what we will need in the future, and make good decisions about how technology supports the long-term success of the business,” it said. Candidates might want to be aware that, if they are lucky enough to be offered the job and they accept the mission, the battle will not be an easy one. The head of IT will take responsibility for core IT environment and information security, advising senior management on technology, security, risk and investment. They will also support the teams to keep “significant technology programs moving, openly tackling the challenges that come with major change, and ensure that we continue to make rapid progress.” The Nottingham-based retailer and manufacturer is in the midst of ERP and supply chain management systems overhauls that were first mobilized years ago and have been beset with delays and over-runs. Back in January 2021, The Register reported that Games Workshop delayed its Microsoft Dynamics-based ERP rollout and appointed a new integrator, having already hoped to go live in 2020. By September that year, it said project issues were impacting the development of new features in online shopping. In January 2022, it added another £500k to the project budget with no end in sight . A year later, it said the business faced ongoing challenges to integrate new IT systems when it was still heavily reliant on working with its legacy tech systems. “Finishing these projects and upgrading our systems continue to be a key area of focus. We are making some progress but it's costing us more time and money – we will remain cost conscious," it told investors . Around four years later, challenges remain ongoing, according to the latest annual report, published in July, for the year ending in May 2026. It said the group’s main financial system is still being supported by a number of legacy ERP applications for which “we have identified control deficiencies in our previous audits.” These still exist, according to a review of IT systems. The report added that the responsibility for delivering IT had moved to its operational manufacturing and supply chain director, under the COO from June, a decision which “helped bring all of the internal departments together.” “Our Systems Improvement Plan (SIP) is on track with very clear milestones for us all to support and deliver,” it added. Games Workshop is famous for the phenomenon of Warhammer 40,000 — also known as WH40K or 40K — thought to be the most popular miniature wargame in the world. Battles are set in the distant future, leaving the technology department to hope the end of its long-running ERP saga comes before that date.

events.title: Bringing predictive analytics to the agentic AI era
events.summary: In 2026, the question for enterprise AI is no longer whether predictive models can outperform statistical forecasts—that argument is settled. The big question now is how to enable predictive systems to act on their own conclusions without drifting from business intent. The frontier has moved from prediction to autonomous decision making, and the gap between leaders and laggards is widening accordingly. “Enterprises are done with a backward-looking point of view; they want to be more forward-thinking,” says Vishal Gupta, partner at research firm Everest Group. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Intelligent analytics, powered by technologies like deep learning and generative AI, are making this possible. Real-time training allows AI to evolve continuously instead of waiting for quarterly refreshes. In addition, the data that newer predictive engines rely upon has expanded to encompass not just neat, numerical records but also messy, unstructured sources of insight-rich interactions. As a result, AI-powered analytics are moving enterprises from passive hindsight to pragmatic foresight. AI takes predictive analytics—a broad discipline that includes predictive modeling, data prep, analysis workflows, interpretation of results, and decision-making applications—to new heights. “In many ways I think the word ‘analytics’ is giving way to AI,” says Gupta. “Everything is becoming AI.” Download the report This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. events.title: Satya Nadella reinvented Microsoft once. Can he do it again in the AI era?
events.summary: Satya Nadella revived Microsoft after succeeding Steve Ballmer in 2014, turning the company into a cloud powerhouse. But almost four years into the artificial intelligence boom, the software giant has yet to find a breakout hit at the model or application layer. Part of Nadella's challenge involves shifting the business model yet again, this time to center it around tokens, the currency of the AI economy. On a sunny day in Seattle in late September, about 50 executives representing large Microsoft customers had a rare opportunity. They could ask anything of CEO Satya Nadella . One attendee wanted to know what Microsoft could do to help companies adapt to the artificial intelligence age. Nadella responded by emphasizing the importance of "diffusion inside the enterprise," meaning AI tools need to be widely deployed. "Like all things, change is always bottom up, top down, and middle up," said Nadella, sporting a tight black crewneck and dark gray slacks, as he strode across the stage at the downtown Paccar Pavilion. For the 59-year-old Nadella, who's spent over half his life at Microsoft, the gathering landed at a pivotal moment, as the software giant tries to magnify its role in the AI boom. Of late, Nadella has been inserting himself more into the AI discourse, posting on X last month about the need for "deliberate pacing" in model development, and days later addressing safety fears at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles. Despite its almost $4 trillion market cap, Microsoft has yet to break out as an AI leader. Nvidia dominates in AI chips, Anthropic and OpenAI boast the foremost models, Meta just released the first mass-market personal agent, and Google's Gemini-powered services are popular with businesses and consumers. Microsoft was aggressively early to AI through an investment in OpenAI, but that alliance has frayed. While the software giant has a big business in renting out chips for AI developers through its Azure cloud, its Copilot technology isn't pervasive in the workplace, and its proprietary AI models remain niche. The company is hosting a Windows and Surface event in San Francisco on Wednesday, describing it in an invitation as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC." Wall Street is lukewarm on the story. Even factoring in a sharp third-quarter rally, the stock is trailing its megacap peers and the broader Nasdaq this year, up just 7% as of Friday's close. Microsoft hasn't beaten the S&P 500 in a calendar year since 2023. Tiffany Wade, co-portfolio manager at Microsoft shareholder Columbia Threadneedle, said there are a lot of unknowns about Copilot, which is the centerpiece of Nadella's AI strategy. "I think there needs to be a little bit more maturity of the product before we figure out actually what the best solution or what pricing is," Wade said in an interview. For longtime Microsoft investors, Nadella has a solid track record when it comes to navigating industry shifts. He was named CEO in 2014, succeeding Steve Ballmer , who had presided over a roughly 33% drop in the stock price during his 14-year tenure, as Microsoft slipped into the beleaguered category of legacy software. Nadella proceeded to turn Microsoft into a cloud powerhouse. He tossed aside perpetual Office software licenses and pushed the company into subscription-based software-as-a-service offerings alongside Azure infrastructure. And he permitted customers to integrate products from bitter rivals like Oracle and Salesforce , rather than insisting on a pure Microsoft stack. Trained as an electrical engineer and computer scientist, Nadella became a savvy deal-maker, expanding Microsoft through acquisitions of "Minecraft"-maker Mojang, business social network LinkedIn and code-sharing service GitHub . In recent months, Nadella has acknowledged to investors that he's got to change the business model yet again, this time to reflect the AI-fueled move toward consumption-based pricing. That means becoming a vendor of large volumes of tokens, which measure computing usage and represent the currency of the AI economy. Success would mean "further expanding our TAM," Nadella said on Microsoft's July earnings call, adopting the acronym for total addressable market. Much of the growth story Nadella preaches involves the production of software. Develop more code and do it faster, boosted by the latest and greatest AI tools. "We went from the code assist to the agentic coding to software factory all within one year," Nadella said at the customer gathering late last month. Now he wants to see Microsoft clients open their own software factories, spending more along the way to help churn out code. He's also hoping to empower nontechnical knowledge workers. Some of Nadella's lieutenants at the event unveiled a Copilot "super app " that can perform increasingly complex tasks, generate simple applications and function as a virtual teammate. Nadella had a preview of what was coming.

events.title: Accept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam Altman
events.summary: Boss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliver Sam Altman says he believes the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for the benefits of the technology. The chief executive of OpenAI cited hacks, scams and “other bad things that will happen” in an interview that sparked an instant backlash from critics of the big AI companies. His comments came after one of his company’s safety experts resigned , saying at the weekend that its “culture is broken”. In an interview released on Monday, Altman was asked about how OpenAI’s approach to safety differed from that of Anthropic, which has called for the industry to slow down after one of its researchers quit , warning that AI experts believed “it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. “I think there’s a lot of daylight,” Altman said. “One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use AI widely]. “I do think the lighter touch regulatory stance we advocate for comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience. “I wouldn’t take a trade of saying we will make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams or all the other bad things that will happen because I think that people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude – more good stuff than bad stuff.” The interview for Politico’s Decoded podcast drew a strong response from Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida. He said he had “no dice” with the idea “a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision [on safety] for the rest of us”. His state last week asked a judge to bar OpenAI from developing new AI models without third-party approved guardrails. Gary Marcus, a prominent AI sceptic and professor emeritus at New York University, said Altman was “saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful”. Altman also reignited a feud with Elon Musk, telling Vanity Fair: “I don’t like bullies, and I think Elon’s a bully.” He had been asked if the AI industry could “grow up” and work together. “I think once in a while you got to punch a bully back in the nose,” Altman said. “And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do. So if you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while, but I will work with Elon, of course.” Altman co-founded OpenAI with Musk in 2015 but earlier this year Musk alleged in court that Altman, OpenAI, and the company’s president, Greg Brockman, unjustly enriched themselves and broke a founding contract. Musk’s claim was dismissed by a judge and jury. OpenAI was hit by multiple safety crises over the summer, including when a swarm of its AI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website. Other agents accessed Australian government data. In the interview with Vanity Fair, Altman warned of “a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems” from rival open-source models. He suggested OpenAI could help its customers defend against the risk. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives The company has scrapped the release of a cutting-edge model but Altman’s comments reflect a more bullish mood ahead of a stock market flotation. The wave of public and political concern last month about the potentially catastrophic consequences of fast-progressing AI agents that act beyond human intent had led to hopes of US-wide or even international safety agreements. However, Donald Trump and AI bosses including Altman and Dario Amodei of Anthropic signed a far more laissez-faire pact at the White House last week. The US president said he wanted the companies to “self-police” to limit the risks from AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons. Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and Google DeepMind and as chief scientist at the UK’s AI Safety Institute, said warnings about AI risks understated the dangers. “There’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems,” he said, adding that actions taken over the next two to 10 years would be decisive. OpenAI’s David Robinson announced his departure at the weekend, saying “the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough” as they sprint from one product launch to the next. His view was endorsed by Miles Brundage, an AI policy researcher who worked at OpenAI for six years. He said he regretted helping “spread the idea of iterative deployment”, which may have made sense when AI was less powerful “but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks”.

events.title: China shuts hundreds of banks as Beijing moves to shore up its financial system
events.summary: China has shut about a quarter of its banks as Beijing accelerates efforts to create fewer, better-capitalized lenders amid the country's economic slowdown. Fitch Ratings said smaller, rural banks remain China’s financial-system weak spot, citing deteriorating asset quality, thin capital buffers and governance shortcomings. China is accelerating its consolidation of smaller, mostly rural banks in a bid to shore up its financial system, amid ongoing concerns over an economic slowdown in the country. Beijing's policy-led consolidation saw a record 670 lenders closed in 2025 — about one-quarter of banks in the country — as authorities ramped up mergers and dissolutions to create fewer, larger and better-capitalized institutions, according to Fitch Ratings analysis . Small and rural commercial banks "remain the weakest part of the system" in China, Fitch said in a report, which flagged their "poor asset quality, low capitalization and governance shortcomings," especially in less-developed regions of the country. The rating agency said the return on assets among rural banks fell to 0.45% in the first half, down from 0.56% in 2021. Meanwhile, non-performing loans among such lenders rose to 2.8% in the same period, ahead of the sector average of 1.5%, with greater exposure to smaller companies, property developers and local government funding vehicles. The consolidation push is aimed at boosting oversight, curbing regulatory arbitrage and improving transparency, Fitch said, noting that stress at smaller lenders is unlikely to lead to system-wide contagion, pointing to their largely localized operations and limited interbank exposure. The measures could "ultimately reshape competitive dynamics among smaller lenders, although their structural weaknesses may persist in the near term," the rating agency added. The move comes amid ongoing signs of strain in the world's second-largest economy. China's GDP grew 4.3% in the second quarter, its slowest pace since 2022 , while industrial profits came in at 4.2% annually in August, their weakest pace this year.

events.title: American investors are touring China’s robot factories to size up the competition
events.summary: AgiBot's factory in Shanghai. (Photo by Tang Yanjun/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images) Tang Yanjun/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images Silicon Valley investors are taking field trips to robot factories in China. The goal is not to scout investments, but to size up rivals to their portfolio companies. Some investors are paying $10,000 for tours with translators, five hotels, and executive dinners. Last year, when Ryan Cunningham, a Silicon Valley investor, floated a trip to China in a WhatsApp group of robotics investors, the response was lukewarm. One person jokingly asked if he could smuggle a humanoid robot home. This year, the jokes have given way to travel plans. Cunningham, the founder of Edgerunner Ventures, a venture capital firm that backs energy and computing startups, is planning an April trip to China for 10 investors. Nearly every investor group chat he is in now trades notes on recent or upcoming excursions to China, he told Business Insider, as venture capitalists gauge China's hardware prowess to see what American robotics startups are up against. "The reason I want to bring them to China is because I want to take them by the shoulders and say, 'Guys, if you want to get serious, this is what we should be learning from,'" said Cunningham, who visited Shanghai last year for the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, an annual gathering for the AI industry. Cunningham is among a growing cadre of Silicon Valley investors heading east to see how China built its edge in robotics and other hardware. For many, the point is not to scout Chinese investments. It is to size up the rivals confronting their US portfolio companies. The excursions range from private VC delegations to $10,000-a-head tours that pair factory visits with translators, five-star hotels, and dinners with local tech executives. Behind the tours is the sobering realization that China has established a formidable lead in crucial parts of robotics, from manufacturing and supply chains to deploying machines and collecting the data needed to improve them. Robotic arms at a BYD factory in Fuzhou. Wan Xiang/Xinhua via Getty Images Chinese companies Unitree and AgiBot together shipped 71% of the world's humanoid robots last year, according to research firm Omdia. China also controls 63% of the key companies in the global supply chain for humanoid-robot components, according to the Mercator Institute for China Studies, a German think tank. Meanwhile, most American humanoids are still in development and not available off the shelf. Most US companies rely on Chinese suppliers for components or assembly, according to Stanford's 2026 Emerging Technology Review . The stakes are high for US investors pouring money into robotics and physical AI . They are betting that advances in AI, cheaper hardware, labor shortages, and the push to reshore manufacturing can mint the next generation of technology giants. Robotics, meanwhile, is increasingly viewed as a national-security concern. In July, the Federal Communications Commission banned new foreign-made "advanced robotic devices," citing "unacceptable risks" to national security. Robotics may be Silicon Valley's latest obsession, but China has spent years building up its industry. "The Chinese have been very hardware focused," Wendy Chang, a senior analyst at the Mercator Institute for China Studies, told Business Insider. "They are trying to own the whole robotics supply chain." In a 2023 policy document, China's government compared the potential impact of humanoid robots with that of computers, smartphones, and electric vehicles. It laid out a plan to deploy humanoid robots across the economy by 2027. China's head start has drawn American investors in for a bit of competitive snooping. In recent months, dozens of VCs, including investors from Eclipse, G2 Venture Partners, and Chemistry VC, have traveled to China. Partners from Founders Fund and Khosla Ventures have also made trips, The Information reported last month . A reality check for Silicon Valley Late last year, partners at Bay Area-based G2 decided they needed a clearer view of China. The firm, which spun out of Kleiner Perkins, invests in growth-stage companies building technology for physical industries, including energy, manufacturing, and transportation. "We knew they were ahead, but it doesn't really hit you until you're on the ground," said Neel Mehta, a G2 investor, who traveled to Shenzhen and Beijing with a colleague earlier this year. Mehta and his colleague built their trip around Morgan Stanley's China Summit in Shenzhen, which included field trips to robotics and autonomous-vehicle companies. They also arranged visits to Xiaomi , the consumer electronics giant that has expanded into electric vehicles, and to EV maker BYD . For years, Mehta said, US investors had dismissed Chinese technology as lower quality. Conventional wisdom held that China might have an edge in manufacturing, but the US would always build better AI. Mehta returned to the Bay Area convinced both assumptions were wrong. AgiBot's factory in Shanghai. (Photo by Tang Yanjun/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images) Tang Yanjun/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images At a Xiaomi dealership in Shenzhen, Mehta saw the company's flagship SU7 electric car, which starts at around $30,000. "The quality and finish is everything you'd expect in a luxury car like Porsche, no exaggeration," Mehta said. The car is not sold in the US, where Chinese EV imports face restrictions and a 100% tariff. Mehta was also struck by China's data-collection efforts. Robotics companies need large amounts of real-world data to train systems to perceive their surroundings and perform physical tasks. At one data-collection farm, he saw hundreds of workers stationed in pods around the clock, teleoperating robots to generate it at scale. "If you think data is the core bottleneck in robotics, there's a world in which they have better models than anyone else," he said. The DeepSeek wake-up call Rui Ma, who runs Tech Buzz China, a podcast and research platform covering China's technology industry, told Business Insider that Silicon Valley's renewed curiosity about China follows years of US-China tensions and a chill in cross-border investment. That has begun to change as powerful models from Chinese AI companies, including DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen, and Moonshot AI's Kimi, have made China's technological gains harder to dismiss. "It's very specific to the DeepSeek moment," Ma said, referring to the Chinese company's 2025 release of an AI model that shook Silicon Valley. "People are like, 'Oh wow, China actually has AI and other technologies worth paying attention to.'" Ma began organizing tours to China in 2019, but paused them during the pandemic. events.title: Russia plague: What we know about the suspected case reportedly linked to a lab worker’s death
events.summary: An employee at Russia's anti-plague institute has died from a suspected case of plague. Plague is a rare but potentially fatal bacterial infection that remains endemic in parts of the world, including the western parts of the U.S. The recent case in Russia appears to be of pneumonic plague, where the bacteria infects the lungs. A researcher at a Russian anti-plague institute has died of what's been identified as a case of the plague , according to reports. Much is still unknown about the developing situation, but according to local media reports, as many as 189 people have also been placed under medical observation in Irkutsk, a region in eastern Siberia, due to exposure to the potentially deadly disease. The World Health Organization said it was aware of reports that a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast died of severe pneumonia on 2 October 2026, and that it had offered support to Russia. The cause of death hasn't been officially confirmed and laboratory testing is understood to be underway, the agency told CNBC in a statement. "All of the patient's contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for illness, and none to date have shown symptoms of illness," the WHO said. What is the plague and how does it spread? Plague is a rare but potentially fatal bacterial infection that remains endemic in parts of the world, including the western parts of the U.S., but can be treated with antibiotics if identified quickly. It's caused by the zoonotic bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals and their fleas, and it comes in many forms. Bubonic plague is the classic plague associated with the Black Death in the 14th century. Without treatment, the bacteria can escape the lymphatic system and enter the bloodstream or lungs, leading to septicemic or pneumonic plague, according to the World Health Organization. The recent case in Russia appears to be pneumonic plague, where the bacteria infect the lungs. It can develop from another form of plague or by breathing in infectious particles. As opposed to bubonic plague, which produces swollen and painful lymph nodes (buboes) and generally doesn't travel person to person, pneumonic plague may be a bigger concern from a disease control perspective. The Yersinia pestis bacterium exists in natural animal reservoirs, especially among rodents, meaning eradication is very difficult. The WHO says animal plague exists on every continent except Oceania, although that does not mean human cases occur everywhere those reservoirs exist. "Potentially this lab-acquired case of pneumonic plague could be transmitted by the respiratory route," Brendan Wren, professor at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, told CNBC. "Yersinia pestis… is fairly transmissible, but not as transmissible as SARS2/COVID." What's happening with the suspected case in Russia? According to Russia's public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor, the employee at the anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk had been diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown aetiology." The situation in the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov was "stable," and measures have been implemented in response to the case, it said in a statement on Sunday. Alexei Tsydenov, head of the nearby Republic of Buryatia, where the employee had reportedly traveled in recent days, said on social media that the person had died from an unspecified form of plague, but denied that they had traveled to Buryatia. CNBC has not been able to independently verify the reports. The Russian Ministry of Health didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. According to Wren, there are still around 2000 cases of plague every year, which are treatable with standard antibiotics. "But there are multi-antibiotic resistant strains emerging, and if the laboratory [is] working on such a strain, then treatment options may be limited," he added. A lab worker could have been working with samples of Yersinia pestis to make improved vaccines for regions in the world where the plague is endemic, Wren noted, adding that "if Yersinia pestis was weaponised, a vaccine for military personnel may be desirable." Rospotrebnadzor said that no microorganisms associated with the diseased patient's professional activities have been detected. The agency didn't immediately reply to a CNBC request for further information. The WHO told CNBC that based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low, and that the risk assessment will be updated once more information is available. — CNBC's Jenny Lee contributed to this report

events.title: Ukraine's robotic gun turrets have scored their first kills of Russia's fastest attack drones
events.summary: Ukraine said an AI-enabled turret shot down Russia's fastest attack drone. Courtesy of United24 Ukraine's robotic gun turrets have achieved their first interceptions of Russia's fastest attack drone. The AI-enabled turrets were deployed around Kyiv amid an uptick in jet-powered drone attacks. Ukraine has struggled to defend against this faster class of Russian strike weapons. Ukraine has used artificial intelligence-enabled robotic gun turrets to shoot down Russia's fastest attack drones for the first time, a senior Air Force official confirmed on Monday. Yurii Inhat, a Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson, said automated gun turrets have intercepted Russian jet-powered drones , including the Geran-5 — a significant development for Kyiv as it struggles to defend against Russia's high-speed weapons. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that more than a dozen turrets were installed around Kyiv, with another eight planned for deployment across the wider region, to counter the rise in Russia's jet-powered drones. Inhat described the turrets as "innovative technologies" that rely on AI and machine vision to enable the interception. Speaking during a national telethon, he said the guns have a limited range, Ukrainian media reported. At least some of the turrets will be installed on Kyiv's bridges, which Russian forces have targeted multiple times with drones over the past week amid a broader escalation of attacks on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure . Ukraine has not disclosed the specific type of turret deployed. The system does, however, feature a .50-caliber machine gun, Zelenskyy revealed, a typical weapon used by mobile air defense units . Russia's jet-powered drones are faster than many Ukrainian interceptors, prompting local companies to upgrade their models. AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka Last year, Ukraine confirmed the deployment of the Sky Sentinel, an AI-powered turret  capable of shooting down Russian attack drones. Russia is increasingly using drones powered by mini turbojet engines to attack Ukraine; Kyiv said Moscow launched 2,800 in August compared to 350 in June. The Geran-5, the newest and fastest of the models in service, can reach speeds of up to 375 mph. The uptick in jet-powered drones over the past few months has presented a significant challenge for Ukrainian air defenses . Inhat said on Monday that the interception rate for these drones is 50% to 70%, compared to over 85% for older, slower propeller-powered models like the Geran-2. The new turret deployment reflects Ukraine's efforts to bolster its air defenses in response to the growing threat of jet-powered drones. Ukrainian defense companies are also upgrading the speed of their interceptor drones. Some next-generation models have already shot down jet-powered drones, including the Geran-5, The "Bars" long-range drone has the highest success rate among the Ukrainian interceptors with a 30% shoot-down rate, Zelenskyy said over the weekend. "Others are catching up as well." Read the original article on Business Insider
