events.title: Is Iran charging a toll to allow oil traffic through Hormuz?
events.summary: Crude exports bypassing Hormuz surged in September, yet oil prices remain high. Could a secret fee be the reason? Middle East oil exports have climbed back above levels seen before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, despite Tehran’s attempts to blockade the Strait of Hormuz and attack vessels. Crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on four days in the final week of September, reaching between 19.5 and 22.5 million barrels per day (bpd), according to provisional data from maritime tracking firm Kpler. Before the war, exports averaged about 18 million bpd. list 1 of 3 Trump vs Europe as US presses for release of emergency diesel stocks list 2 of 3 Iraq grants Iranian airlines 40 daily Najaf flights after US exemption list 3 of 3 Iran says Hormuz to remain closed until US meets conditions This surge in oil exports from the region has so far largely been attributed to US ships shepherding tankers out of the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with increasing ship-to-ship transfers that reduce the risks of being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones. Meanwhile, the fact that oil prices have remained high has been explained by analysts as the result of still-elevated insurance rates — driven by fears of Iranian attacks — and a market factoring in the possibility of a return to a hot war. But a senior Kpler analyst last week offered a different explanation for the rise in oil exports at high prices. Gulf countries, she suggested, may be paying Iran to allow their oil through – potentially handing Tehran a significant portion of the value of the cargo. Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas exports passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Does this explanation hold up, and what does it mean for the war and oil prices? Michelle Brohard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at Kpler, recently said some countries could be paying Iran for passage through the Strait of Hormuz. “I suspect there is a toll that’s being paid, which is giving these ships safe passage,” she said in an interview last week with energy analyst Rory Johnston. “I also suspect that these countries know that this is unsustainable from a perspective of [the] US escorting [ships], and also unsustainable from them paying Iran 10 percent of their cargo, or 20 percent of their cargo,” she added. “So you’re starting to see like what I would call like a race to get out as much as possible, as quickly as possible before the war restarts.” The claim has not been independently verified, and Brohard presented it as speculation rather than a finding backed by evidence. But as early as March, the shipping journal Lloyd’s List reported that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had already imposed a “toll booth” system to control vessel traffic through the strait. The Trump administration, during the course of the war, has repeatedly said Iran will not be permitted to charge a toll under any potential agreement with Washington. Closure of the strait has caused global fuel costs to soar and has tested agricultural sectors across the world. What does traffic in the Hormuz look like? Oil is increasingly getting out of the Middle East, marine trackers report. In the last week of September, the seven-day average climbed above the roughly 18 million bpd recorded before the US-Israel war on Iran began in February – the first time since the conflict started. Kpler said crude exports excluding Iran had also recovered to at least 16.5 million bpd as an average over September. The pattern of increasing oil exports has continued into October. Iraq’s state-owned Oil Tanker Company on Saturday announced that it had transported two million barrels of crude on a very ‌large crude carrier (VLCC) through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general said was the company’s first such operation in decades. According to Kpler, “40 percent now bypass Hormuz, and most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore”, with much of it flowing through Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates pipelines. The export figures also include supplies moved through the Red Sea, which has become an increasingly important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. Moreover, the Kpler figures exclude any vessels that may have crossed the key transit route with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection. Iran, however, disputes suggestions that it has lost control of the waterway. Senior IRGC commander Ali Fadavi said on Sunday only three to four million bpd were travelling along a US-supervised route and described that amount as “negligible” compared with pre-war traffic. Before the war erupted seven months ago, the strait routinely saw about 125 large commercial vessels a day, including tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers and container ships. Oil prices have eased marginally as exports from the Middle East recover.

events.title: Adnoc signs Thai LNG deal after Iran war disrupts Gulf supply
events.summary: Adnoc has agreed to supply about two million tonnes of liquefied natural gas to Thailand ’s Gulf Development, boosting the country's access to the fuel as the Iran war disrupts supplies from the Middle East. Deliveries under the multi-year sales and purchase agreement are to start in 2027, Adnoc said on Monday. The company did not disclose prices, the length of the contract or where the cargoes will be sourced from. The agreement builds on a first LNG supply deal between the companies signed in 2025. The latest deal comes as Thailand seeks to diversify its LNG supplies after the war sharply curtailed shipments from the Gulf. Natural gas accounts for more than 60 per cent of the country’s power generation, while about 24 per cent of its LNG imports – about 2.2 million tonnes a year – normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz, almost all from Qatar, according to Thailand-based Krungsri Research. State-controlled PTT has been exploring alternative supplies, including from Oman, Mexico and Canada. The regional war has upended a global LNG market that was already heading into a period of tighter seasonal demand. The strait, through which about a fifth of global crude and LNG flowed before the war began in late February, remains largely shut. QatarEnergy declared force majeure in early March, while an Iranian missile strike on the Ras Laffan complex on March 18 knocked out about 17 per cent of Qatar's LNG production capacity. Cargo cancellations to some Asian buyers have since been extended through November, helping push prices in Asia and Europe towards their highest levels since late 2022. Gulf LNG exports remain far below their prewar pace of about three shipments a day. “This agreement builds on our first LNG supply agreement with Gulf Group and reinforces Adnoc’s commitment to ensuring reliable energy supplies to Thailand and our Asian customers,” said Nasser Al Muhairi, acting chief executive of Adnoc downstream industry, marketing and trading. Gulf Development chief executive Sarath Ratanavadi said the agreement would help to build a “diversified, resilient LNG portfolio” and gave the company greater flexibility to meet demand. The supplies will be delivered through Adnoc Trading and its LNG marketing and trading platform , launched in Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM in July. Adnoc is targeting 47 million tonnes a year of marketable LNG beyond 2030 as it expands its portfolio and trading operations.

events.title: Trump won Nebraska by 20 points. Now he’s trying to rescue a GOP Senate seat after angering ranchers with his plan to import more beef
events.summary: President Donald Trump is taking his Republican midterm rescue mission to Nebraska on Monday, campaigning alongside GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats . Trump is headed to Grand Island, Nebraska, located in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. It’s part of what the Republican president says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of Nov. 3 that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama . On Wednesday, he’ll make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio. “The president’s coming to Nebraska to help me campaign, so I can get reelected,” Ricketts told the Associated Press last week on Capitol Hill. Ricketts, a former governor of the state, was appointed then later elected to fill Sen. Ben Sasse’s seat when he left to run the University of Florida in 2023. Now he is running for his first full six-year term against independent Dan Osborn — a race that initially was not expected to be competitive but is now being watched by the national parties. Voters across the country are frustrated with Trump’s handling of the economy , including persistently high costs for fuel and groceries. It’s a major issue for rural voters who have backed the president and his party in recent elections. The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers, but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them. “The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.” There are a few Senate races where independents are the challengers In the House of Representatives, the Grand Island area is represented by Republican Rep. Adrian Smith, whose race is not expected to be close. But Nebraska has a competitive House race farther east in Omaha , considered the “blue dot” of the state because the area’s electoral vote in presidential elections often goes to Democrats. Osborn, a former labor union chief, ran against Republican Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024 and lost by 7 percentage points. Though national Democrats support him, he has refused to say what party he would caucus with should he be elected in November. Other independents in the Senate, including Maine’s Angus King on the moderate end and Vermont’s Bernie Sanders on the left, caucus with Democrats for organizational purposes and committee assignments. With the Democratic brand remaining deeply unpopular in conservative states, Osborn isn’t the only declared independent running for the Senate against Republicans this year. In South Dakota, Navy and Air Force veteran Brian Bengs is campaigning as an independent against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Bengs ran as a Democrat for the Senate four years ago and was handily defeated by now-Senate Majority Leader John Thune. It’s a similar dynamic in Idaho, where independent Todd Achilles is challenging GOP Sen. Jim Risch. Democratic voters in Nebraska chose Cindy Burbank as their party nominee earlier this year, but Burbank specifically campaigned on ensuring that no votes would be siphoned from Osborn in the general elections in November, and she has since formally dropped out of the race. Osborn has been traveling across Nebraska to hold meetings in all 93 counties, and has repeatedly criticized Ricketts for not holding town halls to meet with constituents. Ricketts, whose family founded TD Ameritrade and owns Major League Baseball’s Chicago Cubs, served as governor from 2015 to 2023. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Before UK Greens, who else has equated Zionism with racism?
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Israel condemns the move as the party’s vote causes an uproar, including among party members. The United Kingdom’s Green Party has voted to define Zionism as a form of racism, drawing condemnation from the Israeli government. In a binding vote held at the party’s conference over the weekend, members voted to usher in the new definition as well as a series of other strongly pro-Palestine policies. list 1 of 4 Israel lashes out as UK’s Green Party formally defines Zionism as ‘racism’ list 2 of 4 Ireland refuse handshake with Israel and don armbands in Nations League tie list 3 of 4 ‘Did he know?’: Why Israel is rejecting an October 7 reckoning list 4 of 4 Netanyahu’s fight to own the election narrative However, just as the resolution has drawn international criticism, it has also proved internally controversial with four of the party’s five members in parliament opposing it. Israel on Monday banned party leader Zack Polanski from the country just a day before the politician faces a by-election as he runs in the London constituency that former Prime Minister Keir Starmer represented. Zionism emerged as a political ideology in the late 19th century. It called for the creation of a Jewish homeland at a time of rising anti-Semitism and persecution of Jews in Europe. Theodore Herzl, an Austro-Hungarian journalist considered the father of political Zionism, originally proposed an independent and colonial Jewish state in either Palestine or Argentina. Here’s what we know about what the Greens have said: The Greens endorsed the motion to equate Zionism with racism by a vote of 1,022 to 813. In addition, the party restated its “commitment to Palestinian liberation” and called for the “establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine”. The party also recommitted to its support of Palestinians’ right of return as well as to the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement against Israel. “The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians,” a Green Party statement said. A significant number of party members, including four of its five MPs, were against parts of the resolution, exposing divisions within the party. Codeputy leader Rachel Millward said in a post on X that while the party is committed to “stop the genocide”, the term Zionism means “different things to different people, … so I personally do not think the policy helps us do the work we all want to”. Meanwhile, Polanski, who is Jewish and was away campaigning during the vote, told journalists afterwards that if Zionism equates to the displacement of Palestinians, “that is clearly racist.” Polanski said he, however, did not support the reference to a single Palestinian state and external entities should not decide what a future state would look like. Israel has accused the party of legitimising “terrorism”, and senior officials equated it to anti-Semitism. “The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on social media. Israeli President Isaac Herzog said it would “deliberately endanger Jews and Israelis everywhere”. Opposition leader Yair Lapid said the party was “racist”. The Green Party has rejected equating criticism of Israel with anti-Semitism and reiterated its stance against “any form of discrimination or harassment”. “We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people,” Polanski and other senior party members said in a statement on Sunday. Has Zionism been equated to racism before? Yes. In 1975, the UN General Assembly passed a resolution that “determines that Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination”. The vote was sponsored by the Soviet bloc and the Arab League. It passed after 72 countries, largely from the Middle East and Africa, voted for it. Israel and 34 other countries – chiefly from the West – were against it. Thirty-two other countries abstained. Just a year before, at the 1974 General Assembly, Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat had given his “olive branch” speech at the General Assembly. About the same time, African countries opposing the apartheid regime in South Africa, which was increasingly allying with Israel, had resolved separately that the Israeli government was “racist” and both had an “imperialist origin.” Also, in 1975, at the first international women’s conference, held in Mexico City, attendees decided there would be no international peace outside the “elimination of foreign occupation, Zionism, apartheid” and all other forms of “racial discrimination”. However, the General Assembly vote proved controversial.

events.title: KPMG has a new CEO leading its 276,000 staff. Here are the key challenges he faces.
events.summary: KPMG is the smallest of the Big Four professional services firms. Sean Gallup/Getty Images KPMG has a new global chairman and CEO: Gary Wingrove. From AI transformation to an auditing scandal, he's taken over at a turbulent time for consulting. Business Insider spoke to industry watchers about the challenges Wingrove faces as he starts his tenure. KPMG has a new boss. On October 1, Gary Wingrove took over as global chairman and CEO of the Big Four accounting and consulting firm, succeeding Bill Thomas after an eight-year tenure. Wingrove joined KPMG in 2000 and most recently held roles as CEO of KPMG Australia from 2013 to 2021 and international COO. He now oversees more than 276,000 employees across KPMG's member firms. The firms operate as a global network of legally separate firms rather than as a single company, making the role of global chair different from that of a typical corporate CEO. Big Four leaders typically spend decades building the trust, personal networks, and credibility needed to win an internal election — the way Big Four firms choose their heads. Once in the role, they are responsible for holding the network together across geographies, monitoring its performance, and stepping in during high-stakes crises. KPMG did not respond to a request for comment for this story. When Wingrove's appointment was announced in March, he said that he would aim to create an environment where KPMG employees could thrive . AI, AI, and more AI AI is both one of KPMG's biggest growth opportunities and a tricky management challenge. The Big Four have cast themselves as "client zero" as AI changes the workplace — whatever happens to the rest of the workforce with AI, it probably happened inside the firms first. Wingrove will be under pressure to ensure all of KPMG's firms innovate quickly and cohesively, and that the workforce can adapt without weakening its pipeline of future managers and partners. Have a tip or story to share about working in consulting? Contact this reporter via email at pthompson@businessinsider.com or Signal at Polly_Thompson.89. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely . "In consulting, AI is already reducing the value of some of the more junior, research-heavy and analytical work that has traditionally supported the pyramid," said James Ransome, a partner and consulting lead at executive-search and industry-analysis firm Patrick Morgan. That raises a longer-term question: how will firms train junior staff if the work they once learned is increasingly automated? Getting that approach right will involve rethinking both team structures and the development of junior talent, Ransome said. On the business side, KPMG's US arm recently launched a new Client Technology & Innovation group to develop AI-native products and services that it says will move at Silicon Valley-like speed. The wider firm has invested heavily in AI tools and partnerships. Driving growth Wingrove, like his fellow Big Four leaders, is facing down a tougher consulting market. KPMG is the smallest of the Big Four, both in terms of employee numbers and annual revenue. Its latest full-year financial results suggest that it is growing its business slightly faster than rivals PwC and EY. The firm's annual revenue grew 5.1% in 2025 to $39.8 billion. That was driven less by consulting than by KPMG's more traditional business. Audit was up 6%, and KPMG's tax revenues grew notably faster than those of its competitors — up 7.5% compared to around 5.5% at EY and Deloitte, and 1% at PwC. However, advisory grew just 2.9%, lower than its competitors. AI offers a great pipeline of new consulting business as companies turn to consultants for help figuring out how to use AI and retrain workers. However, it's also disrupting the firms' economics and pricing model, putting pressure on time-based fees that have long underpinned the industry. Economic uncertainty is also putting pressure on prices and comes as the firms need to invest more in technology, especially AI, Emma Carroll, a consultant at Source Global Research who advises the professional services sector, told Business Insider. The outlook for consulting services is strong, she said. "There's no shortage of demand. Two-thirds of organizations expect their use of external support to grow in the next 12-18 months; no one expects it to shrink." Working across the world The Big Four's independent network structure is particularly important for the audit function, where firms must navigate local regulations and independence requirements. But global clients increasingly require cross-border coordination and access to shared specialist capabilities and technology. PwC US announced in September that it plans to merge its offshoring center in India with the Indian branch of PwC. At EY, global CEO Janet Truncale has merged 18 geographical regions into 10 superregions. In a video released on his first day, Wingrove announced Connected 2030, a global strategy intended to make KPMG a "more connected, agile and innovative global organization." KPMG has been the least integrated of the Big Four, with practices that are siloed and run by partners who exert more control over their respective businesses, said Tom Rodenhauser, managing partner of K2 Consulting Research. That fragmentation could be an advantage if KPMG focuses on key markets and functions, and specializes its offering for different clients rather than trying to be a one-stop shop, said Rodenhauser. Wingrove is probably well-suited to the challenge of balancing the tension between independence and global cooperation, given his previous role as Global COO, where regional integration and global investment were already part of his remit, James Ransome said. Dealing with trouble Down Under KPMG's office in Sydney has been at the center of recent scandals in its business Down Under. Bloomberg/Getty Images One of Wingrove's most pressing challenges will be rebuilding trust after an audit-confidentiality scandal at KPMG Australia. In March 2026, Australian Labor senator Deborah O'Neill aired whistleblower allegations that KPMG partners had accessed and shared confidential client information internally to help pursue audit work. The whistleblower had raised concerns with KPMG internally from 2024, but the crisis became public after O'Neill's disclosure. KPMG has since acknowledged that its initial investigation of the whistleblower's concerns wasn't rigorous enough and confirmed that client information was inappropriately shared inside the firm. Reporting of the scandal has been led by The Australian Financial Review. The fallout has prompted resignations of several leaders, regulatory and parliamentary scrutiny, and reviews of KPMG relationships by some of its biggest clients and public-sector customers. events.title: From Scan to Treatment Plan, AI Helps Close Breast Cancer’s Deadliest Gaps
events.summary: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among American women — yet the gaps in care are wide. A majority of women over age 40 skip the recommended annual screening. Radiologists are reading more mammograms with fewer colleagues. And when a diagnosis arrives, the tests that inform treatment can take weeks to return results. Companies in the NVIDIA Inception program for startups are building AI applications to support clinicians at each of these friction points, including imaging, risk assessment and treatment planning. About 40 million mammograms are performed in the U.S. each year, but a projected shortfall of tens of thousands of radiologists over the next decade is straining the system’s capacity to read them. At the other end of the care timeline, treatment decisions often hinge on genomic assays sent off to outside labs — assays that take weeks to process, at a moment when speed and certainty matter most. The companies below are addressing both ends of that gap, and everything in between, accelerated by NVIDIA AI infrastructure. Automated Imaging Delivers AI-Powered Insights For women struggling to find time or a nearby location for breast cancer screening, access is a practical barrier that translates into missed diagnoses. NVIDIA Inception startup iSono Health was built around simplifying this imaging workflow. The company’s FDA-cleared ATUSA platform — a wearable, automated 3D quantitative ultrasound system — captures a standardized breast volume in approximately two minutes per breast, compared with up to 45 minutes for a conventional handheld ultrasound. The system’s AI, trained on thousands of full-breast scans comprising over 1.5 million ultrasound frames, automates image acquisition. It uses NVIDIA GPU acceleration and open source medical imaging technology to deliver a 3D scan that the company says is 28% more sensitive than a handheld 2D ultrasound. Handheld ultrasound depends on whoever holds the probe, so a woman’s scans typically can’t be compared from one year to the next. ATUSA captures the whole breast the same way every time, creating a repeatable view of breast tissue that could help clinicians analyze how a patient’s tissue changes across successive scans, while also reducing operator errors and variability. ATUSA is commercially available through partner clinics across California, Texas, Georgia, Tennessee and Washington D.C., with new sites coming online regularly. “Getting the scan closer to the patient is the first breakthrough,” said Neda Razavi, CEO of iSono Health. “Our vision is to make that scan increasingly informative: helping clinicians see what is there, understand what has changed and make more informed decisions.” iSono Health has developed AI capabilities for lesion detection, 3D segmentation and lesion classification. It next plans to extend its AI pipeline into multimodal diagnostic intelligence spanning 3D ultrasound, mammography, MRI and clinical information. The company has a multicenter clinical study with 3,200 patients underway to further validate the platform’s performance, with lead research sites at UC Davis and Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Finding Cancers, Cutting False Alarms Another NVIDIA Inception company, Whiterabbit.ai, develops AI technology for breast cancer screening. Its FDA-cleared WRDensity software automatically assesses breast density from mammograms and has been used in the care of hundreds of thousands of patients. The company has also developed WRRisk, a clinical decision support software for estimating patients’ long-term risk of developing breast cancer — and is researching a new generation of AI for mammography that could help radiologists detect more cancers while automating the screening of mammograms that are negative for breast cancer. The goal is to reduce the burden on a strained radiologist workforce, accelerate results and reduce avoidable callbacks for patients, and lower downstream healthcare costs. “Every day, breast radiologists face a needle-in-a-haystack problem, trying to find roughly one cancer in every 200 mammograms,” said Jason Su, cofounder and chief technology officer of Whiterabbit.ai. “We hope AI can be a powerful sidekick to radiologists, helping to clear away the hay so they can focus their expertise where it matters most.” Whiterabbit trains its AI models on a cluster of NVIDIA GPUs housed at Washington University in St. Louis, supplemented by additional GPU capacity in the cloud. Inference runs on NVIDIA GPUs deployed directly in the clinic. Predicting Which Treatments Will Work Once a patient is diagnosed with breast cancer, the next question is what to do about it — and the answer depends on predicting how the cancer will respond to treatment. Today, these predictions are limited in scope and accuracy, and often require a separate tissue biopsy with a two- to four-week wait. Ataraxis AI is building clinical intelligence that predicts patient outcomes and response to different therapies using digital data, including pathology slides that are already part of the standard patient workup. “The tools oncologists rely on today to guide therapy decisions were largely trained once, fifteen years ago, and never updated. Our models get stronger every time we acquire more clinical trial data,” said Joseph Cappadona, member of technical staff at Ataraxis AI. “But as we scale our models, the bigger shift is being able to answer more questions to help oncologists personalize therapy across all cancers.” Ataraxis’s AI models analyze digital pathology slides and standard clinical variables to predict treatment response and recurrence risk. One model predicts whether presurgical chemotherapy is likely to shrink a patient’s tumor to the point of response before the operating room. After surgery, another model estimates a patient’s five-year recurrence risk and the likely benefit of chemotherapy as a next step. Both models have been validated across more than 10 institutions and multiple clinical trials, and are in active clinical use. They run on NVIDIA GPUs on premises, in an offsite data center and in the cloud — using PyTorch accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA throughout. Providing Tumor Insights With 3D Visualization Another NVIDIA Inception company, SimBioSys , joined NVIDIA on a recent panel marking Breast Cancer Awareness Month. The company builds AI-powered precision medicine technology that creates accurate 3D models of breast tumors, veins and other soft tissue, delivering important insights to help guide surgeries and influence treatment plans. It has also built a tool to estimate the risk of breast cancer recurrence based on 3D volumetric data from a patient’s breast MRI, tumor pathology and clinical data. “We’re building a platform that now allows us to take multimodal data — imaging exams, pathology results, genomic testing when applicable and other biological inputs — and, using AI, bring that all together,” said Stacey Stevens, CEO of SimBioSys, at the event.

events.title: Trump reiterates pledge to send $5,000 checks, and hands out smaller payments, as midterm elections loom
events.summary: President Donald Trump is touting two federal cash-payment programs already underway while renewing a much larger $5,000 check promise contingent on Republicans retaining Congress. The cash offers come as Republicans head into the final stretch of a midterm campaign dominated by concerns about prices and the economy. Trump has previously claimed Americans would receive checks that never materialized, and some polling shows voters are skeptical. With Election Day less than a month away, President Donald Trump is touting two federal cash-payment programs already underway while renewing a much larger $5,000 check promise contingent on Republicans retaining Congress. On Friday, Trump announced one-time $90 payments to 20.8 million Medicare beneficiaries. A day later, he revived an earlier promise to give every adult U.S. citizen $5,000 — but only if Republicans retain control of Congress in November. "If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate in the 2026 Midterm Elections, I'm going to give all Adult Citizens in the United States of America, $5,000," Trump said in a Truth Social video post Saturday. The president made a similar pledge at the Republican National Committee's first midterm convention in Dallas last month. Trump hasn't provided any details on who would authorize the payments and where the money would come from. Those claims came on the heels of $500 Obamacare "refund" checks that began going out last week to roughly 950,000 people who bought unsubsidized coverage through the federal marketplace. The $90 payments to certain eligible Medicare Part B enrollees are scheduled to arrive this month, funded through the Medicare Improvement Fund. The $500 Obamacare payments are already being distributed to certain full-price HealthCare.gov customers. Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' Supreme Court Justice Alito said he's 'thought about' retirement as Senate control hangs in balance Trump taps Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as AI czar A Reuters analysis found 71% of the Obamacare money — $339 million — is going to residents of 13 states with some of the country's most competitive Senate and gubernatorial races, though eligibility is based on insurance status, not voting status. Together, the flurry of offers of direct cash payments comes as Republicans head into the final stretch of a midterm campaign dominated by concerns about prices and the economy . But the $5,000 "Trump dividend" remains just a promise and Trump has been extremely light on details, particularly on where the money would come from and who would need to authorize it. Sending $5,000 to every adult citizen would cost roughly $1.2 trillion and require congressional approval. Some Republicans have also raised concerns about its effect on the deficit and inflation. Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., told Reuters last month he would "throw everything of my heart and soul" into stopping the proposal, warning it could push interest rates higher. And Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., called the plan a "political bribe" in a Sept. 10 interview with CNN , and said Congress controls federal spending. The White House and offices of Reps. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., and Jamie Raskin, D-Md., did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Polling suggests the idea isn't a sure-fire political winner. A Rasmussen Reports survey found likely voters essentially split, 47% to 48%, on the proposal. Just 15% said it would affect their vote. A Marquette Law School poll in Wisconsin found 70% opposed the payments, while an Economist/YouGov survey found 57% of registered voters doubted Trump would actually deliver them even if Republicans retained Congress. In the past, Trump has made several promises to send cash payments to Americans — and didn't deliver. In February 2025, the Trump administration floated a $5,000 "DOGE dividend" check, claiming the money would come from savings from the cuts enacted by the now-defunct, Elon Musk -led "Department of Government Efficiency." Those payments never materialized. Then, in November, Trump proposed a reciprocal tariff -funded dividend payment of at least $2,000 per person . The Supreme Court struck down the tariffs in February of this year, and no checks were ever issued. The pattern of offering cash payments directly to voters stretches back to Trump's first term. Six weeks before the 2020 election, Trump promised 33 million Medicare beneficiaries $200 prescription-drug cards "in coming weeks" — but the cards never went out . Still, the Trump administration delivered a $1,776 " Warrior Dividend " to roughly 1.5 million service members last year, and Congress approved pandemic stimulus payments during his first term.

World Investor Week is a global effort by the International Organization of Securities Commissions to bring together regulators across six continents to raise awareness about the importance of investor education and investor protection. This year marks WIW’s tenth anniversary. events.title: Bolsonaro favourite to win: What Brazil’s first round of elections tells us
events.summary: Analysts say Flavio Bolsonaro is projected to win a run-off vote on October 25 and become Brazil’s next president. Right-wing Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has exceeded expectations in the first-round vote with a slight lead over the incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio ‌Lula da Silva, triggering a run-off later this month. “Brazil wants change, and I am very happy with the results,” Bolsonaro told reporters in Brasilia on Sunday as he saluted “the end of the era of [Lula’s] Workers’ Party”. list 1 of 3 Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro close campaigns ahead of critical election list 2 of 3 Will Brazil’s Lula halt the right-wing wave sweeping Latin America? list 3 of 3 Polls close in Brazil’s polarised election pitting Lula against Bolsonaro The 45-year-old ⁠son of right-wing former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year jail sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, now faces an October 25 showdown with the 80-year-old Lula, who is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term. ‌In the run-up to Sunday’s first-round vote, a series of polls showed a close race between Lula and Bolsonaro, with the incumbent president poised to win by about 3 percentage points against his right-wing challenger. In a surprise result that defied opinion poll projections, Bolsonaro beat Lula with 47 percent of the vote, while Lula got 45.1 percent. Neither reached the 50 percent threshold needed to win in the first round. That sets up another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown, four years after Lula narrowly defeated Jair Bolsonaro. Why is Bolsonaro favoured to win Brazil’s election? Bolsonaro’s stronger-than-expected performance is likely to buoy his campaign and may bolster Brazil’s currency and stock market, which have risen on the prospects of the business-friendly challenger. Oliver Stuenkel, professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) in San Paulo, Brazil, said Lula was in a difficult position as he could not count on voters who backed one of the other 10 candidates to vote for him in the second round. “Not only is he behind now after this first round, but the other candidates who received a total of nearly 8 percent are largely centre-right, which means that the people who voted for these other candidates are very unlikely to shift for Lula,” Stuenkel told Al Jazeera. “So he must change his campaign tactics and above all mobilise a significant part of people who stayed at home,” he added. About 30 million Brazilians – 21 percent of the electorate – did not vote in the first round. Al Jazeera’s Monica Yanakiew, reporting from Rio de Janeiro, said Lula supporters felt their candidate had not used social media as effectively as the right-wing camp. “This is something they have to work on in the second round,” Yanakiew said. From a historical perspective, however, such efforts are unlikely to change the outcome. “Unless something very unusual happens in the next three weeks, Flavio Bolsonaro is set to win,” Stuenkel said. “In Brazilian presidential politics, no candidate who came second in the first round ended up winning the presidency since 1989.” Has the Bolsonaro family taken hold of Brazil? Several politicians from the Bolsonaro family have won congressional races taking place as part of the broader nationwide general elections. Michelle Bolsonaro, wife of former President Jair Bolsonaro and stepmother of Flavio, won a Senate seat in the Federal District, home to the capital, Brasilia. In June, the 44-year-old, who has never held government office, had a public falling out with her stepson, whom she accused of disrespecting her in lengthy videos posted on her social media. The pair later made up. Ex-leader Bolsonaro’s second son Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, was the second most-voted senatorial candidate in the southern Santa Catarina state and won a seat in the Senate. The fourth and younger son, Jair Renan Bolsonaro, was elected to the lower house of Congress. Some experts credit “antipetismo” — a trend of hostility against Lula’s PT movement — with fuelling the Bolsonaro family’s rise to political power. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) won 121 of the 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies while Lula’s PT got 70. What are the implications of a Bolsonaro win? Brazil’s presidential election carries significant regional and geopolitical implications. Reporting from Sao Paulo, Al Jazeera’s Lucia Newman said Lula has been “on a collision course” with United States President Donald Trump, who is a vocal and ardent supporter of the Bolsonaro camp. “That puts Brazil in the middle of a fierce competition between Washington and China for political, diplomatic and economic dominance, especially since Brazil is a powerhouse on all these fronts,” Newman said. While Bolsonarism is strongly aligned with the US and Israel, Brazil also has a tight economic relationship with China, its largest trade partner.

events.title: Lionel Messi to join Argentina for farewell match against Benin
events.summary: The friendly marks a symbolic passing of the torch for a player whose international legacy includes a World Cup title. Lionel Messi will bring the curtain down on his glittering Argentina career with a farewell friendly against Benin that marks the dawn of a new era for the South American champions. After more than two decades of service to his country, the 39-year-old superstar will hand over the captain’s armband for good as he makes his final appearance in the Albiceleste jersey on Tuesday at the Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires. list 1 of 3 ‘You are eternal’: Football world pays tribute to Argentina’s Lionel Messi list 2 of 3 Lionel Messi’s Argentina career in numbers: Records, goals, trophies list 3 of 3 ‘The time has come’: Messi retires from international football Messi will be joined for his international swansong by 85,000 spectators and several of the teammates with whom he reached the pinnacle of football at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar , alongside members of Argentina’s emerging generation. The friendly marks a symbolic passing of the torch for a player whose international legacy includes a World Cup title, two Copa America crowns and the Finalissima. Messi will also bow out as Argentina’s record appearance-maker and leading scorer with 125 goals in 207 games as well as a record 68 assists. His farewell comes two and a half months after Argentina’s ill-tempered World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression. “I gave it my all. I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance,” Messi wrote when announcing his international retirement in August. Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028 although after the death of his father , Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated. Members of Argentina’s 2022 World Cup-winning squad and their families will join Messi for Tuesday’s farewell against Benin, ranked 93rd in the world. Veterans of that Doha triumph, such as Angel Di Maria, who retired from international football in 2024, will be there to witness the passing of the torch to a new generation charged with extending the Albiceleste’s golden era. Several of the newcomers, including Franco Mastantuono and Leonel Flores, were not even born when “La Pulga” (“The Flea”) made his Argentina debut in 2005 for a team whose history had for so long been dominated by Diego Maradona. “It’s going to be an unforgettable day for everyone. Everyone wants to be at this match, and now it’s just about enjoying it,” Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni said. Argentina’s new generation has already shown what it can do without its captain although nobody is pretending that replacing a man regarded by many as the greatest footballer in history will be straightforward. “Collectively, we will try to fill the void left by Leo,” said Scaloni, who is negotiating a contract extension after leaving his future unresolved following the World Cup defeat in July. Scaloni, who mastered the art of building the right supporting cast around Messi, will also say goodbye on Tuesday to 38-year-old vice captain Nicolas Otamendi. Like Messi and Otamendi, midfielders Rodrigo De Paul and Giovani Lo Celso were called up solely for the Benin game, raising the possibility that neither will represent Argentina again. Those certain to be involved, at least from the bench, include other veterans of the 2022 World Cup who will be the standard-bearers for Argentina after Messi: defender Cristian Romero, midfielders Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernandez, and forwards Julian Alvarez and Lautaro Martinez. Tenacious centre back Romero is set to inherit the captain’s armband, first worn by Messi at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa. Goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez and Lautaro Martinez are next in the captain hierarchy. They have already begun to rally around Messi’s heirs, who showed their appetite for success in Argentina’s first game since the World Cup final, against Bolivia in Cordoba on Wednesday. Argentina swept the Bolivians aside 4-0 with young talents Nico Paz and Jose Manuel Lopez among the scorers. They followed that victory with a 7-0 rout of Burkina Faso at the Monumental on Saturday with Mastantuono and Gianluca Prestianni scoring their first international goals. While Argentina’s future is beginning to take shape, one small but symbolically significant question remains: Who will inherit Messi’s number 10 shirt ? “We won’t give the number 10 to anyone until Leo’s match takes place,” Scaloni said. “After that, we’ll see.”

events.title: GM says hybrid vehicles are coming: 'We're not tone deaf to our customers'
events.summary: General Motors plans to introduce hybrid models into its U.S. lineup as consumers deal with elevated gas prices and the industry faces a lack of interest in all-electric vehicles. Hybrids are growing in popularity, as sales of the vehicles keep climbing. GM has largely been absent from the hybrid market this decade, but Mike Anderson, GM's vice president of propulsion engineering, told CNBC the automaker is listening to the market. DETROIT — General Motors plans to introduce hybrid models into its U.S. lineup as sales of the vehicles continue to grow amid inflated gas prices and a pullback in all-electric cars. Mike Anderson, GM's vice president of propulsion engineering, reconfirmed the automaker's hybrid plans, but declined to discuss timing for such vehicles, which had previously been expected as soon as next year. "It's fair to say that [hybrids are] part of the plan," Anderson, a 35-year GM veteran, told CNBC during an interview. "We're not tone deaf to our customers. We know what they want and we want to give that to them as quickly as we can." GM has largely been absent from the hybrid market this decade, instead using its resources to go "all-in" on all-electric vehicles . But amid lackluster EV demand, industry deregulation and increased hybrid popularity, Anderson said the company needs to meet customer demand wherever it may be. "Our long-term vision is an all-electric future. That's our goal," Anderson said. "That's the end state, but it's going to be a journey that involves technology diversity." GM CEO Mary Barra in January said the automaker was still studying plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, or PHEVs, for its U.S. lineup as well as traditional hybrids but remained critical of the technologies. She also told Bloomberg later that month that a "handful" of such models were coming but did not give a timeline. In mid-2024, GM announced plans to introduce PHEVs by 2027. At that time, GM was under pressure to meet stricter federal tailpipe emissions standards that have since been lowered or eliminated by the Trump administration. AutoForecast Solutions, an automotive data and consulting firm, expects GM to begin offering PHEVs in late 2027 to early 2028 with a 70-mile EV range "throughout its portfolio," according to Casey Selecman, director of powertrain forecasts for the company. "GM has several PHEVs planned throughout the portfolio from the Equinox to the Silverado but has been very cautious in rolling them out due to fears of customer technology preference changes that have burned them in the past," he said. Anderson declined to discuss potential products or timing for GM's first new hybrid model. "You can see, without me saying what our future plans are, where the customers are clamoring for these things and really, really going for them," he said. "We want to meet them where they want things." Sales of hybrid models in the U.S. have jumped amid dimming EV demand, inflated gas prices and more offerings in the market, which GM has been missing out on. Cox Automotive reports hybrid vehicle sales from the second quarter of this year increased 23% from a year earlier to represent a record 16.3% of U.S. sales from April through June. That compares with roughly 5.8% of sales for EVs, Cox said. The automotive industry has more powertrain and "propulsion" options than ever before. Here's a breakdown: Internal combustion engine (ICE): A "traditional" vehicle with an engine that's fueled with gasoline or diesel. Mild-hybrid electric vehicle (MHEV): An ICE vehicle that functions largely like a nonhybrid vehicle but may include minimal electrified features such as a small battery, regenerative braking or electric motor. Hybrid electric vehicle (HEV): Think of the Toyota Prius, a vehicle that has a hybrid powertrain system combined with an engine. Plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV) : These vehicles feature an internal combustion engine combined with a hybrid system, including a larger battery than traditional hybrid vehicles as well as a plug to recharge the vehicle's battery. They typically allow drivers to travel a certain number of miles using the battery before the engine is needed to power the car or truck. Battery-electric vehicle (BEV): These all-electric vehicles do not feature an internal combustion engine. Instead, they contain an electric motor that's powered by a large battery. They need to be recharged using an electrical outlet and charging port or charging station. Fuel cell electric vehicle (FCEV): Hydrogen fuel cell electric vehicles and equipment operate much like BEVs but are powered by electricity generated from hydrogen and oxygen instead of pure batteries, which commonly include lithium. They're filled up with a nozzle, similar to traditional gas and diesel vehicles.

events.title: NVIDIA Head of Sustainability: how to accelerate America’s nuclear energy renaissance
events.summary: For most of the last few decades, electricity demand in the United States has been relatively flat. Our energy system, infrastructure, and in many ways, our policies were built around the assumption it would not grow dramatically.  That era is ending.  AI is one visible driver of new electricity demand, but it is far from the only one. We are electrifying more of the economy. Manufacturing is returning to the United States. Robots and physical AI are moving quickly from research labs into the real world.  We are simply going to need far more electricity than we have today. And that is why we need to re-evaluate nuclear energy. At NVIDIA, we see both sides of this transition. The AI and accelerated computing we develop with our broad ecosystem of partners can also help energy developers design, simulate and operate infrastructure. This perspective that shapes our belief that the nuclear debate must move beyond whether to build—and focus on how technology can help the industry build safely, faster and at scale. Why Nuclear, Why Now  Support for nuclear power is converging in Washington in a way we have not seen in decades. Nuclear energy is increasingly viewed as a tool for mitigating climate change, while meeting increasing demand for energy abundance and economic growth. But the case for domestic nuclear expansion is stronger. Nuclear promises clean, firm, abundant energy that can meet growing demand and serve large industrial loads. The nation that sets the standard for safe, affordable, modern nuclear power will have strategic, security and commercial advantages. France’s long-term commitment to nuclear has already demonstrated that it can provide safe and reliable power at scale and maintain public support. AI is now accelerating interest by creating a massive, well-capitalized customer base that is willing to invest in clean power and next-generation nuclear technologies. A New Wave of Investment and Innovation The funding behind this new era of nuclear is coming from a mix of federal agencies and national laboratories, venture-backed startups, and companies investing in the clean power they will need. The first megawatt of a new nuclear technology is extraordinarily expensive, but once a design is developed, tested, and proven viable, economies of scale can help bring costs down. Companies are pursuing everything from advanced fission technologies like microreactors and small modular reactors to fusion. At NVIDIA, we’re witnessing far more demand for energy than available supply, in addition to construction and timing delays. Designing reactors, interpreting technical and regulatory information, simulating plant operations and integrating new power sources all require the ability to process increasingly complex data. NVIDIA works across that entire computing stack, giving us a view of how these pieces can work together. TerraPower , for example, is connecting an NVIDIA Omniverse-powered platform to use digital twins to compress parts of advanced nuclear siting and design. Atomic Canyon is using accelerated computing to build AI-powered knowledge tools for reactor operators, turning procedures, regulatory guidance, licensing records, and other nuclear data into a usable knowledge layer. Commonwealth Fusion Systems is using Omniverse libraries and OpenUSD to compress years of fusion experimentation into weeks.  We do not yet know which approaches will prove most successful. We need an environment where they can safely compete and prove what works — while rebuilding U.S. industrial capacity, skilled talent, and manufacturing supply chains along the way. A New Technological Era Requires a New Risk Calculus  Safety remains the central hurdle. But we are in a new technological era of reactor design, and the old risk calculus no longer reflects what many of these systems are designed to do. Many advanced reactors are being built with passive safety mechanisms, where the fail-safe state is the default rather than something dependent on active intervention. Waste management is also part of the equation, with advances in reactor design and waste management helping minimize radioactive waste and safely contain what remains. The right approach is to minimize both the probability and magnitude of an incident: make failures extremely unlikely while ensuring even worst-case scenarios can be contained and mitigated. Modular and advanced designs could also enable smaller, safer facilities with broader applications. AI can play a role in that work, but only within clear boundaries. Argonne National Laboratory is testing PRO-AID, a system that combines AI with physics-based models to identify and explain equipment problems in real time. In testing, it detected simulated sensor and component failures as they occurred, while leaving verification, response and operational decisions to trained personnel under established safety and regulatory procedures. The government also has a tremendous opportunity to build public trust. Early projects and pilots at Idaho National Laboratory and Department of Defense sites demonstrate that advanced nuclear technologies can operate safely and reliably in the real world.  How Do We Accelerate the Deployment of Nuclear Energy?  The biggest constraint on nuclear development today is regulation. Many of the rules governing nuclear were built around older reactor designs and do not reflect the technical reality of the advanced systems being developed today.  There are signs of progress. The NRC has moved toward 18-month review milestones for new reactor licenses and construction permits. TerraPower’s Kemmerer 1 construction permit, originally scheduled for a 27-month review, received its final safety evaluation in 18 months. Now we need to make that speed and predictability the norm. The NRC should continue moving toward risk-informed regulation with predictable review timelines appropriate to advanced technologies. Congress should ensure the bipartisan ADVANCE Act, signed into law in July 2024, is fully implemented by providing the resources, oversight, and direction needed to make its reforms real. That includes completing work on efficient license reviews, creating an expedited process for qualifying new reactor applications, finalizing lower fees for advanced-reactor applicants, and developing clear frameworks for microreactors, fusion machines, advanced fuels, and environmental reviews. The NRC will also need the technical staff and budget flexibility to do this work effectively. The law provides the direction; the remaining challenge is turning it into rules, guidance and review practices that developers can rely on. DOE can help technologies prove themselves before commercial deployment. Its Reactor Pilot Program recently enabled Valar Atomics to achieve criticality with an advanced reactor in Utah — the first DOE-authorized reactor built outside a national laboratory. events.title: Anthropic says its IPO could herald the end of the world as we know it
events.summary: Anthropic's IPO prospectus leaked this week, and boy was it filled with interesting details. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle on this page, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or YouTube. You can also subscribe on those platforms to be notified when a new episode goes live For starters there's the fact a third of it is all about existential AI risks, then there's the fact that, despite some impressive revenue growth the company still has yet to turn a profit. Combine that with massive capex predictions, and you have an IPO with massive valuation, yet a long, hard road toward anything resembling earnings. Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, El Reg editor in chief Matt Rosoff, and enterprise IT reporter Lindsay Clark on this week's episode of The Kettle where they discuss the revelations, what they mean for the state of the AI industry, and just how much distraction from its actual problems Anthropic can eke out by keeping that doomsday narrative front and center. With me to talk about the revelations are our editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff and enterprise IT reporter Lindsay Clark who brought us news of this whole mess. Thank you both for joining me. Lindsay Clark (00:36) Thank you. Matt Rosoff (00:37) Thanks for having us. Brandon (00:38) Yeah. So Lindsay, I know we didn't break this story. This was, I believe, a Financial Times exclusive, but what was reported about those IPO docs, in the story you wrote and just how apocalyptically optimistic is this whole thing? Lindsay Clark (00:53) Well we have this scenario where a company, Anthropic, is trying to sell itself by telling people that there's an existential risk to its technology, which I think is a bit of a weird way to go about it. Anthropic is still massively loss-making as far as we know. Brandon (01:22) There was what, I think you said, $8 billion loss on $4.6 billion of [revenue] or something? Lindsay Clark (01:28) That's right, and it says it plans to spend $500 billion or so on cloud computing over the next few years. So I don't know what you make of those numbers, but it's hard to get them to add up in my head. Brandon (01:40) I mean it's interesting just how it's still not a profitable company. But Matt and I were discussing earlier, I was saying that I think it's interesting that Anthropic is pushed ahead with this IPO despite OpenAI pausing it, because I feel like Anthropic has long had this reputation as sort of being the more safety-conscious, the more conservative AI company. But here they are with OpenAI kind of saying, Well, we're gonna pump the brakes on our IPO until we can make sure our models are safe, but Anthropic is plowing ahead. And Matt, you had an interesting take on that and it was more to the financial end, right? So what were you saying to me about that earlier? Matt Rosoff (02:21) I think that if you probably were to look at OpenAI's numbers, they would be even worse than Anthropic's. And I can't overstate based on the leaked prospectus information that we've seen. It seems as if the more money they earn, the more they have to spend. So the margins seem pretty bad. Now there was a report that they had actually turned profitable on an adjusted basis [in] Q2 this year, but that's if you strip out all of the training costs. So I guess if it's just inference alone, without the training costs and without certain other costs, they have decent margins. So maybe there is a path to profitability. Now it looks as if their operating loss last year was almost double their revenue. So if their revenue continues to increase at the rate that it is, which is, it seems like it's going up 4x, 12x per year, something like that, depending on the period you're looking at. If they can't get the expenses under control, the business doesn't seem to make a whole lot of sense. Nonetheless, I think they are growing faster because they were earlier to enterprise and they have become more essential to more companies than OpenAI did. And I think OpenAI is still sort of adjusting its business model and maybe not growing at quite the same rate. So that's my suspicion is that those numbers would look even worse. Brandon (04:01) Yeah, so the safety argument is probably just some spackle slapped on top of the bad financials to try to kinda hide it, I guess. If what you're saying is correct. Matt Rosoff (04:12) That's my speculation. It doesn't seem to make a whole lot of sense to say, well, we're so worried about this amazing thing that we've built that we don't want to show you our books and we're not gonna go public yet until we have that all figured out. That seems like a strange argument to make. Brandon (04:31) Yeah, I would have to agree with that. So speaking of economic impact, Lindsay, you were talking a bit more in your story about some of the broader sort of economic scope of the AI industry. And I'm curious, could you go more into some of the numbers you discussed in your story? Lindsay Clark (04:51) Yeah, sure. So it was a few months ago, I think in August, ING. events.title: The AI industry ‘hates crypto people’—but they may need them all the same
events.summary: Tricia Wang spends a lot of time in the Bay Area. A longtime veteran of the region’s tech scene, she has noticed that those who work in the ascendant artificial intelligence sector have strong views—including on crypto. According to Wang, “AI people hate crypto people. I can’t explain how much they hate crypto people. If the word ‘blockchain’ or ‘crypto’ is mentioned, they think you’re a total loser.” Harsh words! Still, the AI crowd’s antipathy is perhaps understandable given the barrage of scams that have long dogged the crypto world—not to mention the cringe behavior of many of its leaders. Still, the haters may want to soften their views, if only because the blockchain technology on which crypto is built may offer solutions to some real problems in the AI world. That’s the view of Wang, who is well versed in crypto, and currently leads an organization called the Advanced AI Society . The group’s goal is to build “proof of control” infrastructure that can limit the mischief of marauding agents like the ones at OpenAI that recently escaped their sandbox in order to plunder third-party sites. Until recently, experts proposed “human-in-the-loop” as the key to preventing such incidents. Wang, though, says this is not practical as AI scales to trillions of transactions, and makes the case that machine-to-machine monitoring is the only viable option. But whose machines will carry out that monitoring? According to Wang, the prevailing solutions are typically limited to “trust me, bro”—where we rely on hyperscalers like OpenAI and Anthropic to contain their agents—or “trust those bros,” where a third party like METR keeps tabs on what agents are doing. What she and the Advanced AI Society propose instead is to rely on decentralized tools that require agents to verify they are authorized to carry out whatever they are undertaking. The group describes this process, which also ensures agents can’t falsify their own logs, as “proof of control.” This sort of verification can be carried out at scale, Wang says, in part by relying on technology developed by the crypto industry such as distributed ledgers and zero-knowledge proofs. It may be tempting for some—especially AI-native crypto haters—to dismiss this as a self-serving solution proposed by a group whose ranks include numerous blockchain figures, including former CFTC Chair Chris “Crypto Dad” Giancarlo and one-time crypto evangelist Sheila Warren. The Advanced AI Society, however, appears to be attracting some big-name support outside of the crypto world. Its advisory board includes OG cryptographer Bruce Schneier and tech theorist Clay Shirky—neither of whom has a track record of attaching their name to fly-by-night projects. And most notably, the first version of the group’s proof-of-control standard is being housed by the Linux Foundation, whose decades of open-source advocacy have made it a pillar of the tech world. I confess that pronouncing the optimal technical and regulatory solution for rogue AI agents is above my pay grade. But I am confident in saying blockchain developers have a proven track record of producing decentralized and battle-hardened technology—most notably Bitcoin—and that the AI world shouldn’t be too quick in writing them off. Jeff John Roberts jeff.roberts@fortune.com @jeffjohnroberts This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: In Russia-occupied Oleshky, Ukrainians face hunger, drones and landmines
events.summary: Ukrainians suffering from food shortages are turning to weeds for sustenance in a town where bodies are reportedly eaten by dogs. Kyiv, Ukraine – On the day of her 41st wedding anniversary, Vera Gulyaeva recalled her husband’s life and death. In March, a Russian drone plunged into a bread line in the southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky, killing several people and wounding Serhiy Gulyaev, a retired 63-year-old driver. list 1 of 4 Row between Ukraine, South Korea mounts over North Korean POWs list 2 of 4 Ukraine calls for tighter sanctions as Russian attacks spark Kyiv gridlock list 3 of 4 Russia’s ‘new doctrine’ targets civilian sites in Ukraine, Zelenskyy says list 4 of 4 Ukraine ready for US-backed talks with Russia: Zelenskyy The town in the Kherson region had already been occupied for more than four years, and its 2,000 remaining residents spent the last two and a half years without electricity, running water, natural gas or healthcare. The Gulyaevs, who had met at a friends’ wedding in 1985, lived in a small house they had built. They were reluctant to leave even after their children fled to Kyiv-controlled areas. They had an orchid, a vegetable patch, five hens, a water well and a power generator that ran on the overpriced gas they occasionally bought from middlemen. “I almost never left the house,” Gulyaeva, a stately 64-year-old retired schoolteacher told Al Jazeera. “The husband occasionally went out to buy bread.” The bread-line attack left him with deep cranial wounds. She tried to get him to a hospital 80km (50 miles) away in the city of Skadovsk but failed as the ambulance ran over a landmine on the road. Days later, a second attempt worked – but Gulyaev died in the hospital. She recovered his remains, had them cremated and returned home with his ashes. Now, she lives in western Ukraine with her daughter-in-law and two grandchildren while her son fights Russian forces. Gulyaeva left behind all her family photos, friends and neighbours – several of whom have since died. “People ate all of the food they’d stashed. People are starving,” Gulyaeva said of the food shortage stalking the town. After four decades of teaching in the elementary school she had attended as a child, she still cannot fathom “how people can kill other people”. Some residents survive on what they have farmed, stashed or found in abandoned apartments or houses. Others try to reach the nearest functioning grocery shop in the neighbouring village of Radensk, 20km (12.4 miles) away, to buy food. A resident who fled the town but remains in contact with some residents told Al Jazeera that people have been killed by Russian drones or landmines. The bodies left out in the open are eaten by feral dogs. On Thursday alone, there were four casualties. As they tried to get to Radensk, two people were killed and two were injured and brought back on a wheelbarrow and a bike. “The choice that Russia leaves every day to civilian residents – stay and starve to death, leave and risk getting blown on a landmine,” Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, wrote on Telegram on Saturday. European officials said the situation in Oleshky proves that Kyiv should not give in to Moscow’s demands to cede its land. “When someone says: ‘Why don’t they just give up these territories?’ it sounds so simple. Right? But in reality, this is about the people who will suffer on those territories,” European Union High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said on September 28. Moscow, which has denied targeting civilians throughout the war, has acknowledged the humanitarian disaster but blamed Kyiv. “There are, indeed, problems with delivering food and medical drugs [because] the Kyiv regime literally does everything to thwart these deliveries,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed on September 20. “Drones always hover in the air, killing people.” Pro-Russian figures in occupied areas support his claims. “Those who wanted to leave have left. No one is being held here,” an anonymous pro-Russian woman who runs a Telegram channel on life in Oleshky wrote on September 28. “Unfortunately, locals are afraid to speak on camera” because they have relatives on the Ukrainian side, she claimed. “The elderly live under Ukrainian shelling but are afraid to talk.” Her claims are a far cry from what Ukrainian officials say. Most Oleshky residents eat once a day, according to Tetiana Khasanenko, Oleshky’s mayor, who fled to the Kyiv-controlled side but maintains constant contact with the remaining residents. Some have found old, dried macaroni to sustain themselves. Some eat whatever they manage to grow next to their houses. And some resort to common purslane – a watery weed that contains next to no protein and can be eaten raw. “There’s no flour, no meat, no oil, no sugar, no salt,” Hasanenko told Al Jazeera. “There’s nothing.” She accused Russia of using the residents as human shields.

events.title: Students continue to protest in France as hundreds of schools close
events.summary: Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday about 500 schools likely to be fully or partially closed on Monday. Hundreds of high schools in France are closed as student protests continue against rundown schools and teacher shortages. Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon told CNews television on Monday that the priority was to “restore order”. list 1 of 3 What’s behind French student protests that turned violent? list 2 of 3 School protests spread as fires, blockades deepen unrest in France list 3 of 3 What’s behind France’s school protests? Earlier, National Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday evening, of the 3,700 schools, 400 to 500 were likely to be closed fully or partially on Monday. Geffray said 24 schools had been burned or ransacked, while 78 teaching staff had been injured since the beginning of the protests. Nationwide demonstrations erupted at the end of last month at a high school in a Parisian suburb over teacher shortages, before spreading nationwide. Reporting from a high school in Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said students had set up a barricade in front of the building’s entrance using dustbins and fences. “We’ve been talking to many of the students who have come out here, and what they say is that they are here to have their demands heard by the government. They say they are fed up with teacher shortages and often don’t have teachers for subjects like maths and English,” she said. “They also tell us that they’re here to demonstrate to show solidarity with other high school students who are in perhaps poorer areas in France with less adequate facilities or in France’s overseas territories. They say all young people should have an equal right to education,” Butler added. French news channel BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille, northern France, tear gas being used in Toulouse in the southwest and of a fire being set alight as people tried to break into a school in central Paris. Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalised Lycee Vauquelin in Paris’s 13th district, said a “very determined” group wearing hoods and masks attacked her school. While police and firefighters quickly put out the fire and the school was evacuated, suspending classes, Zerbib said it was “very violent and happened very quickly”, adding that the attack lasted 15-20 minutes. Since September 28, about 5,000 people, mostly teenagers, have been arrested across the country and dozens have been injured. French newspaper La Voix du Nord reported on Monday that a teenager lost a hand after picking up a police stun grenade. Teachers and members of the public have also been attacked, while estimated costs of property damage are in the tens of millions of euros. Student unions have called for a national day of demonstration on Tuesday.

events.title: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta execs set to testify at NYC Council hearing on AI risks
events.summary: Senior leaders from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta are slated to testify under oath during a New York City Council hearing. The companies will be asked to explain the risks posed by AI and to weigh in on potential legislative solutions, New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin said in a release. Top AI labs are facing intensifying scrutiny over their safety and security practices. Senior leaders from Anthropic , OpenAI, Google and Meta are slated to testify under oath during a New York City Council hearing about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence on Monday, following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models. The testimony will take place during a rare "Council Committee of the Whole" hearing, which means that all 51 members are expected to attend, according to a release from New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin. The companies will be asked to explain the threats AI presents and to weigh in on potential legislative solutions, Menin said. The session is scheduled to begin at 11 a.m. ET, according to the agenda for the meeting posted online. Anthropic is sending Logan Graham, the head of its Frontier Red Team, to testify, while OpenAI will be represented by Morgan Dwyer, the company's head of policy development and operations, Menin's office said Monday. Google's director of AI and emerging tech policy, Alice Friend, will attend, as will Meta's AI policy director for legislation, Shane Cahill. Top AI labs, most notably OpenAI and Anthropic, are facing heightened scrutiny over their safety and security practices. Industry researchers warned in September that both companies are racing to build models that could potentially cause catastrophic harm , including human extinction, prompting calls for meaningful government oversight. One researcher, Jacob Coxon, quit his job at Anthropic and set off a firestorm on social media by claiming that the company, and OpenAI , are " gambling with our lives ." Coxon will be at the hearing on Monday, CNBC confirmed, as will Alex Turner, a former Google DeepMind research scientist and Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher. Concerns began swirling over the summer after OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face . Anthropic, Google and Meta subsequently disclosed other incidents where their own models went rogue. "Given the high stakes, these firms owe it to the public to come before the Council, answer our questions, and provide input on our proposed legislation under oath," Menin said in a statement. While Meta confirmed it would participate in the hearing late last month, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google only agreed to appear after the council threatened to subpoena them, Menin said. The city issued a subpoena to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk last week, requiring that he or another representative of the company's AI unit, SpaceXAI, testify. Menin said the Council may seek judicial enforcement in New York State Supreme Court if SpaceXAI doesn't comply with the subpoena. events.title: Qatar’s luxury market attracts 34,000 visitors
events.summary: Many Gulf events have been postponed or canceled because of the war, but Qatar’s annual bonanza of bling was lively last week. More than 34,000 people attended the six-day Doha Jewellery & Watches Exhibition, and many — unlike this reporter — weren’t lookie-loos. Doha’s exhibition center was transformed into a gallery of coveted gems and timepieces, with the cars at the valet reflecting the wealth of the clientele inside. Shoppers were reluctant to talk, but several said they attend every year because exhibitors (there were more than 50 representing 500 brands) bring in inventory that isn’t usually available in Qatar. One jeweler said sales in a single week were like Valentine’s Day, Mother’s Day, and Christmas all rolled into one. For those seeking iced-out Pateks, or more modest trappings, the exhibition returns in late April. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Abu Dhabi's XRG invests in Argentina's LNG expansion
events.summary: Abu Dhabi’s XRG is backing Argentina’s bid to become a major liquefied natural gas exporter. ADNOC’s international arm agreed in June to take a 32% stake in three Argentine gas blocks . They will feed the country’s first LNG export terminal, designed to produce 12 million tons a year in its initial phase. “ No country or company secures its energy future alone ,” Executive Chairman Sultan Al Jaber said in Paris last week. At a time when exports from their home markets have been severely constrained, such international investments are only increasing in importance, helping Gulf producers meet customer demand and benefit from higher prices. This year, QatarEnergy took a stake in Golden Pass LNG in Texas, Saudi Aramco acquired an interest in the nearby Port Arthur LNG terminal, and XRG has bought into LNG projects in Texas and Mozambique. — Ed Clowes
