events.title: Gulf SWFs on track for major investments despite war
events.summary: Gulf sovereign wealth funds are on track for one of their most active years of dealmaking ever, even as war disrupts businesses and economic growth. Regional funds are forecast to invest $136 billion by year-end , making 2026 their second-busiest on record, according to consultancy Global SWF. Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala leads with $26.2 billion invested so far this year. Nearly half of Gulf sovereign fund investment went to the US, showing that American assets remain attractive despite the debate about the future of Gulf states’ relationship with their main strategic ally. Gulf funds are major backers of the $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Kuwait’s and Qatar’s funds may also be called on to transfer money to their government budgets to help prop up state finances, hit by the decline in oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, Global SWF said. That won’t stop the funds from expanding rapidly in coming years, with Gulf funds set to control $8.8 trillion by 2030, up from $6.1 trillion. — Matthew Martin

events.title: Fewer Americans are getting help buying groceries from SNAP benefits as states grapple with the program’s cascade of changes
events.summary: As of Oct. 1, 2026, states must pay more to run SNAP. AP Photo/Allison Dinner The number of people enrolled in the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program is falling fast. The program formerly known as food stamps helped roughly 42 million Americans put food on the table in 2025. As of June 2026, the most recent data available, the number of people enrolled in the program in the whole country had declined by almost 13% to 36.4 million . Among those no longer getting benefits are an estimated 1.5 million children . What explains this decline? President Donald Trump says a strong economy has driven down demand for the program. It’s possible that some people have left the program because their incomes rose. But the enrollment decline has a lot to do with the big tax-and-spending package the president signed into law in July 2025 . States are struggling to keep up For example, the law caused some immigrants residing legally in the country, such as refugees and those seeking asylum, to no longer be eligible for SNAP benefits. In addition, more people enrolled in SNAP now may only get up to three months of benefits if they don’t work, engage in training programs or volunteer at least 80 hours a month. These work requirements previously applied only to adults up to the age of 54; that cutoff is rising to 64. Another change is that parents of older children ages 14-17 are now expected to meet these work requirements . All states are phasing in these restrictions, but the number of people getting SNAP benefits is falling much faster in some states than others. That includes Arizona, where enrollment has fallen by almost half , along with Louisiana and Illinois , where it’s down by about one-fifth. And now, states must pay more to run SNAP , which is federally funded but state-administered. In my research on the history of SNAP, I’ve found that changes in the way states run their programs have a big impact on who can get help. States are struggling to adapt to new federal policies. As additional changes roll out, more families may lose access to SNAP. Covering more of the administrative costs As of Oct. 1, 2026, states have to pay 75% of all administrative costs, which include paying staff who manage the enrollment process and maintaining the program’s computer systems. Previously, states paid 50% of those costs. The federal government estimates that states and local governments will pay roughly US$17 billion more in administrative costs over the next five years. In the 2027 fiscal year, which began on Oct. 1, California – with the largest population of any state – will be responsible for paying roughly $670 million more to run the program. Wyoming, with the smallest number of residents, will pay about $3 million more . Costs will be shifted to local governments in nine of the 10 states where SNAP is administered by counties. Looming changes tied to ‘payment error rates’ State agencies and some state legislatures are imposing stricter rules and requiring applicants to provide more paperwork documenting their income, expenses and the number of people in their household. Caseworkers in states such as Arizona have reportedly been overwhelmed with the paperwork. Those seeking help have spent hours trying to get through on phone lines and have faced monthslong delays. States are taking these steps to get ready for another change that will roll out in October 2027. At that point, many states will also have to cover up to 15% of the costs of benefits for the first time since the program began in the 1960s. This cost is much larger than the administrative costs and could be staggering for many states . How much a state pays will be based on its “payment error rate.” These error rates measure how much in benefits are paid above or below what families are actually entitled to based on their household size, income and expenses. It is calculated based on an in-depth review of a small sample of a state’s benefits payments each year. These inaccurate payments are generally a result of mistakes on the part of the applicant or their caseworker – they rarely are the result of fraud. The payment error rate includes benefits paid to ineligible participants. It does not include payments never made to applicants who were eligible for benefits but wrongly denied them or incorrectly dropped from the program. Supporters of SNAP argue that this makes states err on the side of denying benefits. Range of rates States with an error rate less than 6% won’t face new costs for benefits. But only nine states had rates that low in 2025. States with an error rate between 6% and 8% will be responsible for 5% of the costs of their residents’ SNAP benefits. States with an error rate between 8% and 10% will have to cover 10%. States with error rates over 10% will have to cover 15%. There’s a weird twist: If a state has an error rate over 13.32% , it won’t have to pay part of the cost of residents’ SNAP benefits for up to two years as they would have had it been in the 6% to 13.32% range. Farm bill politics could play a role To reduce their error rates, states need to invest in more staff, training, technology and better application and verification procedures. But states had little time to do all that. The states’ share of costs slated to kick in as of October 2027 is based on the error rates in the fiscal year that ended in September 2026. Organizations representing state and local governments and social workers are pushing for an across-the board two-year delay. What’s more, legislation known as the “ farm bill ,” which sets policies for agriculture, conservation and food-related assistance like SNAP, is now ensnared in the dispute. Democrats, whose support is needed to pass the legislation in the Senate, would like to see most of the new SNAP changes repealed. Congress aims to pass a farm bill roughly every five years, but the most recent one, which was finalized in 2018, has expired . Short of rolling back all the SNAP policy changes, many Democrats have refused to vote for the farm bill unless it includes a two-year delay for all states in shouldering part of the cost of SNAP benefits. If the Democratic Party holds a majority in one or both chambers of Congress after the 2026 midterm elections, their leverage could increase in these negotiations. The Republican Party’s version of the farm bill now pending in the Senate includes a one-year delay in the benefits-funding changes. But it would increase the states’ burden even more than the policy planned for October 2027. That’s a nonstarter for Democrats. What states can do about all this Meanwhile, there are many signs that a large share of the people who have lost their SNAP benefits are struggling to feed their families. More people, for example, are seeking help from food pantries and banks , which fear they will not be able to keep up with growing demand. It’s hard to predict what might happen next. events.title: Why it’s more important than ever to jump-start entrepreneurial careers from the college classroom
events.summary: By teaching entrepreneurship, colleges can better prepare students for a fast-changing job market and technological disruption. Igor Golovniov/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Recent college graduates are facing a job market that’s only getting tougher. Their unemployment rate hit 5.7% , compared to 4.1% for all workers, in June 2026. That may not sound like much, but it’s one of the worst rates in the past 20 years. Meanwhile, roughly 4 in 10 graduates are underemployed, which means they work in jobs that typically don’t require a college degree. That’s the highest rate since the COVID-19 pandemic. As an educator for more than 25 years, I see the growing anxiety every day. In a change from years past, parents are now peppering me with questions: How can their kids leverage their college education in such a fast-changing world? Will they learn skills in school that will soon be antiquated once they graduate? What’s essential to understand is that technology adoption cycles have accelerated at a breathtaking rate over the past few years. While the telephone and television took decades to reach 100 million users, ChatGPT and TikTok attained that threshold in a matter of months. Colleges need to adapt their curricula accordingly. Georgia Tech, where I teach engineering, has focused on pushing entrepreneurship across our campus since 2014. We’re seeing encouraging signs from our follow-ups with graduating students that it’s helping their early careers. I believe one of the best ways to adjust to these changes is to embed entrepreneurial experiences throughout college. Such hands-on learning, in turn, develops versatile, adaptable talent, producing graduates who can pivot across jobs as industries, technologies and opportunities evolve. And this needn’t be confined to business students – young people in all majors can benefit. 3 core lessons The educational value of entrepreneurship isn’t principally that every student will be able to start a company. It’s that entrepreneurial experiences develop the capabilities students need in a rapidly changing economy – and ultimately build more resilient careers. Here are some ways educators can future-proof the college experience, based on what I’ve learned and applied at Georgia Tech. Making adaptability a core skill: Students need to learn how to be nimble . This means recognizing important changes in the landscape, identifying new problems and the opportunities they create, articulating a response and mobilizing the necessary resources. Ultimately, this approach will help students be prepared for the real world. To impart these lessons, I believe colleges should provide hands-on opportunities to help students learn through experience before they enter the workforce. For example, they could encourage students to develop a business venture idea that addresses a newly created opportunity in the marketplace through accelerators, or short-term “boot camps” for young companies to help them grown quickly. One example is Greptile, a startup that came out of the Georgia Tech CREATE-X accelerator . The goal isn’t that a startup will be launched – that depends on several factors coming together – but that the student gains the experience to understand a changing landscape. Understanding customer value: Colleges can also teach students how to think about customer value – namely, why the solution they’re working on matters to the consumers buying it. This isn’t just for business students. All students can gain from learning to think about the customers or clients they will deal with in their careers. In fact, students from 38 majors have participated in the entrepreneurship programs at Georgia Tech . Through on-the-ground experience that requires them to find customers, students can learn about the real-world impact of the products and services they create. When students spend hundreds of hours selling their young startup to the outside world, they learn to understand value at a deep level. Emphasizing fundamentals: Fundamental skills are key because they outlast the technology underpinning the business. In fact, the more quickly specific technologies change, the more important a strong grounding in fundamentals becomes. This means it’s a smarter investment to offer, say, a fundamental course on wireless networking or deep learning concepts over a course that teaches specific wireless technologies or emphasizes the use of a specific model. A strong foundation gives students the tools to adapt to technologies that may not yet exist when they graduate. Students in startup training have to deal with uncertainty, resource constraints and customer interaction, all of which will make them more nimble in their careers. David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images The many paths toward entrepreneurship Another great advantage of entrepreneurial experiences is that they force students to deal with uncertainty, recognize opportunities, work around resource constraints and learn how to create value. But other strategies work as well. A few examples are project-based learning, internships and interdisciplinary capstone classes that let students pursue independent research projects as their final course. That said, entrepreneurial experiences provide an unusually concentrated and effective environment that requires students to solve problems, engage with customers and mobilize resources they don’t directly control – all while getting real-world feedback. More and more universities and colleges understand this point and have ramped up support for entrepreneurial activity for their students, such as Cornell and the University of Washington . At Georgia Tech, we have a playbook that we have developed through our experiences that follows the following principles: Embed entrepreneurship into the curriculum: One simple way for colleges to incorporate entrepreneurial experiences into their coursework is to offer an entrepreneurship minor to all students, regardless of major. This would offer the opportunity to a broader range of students who otherwise might miss out. Build a pathway to business creation: Entrepreneurial education is most effective when it leads to something bigger. To that end, many colleges are now offering a startup accelerator, including MIT , Rice University and the University of Texas . But more is needed: A startup pathway that caters to students at all stages can substantially broaden participation and impact, regardless of whether a business results. At Georgia Tech, we have a learn/make/launch/scale pathway that offers programs and resources for learning about entrepreneurship, building solutions, launching new ventures and eventually scaling them. Offer real venture experience: A successful model combines theoretical learning with hands-on experience. The confidence that students gain through that experience may be at least as important an educational outcome as the viability of the startups they launch.

events.title: Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election
events.summary: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for November on Monday, as analysts said he may be betting on last week's parliamentary rejection of his property sector reforms to mobilize public anger. Sánchez has clashed with U.S. President Donald Trump this year after he criticized the White House's war with Iran, with Trump slamming Spain's NATO spending. Polling suggests a right-wing coalition could take power in Spain, raising key questions for investors over the European country's position on trade with the U.S. and China. Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for Nov. 29 on Monday after parliament rejected measures intended to quell public anger and mass protests over the country's housing crisis. Sánchez garnered both fans and foes on the international stage after he emerged as Europe's most vocal critic of U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East earlier this year. To some, his warning of "repeating the mistakes of the past" and refusal to be "complicit in something that is bad for the world" was an example of Europe standing up to a hawkish administration regardless of potential reprisal. Others — not least U.S. President Donald Trump — slammed Sánchez and his administration, accusing Spain of putting "American lives at risk" and failing to pull its weight on NATO spending . Trump threatened to cut off Spanish trade and diplomatic relations. Sánchez — also a fierce critic of Israel's war in Gaza — continued to take aim at the White House, saying of a now-defunct U.S.-Iran ceasefire that he would "not applaud those who set the world on fire just because they show up with a bucket." But such geopolitical maneuvering is far from the agenda this month in Spain. Public debate, as elsewhere in Europe, is increasingly defined by discontent over housing, wages and the cost of living. Immigration is also a growing political flashpoint, with the Spanish government still grappling with the aftermath of the arrival of tens of thousands of migrants into the North African enclave of Ceuta in July. On headline figures alone, Spain's economy has bounced back strongly since the pandemic and continues to outpace the euro area average, with growth coming in at 0.7% in the second quarter this year. Tourism is booming, investor interest in its assets has been robust and the jobs market is strong . Yet tens of thousands of people took to the streets over the weekend in a culmination of protests that have swept up all sides of the political spectrum, from left-wing housing campaigners who remain camped out in Madrid to far-right activists reported to have performed Nazi salutes . Public discontent and calls for a general strike have mounted following the September eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her home of 70 years. News of the dramatic event brought longstanding complaints about unaffordable rent increases and a lack of housing stock — especially in tourist hotspots — to a head. Sánchez, leader of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party, has served as prime minister since 2018. He currently leads a fragile left-wing coalition formed in November 2023 reliant on numerous smaller, regional parties, which has made it difficult for him to pass reforms despite his reputation for political savvy. A parliamentary deadlock has left the country unable to pass a budget for more than three years . Sánchez's popularity has been further dented this year by a probe into alleged misuse of funds by the Socialist Party and a corruption investigation into Sánchez's ally, former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero . Zapatero denies wrongdoing. In a bid to address the housing protests, Sánchez last week attempted to hurriedly pass measures to protect renters, including the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, tax increases for apartments intended for tourist rents, a two-year extension on rental leases with expiry before 2028, and a restriction purchases of residential properties by investment firms. The bills were voted down following opposition by parties including the center-right People's Party, the far-right Vox party, and pro-independence Together for Catalonia, further stoking public anger. With a fresh parliamentary election required to be held before August 2027, analysts had been anticipating a vote would be called soon, Carsten Nickel, managing director of consultancy Consello, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday. "Clearly with this housing market related issue, [Sánchez] really sees this as an opportunity now — doesn't mean he's going to win it — but to rally the center-left vote on this typically center-left topic, and that's a better backdrop than say corruption allegations or regional election losses," Nickel said.

events.title: The Download: AI’s popularity paradox and EmTech Future 2026
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. People really hate AI, so why can’t they get enough? —Will Douglas Heaven Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM designed to come up with a wide variety of responses . He said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.” My reply? “I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist.” It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype, steered by zealots, inescapable —and I’m far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now. Public sentiment is souring fast, with more people saying AI will have a negative impact than a positive one. At the same time, AI use is skyrocketing. So why do people hate AI but keep coming back for more? Here’s my theory . To stay up-to-date with the latest in AI, sign up to get The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter, in your inbox every Monday. EmTech Future 2026: when AI meets everything Last week, EmTech Future 2026 explored some of the biggest questions shaping technology right now: how AI is changing industries, where quantum is heading, what new energy systems could make possible, and how robotics are evolving. It also looked at what happens when these technologies start to converge. The full program is now available on demand. And today, we’re releasing two sessions exclusively to subscribers: a chat with Google Research’s Yossi Matias on how AI is reshaping biology, infrastructure, manufacturing and science, and a special panel with MIT Technology Review editors that takes you inside our newsroom. events.title: Why airfares could rise even more, but airline profits won't
events.summary: U.S. airfares rose 23.4% in August from a year earlier, while Thanksgiving and Christmas fares are also sharply higher. Elevated, volatile jet fuel costs and constrained capacity are giving airlines more reason to protect higher ticket prices. Higher fuel expense is offsetting revenue gains, prompting analysts and carriers to cut or reassess profit expectations. Volatile fuel prices and resilient travel demand are threatening to keep airfare high this year. Airline profits will be harder to come by. The Iran war that began at the end of February sent fuel prices to multi-year if not record highs, including for diesel, gasoline and jet fuel, airlines' biggest expense after labor. Supply scares with the Strait of Hormuz disruptions lasting most of this year and high demand have sent jet fuel prices and other distilled products up more than crude oil. Airline executives aren't expecting much relief in fuel costs anytime soon, or a drop in travel demand. "You can't run the business on the hope that the Strait of Hormuz is going to open at a certain time," Qantas Airways CEO Vanessa Hudson told CNBC in an interview late last month. The Australian airline operates some of the world's longest flights and is planning even longer ones for next year and 2028, starting routes between London and Sydney and New York and Sydney. "There's a backdrop of resilient demand in in this environment. We're making sure that we've got our capacity settings right," she said. Airlines have been passing higher fuel costs along to consumers by raising fares, adding fuel surcharges or increasing their checked baggage fees . The United States' on-again-off-again truce talks with Iran since the spring have kept fuel prices volatile, but airlines are holding onto those fare gains as customers continue to book. Carriers have also raced to add more luxurious seats on board to capitalize on demand for pricier and roomier offerings, sometimes taking down the number of standard coach seats to do so. Slightly fewer people are flying this year compared with last, but demand overall remains strong, even with higher ticket prices. Security screenings at U.S. airports were down 1% this year through Sept. 20 compared with the same period of 2025, according to a Sept. 23 Bernstein note. Still, the latest U.S. inflation read showed airfare rose 23.4% in August from a year earlier. Holiday travel could be up even more. As of Sept. 24, fare-tracking platform Hopper said domestic, round-trip tickets were going for $402 over Thanksgiving, up 31% from last year. U.S. Christmas fares, meanwhile, are up 23% at $452 a round-trip. Those holiday visits are essential to many families, said Hopper economist Hayley Berg, so a lot of flyers might not like the fare but book it anyway. Berg said many customers have been locking in their Thanksgiving and Christmas flights earlier than usual. While business travel demand has been strong in recent months and off-peak trips are no longer a savvy traveler's secret, customers' focus on those key holiday trips this year could mean there are deals in the interim, Berg said. "To me, that signals that they're already thinking about end of year travel and not thinking about any of those filler trips, fall shoulder-season trips," she said. Airline revenue surges, profit forecast dims Carriers are forecasting double-digit revenue growth for the third quarter as customers spend more. That's even with slightly fewer people flying. "I've never seen in my career, outside of recovery after maybe the pandemic or 9/11 ... seen a revenue environment in terms of year-over-year improvement," American Airlines CEO Robert Isom said at a Morgan Stanley investor conference last month. The carrier has been revamping its cabins to add more premium seats and other changes to catch up to rivals. But despite the higher fares, Wall Street analysts have cut their profit estimates for U.S. carriers since another hike in jet fuel in the summer. American in July said it expects to lose between 10 and 70 cents a share, on an adjusted basis, for the third quarter and cut its profit outlook for 2026. Investors and anyone looking to buy a plane ticket in the next few months will get an updated view of what's to come when airline earnings season kicks off on Friday with Delta Air Lines . The most profitable U.S. carrier, which also stands to benefit from its owned refinery, will report third-quarter results and will give a fresh outlook for the end of the year. Wall Street's focus will be on the fourth quarter and beyond. Airlines are likely to lower their earnings outlooks for that quarter, said Savanthi Syth, airline analyst at Raymond James. She said carriers aren't likely to make as many broad-based fare increases now, but if jet fuel remains in the $4 to $4.50 a gallon range, they're likely to cut more flights, which can end up raising fares with customers facing fewer seats to choose from.

events.title: Booking Holdings spends nearly $9 billion a year to reach travelers. Its CFO explains how AI is changing trip planning
events.summary: Good morning. The biggest impact of AI on travel may happen before the traveler ever checks into a hotel or boards a plane. At the Fortune AIQ Summit on Oct. 1, I interviewed Ewout Steenbergen, EVP and CFO of Booking Holdings ( No. 169 on the Fortune 500), which owns and operates several major online travel brands, including Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, KAYAK, OpenTable, and Rentalcars.com. Steenbergen described a future in which AI makes travel planning more seamless, personalized, and proactive. That could mean suggesting an indoor visit to the Louvre when rain threatens a Paris itinerary, automatically moving a restaurant reservation after a delayed flight, or recommending an activity based on a traveler’s preferences and open time. The prize is not simply a better chatbot. It is what Booking calls a “connected trip”: an integrated experience that ties together flights, hotels, restaurants, rental cars, and activities. And, in doing so, potentially creates more loyalty, trust, and frequency of engagement. From AI pilots to unit economics For finance leaders, Steenbergen’s comments offered a practical framework for judging AI investments. His message: Move past isolated pilots, but keep a close eye on unit economics. Booking spends roughly $8 billion to $9 billion annually on paid customer-acquisition channels, including search, social, and metasearch platforms, Steenbergen said. About one-third of its consumer traffic comes through paid channels, while the other two-thirds comes directly to its platforms. As consumers turn to more AI tools and agents for discovery, he sees greater channel diversification as potentially positive for Booking’s unit economics. Early signals are encouraging. Customers using Booking’s AI tools are booking somewhat faster, converting at somewhat higher rates, and canceling less often, Steenbergen said, while cautioning that the data remains early stage. I asked him how he’s measuring the financial return on investment when it comes to AI. “I think in this area there isn’t a perfect answer,” he said. He continued, “I even think that the hyperscalers that spend hundreds of billions on the development of their large language models, they don’t really know what is going to be the ROI,” Steenbergen said. “They have maybe some assumptions and some hypotheses, but the whole point is, you don’t want to fall behind.” He argued that the biggest returns come not from layering AI onto existing processes, but from rebuilding processes end to end. In customer service, Booking has seen booking units grow at a high single-digit rate while total customer-service costs declined slightly, he said. Customer satisfaction increased at the same time, driving down average servicing cost per booking. In engineering, the company’s roughly 9,000 technologists have used AI tools to increase the number of merge requests put into production by about 30%, Steenbergen said. Crucially, that figure reflects code that has been tested and cleared quality controls—not merely generated. The CFO’s job, then, is to measure both sides of the ledger. Steenbergen said Booking monitors token and licensing costs and uses “effective model-cost routing,” reserving lower-cost or open-source models for simpler tasks and more expensive models for complex ones. One engineering metric combines human and AI costs: total IT cost per merge request. That is the more mature AI-finance question. Not whether a model costs more in isolation, but whether it lowers the all-in cost of producing a valuable outcome. Steenbergen is applying the technology personally, too. He has an “AI coach” and uses two AI agents: a “strategic thought partner” for board materials and strategic analysis, and a “critical equity research agent” to pressure-test earnings-call preparation. Watch the full video of my interview with Steenbergen at the Fortune AIQ Summit here . Sheryl   Estrada Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: CEOs are threatening to take their jobs and their billions elsewhere. That leverage has limits
events.summary: When a company brings thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in economic activity to a city or state, its CEO gains a powerful bargaining chip with the government. Knowing when to use that power requires the kind of judgment that increasingly defines the corner office, weighing political influence against the interests of employees, the needs of the business, and the company’s ties to the place it calls home. CEOs are increasingly making the economic stakes explicit , tying decisions about jobs and future investment to clashes over taxes, regulation, social policy, and corporate deals. Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison raised the prospect of leaving California amid the legal fight over the company’s Warner Bros. Discovery deal. Citadel founder Ken Griffin warned that future growth could favor Miami amid a clash with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Elon Musk moved the headquarters of SpaceX and X to Texas after criticizing a California law concerning transgender students. Corporate America has wielded this kind of influence for decades. In 1964, Coca-Cola used its economic clout in Atlanta to pressure the city’s business establishment to attend a dinner honoring Martin Luther King Jr. What has changed since then is CEOs’ growing willingness to make the stakes public, openly connecting jobs and investment to policymakers’ decisions. Still, a relocation threat only works if it’s credible. A company needs somewhere else to go and must be prepared to leave. Following through, however, can come at a steep cost. Companies rooted in industry clusters can be especially difficult to move. Hollywood’s century-old entertainment ecosystem, for example, cannot simply be recreated elsewhere. Relocation can also mean losing skilled employees unwilling to uproot their lives, along with institutional knowledge and employee trust. Governments have plenty at stake too. UC Berkeley economist Enrico Moretti estimates that every tech job lost can cost a community another four to five local jobs, giving elected officials a powerful incentive to keep major employers in place. The strategic challenge for CEOs is knowing the strength of the hand they are holding before playing it. Jobs and investment can provide formidable negotiating power, but putting them on the table can expose just how much a company depends on the people and places it is threatening to leave. Read the full magazine article in Fortune ’s October/November 2026 issue . Ruth Umoh ruth.umoh@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Hungary’s former foreign minister grilled over ties to China's BYD automaker while in office
events.summary: Péter Szijjártó, Hungary’s former foreign minister, is appearing before a parliamentary committee to answer questions about his dealings with Chinese automaker BYD while in office BUDAPEST, Hungary -- Hungary’s former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó appeared before a parliamentary committee on Monday to answer questions about his dealings with Chinese automaker BYD while still in office. He left politics in July to take up an executive position with the company. Szijjártó, who served as Hungary's foreign minister for 12 years under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán before an election defeat in April, announced in July that he would resign his seat in Hungary’s parliament to take the job at the world’s top electric carmaker . The announcement prompted accusations of a conflict of interest, and criticism of his central role in facilitating substantial government subsidies for the company while in office. In addition to securing the deal allowing BYD to open its first European factory near the southern Hungarian city of Szeged, Szijjártó also announced in 2025 that the company would locate its European headquarters and a research and development center in Budapest, and receive 20 billion forints ($63.7 million) in government assistance. Upon arriving at the closed-door National Security Committee hearing on Monday, Szijjártó told reporters that there had been “serious misunderstandings” related to BYD’s investment in Hungary. He made no mention of his new position at the company, which he earlier described as an “executive responsible for the group’s external relations and the development of new business lines.” “I consider it a great success that this factory came to Hungary,” Szijjártó said on Monday. “I would also like to point out that the proposed and awarded government subsidies for the construction of the BYD factory in Szeged have remained well within the framework of the usual subsidies for investments of this magnitude.” Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials US Marine arrested on suspicion of murder after 'brutal and heinous' death in Japan District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, told lawmakers in July that Szijjártó had helped BYD “with hundreds of billions (of forints) in public money, diplomatic support and state infrastructure,” and that an investigation would be launched to “examine all the decisions, negotiations and state commitments” made by Szijjártó related to the BYD investment. While in office working under Orbán, Szijjártó concluded numerous foreign investment deals with Chinese companies to open factories in Hungary, largely related to battery production for the electric vehicle industry. Orbán’s government hoped the investments would make Hungary a global hub of lithium-ion battery manufacturing, yet decreased demand and other market pressures have so far prevented those investments from paying high dividends. Since taking office in May, Magyar’s government has promised increased regulation and tighter oversight of the battery production sector following some workplace accidents and findings at several plants that showed contamination levels over legal limits. events.title: WMA members must call for release of detained Palestinian medics
events.summary: Members of the World Medical Association have a duty to uphold their commitment to the protection of healthcare workers everywhere. More than 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed during the genocide in Gaza. Israel has detained hundreds more without charges. Doctors, nurses and paramedics who stayed to treat the wounded have themselves become casualties of this war. When medical staff are killed, imprisoned or disappeared, it is not only they who pay the price. Patients lose the people they rely on to keep them alive. This is something delegates who gather in Rotterdam this week for the General Assembly of the World Medical Association (WMA) must remember. The fate of their Palestinian colleagues should be put on the table, not as a debating point, but as a test of whether the world’s governing body of medical ethics still means what it says. The WMA already recognised the seriousness of these issues last year by adopting a resolution on the protection of healthcare in conflict. That was an important step and a welcome reaffirmation of the principles of medical neutrality. The challenge now is to ensure this is followed by the commitment of every medical association to explicitly support it and to use its influence to pressure governments to act. If the WMA Assembly needs a single face for this file, it could be the one of Dr Hussam Abu Safia, the paediatrician who was the head of Kamal Adwan Hospital, the last functioning hospital in northern Gaza until Israeli forces stormed it in December 2024. He’s been held now for more than 22 months without charge under Israel’s Incarceration of Unlawful Combatants Law, which permits indefinite detentions. He reportedly continues to endure prolonged solitary confinement, beatings, severe weight loss and untreated pre-existing conditions. An international petition for his release has drawn the signatures of more than 970 medical professionals from 41 countries. Alongside him stands Dr Mazen al-Rantisi, the 71-year-old family physician from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, known as the “doctor of the poor”. He was arrested in June in a predawn raid on his home. In addition, our longtime Doctors Without Borders (MSF) colleague, Dr Mohammed Hassan Ali Obeid, a respected 43-year-old Palestinian orthopaedic surgeon and father of three children, has been detained under the Unlawful Combatants Law in Israel for more than 600 days without charge. Although detained health workers have been released, more than 80 remain in Israeli custody alongside at least a dozen arrested from the West Bank. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recorded 1,000 attacks on healthcare, which have resulted in more than 1,000 deaths and 1,700 injuries in Gaza since October 7, 2023. Roughly 90 percent of Gaza’s health infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged. In August 2025, United Nations experts stated that the systematic destruction of the health system amounts to “medicide”. In the West Bank, where no wartime emergency provides cover, the WHO also documented more than 1,000 attacks on healthcare since October 7, 2023, with 42 deaths and at least 218 injuries. Ambulances are stopped at checkpoints and their crews taken. Medics trying to reach people injured in settler attacks have themselves been obstructed. Dialysis and oncologic patients stay home because the checkpoints make the journey to treatment impossible. Healthcare workers have been shot, detained and killed during Israeli military raids. All of this represents Israel’s deliberate and systematic endeavour to dismantle Palestinians’ capacity to provide care. This is consistent with its clear and blatant disregard for Palestinian life. The WMA Assembly should speak plainly about what is happening. It should call publicly for the release of detained Palestinian doctors, including Abu Safia, al-Rantisi and Obeid. It should press for independent access to those still being held. And it should back independent investigations into attacks on healthcare in Gaza and the West Bank with the findings made public regardless of where they lead. This is an opportunity to collectively pressure fellow medical associations, political authorities and any relevant bodies to take action. What lies before the Rotterdam assembly is a duty. One that reaffirms loudly, structurally, universally the founding proposition of the WMA: that membership carries an ethical responsibility, which does not flex with geography or alliances. Healthcare workers are not targets. Either a white coat is worth protecting everywhere, or it is protected nowhere. The test is not simply whether we affirm these principles, but whether we uphold them when it matters most. The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

events.title: The job market is brutal. But nearly 1 in 3 workers still want to quit
events.summary: Good morning! With job seekers facing one of the toughest markets in years, employers might assume they can worry less about keeping workers from heading for the exits. New data suggests otherwise.  A Workday report released today finds that employee retention is eroding across industries, even at companies that are still growing headcount. Nearly one-third of employees surveyed said they’re likely to look for a new role externally in the next 12 months. Put another way, roughly two employees are weighing an exit for every one who accepts a job at a company. And some two-thirds of employers saw people staying for shorter stints this year than last year. What’s driving the retention slide? Phil Willburn, Workday’s vice president of people systems, intelligence and support, points to two problems: employees aren’t seeing career progression, and they don’t understand where the company is headed. Workday found that communicating a clear strategy is one of the most powerful levers leaders have to improve how employees feel about the workplace. Yet it is also the only factor Workday measures that has flatlined since 2021. Trust in a time of uncertainty may also be at play. Employee trust in colleagues, managers, and CEOs has fallen to a record low, according to Edelman’s latest Trust at Work study , which will be released tomorrow. Only 66% believe they are paid fairly for the work they do, and 61% believe there are many opportunities to move up in their organizations, the study found. What makes this moment unique, Willburn says, is that workers are dealing with economic uncertainty and AI fear at the same time. “When you compound those two together with many companies having a squishy AI strategy, it creates worker anxiety,” he says. “Workers already know that their jobs are changing, and they want their employer to step in and help with that transformation.” Even workers who choose to ride out the uncertainty aren’t happy about it. Workday found that those employees are less likely to recommend their employer—a warning that a weak job market can keep people in their seats without making them more committed to the company. So what can HR leaders do? Willburn says it starts with a candid acknowledgement that work is changing and explaining how AI will transform employees’ roles. Leaders then need to lay out a clear strategy for how the organization plans to compete in an AI-driven economy and what that means for the people working there. The final step is to give employees agency over their career progression. At Workday, for example, employees have access to a personalized AI coach designed to help them identify new skills and potential career paths. Once they identify a route, the company provides up to $2,500 to pursue relevant development. Kristin Stoller Editorial Director, Fortune Live Media kristin.stoller@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Instinct users say its new shopping feature is pushing products they never asked for
events.summary: Instinct users flagged unsolicited shopping recommendations, raising questions about how personal AI agents will monetize their platforms. Gabby Jones/Bloomberg via Getty Images Instinct users say it texted them a shopping list pulled from chats they thought were private. Instinct's CEO says agents shouldn't push purchases users don't want. But users say they got them. Marketing and media analysts say the shopping suggestions may hint at monetization. If Instinct has suddenly texted you a shopping list you never asked for, you're not alone. Three early users, among dozens of X users, told Business Insider that the personal AI agent sent them unsolicited product recommendations based on details from earlier conversations. Shruti Gandhi, a general partner and founding engineer at AI-focused venture firm Array Ventures, said Instinct sent her a shopping list despite not requesting one. "I didn't ask for anything," Gandhi told Business Insider, adding that the agent knew she had a trip coming up. Screenshots Gandhi shared on X show Instinct using details about her upcoming conference and keynote to create a five-item list, including a $250.75 carry-on suitcase, sunscreen, and a power bank. The recommendations — reviewed by Business Insider — come as Instinct expanded its shopping tools through a Shopify partnership and began rolling out Instinct Selections , a feature that Shinn says draws on recommendations curated by chefs, designers, architects, and local guides. They were not labeled as ads, and Business Insider could not determine whether Instinct earns money from resulting purchases . But they could test a red line set by Instinct CEO Noah Shinn. In an interview on "Invest Like The Best" posted last week, Shinn said agents should not use their knowledge of users to steer them into purchases they do not want. He criticized platforms that use paid ads to persuade people to buy products they "may or may not want." "I think it would be a very dangerous world if Instinct were influencing the user's behavior to purchase something that they don't want to purchase or to subscribe to something that they don't want," he said. Instinct didn't respond to a request for comment. When a recommendation feels like a pitch Ghandi isn't the only Instinct user to have flagged such unsolicited recommendations. Tanmaye Bhatia, AI lead at Primary Venture Partners, said Instinct texted him unsolicited product recommendations on Tuesday. A screenshot he published on X last Tuesday shows the agent offering picks "for the range and the road," including $15 golf alignment sticks, after drawing on earlier discussions about his golf swing and upcoming travel. Bhatia told Business Insider he did not believe the recommendations were ads, but said they were "a bit of a turnoff." He said Instinct should have first asked whether it could make occasional recommendations based on his personal history . Girum Tihtina, the cofounder and CEO of medical-tourism marketplace Doctours, posted a screenshot on X last Wednesday showing Instinct recommending a "first office kit," including a monitor he said was worth roughly $200. Tihtina told Business Insider that the message arrived randomly, when he had not been discussing shopping, and that he could not connect the recommendation to any previous conversation. "I have no idea why it chose what to show me," Tihtina said. "I just shrugged it off as they're probably experimenting on how to make money." The price of a personal agent So, is this Instinct's attempt to monetize its personal AI agent? On "Invest Like The Best" last Monday, Shinn described a business model in which Instinct stays free for users while merchants pay it a cut when it brings them a customer and helps complete a purchase. That does not establish that Instinct earned money from the unsolicited recommendations. But marketing analysts told Business Insider the shopping suggestions highlight a potential conflict: An agent is supposed to advise its user, but may also have a financial incentive to turn that user's personal information into a purchase. Davood Wadi, an AI research scientist at General Motors and a research affiliate at McGill University's Desautels Faculty of Management, said the key unanswered question is whether Instinct makes money when a user buys something it suggests. If it does, "then yes, this is monetization, even without any ads," he said. Kirk Plangger, chair and head of marketing at King's Business School, urged caution. There is "no evidence that these particular recommendations were paid placements or that Instinct made money from them," he said. Still, he said, the bigger shift is that an agent can use what it knows about a user to "initiat[e] the shopping occasion itself." Even if products are selected in the consumer's interest, Instinct could have an incentive to create more opportunities to shop if it benefits whenever a purchase is made, Plangger said. Carlos Diaz Ruiz, an associate professor of marketing at Hanken School of Economics, said the messages do not prove covert advertising. But they create a "structural tension" if future commissions give Instinct an incentive to turn personal conversations into purchase leads, he said. Ari Paparo, founder and chairman of Marketecture Media, said his "best guess" was that Instinct was testing whether these recommendations generate consumer interest before potentially moving toward an affiliate model. David Rand, a Cornell professor of information science, marketing, and psychology, was more agnostic. The suggestions could be a genuine attempt to help, or a monetization play, he said. "Without transparency" into the agent's instructions, "there's really no way of knowing," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Average five-year fixed mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
events.summary: Banks and building societies raise prices as turmoil in bond markets increases expectations of base rate rise The average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage has hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years, as jitters in the money markets make the loans more expensive for lenders to offer. Figures from financial information provider Moneyfacts show the average is now 6.00%, its highest point since September 2023, while the average two-year fixed rate is not far behind at 5.98%, its highest since December of the same year. In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put up prices as turmoil in global bond markets has increased expectations of a base rate rise . Meanwhile, borrowers in Great Britain have seen their choice of fixed-rate mortgages costing below 5% shrivel to only nine options, according to Moneyfacts. That marks a 99% plunge in the market since the start of last month, when there were 1,494 deals priced below that level. There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages . Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfacts, said the impact on rates had been “brutal”. She said: “Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers. Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed.” The rise in prices is bad news for borrowers finishing existing fixed-rate deals who at the start of the year may have been looking forward to falling costs, as well as those hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a property. Figures from the HomeOwners Alliance show the monthly cost of a £250,000 loan fixed at 6% for five years is £158 higher than the same-sized loan locked in at 4.94%, which was the average rate reported by Moneyfacts at the start of February. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning There are already signs that higher mortgage costs are weighing down the housing market, with Nationwide building society last week reporting that annual price growth had halved in September . Ian Harris, the president of the estate agents’ body NAEA Propertymark, said members were “seeing first-hand how sensitive buyers are to mortgage rates”, and the rapid disappearance of sub-5% deals would add further pressure to affordability. He said: “For some buyers, even a relatively small increase in monthly repayments can mean they have to reduce their budget or step back from a purchase altogether. Equally, homeowners coming off fixed-rate deals may face significantly higher repayments, which could affect their decision to move.”

events.title: UK reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align with EU
events.summary: Move would strengthen Britain’s case to be included in new legislation to protect European manufacturing The UK is reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align itself with the EU and strengthen its case to be included in new legislation designed to protect the European manufacturing sectors including autos and chemicals. It is understood the EU has raised the question of tariffs with the UK as part of the discussions on the “Made in Europe” legislation , known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely . Brussels believes the UK would have to introduce tariffs to create a level playing field to qualify for inclusion in the scheme and match the tariffs of up to 45% it has levied on Chinese cars since October 2024. Imposing tariffs on Chinese cars would probably prompt a hostile response from Beijing and test Andy Burnham’s desire for a reset in the post-Brexit relationship with the EU. It would also involve a lengthy World Trade Organization process. It took the EU 13 months between the launch of the investigation into state subsidies in production and transport lines and finally imposing tariffs in October 2024. The UK has been lobbying hard to be included in the legislation, which will require manufacturers to procure components from the continent to protect against the growing presence of China in supply chains, particularly the auto and chemicals sector. A government source pointed to comments from the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, last week, saying tariffs on Chinese EVs were “always kept … under close review”. If tariffs were to be imposed, the move would be a break with the previous government policy. Keir Starmer’s government positioned itself as a strong ally to China, viewing it as an important source of economic growth rather than a risk to British manufacturing. The UK has consistently argued it does not need trade barriers in the way Brussels does because it does not have the huge trade deficit – now running at more than £1bn (€1.18bn) a day – that the EU is struggling to contain. China’s increasing trade with the EU – not only in finished products such as cars but also in components – is causing deep concern about cannibalisation of native industries in European capitals. The EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, is visiting Beijing this Wednesday for talks over a reset in trade relations. Experts said last week the UK car industry faced a “difficult trade-off” , with Chinese investment a potential “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers. However, Nissan’s chair in Europe, Massimiliano Messina, recently said Europe “cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market” through imports via Great Britain. Nissan is in talks with the Chinese company Chery to manufacture cars in its Sunderland plant, but this would still align with the EU’s Made in Europe policy. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The EU views Chinese manufacturers based in Europe, employing EU staff, as less of a threat to its indigenous industries. Chinese brands made by BYD in Hungary, for example, will not be subject to import duties. Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said any consideration of tariffs needed to be based on “robust evidence” and maintain a rules-based open and competitive market, adding: “Trade restrictions can have unintended consequences. “The immediate priority is a pragmatic agreement recognising the UK as a trusted ‘Made in Europe’ partner as the exclusion of UK-built vehicles would severely damage both our highly integrated industries, jeopardising the €80bn trading relationship.” Brands such as BYD, Leapmotor and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to the latest industry figures. BYD has almost doubled its share of the UK market in September 2026 compared with September 2025, with 5.75% of the market, according to figures from the SMMT released on Monday. In the year to date, BYD’s share has gone up from 2.2% to 3.93%, with 68,000 BYD cars sold up to the end of September, closing in on BMW, which shifted 91,000. Jaecoo’s share has rocketed, increasing by 223%, with 58,000 new cars sold in the year so far, while Leapmotor sales have soared by a phenomenal 765% – up from about 1,500 cars sold in 2025 to more than 13,000 in the year so far. A UK government spokesperson said: “We have not put tariffs on Chinese EVs. We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector’s and UK’s national interests.”

events.title: Washington has picked a side in Ethiopia's new war
events.summary: There is new cause for alarm in the Horn of Africa. A week after a coalition of seven opposition groups announced an alliance to overthrow the government of Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, fighting has broken out across several regions of the country of 130 million people. Led by the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front, the militias of Ethiopia’s largest regions of Amhara and Oromia have also pledged their support. Early battles have taken place along a critical commercial route leading east to the port of Djibouti, while drone strikes were carried out around the army’s main airbase near the capital, Addis Ababa. The choice of economic and political targets reflects the reality that even though the Tigrayans are weaker militarily than in their previous war that ended in 2022, they can still create asymmetric pressure on the government. Ethiopia’s army is now quickly regrouping and is pushing the TPLF back into Tigray, where government forces have retaken the regional airport and now occupy the capital, Mekelle. As the conflict moves into urban areas, the risk of displacement and civilian casualties grows. And in a region already suffering from aid shortages, and anticipating even greater food insecurity from this year’s El Nino, humanitarians are rightly nervous about a potential catastrophic fallout. But the Tigrayans and their “Alliance for Survival” allies believe they have an ace up their sleeves. A coalition of neighboring states, led by Egypt and including Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia have reportedly been working in the background to support the Prime Minister’s armed opponents. Abiy’s announcement of building three new hydroelectric dams on the Nile, along with his threatening claims on the Eritrean port of Assab, and his army’s support for the Rapid Support Forces militia next door in Sudan have made him no friends across the region. All would like to see his ambitions contained. With a fully internationalized conflict already raging in neighboring Sudan and long-time foe Eritrea poised to enter the fight on the side of the Tigrayans, the risk that Ethiopia’s conflict converges with existing regional instability and animosities is high. The fallout from a regional war on US priorities from counterterrorism to Red Sea security would be disastrous, which raises the question why isn’t the Trump Administration doing more to stop it? On Oct. 4, the State Department urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to “exercise maximum restraint,” though curiously did not address the current fighting by Ethiopia’s internal armed groups. But back in June, the State Department sanctioned a group of Tigrayan officials for “undermining resolution to the crisis in Tigray” and last week the US ambassador in Addis blamed Tigrayans for their “poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive.” None of this suggests an even-handed approach this time around that would enable Washington to mediate an end to the violence as it did in 2022 to end the last Tigray war. This time, Washington has picked a side. Rubio’s newfound prioritization of commercial diplomacy , reflected in the announcement last week of the sale of $5 billion in Boeing aircraft to Ethiopia’s national airline, speaks to Washington’s focus on economic returns over peacemaking. But that view is shortsighted. Ethiopia’s double-digit economic growth and large infrastructure plans are vulnerable to the threat of nationwide war and regional meddling. The African Union has called for calm , but only Washington has the political leverage to manage a regional crisis. With Red Sea instability occupying more of Washington’s strategic focus, it would do well to prioritize peacemaking and ensure that Ethiopia’s economic potential is not undone by a descent into a region-wide conflict.

events.title: Growing outrage in Japan after US Marine arrested in woman’s killing
events.summary: The 20-year-old soldier denies the charge as protests held on Okinawa and in Tokyo. Japan’s prime minister says the killing of a woman , allegedly by a US Marine stationed in Okinawa, is a “heinous crime”, and she has called on the United States to “thoroughly enforce discipline” amid growing outrage in Japan. Sanae Takaichi told lawmakers on Monday that the government has urged the US to provide “full cooperation with the investigation” and called for “strict discipline among US military personnel”. list 1 of 4 Japan turns to Canadian crude as Asia feels Hormuz supply pinch list 2 of 4 US aircraft carrier expected to relieve USS Lincoln in Middle East list 3 of 4 Japanese PM-backed candidate wins Okinawa gubernatorial election list 4 of 4 Japan summons US envoy as Marine arrested over killing in Okinawa About 54,000 US military personnel, including 18,000 Marines, are stationed in Japan. The majority of these forces are based in Okinawa, a Japanese island that came under US administrative control at the end of World War II and was returned to Japan in 1972. Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drink-driving incidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on the island. The new case involves a 20-year-old Marine who was arrested on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in the city of Naha and stealing her wallet, police said on Sunday. The Kyodo News agency, quoting police, reported that the woman’s body was found in a hotel room and she appeared to have been strangled. The Marine was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday and sent to prosecutors on Monday, according to Kyodo News. He has denied the charges. “The occurrence of such a heinous crime is extremely regrettable,” Takaichi said. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Monday that Tokyo will “continue to urge the US side to thoroughly enforce discipline” among its soldiers in Japan. Kihara, who is in charge of mitigating the impact of US forces in Okinawa, said Tokyo has protested to the US at “various levels”. The incident has caused outrage across Japan, and the Japanese Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Defence have summoned the US ambassador and the commander of US forces in Japan. According to Jiji Press, about 100 people held protests outside the Okinawa prefectural government building on Sunday and shouted: “How much longer do we have to bear all of this?” Another 100 people participated in a rally in Naha on Sunday, Japanese media reported. Okinawa native Sorane Sakihama, 24, who organised a similar rally in Tokyo on Sunday, said she cried upon learning about the woman’s death. “We couldn’t protect her. That made me so angry and sad,” the university student told the AFP news agency, adding that she was planning to organise another protest in front of the US embassy on Tuesday evening. “I want to ask them: What are these soldiers stationed here for? They might say they are here to protect lives or boost security. But how can they say that when a life was taken by one of their own?” Since Okinawa was returned to Japan, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested in Japan, according to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper.

events.title: Ubuntu 'Stonking Stingray' beta swims out: Deeper Rust 'oxidization' plus LLM speech-to-text
events.summary: Ubuntu 26.10, “Stonking Stingray,” has entered beta testing, slightly later than planned – it is in fact scheduled to be released on October 15. While many people will stay with the LTS version, there’s some interesting stuff in there. There are already some release notes, but like the OS itself, they aren’t final yet, and there are still some gaps. Canonical does note that the "oxidization" process – exchanging core Unix tools written in C with new Rust replacements – goes further in this edition: now, the stock OpenPGP encryption support is via the Rust-based Sequoia-PGP. Perhaps one of the most daringly different new features is Canonical’s promised LLM-powered Myna speech-to-text tool. This isn’t installed by default, but you can add it, and a choice of speech-recognition models. We found various sets of instructions, including the unofficial “Ubuntu Handbook”. Our geriatric testbed was a little old for this, though, and we couldn't try it. A couple of weeks ago we took at look at the beta of what will become Fedora 45. Both Ubuntu 26.10 and the default workstation edition of Fedora will use GNOME 51, but since the Fedora beta, the final release of the latest GNOME is here: GNOME 51 “A Coruña”. The version in the Ubuntu beta isn’t working completely smoothly. We saw a persistent error about missing themes, and although the OS offered to install whatever was missing automatically, this failed. Since it doesn’t actually say what is missing, we can’t install it ourselves. The problem is only cosmetic: just some missing icons in applications, very similar to what we saw in Alpine Linux 3.16 four years ago. Sadly, problems around GNOME themes are a long standing issue. As we reported earlier this year, the Linux Mint developers are still struggling with them. The occasional missing icon aside, though, Stonking works pretty well. We tried both in a Virtualbox VM and on bare metal on our old testbed Thinkpad W520, and it ran well in both. The new installation program that arrived with the 2024 LTS version works fine, and now makes it much clearer which control is currently selected with an orange highlight. We do wish the window was resizable, though. The testbed machine has two SATA drives and we had to do a lot of scrolling to choose the right partitions. It also failed to use our dedicated swap partition, although we selected it during installation. Although GNOME 51 removed their support for old Nvidia devices in this development cycle, it still picked up and used the machine’s Nvidia-controlled Displayport output. It didn’t work perfectly: GNOME couldn’t report on the model or properties of our Quadro 1000 GPU, or the CPU-integrated Intel one for that matter, but at least the second screen worked. More surprisingly, it even worked in the Fallback session, even though that uses the Metacity X11 window manager – and while logged into to a Fallback session, it could identify both GPUs. GNOME 51 isn’t a very feature-heavy release, but the Settings app has some useful additions, such as the ability to automatically disable the trackpad when an external mouse is connected. In our testing, it picked up and let us configure mouse, trackpad, and trackpoint, each in a separate tab. GNOME 51 no longer supports Wi-Fi networks with the old WEP encryption system, though. Modern Linux continues to move away from being an OS for old and low-end hardware. If the machine is online during installation, the installer fetches any package updates as it works, so the first update post-install is much quicker. However, this doesn’t apply to Snap packages: the .deb package phase of our first update was very fast, but we got various new snaps. One detail we haven’t noticed before is that while a snap application is updating, its dock icon temporarily gets a progress bar to tell you it’s being updated. We did a full install with all the optional extras, so this applied to Thunderbird as well as Firefox. A full installation took a fairly hefty 13 GB of disk space, although to be fair, that included 4GB of swap space – so in real money, it’s about 9 GB, which isn’t too bad for 2026. According to the htop command, it idles at about 1.2 B RAM, which is quite high, but then GNOME is no lightweight. Linux kernel 7.3 is still in development, but at the time of writing it’s up to RC5, and our testing ran without a hitch. The final version may be out before “Stonking” is completed, but if not, users will get it very soon afterwards. We also gave the Kubuntu desktop a very brief try. In this release, it uses Plasma 6.7.5, and ran well – it was fast, smooth, and happily drove both screens of our testbed machine; helpfully, on our first login, it asked where the second display was relative to the first. If you want modern Wayland niceties such as different dots-per-inch settings on different screens, but you also want a traditional Windows-style layout, KDE is currently the way to go. Plasma 6.8 is scheduled for later this month, and totally drops X11 support. It’s likely to be the desktop in Kubuntu 27.04, making it Wayland-only – so 26.10 is probably the last ever version of Kubuntu in which displaying your desktop thanks to X.org is a supported option. We installed X11 support, which is just one command: sudo apt install -y plasma-session-x11 This brings in multiple extra dependencies, which is why we specified the -y switch, but it took just seconds. We logged out, logged back again choosing “Plasma (X11)”, and… Everything looked absolutely identical. Which is how it should be, of course. Both screens were working normally, thanks to the Nouveau FOSS NVIDIA driver. The only visible differences are the classic “wobbly window” effect when moving windows around, and that the title-bar context menu regains the option to “shade” a window: roll it up, leaving only the title bar visible. You can’t do this in a Wayland environment. Under Wayland, htop reports about 1.2 GB in use; under X.org, about 1.3 GB. The resurrected Oxygen theme from KDE 4 is built in, if you want a bit more visual bling, but we preferred the flatter grayer look of the default Breeze theme. The only freeze that we saw in all our testing of the Stonking beta was after logging out of a Plasma (Wayland) session and trying to log back in using Plasma (X11). To be fair, we suspect most people wouldn’t chop-and-change this much. Ubuntu Stonking is shaping up well. Aside from the small theme-related glitches, GNOME worked fine, and KDE didn’t even have those minor issues. The equivalent beta versions of all the official flavors are also available, including both Ubuntu Unity 26.10 and Ubuntu MATE. Despite a hundred other distros, Ubuntu remains the go-to desktop Linux for most people. While Canonical is getting slightly more experimental with interim releases again, this is a mature product now and they’re a pretty safe bet. ®

events.title: Reforming UK capital markets to ensure they work well for our economy
events.summary: Speech by Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges, at the Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026. The Economic Secretary to the Treasury has discussed the contribution of UK markets to economic growth.I want to build on that by talking about the FCA’s role in reforming capital market rules.The headline is that we've been very busy over the past few years.We’ve now completed major aspects of a multi-year programme of work, to ensure capital markets work well for our economy and support growth.This has already delivered positive changes. But there’s plenty more to come.We are working on further reforms, while also adapting to rapid changes in markets and use of technology.In fact, areas such as tokenisation, AI and markets for trading private company shares have become central to our capital markets policy programme.And that tells us something important. As markets change, our approach has had to change too.The question has not been whether regulation changes. It has been how we adjust in a way that preserves trust while also supporting innovation and growth.Let me start by talking about our approach to the work.We have been working with the Treasury, the Bank of England and in close dialogue with the private sector, on a raft of wholesale market reforms.These draw on formal reports, like the Wholesale Markets Review, our process of reviewing inherited EU regulation, and issues raised by market contacts.Some have suggested the work programme is a list not a strategy. But I think that underestimates it. There are some key principles running through it.

events.title: Euro falls to 17-month low against dollar amid French debt fears
events.summary: France’s Cac 40 index slides as announcement of snap election in Spain also helps fuel eurozone uncertainty The euro has slumped to the lowest level against the dollar in 17 months amid growing concern France’s debt position could threaten the stability of the wider single currency bloc. The single currency fell as much as 0.8% against the dollar in early trading on Monday to below $1.12, its lowest level since May 2025, before recovering slightly. It has slumped by about 1.2% this month, accelerating a drop of about eight cents against the greenback from a peak of $1.20 in January. Investors said the sell-off in the euro was fuelled by concerns over France’s rising debt costs as the government battles to control its stretched public finances in the run-up to next year’s presidential election. France’s blue-chip Cac 40 index of leading company shares fell by 1% on Monday, as markets elsewhere across Europe rallied. The FTSE 100 was up 0.2%, while Germany’s Dax was little changed. Monday’s announcement of a snap election in Spain by the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency housing legislation last week has also fuelled eurozone uncertainty. Madrid’s benchmark Ibex 35 index rose by 0.5%. “Europe is taking the spotlight at the start of the week, as fiscal and political concerns hit the bloc,” said Kathleen Brooks, the research director at XTB. “France is the epicentre of the concerns; however, Spain is also set to get ready for an early election, which is adding to investor worries.” Amid a global sell-off in sovereign debt as the Iran war rattles markets, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on French 10-year government bonds last week hit the highest level since 2002, before dipping back on Friday. This pushed the gap between France and Germany’s borrowing costs, an important measure of investor concern, to its widest level since 2012 at the height of the eurozone sovereign debt crisis . Investors are focused on Paris’s fiscal position and concerns that the presidential election and a hung parliament – with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party gaining ground – could make it tougher for the government to curtail a yawning budget deficit. The minority government of the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, announced plans last month for a €54bn (£45.8bn) savings drive to curb borrowing levels, setting the stage for a fierce political battle. With President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration under pressure amid strikes and protests across the country , the budget measures involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. Lecornu said the savings would result in limiting a budget deficit of 5.5% of GDP this year to 5% next year. He warned that without action the shortfall between public spending and revenue could reach 6.5%. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning However, investors fear political pressures could derail fiscal consolidation, threatening to push up borrowing and adding to France’s debt pile at a time of soaring government borrowing costs. Analysts warned the stresses in the French bond market could spread to other countries in the euro area, stoking fears over a return to the dynamics of the 2010s sovereign debt crisis. It comes amid concerns over the test facing the European Central Bank from mounting inflationary pressures from the war in the Middle East and the risk France’s debt problem spreads throughout the euro area. Roberto Mialich, a currency strategist at the Italian bank UniCredit, said: “Investors still do not rule out riding a further decline of the euro, making a retest of $1.10 possible in the near term. “This is also because growing political tensions across the eurozone (primarily in France and Spain) and fears of contagion across the European sovereign debt market are putting pressure on the euro.”
