events.title: Why are data centres such a big deal in Scotland?
events.summary: A Google Data Centre in Cheshunt in Hertfordshire Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes. Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them - on a massive scale. The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new "hyperscale" data centres, including some which would rank among the biggest in the world. Plans are in place to build at least 23 giant AI-powered data centres. Supporters say they are vital for the future and could bring billions of pounds in investment, as well as thousands of jobs. Opponents fear the impact of their size on local communities, the vast amounts of energy they use and even the noise they will make. So what exactly are data centres, and why have they become one of Scotland's most controversial planning battles? The data centre proposed at Chapelcross would be one of the biggest in the world if it went ahead From the outside, data centres look like a factory or a warehouse. On the inside, thousands of flashing lights blink and fans whirr as rows of computer servers power AI. While some are built by tech giants like Amazon, other developers claim commercial sensitivities when asked what they are actually powering. Scotland's centres are currently quite small, but some of proposals for the hyperscale versions are immense. One of the biggest is at Auchtertool in Fife . The site would span 60 hectares (150 acres) - about the size of 84 football pitches. There have been a number of protests against data centres AI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. But Scotland's data centre debate is not really about the technology inside the building - it's about the scale and impact of the centres themselves. At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie , which has a capacity for 12MW. The new data centres being proposed are a whole new level. If one planned for Chapelcross in Dumfries and Galloway goes ahead, it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world. At Auchtertool, the planned 600MW data centre would be the same size as the neighbouring village. their size and impact on the landscape the amount of electricity they require noise generated by thousands of servers and cooling systems The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies. The Scottish government has so far refused to impose a moratorium. One of Scotland's biggest selling points for data centre developers is its strong renewable energy sector. Scotland generates huge amounts of electricity from wind, and some of that power is currently wasted because the grid does not have enough capacity to move it from where it is produced to where it is needed. However, experts caution that this does not mean data centres would run entirely on renewable energy . During periods of low wind or when clouds are blocking the sun, it may mean having to fire up fossil fuel power stations to provide the energy required to keep the servers blinking. Don't data centres use a lot of water? The scene inside a Meta data centre in Temple, Texas. As well as using huge amounts of electricity, the giant data centres can require large quantities of water to prevent them from overheating. While the tech industry says it is developing more efficient cooling systems, industry sources told the BBC last year the UK government's plan to make the UK a "world leader" in AI could put already stretched supplies of drinking water under strain. An expert recently claimed that Scotland's current data centres use less water each day than its libraries, but there are significant concerns over what the water consumption could be if any of the hyperscale centres were given the go-ahead. Data centres have many fans cooling down the servers inside and people in the US who live near them have reported hearing a constant noise, with concerns it has also driven away wildlife. What are the potential benefits of data centres? Many of the proposed data centres are in Scotland's central belt - including an expansion of the company DataVita's site in North Lanarkshire As well as having a stake in a key future technology, those behind AI data centres say they will create jobs. Lanarkshire has been designated an AI growth zone by the UK government, with data centres at its heart. When it was announced in January , external , £8bn of investment and 3,400 jobs were promised. The type of jobs a data centre creates has also been debated. About 800 are expected to be in AI, with 50 apprenticeships.

events.title: Trump chooses top spy boss to run new AI taskforce
events.summary: Published 5 October 2026, 02:33 BST US President Donald Trump has named the director of national intelligence as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will coordinate government engagement with consumers, companies and "religious organizations". Jay Clayton will head a taskforce that has drawn criticism from the likes of Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren who has called for regulation of AI. Trump has rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity. Last week, the president and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document, making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology. Trump - who is unilaterally attempting to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" - wrote on social media: "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies." As well as Clayton, a former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission, Andrew Ferguson, head of the Federal Trade Commission, will be on the taskforce along with Emil Michael, undersecretary of defense for research and engineering. It will report directly to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. Trump has pushed back against any kind of slowdown on AI development. He said the US is leading the race ahead of China, adding: "And, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins." President Xi Jinping recently travelled to Washington for a state visit. Days later, Trump ruled out a joint venture between the US and China to develop AI. "If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology. Trump first announced the taskforce in September, prompting Warren to state: "Congress cannot meet the pressing threat of AI by just forming another committee or continuing to have drawn-out discussions about it." She added: "Let's actually pass some meaningful regulations on AI to protect people." US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public. "The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded. The company recently admitted that a rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the agent "infiltrated" a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare. Despite the incident occuring in June, Albanese said the government only learned about the breach in August. He said there will be "legal consequences". OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon is due to appear as part of an AI inquiry in Australian on Tuesday. Over the weekend, a former leader in OpenAI's safety systems team wrote in an article for the Atlantic magazine that he had left the firm because its culture was "broken". "As [OpenAI] sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," wrote David Robinson, who was involved in safety and transparency reporting. The BBC has contacted OpenAI for comment. Last month, the ChatGPT-maker pulled the release of its latest AI model due to safety concerns. Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit Published 5 days ago OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns Published 6 days ago Trump has largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves. A pact signed on 29 September included the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google. On the same day, the president signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence. SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said. Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding, arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems. Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI.

events.title: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
events.summary: AI data centers are driving demand for memory chips, pushing phone makers to raise prices and abandon some of their most affordable models. The world’s cheapest smartphones are disappearing because AI infrastructure is absorbing the components. Prices of existing smartphone models have risen by about 15% globally this year , while newly launched models are roughly 25% more expensive than last year. A global memory chip shortage, driven by demand from AI data centers, is pushing up the cost of making smartphones. Chinese smartphone makers — which have championed affordable, feature-rich devices and account for approximately 60% of all smartphones shipped globally — have “drastically reduced” their entry-level projects this year as memory-chip costs have risen, Ivan Lam, senior analyst at research firm Counterpoint, told Rest of World . They are instead prioritizing more profitable premium devices. The smartphone price increases vary sharply by region: They have risen by 21% in India, 19% across Asia-Pacific, and 18% in the Middle East and Africa. In the U.S., they have gone up by just 5%. The shift could affect more than consumers looking for cheaper phones. For people who have yet to buy their first smartphone, higher prices could make it harder to get online at all — potentially widening the digital divide. The consequences will also reach the U.S. as more essential services move online and the global supply chain for smartphones becomes more expensive. GSMA, the global mobile industry association, had earlier said nearly 800 million more people will use mobile internet by 2030. But it is concerned that rising smartphone costs would affect this projection and widen the gap of digital inequality, Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at the group’s nonprofit foundation, told Rest of World . “We live in an increasingly digital world, and the proliferation of technologies such as AI is creating greater digital divides and inequities,” Sibthorpe said. “Stakeholders are increasingly using AI to provide access to important services, but people won’t be able to benefit without access to an internet-enabled phone and the internet.” In 2025, more than one in four smartphones shipped globally cost less than $150 . That market is now shrinking. Chinese phonemakers including Xiaomi i Xiaomi Xiaomi is a Chinese consumer electronics company that leads the country in smartphone manufacturing and sales. READ MORE , Oppo, Vivo, and Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE have built their businesses around offering affordable phones with increasingly sophisticated features. But the economics of that strategy are changing. What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300.” Ivan Lam, senior analyst, Counterpoint Chinese companies “would rather reduce investment in products below $150 or $200 and put more resources into higher-margin phones, branding, user experience, and AI,” said Lam. In India, Xiaomi raised the price of a 128GB Redmi 15C from 12,499 rupees ($140) at launch last December to 16,999 rupees ($190) in June, a 36% increase. In Southeast Asia, Oppo’s sub-$100 phone shipments plunged 96%, and Vivo moved its main entry-level model above $100 in most markets, according to research firm Omdia . In Africa, where 81% of smartphones shipped last year cost less than $200, shipments of sub-$100 phones fell 34% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. “What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300,” Lam said, adding that he does not expect costs to return to their pre-2025 levels. The memory-chip shortage is unlikely to ease soon, Ramon Llamas, research director in mobile devices at market research and advisory firm IDC, told Rest of World. “ There are three primary manufacturers of memory, and in late 2025, all of them pivoted the vast majority of their supply towards AI centers instead of consumer electronics,” Llamas said. “That left many companies scrambling for inventory. … Scarcity of memory has driven up prices for memory, and those price increases have been passed on to the consumer.” Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology make up more than 90% of the global memory chip market. These companies have entered several partnerships with U.S. AI giants in recent years. S&P Global has estimated that the capital expenditure of U.S. hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, and SpaceX — will exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027 , up from a projected $870 billion in 2026 and $470 billion in 2025. Shipments of sub-$100 smartphones are already falling sharply. The 173 million sub-$100 smartphones shipped globally last year are disappearing, with shipments falling almost 60% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to IDC.

events.title: Three tax votes in November that will affect high earners
events.summary: In November, voters will head to the polls in California, Colorado, and Washington State to decide on ballot measures that could significantly affect high earners and wealth migration. The K-shaped economy has stirred a rise in populism and calls for the wealthy to pay their "fair share," especially in Democratic-led states. At the same time, rising competition among states to attract high earners is leading to ballot initiatives to cap or even lower taxes. Get Inside Wealth directly to your inbox The Inside Wealth newsletter by Robert Frank is your weekly guide to high-net-worth investors and the industries that serve them. A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. Voters will decide whether to raise or lower taxes on the wealthy in multiple states next month, with California leading the way with a potential wealth tax. The K-shaped economy has stirred a rise in populism and calls for the wealthy to pay their "fair share," especially in Democratic-led states. At the same time, rising competition among states to attract high earners is leading to ballot initiatives to cap or even lower taxes. "Over the last few years, we've seen a divergence in state income taxes and taxes on high earners," said Jared Walczak of the Tax Foundation. "We've seen many states cut individual taxes and others going in the opposite direction. It used to be the average tax rate was 6%. Now that middle has been hollowed out." The votes add fuel to the national debate over taxing the wealthy. In Massachusetts, a millionaire tax passed in 2022, imposing an extra 4% levy on those making more than $1 million a year. The tax has raised far more revenue than predicted, generating over $3 billion in the 2025-2026 fiscal year. Yet a study of IRS data by the Boston-based Pioneer Institute found that Massachusetts lost over $4 billion in adjusted gross income in 2023 from high earners leaving the state. Rhode Island joined the "millionaire tax" club this summer, passing legislation that added a phased, 3% surcharge to $1 million-plus earners, creating a top rate of 8.99% by 2029. New York's tax on high-end second homes faced new legal challenges this week, as a state judge ruled that the city needs to re-do notifications to potential taxpayers and businessmen Wilbur Ross and Steve Wynn filed suit against the tax claiming it's unconstitutional. At the other end of the political spectrum, more than a dozen states are in the process of reducing or eliminating their income taxes over time. South Carolina, Arkansas, West Virginia, Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, and Utah passed income tax reductions this year, with others approving revenue triggers that lower rates based on state revenue. In November, voters will head to the polls to decide on ballot measures that could significantly affect high earners and wealth migration. Three states to watch: California's Billionaire Tax Act has divided Democrats, split Silicon Valley and driven several of the state's billionaires to move to Florida. The measure would impose a one-time tax of 5% on the total net worth of California residents worth $1 billion or more. Since it needs only a simple majority of voters to pass, and would tax about 200 of the state's richest residents, many experts predicted it would pass. Yet a recent University of California, Berkeley poll shows 45% in favor and 43% opposed. Two competing ballot measures are likely to sow confusion and possibly defeat the billionaires tax if they receive more votes. California's billionaires are fighting back. Sergey Brin, John Doerr, Patrick Collison, Michael Moritz, Eric Schmidt, Max Levchin and others have contributed a total of more than $180 million to groups opposing the tax. Tax advisers are also counseling the state's billionaires on strategies to lower their taxable net worth, such as investing in Treasuries or transferring real estate to personal ownership. Voters will decide whether to replace Colorado's flat tax of 4.4% with a graduated income tax that raises the rates for high earners. The tax would increase to 7.4% for those making more than $500,000 a year and to 8.4% for income over $1 million. The income thresholds apply to both single filers and joint filers. So a couple making more than $500,000 a year combined would be subject to the 7.4% rate on income above the threshold. Analysts estimate the higher rates would impact the top 3% of taxpayers. Individuals or couples making less than $100,000 a year would get a tax cut, with a rate as low as 3.7% depending on income. The changes are projected to raise about $2.7 billion a year for education, healthcare and other public services. Opponents of the measure, including the state's Democratic Governor, Jared Polis, and the Colorado Chamber of Commerce, argue it will reduce the state's competitiveness and drive businesses to other states.

events.title: How ProPublica Reporters Became Private School Owners in 24 Hours
events.summary: The only requirement to open a private school in Arkansas is displaying a flag and flagpole, so the reporting team visited the local flag shop in Little Rock. Brian Chilson/Arkansas Times It began as a casual question — and a flicker of curiosity — uttered during a meeting of ProPublica journalists who this year are reporting on publicly funded private schools. We were discussing how, in many states, basically anyone can open a private school wherever they want. No experience, no training, no curriculum required. One of our editors jumped in and asked: What if ProPublica tried to establish a private school? We were intrigued. We are longtime education reporters, not educators. Would that matter? Where, if anywhere, do states draw the line on who is fit to run a school — and in some cases, collect public money to fund their ventures?  We decided that testing the thesis that anyone can open a school would be valuable to our ongoing reporting, particularly at a time when we have found that private schools are growing rapidly across the country — in barns, farms, co-working spaces, people’s homes and parks. These new schools are fueled by taxpayer-funded vouchers and other programs, and our reporting has revealed states have little interest in monitoring them .  We had some inspiration to draw from: In 2015, comedian John Oliver founded a tax-exempt church to show how easy it was for televangelists to avoid paying taxes while soliciting millions of dollars.  Some of us live in Chicago and are well aware of the lore of the Mirage Tavern , a real bar that undercover reporters operated in the 1970s to expose corruption in the city. While that investigation had a substantial impact, and led to a new city oversight agency, it also drew criticism for its deceptive practices.   We drew lessons from that reporting and set some ground rules at the start of our experiment. To be clear, we had no intention of operating schools. We won’t enroll any students.  Most importantly, it would be critical for us to be transparent about who we were in our applications, using our newsroom phone numbers and email addresses. In one state, we even disclosed that we were “journalists exploring opening a microschool.” We also decided we would stop the experiment if it would require doing something illegal or using public resources for our own benefit. Help ProPublica Report on Education Have you had trouble finding a school or using a voucher-style program? Do you have concerns about schools — public or private — in your area? Help us understand how families across the country are navigating their school options. Get in Touch Here’s how we went about the experiment in Arkansas, West Virginia and North Carolina:  First, we partnered with newsrooms in the three states — the Arkansas Times , Mountain State Spotlight in West Virginia and The Assembly in North Carolina — and pursued creating the schools together. No one knows their states better than reporters who live there, so we wanted to work with the experts. Plus, the school applications required local addresses and we reasoned that newsroom addresses, which state officials could easily look up, would be extra transparent.  Then, we came up with names for the schools. We aimed to call them Curiosity Academies to reflect our curiosity as journalists. We succeeded with the ProPublica-Arkansas Times Curiosity Academy and ProPublica-Mountain State Spotlight Curiosity Academy. A word-count limit required us to scrap curiosity for our school in North Carolina. We simply called it the ProPublica-Assembly Academy.   Next, we filed paperwork with each state. That turned out to be easier than working through the legal and ethical questions with our editors, our legal team and our standards editor to design our experiment in the first place.  In Arkansas, we didn’t need permission from the state Education Department, which does not regulate private schools. All it took was filling out a form on the Arkansas secretary of state website, $45 and an American flag to be recognized as a private school business (yes, Arkansas requires all schools to have an American flag — but only public schools also are required to have the Arkansas flag). The secretary of state’s office even emailed us a certificate. The official certificate acknowledging our school Secretary of State/State of Arkansas But when it came to applying for our private school to become eligible for public funds, a process that does add some guardrails, we didn’t think we could do it. In Arkansas, private schools participating in the voucher-like program have to be accredited or working toward it, which often requires creating curriculum and school handbooks. That seemed like a step too far since we weren’t actually opening schools.  However, we discovered that Arkansas allows a subset of schools called microschools to use public money with fewer requirements. So, we decided to apply for public funds as a microschool. That process also took only about 10 minutes. We didn’t need to provide our credentials or a background check, prove our fiscal stability or assure that the newsroom was a safe place for students. (If approved, we would not take the next step and register to receive public money.) Want Your Own ProPublica Academy Merch? Visit Our Store A state employee who reviewed our application, which we submitted in early September, said we missed the deadline for this school year but could apply for next school year. He also suggested another way we could tap into public money. Kaelin Clay, the Arkansas Department of Education spokesperson, said the agency reviews applications to the voucher-like program to determine if the schools meet state requirements. She said microschool families have the “freedom to choose” where and how their children learn. In West Virginia, we spent little time handwriting the required information on notebook paper and submitting it to the state Education Department. We eventually established our school as a microschool after a state employee shared that, unlike the regulations for private schools, we would not need an inspection.  We did need proof of at least a high school diploma, and we shared one of our real college transcripts from the late 1990s with the local school district, which then notified the state of our new school. (We couldn’t find the high school transcript; does anyone keep them?)  In an official statement, a spokesperson for West Virginia’s Department of Education said it “does not approve or deny the operation of microschools for any reason, including the qualifications of the owner/operator.” State law includes no mechanism for oversight of microschools. events.title: I was 16 when I started reselling online. A few months later, my garage was a warehouse and I was making $25,000 a month.
events.summary: Courtesy of Ethan Alexander Ethan Alexander was a high school sophomore when he started reselling goods on Amazon. He did $125,000 in sales last year, before the business became overwhelming. He's invested much of the money and plans to use what he learned from the business. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ethan Alexander . It has been edited for length and clarity . Each year, I get a $500 gift from an investment account that my great-grandfather set up for all of his great-grandkids. My gramps — Jack Davis — owned his own company and left a legacy of entrepreneurship in our family. I get the money on his birthday, May 9th. In 2025, my sophomore year of high school, I came across a video on Instagram about making a profit by reselling items online shortly after I received Gramp's gift. I had stopped playing lacrosse, my typical spring sport, and I was looking for something to fill my time. I used the $500 to pay someone to teach me how to resell. I didn't do much research, just thought "what's the worst that can happen?" The business took off immediately, and I generated just under $10,000 in revenue that first month. In August, I did more than $25,000 in revenue. I resold lots of goods at a relatively small profit Success reselling on Amazon comes from volume. I would find a product where I could make a relatively small profit margin — about $2 to $4 — and sell lots of it. To find these products, I utilized software that many Amazon sellers use. I also used AI to create my own system for finding products. The first product I sold was laundry detergent , which I could buy at Walmart and resell on Amazon for about a 25% profit. I'd spend hours driving my truck to all the Walmarts in Greater Kansas City, buying as much detergent as I could fit. The garage at my home looked like a warehouse. Ethan Alexander turned his family's garage into his warehouse. Courtesy of Ethan Alexander After spending afternoons buying the goods, I'd stay up until the early morning packaging them. Then, I'd wake up in the early afternoon and bring my shipments to the post office. Before long, they knew me by name. I learned about the rewards of business and the risks The work wasn't glamorous. I was essentially working a warehouse job in my own house. I didn't see much of my friends that summer, because I was focused on scaling my sales. My mom was a huge asset. She runs her own health and wellness business and is also a business coach. I'm always willing to learn, so I listened to what she told me, and also drew on the skills you learn growing up in an entrepreneurial family. Still, there were lots of little challenges. I was a minor, and some months I was making $45,000 in purchases. At first, I used my mom's credit card for those transactions, but it kept getting flagged as fraud . Eventually, I had to go to the bank and take out a large amount of cash for my Walmart runs. Ethan Alexander used his mom's credit card at first to make the purchases. Courteys of Ethan Alexander I hired a few people to help me pack items, but one of them put the wrong labels on products, a mistake that cost me thousands. I learned about not mixing friendships and business that way. I also had frustrations with the backend of Amazon's seller platforms. I was making good money and incredibly proud of what I had built — but I also learned a lot about the risks of business, not just the rewards. I want to own my own business in the future By February 2026, running the business became overwhelming. My grades were suffering. As a seller, I needed to keep the momentum up to get more sales, so there wasn't really a way to scale back. I decided to stop the business for now. I spent some of the money on splurges, like clothes and Meta glasses. I've also invested a lot of it. Now I'm 18, and entering my senior year of high school. I plan to go to college, because I don't see a reason not to — especially since my parents have a college savings account for me. I'm curious, though, whether I'll learn more in business school than I did from running my own business. I know one thing for certain: I plan to be an entrepreneur. There's no other option, as far as I'm concerned. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Average five-year mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
events.summary: Published 5 October 2026, 10:02 BST The average interest rate on a new five-year fixed mortgage deal has hit 6% for the first time in three years, figures show. The cost of home loans has been rising in recent weeks, as lenders face higher costs amid international concern over rising prices, interest rates, and government borrowing costs. It means home buyers and anyone renewing a fixed deal have seen about 1,500 mortgage deals priced below 5% vanish since the start of September, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts. It described the situation as "brutal" for borrowers, with the average rate on five-year deals now at 6%, and at 5.98% on two-year fixed mortgages. For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage. Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals. Moneyfacts said that the biggest High Street lenders had made repeated fixed rate increases during September. Barclays increased selected fixed rates on four occasions, while HSBC, Lloyds Bank, Nationwide, NatWest, Santander and TSB each made three rounds of increases. It meant that the average rate on a new five-year deal was at its highest since September 2023. On two-year deals, the average rate is at its highest since December 2023. How much could my mortgage payments change? At this rate, your payments could change by… The information you provided on your monthly payments would not be sufficient to pay off your mortgage within the number of years given. This calculator does not constitute financial advice. It is based on a standard mortgage repayment formula dependent on the mortgage size and length and a fixed interest rate. It should be used as a guide only and does not represent the suitability, eligibility or availability of mortgage offers for users. For exact figures, users will need to approach an official mortgage lender. Interest rates fluctuate based on the Bank of England's base rate and market conditions "Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers," said Rachel Springall, finance expert at Moneyfacts. "Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed." She said that those coming to the end of a fixed deal would be "wise to seek advice and compare deals carefully". Some lenders could allow people to lock in a rate three months before their current deal ends, while others could allow six months, she said. Springall said rate rises were "inevitable" because lenders' wholesale funding costs had climbed as a result of rising gilt yields . Interest rates - known as the yield - on government bonds have been going up, meaning it costs the government more to borrow over the long term. The knock-on impact of this on the mortgage market has meant that the number of fixed-rate deals priced below 5% has plunged by 99%, from 1,494 since the start of September 2026 to nine now. In contrast, the number of sub-5% variable rate mortgages has remained broadly stable, Springall said, leading some borrowers to chose deals that track the Bank of England's base rate. Millions of mortgage-holders are coming to the end of their current deals in the next two years. Just over five million homeowners should expect their monthly mortgage repayments to increase by the end of 2028, according to Bank of England forecasts. Some may have expected rates to have fallen this year, owing to improved economic conditions, but the Iran war has upended many of those expectations. It has also led to wider pressure on the cost of essential bills. On Friday, drivers saw the average cost of diesel rise above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group. Domestic energy prices also rose by 4% at the start of October, and forecasters have predicted a 16% increase when regulator Ofgem sets its next price cap for January. The government is under pressure to support those most likely to struggle to pay at the Budget later this month. BT says it acquired TalkTalk Telecommunications Limited and PlatformX Communications Limited on a debt-free basis. It expects a total cash impact of approximately £400 million in its current financial year, including the acquisition consideration and other costs. BT said it stepped in after a prolonged sale process failed to find a buyer for the consumer and wholesale operations. The UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) said a collapse could disrupt emergency calls, hospital communications, and medical alarms. DCMS Secretary of State Lisa Nandy stated: "Phone and broadband services are vital national infrastructure. If TalkTalk services fail, there is a genuine risk to life and public services – including to hospitals, schools, and emergency care." Nandy issued a Public Interest Intervention Notice under section 42 of the Enterprise Act 2002, allowing her to consider the wider public interest alongside competition concerns. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) must report to her by October 19. BT says the businesses will operate separately and continue to compete pending the regulatory review. Kester Mann, director of consumer and connectivity at FDM CCS Insight, said: "Given BT's strong position in the broadband market, it will inevitably also evoke scrutiny from regulators keen to ensure a fair and competitive playing field. Last week, the CMA provisionally identified competition concerns in wholesale fixed broadband services over nexfibre's proposed acquisition of Substantial , Netomnia's parent company. Clive Selley will lead the stabilization and integration planning with immediate effect. Martijn Blanken takes over his role as CEO of BT International. events.title: I toured Qatar's new Qsuite business class, which passengers are still waiting to fly. These are the 7 best upgrades.
events.summary: The new Qsuite is impressive, and I particularly liked the two-person window suite and personal safe. Angelo De Guzman Qatar Airways debuted its new Qsuite Next Gen business class in 2024, but it's still not flying. The airline said the cabin was planned for the Boeing 777-9, a plane years behind schedule. I toured the new seat to see what flyers can expect once it launches and found surprising upgrades. Qatar Airways hoped to debut the next generation of its famous Qsuite business class last year — with lockable drawers and two-person window suites — but it still hasn't flown a single passenger. The Doha-based airline unveiled its reinvented Qsuite at the UK's Farnborough Airshow in 2024, promising a new level of luxury for its Boeing 777-9 jets by 2025. The 777-9 is the larger variant of the 777X. But Boeing's new widebody still isn't certified. The 777X is seven years behind its original schedule, while Boeing continues to grapple with safety, quality, production, and supply-chain problems. Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said at a September Morgan Stanley conference that the 777-9 was still on track for 2027, but an engine issue discovered earlier this year could slightly push the timeline. "I don't see that as a major challenge for us, but we still got a lot in front of us on the flight test program," Ortberg said. "Not done until we're done." Neither Boeing nor Qatar Airways responded to a request for comment from Business Insider. While passengers continue to fly in the original Qsuite — introduced nearly a decade ago and already considered one of the world's best airline business class cabins — I toured Next Gen at the Arabian Travel Market trade show in Dubai in September. Qatar Airways Group CEO Hamad Ali Al-Khater told Euronews the same month that Qsuite Next Gen is due in summer 2027, though the airline has not announced any specific routes. Upgrades include new combinable suites, improved tech, and smarter storage. Seeing these features up close revealed interesting differences that weren't immediately obvious. Here are the seven things that stood out most on the Qsuite Next Gen. The Companion Suite connects two window passengers. The dual window seats. Angelo De Guzman The current Qsuite lets passengers open center seats into shared configurations. Next Gen brings that concept to two window passengers with the Companion Suite. One faces forward and the other backward, situated diagonally from each other instead of directly opposite. I could see my companion without leaning or turning, with enough separation that we didn't feel unusually close. The screens are designed to latch fully aside, opening the sightline between both suites. I had plenty of personal space. The walls weren't close to my shoulders, and the curved architecture made the suite feel enclosed without becoming claustrophobic. The Quad Suite feels enormous. Quad-seating is already a feature of the current Qsuite. Angelo De Guzman Next Gen redesigns Qsuite's existing four-person layout with larger shared surfaces, movable screens, bigger beds, and digitally controlled dividers. The open Quad felt massive. I could easily speak with someone beside or opposite me, while someone diagonally across required me to lean forward and speak up. I could imagine a family spreading a board game across the middle. The dining table felt solid and easily fits a large laptop, with room for phones and belongings. Climbing into the fully flat bed , my shoulders and feet had plenty of room, so that I could roll comfortably to my side. The 4K screens physically swing aside. The television in combinable suites moves out of the way. Angelo De Guzman Qatar upgraded Next Gen with 4K screens, though watching them disappear was more memorable. The Quad's screens looked bright and colorful, responded well, and moved smoothly as I operated them. I slid them until they met back-to-back, then swiveled them 90 degrees toward the rear-facing side and nested them into the surrounding architecture, fully opening the space. A separate touchscreen remote beside the seat provides another way to control the entertainment system . The Quad becomes private again with digitally controlled dividers. One or more of the quad seats can be closed off while the others remain open. Angelo De Guzman That openness is reversible. Digitally controlled internal dividers restore passenger privacy in the Quad. They rose quietly and slowly, extending above my head. With the screen returned to position and the divider raised, the enormous shared space felt like my own cocoon again. I discovered a useful safety feature when my hand blocked the rising divider's path: It stopped automatically. The aisle door remains manual and slides smoothly. It provides substantial privacy while seated, although you could still see taller passengers as they walked past. There's a small safe in the sky. A number pad locks the drawer. Angelo De Guzman One of my favorite additions was a concealed drawer secured by a four-digit PIN entered through the suite's touchscreen. There's easily enough room for valuables like my passport, a watch, and jewelry. It essentially gives passengers a small safe in the sky. Wireless charging and USB-C come to Qsuite. One wireless charging surface had a soft, cloth-like texture, while the other had a harder finish. Angelo De Guzman The current Qsuite uses USB-A ports, while Next Gen replaces them with USB-C and wireless charging. Sitting in different seats revealed another difference. The consoles around the forward- and rear-facing Quad seats aren't identical. I found the forward-facing configuration offered more usable surface area for a laptop, a phone, a menu, a book, or an amenity kit. The seat wasn't more spacious; I simply had more places to put my things, something I'd consider when choosing a seat. An open storage shelf and universal AC outlet sit underneath the main console. 'Make My Bed' makes turndown obvious. The panel on the Qsuite controls most of the functions in the little pod. Angelo De Guzman I didn't press it, but I immediately understood its value. I've flown business-class products where passengers need to ask for turndown, and first-time flyers may not know it's available. Seeing "Make My Bed" removes that guesswork and lets passengers request the service without feeling shy about asking the crew. I liked the Companion Seat most. This is the seat I'd book once the new Qsuite finally flies. Angelo De Guzman After exploring the different configurations, I'd choose the forward-facing window seat in the Companion Suite. It feels more natural to me, with better surrounding surfaces and the option to open the space toward a companion when I want company. But getting a Qsuite seat comes at a significant premium. Round-trip fares in April between New York and Doha on Qatar's Boeing 777-300ER cost around $4,000 in business class, compared with about $600 in economy. events.title: A Trump-sized shadow looms over the Supreme Court's new term
events.summary: The Supreme Court 's next chapter begins Monday, with the justices set to decide key questions involving President Trump's immigration agenda, climate -change litigation and gun control in their new term. The big picture: But one of the most closely watched fights may be on Truth Social, rather than the docket, as an increasingly agitated Trump chastises the high court he helped shape. The executive and judicial branches are set for another round in the white-columned ring with a president who moves at breakneck speed . State of play: The court recently agreed to hear two major immigration cases, one over mandatory detention for certain immigrants and another over deporting immigrants to third countries where they lack ties. On the latter, the high court allowed the administration to restart its fast-tracked third-country deportations late last month while it considers the underlying legal questions in December. The court agreed Thursday to take up the detention case, setting the stage to test the Trump administration's legal interpretation that noncitizens who entered the country illegally, but have been living in the U.S., are to be held without bond. While federal appeals courts have been divided on the issue, a vast majority — nine of the 11 — have rejected the Trump administration's interpretation. Flashback: While the Supreme Court shot down Trump's attempt to undermine birthright citizenship last term, it handed him a number of immigration wins and green-lit policies on its shadow docket. Those victories for Trump allowed the administration to end temporary protected status , enforce stricter asylum rules and use a revamped tool to check voters' citizenship . Zoom out: Before those cases come to the bench, the court will hear arguments Monday in a key climate case that could determine the fate of state-court lawsuits nationwide seeking climate damages from oil giants, Axios' Ben Geman reports. The court also added two other cases to its lineup Thursday, on top of the mandatory detention debate: One is about a federal law protecting land use by religious groups brought by a missionary organization, and the other is about military benefits in divorce settlement agreements. Later this year, the court will weigh the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style weapons and consider whether Arizona can mandate proof of citizenship for people registering to vote. More disputes over other Trump policies are sure to reach the court this term. Friction point: Though the high court has inflated executive power and gave the president a number of summer shadow docket wins, it also checked some of his most audacious actions last term. He didn't like that. After the justices blocked the administration's pre-midterm attempt to rewrite mail-in voting rules, the president raged against his own Supreme Court picks. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves," he wrote on Truth Social. In a recent interview with Time, the president said he regretted nominating them, saying, "I gave them the chance of a lifetime, and it's unfortunate what they did." events.title: Yemeni forces reclaim Dhubab, key positions near Bab al-Mandeb from Houthis
events.summary: The army of the internationally recognised government says it seized key positions near the waterway before Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials’ meeting in Riyadh. The army of Yemen’s internationally recognised government says it has reclaimed control of the Dhubab district and key positions near the Bab al-Mandeb strait and also launched a “strategic offensive” on the capital Sanaa, a day after the government announced the launch of a major military operation against the Houthis. “Forces from the Homeland Shield Forces and the Giants Brigades carried out a large-scale military operation with air cover targeting Houthi militia positions and movements in several areas of the district,” Yemen’s Saudi-backed military said in a statement carried by Yemen’s news agency Saba on Monday. list 1 of 4 Saudi-led coalition dismisses ‘misleading’ Houthi claim of Riyadh attack list 2 of 4 Inside the ‘kill box’: The Yemenis who stayed behind in Houthi-held Mocha list 3 of 4 Yemen’s leader announces military operation to retake Houthi-held territory list 4 of 4 Why is fighting intensifying in Yemen’s Taiz governorate? “During the operation, they advanced and seized important positions – cutting off supply lines and roads leading to Bab al-Mandeb,” an unnamed army source told Saba. The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, meaning Supporters of God in Arabic, lost many fighters and several others were wounded in the clashes, with military equipment destroyed or damaged, according to the source. Government forces are “continuing to comb and secure the liberated areas and cut off supply routes to the Houthi terrorist militia”, Saba reported. Shortly after the announcement, the Saudi Arabia-led military coalition an air campaign was under way against the Houthis. Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the Yemeni forces. He said the coalition has secured “air protection” of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets. Later, government forces announced the launch of a “strategic offensive” on Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, which has been controlled by the Houthis for more than a decade. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the battlefield reports. Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the government to retreat to Aden. The war escalated after a fragile truce struck between the government and the Houthis in 2022 collapsed in July. In mid-September, the Houthis swept across parts of western Yemen, seizing the port city of Mocha and key strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Since then, anti-Houthi forces have largely stabilised the front lines. On Sunday, ⁠⁠Rashad al-Alimi, the chairman of ⁠⁠Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, the executive body of the internationally recognised government, announced the start of military operations to retake the ⁠⁠remaining territory held by ⁠⁠the Houthis. The battlefield reports come as Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar arrived in Saudi Arabia for a meeting with Saudi and Turkish officials under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement . Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif and military chief Asim Munir will accompany Dar at Monday’s talks in Riyadh with their counterparts from Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, the Pakistani Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on X. Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the defence pact on August 7 to strengthen collective deterrence and expand defence cooperation in the region. The pact stipulates that an attack on one of the three countries is considered an attack on them all. Pakistan’s Dar said last week the “ urgent talks ” would address a proposal for political engagement with the Iran-aligned Houthis as an alternative to the military option, following an approach by Tehran. Al Jazeera’s Michael Appel said the Yemen war is expected to feature prominently in the Saudi-hosted talks. “Civilians remain caught up in the fragmented front line of this war, and the announcement of an expanded military operation leaves tens of thousands with the prospect of continued displacement and hunger as a humanitarian crisis takes hold,” he said.

events.title: ﻿The UK’s G20 presidency will push Andy Burnham to the centre of the global stage. What will he use it for? | Michael Jacobs
events.summary: ﻿The UK’s G20 presidency will push Andy Burnham to the centre of the global stage. What will he use it for? This is a chance for the PM to advance his progressive agenda and tackle urgent issues such as AI regulation and climate action A mong the many crucial decisions Andy Burnham has to make over the next few weeks, one has gone almost completely unremarked: what Britain’s priorities will be when it assumes the presidency of the G20 next year. Burnham has said he wants to concentrate on domestic policy. But with the world in turmoil, chairing the group of the world’s largest economies will be one of his most important responsibilities. The last time the UK chaired the forum was in 2009, when Gordon Brown presided over the rescue of the global economy after the financial crash. Before the London summit in April 2009, the French president, Nicolas Sarkozy, had wrung his hands, saying that “none of us has a plan”. Barack Obama had a quick response to this: “Gordon has a plan.” He did. Brown got the G20 to agree to a $5tn fiscal stimulus among its member states, increase International Monetary Fund lending to developing countries and create a new global coordinator for financial regulation, the Financial Stability Board. But 2009 was a rare year for the G20, in that it actually achieved something. In general, the long communiques issued at its annual leaders’ summits reflect only the lowest-common-denominator agreement on broad principles. The G20 rarely commits its members to doing anything they were not planning to do anyway, and only occasionally makes genuinely collective decisions. One of the most consequential was the suspension of developing countries’ debt during the Covid pandemic in 2020 and the subsequent establishment of a “ common framework ” for debt treatment. Indeed, for what is meant to be the effective executive committee of the global economy, the G20 is an oddly weak institution. Its 19 members (plus the EU and the African Union) have no HQ or staff and do not even have a standing website: if you want to know what the G20 has agreed over the past 20 years you need to go to a set of unofficial webpages hosted by some enterprising academics at the University of Toronto. For most countries, hosting the G20 summit is a chance to impress its domestic audience by showing that its head of government bestrides the world stage. Last year Donald Trump boycotted it ; the South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, was glad simply to get any kind of agreed communique. This year, the US is the host, with one of Trump’s own properties near Miami the summit venue in December: expect a show of personal and US power and very little attempt to achieve anything by way of multilateral cooperation. But that makes Burnham’s task next year even more critical. The UK needs to show that it is still possible for the world’s leading nations – including the US and China – to work together to meet the key challenges facing the world. So what should the UK’s presidency priorities be? First, agreement on the need for, and a process towards, a global treaty on the regulation of artificial intelligence. After the recent alarm over the existential risks of AI, the UK has a chance to lead the world towards a global agreement on its control. Even if Trump is unwilling to sign up, getting the rest of the world to do so, seeking a form of global “technological security”, would be a vital achievement. A future US president might well wish to accede later. Second, acknowledgment of the growing risk to food security and a plan to deal with it. The incoming “supersized” El Niño weather pattern is combining with the climate crisis, soil and biodiversity loss, and the impact of the war in the Middle East on diesel and fertiliser costs to create a perfect storm for the world’s food system. Agricultural yields are falling and food prices rising, leaving millions of people at risk of hunger. The G20 needs to act to prevent it. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more Third, acknowledgment of accelerating climate insecurity – the severe risks posed by the climate emergency to all countries’ economies and societies – and agreement on coordinated measures to improve climate resilience. Though the Trump administration does not support emissions reduction, it does accept the need to adapt to climate change, and this year’s extreme weather events have impressed on all governments how urgent this is. The G20 should agree to provide more support to the most vulnerable countries. Fourth, agreement on a debt restructuring programme for low- and middle-income economies whose debt – through no fault of their own, but because of rising global interest rates – has now become unsustainable. For too many countries the compounding of debt burdens with rising energy and food prices has made sustainable economic growth all but impossible.

events.title: Yemen war: What’s the latest, as government forces claim advances?
events.summary: After launching major military offensive to reclaim Houthi-held areas, Yemen’s government says it has retaken a key district. Yemen’s internationally recognised government has announced a major military campaign to retake all territory controlled by the Houthis, marking a new escalation in a civil war that had largely been frozen for several years before battles intensified in recent weeks. The announcement by Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), the executive body of the Yemeni government, comes after weeks of heavy fighting and major Houthi advances along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategically important city of Taiz. list 1 of 3 A Yemeni family spends a week on the road fleeing another Houthi offensive list 2 of 3 Houthis claim strike on Aramco site as Yemen fighting intensifies list 3 of 3 Saudi-led coalition dismisses ‘misleading’ Houthi claim of Riyadh attack On Monday, Yemeni government forces said they were launching a “strategic” offensive on the country’s capital, Sanaa, which the Houthis have held since 2014. Earlier in the day, the Yemeni forces — who are backed by Saudi Arabia — said they had regained control of the Dhubab district on the country’s west coast near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, though the Houthis denied the announcement. The fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, meaning Supporters of God in Arabic – and Yemeni government forces has expanded since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July, displacing more than 100,000 people since then. Last month, the Houthis launched a rapid offensive that captured about 150km (93 miles) of Red Sea coastline and areas around Bab al-Mandeb, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, which is a critical route for international shipping. On Monday, the foreign minister of Yemen’s internationally recognised government requested more support from the international community to defeat the Houthis, saying it is “in the world’s interest” for the country to be stable. “We call upon our brothers, friends and the international community to support the Yemeni people, their state, and their national institutions in confronting the terrorist Houthi militia, which seizes their will by force of arms and lays waste to the lives of their sons – after exhausting all opportunities for de-escalation and peace,” Afrah al-Zouba said in a post on X. So what is the latest on the fighting, and what does Yemen’s government hope to achieve? What is the latest on the fighting? The Yemeni government army said on Monday 1,747 Houthi fighters had been “neutralised” in 1,122 military operations in the Saada, al-Jawf and Taiz governorates and along Yemen’s western coast. Military spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said the attacks targeted artillery and rocket positions, fortifications, supply lines, reinforcements and command centres. Al-Nuzaili said warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers were involved and 364 military and logistical vehicles had been destroyed or disabled. The casualty and equipment figures could not be independently verified. Yemen’s internationally recognised government also announced that its forces had taken control of Dhubab on the Red Sea coast and were launching a major offensive on Sanaa. Elsewhere, the front line in Marib governorate in northeastern Yemen witnessed an escalation in fighting on Monday. A military source told Al Jazeera that government forces launched an attack on Houthi positions on the Raghwan front in the north of the governorate, coinciding with air raids on Houthi positions and reinforcements. The source said the raids targeted Houthi positions near Mount Helan as well as an arms depot and military reinforcements northwest of Marib. On Sunday, a Saudi-led coalition said its forces carried out 97 attacks against Houthi reinforcements around Taiz and the Tor al-Baha front using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers. On the developments in Taiz, Al Jazeera’s Yemen bureau chief, Saeed Thabet, said Houthi operations in the rural areas around the strategic city are based on guerrilla tactics aimed at easing pressure on the coastal front and tightening the blockade of the road to Aden. What has Yemen’s government announced? Al-Alimi said on Sunday that government forces had been ordered to launch military operations to regain Houthi-controlled territory and restore state authority across Yemen. “We have instructed the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned tasks under an approved plan until the country is liberated from the Houthis,” al-Alimi said. Military sources told the Reuters news agency that over the previous 48 hours, the Houthis advanced against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Taiz, pushing forward along the last remaining road linking the city with Aden on Yemen’s southern coast.

events.title: America's EV graveyard has grown by nearly 20 discontinued vehicles this year
events.summary: Several EV models have been pulled from automaker's lineups in 2026. It extends a trend that stretched from September 2025. Hyundai USA Automakers have reorganized their EV lineups since September 2025, when federal tax credits ended. Sagging demand, tariffs, and a new generation of EVs have also led to several product cancellations. Business Insider compiled a list of EVs that have been killed or indefinitely delayed in 2026. American EV sales aren't looking too hot . Since September 2025, when the federal $7,500 tax credit for US-made EVs ended, fewer shoppers have chosen a battery-powered car for their next set of wheels. In the second quarter of 2026, deliveries dropped 20.5%, according to Cox Automotive data. That follows a 27% drop in first-quarter 2026 EV sales and a 36% plunge in EV sales in the final quarter of 2025. The slowdown began reshaping which new car models appeared on US dealership lots last year. By the end of 2025, Ford ended production of the F-150 Lightning, Nissan axed the Ariya, Acura stopped building the ZDX, and Volkswagen paused the ID. Buzz until 2027. That shake-up has continued into 2026, but the lineup changes aren't a  wholesale retreat from EVs . "It's a part of many legacy automakers retooling their EV strategies," Seth Goldstein, an analyst at Morningstar, told Business Insider. "A lot of automakers are going back to the drawing board. They're looking to discontinue unprofitable EVs and replace them with more affordable, long-range EVs." Business Insider is tracking every EV canceled or postponed since January 1, 2026 — a list we'll keep updating as the industry redraws its all-electric road map. Hyundai Ioniq 6 Standard Hyundai. confirmed to Business Insider that the Standard model Ioniq 6 is discontinued in the US. Sjoerd van der Wal/Getty Images Hyundai confirmed to Business Insider that it will stop selling the Korean-built, standard Ioniq 6 in the US. The retro-styled sedan never matched the success of its crossover sibling, the Ioniq 5, which has sold more than 30,000 units this year. Hyundai said it sold just 229 Ioniq 6s in February, its final full month of sales. "Sedan sales have declined a lot over the past decade, and the Ioniq 6 is no exception," Sam Abuelsamid, the vice president of market research at Telemetry, told Business Insider. "Without enough sales to justify US production, the numbers just don't add up for Hyundai." Hyundai said it plans to import a limited number of high-performance Ioniq 6 N models to the US — a pricier variant with more oomph in the electric motor and track-focused upgrades. "In the meantime, 2025 Ioniq 6 sedans continue to be available at dealers alongside our award-winning, US-assembled Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 9 SUVs," the automaker said. The Ioniq 6 will still ship to Canadian dealerships. 2026 Hyundai Kona Electric Hyundai also paused imports for the 2026 Kona Electric. It is expected to return next year. Hyundai In 2019, Hyundai electrified its popular Kona crossover, swapping the gas engine for a battery-powered drivetrain. It became one of the automaker's first mass-market EVs. That run is now on pause. Hyundai said in February that it would not ship the 2026 Kona Electric from its Korean plants to US dealerships. Like the Ioniq 6, the Kona Electric remains available in limited numbers as a 2025 model. The model could return for the 2027 model year. With a starting price around $33,000, it was one of the cheapest EVs on the US market in 2025. Kia Niro EV Kia's Niro EV is reportedly on the chopping block. The Korean automaker is planning on keeping the hybrid version around. Kia The Kia Niro EV has been discontinued in the US, InsideEVs reports. First introduced in the US for the 2018 model year, the Niro EV was developed from Kia's small Niro crossover, which was also offered in hybrid and plug-in hybrid variants. The model received a facelift for the 2026 model year, and the plug-in hybrid version was discontinued as part of the lineup adjustment. The Niro EV was imported from Kia's Hwaseong plant in South Korea, leaving it exposed to ongoing US automotive tariffs. Those added costs, combined with slowing sales in the EV segment, reportedly made the model increasingly difficult to justify at American dealerships, according to InsideEVs. Kia has not responded to a request for comment from Business Insider. Tesla Model S Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced the automaker would kill the Model S - the company's first ground-up vehicle - this year. VCG/VCG via Getty Images The Model S was critical to Tesla's historic ascent. When the sedan debuted in 2012, it was the company's first ground-up vehicle — and a sharp break from the slow, quirky EVs that came before it. With hypercar-like acceleration, sleek body lines, and a tech-forward cabin, the sedan made going electric feel aspirational rather than a legacy automaker's compliance exercise. That shift helped propel Tesla into America's dominant EV automaker. Now, despite its historic role, CEO Elon Musk says the $94,990 sedan is headed for an "honorable discharge" after years of sliding sales . Tesla Model X Tesla is also ending production of the high-priced Model X SUV. Tesla The Model X is also going the way of the dodo. Tesla's second built-from-scratch vehicle will end production in the second quarter of 2026 amid soft demand. The SUV starts at $99,990. Launched in 2015, the Model X was ambitious. And complicated. Its signature second-row falcon-wing doors — which opened by pivoting upward via electronically connected hinges mounted to the roof — became a production headache. Musk once called the car a " Fabergé egg. " The production lines that made the two vehicles will now build the company's Optimus robots. "We're really moving into a future that is based on autonomy," Musk said while announcing their final days, adding that the decision was "slightly sad." Kia EV6 GT and EV9 GT Kia is also ending sales of its highest-powered EV6. David Benito/Getty Images Kia's flagship EV portfolio is also getting tweaked — but more narrowly. The Korean automaker is delaying the GT trims of two models, the EV6 and EV9. Those versions are the highest-performance variants in each lineup. Kia confirmed to Business Insider that the GT trims are delayed "until further notice" due to "changing market conditions." Other trims — which are made at Kia's plant in West Point, Georgia — remain on sale in the US. "This delay does not impact the availability of other trims in the EV6 and EV9 lineups," the company said. Volvo EX30 Volvo will stop selling the EX30 in the US. Volvo Volvo has confirmed to Business Insider that it's discontinuing the EX30 in the US. The small SUV was meant to be a breakthrough in America's electric car market: a ground-up EV with a starting price under $35,000. Tariffs — spanning both the Biden and Trump administrations — upended those plans. Volvo first intended to build the EX30 in China, then shifted production to Belgium,

events.title: A Prediction Market About the Past? Sure, Why Not!
events.summary: Would you put money on whether Covid-19 originated from a lab ? How about whether some of the footage from the Apollo 11 moon landing was actually filmed on Earth? Verifact Markets, a new startup that bills itself as a “prediction market for disputed facts,” is betting that people will be eager to weigh in on questions like these. The company’s premise is so quirky it sounds like something a couple of philosophy and economics majors dreamed after too many bong rips in their dorm room: Instead of wagering on the future, why not trade on stuff that already happened? When Verifact Markets launched on Friday, some of the initial topics traders could take a position on included whether Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide and whether insurance behemoth State Farm “intentionally delayed” claims related to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires . The featured market during beta testing was, indeed, about the origins of Covid-19. (As of writing, the market is still open, with “true” priced at 76 cents and “false” at 32; the majority of participants had put money on the pandemic beginning at Wuhan Institute of Virology.) Verifact Markets is being funded and incubated by Positron Capital Management, the family office of tech investor Peter Wokwicz. He envisions the startup as a way to settle debates over hot-button issues like the amount of energy consumed by AI data centers. “I’m excited, because nobody’s done this before,” Wokwicz says. “We’re not going to shy away from controversial markets.” In a regular prediction market , participants buy financial instruments known as event contracts, which are pegged to whether a specific event will take place in the future. Topics range from which team will win the Super Bowl to what the price of bitcoin will be in 15 minutes to whether the US and Iran will reach a nuclear deal. Someone who buys a “yes” contract on Polymarket that the Bears will start Case Keenum next week will make money if that happens. Similarly, someone who bets “no” on Kalshi that it will rain in Miami tomorrow will lose money if there’s a downpour. Each prediction market has its own rules about how it resolves events, and sometimes things can get messy, like when Polymarket bettors tussled over whether Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky actually wore a suit , or when Kalshi traders revolted over how the platform settled a market on whether Iran’s supreme leader would leave power. Verifact Markets’ setup is even messier. That’s by design, since the platform focuses specifically on scenarios where people disagree on what took place. It lists markets for past events that it considers “disputed” and lets its customers wager “true” or “false” on whether they really happened. People can also submit “evidence” for or against their position, and the company plans to offer rewards for credible documentation that helps resolve markets. If Verifact Markets determines that there’s enough evidence to make a call, it does so. If it still can’t tell, the company will “expire” a market and pay out users based on its calculation of the odds at the time. According to Verifact Markets chief executive and cofounder Rodrigo Aquino, the markets themselves won’t determine whether something is true or false. That means even if all of the customers in a given market voted “true,” that won’t necessarily make it so. Trading prices will be factored in alongside other evidence and documentation that is submitted to the company by users. It is also planning to launch its own research system, which Aquino describes as “patent pending.” When I ask Aquino how the system works, he keeps the answer impressively vague: “We are analyzing, multi-dimensionally, a multitude of data points,” he says, noting that the process is “very mathematical, very quantitative” and also “very secretive.” When I point out that credibly determining how the Covid pandemic started would be a massive news story, resolving a mystery that has eluded scientists for years, Aquino remains upbeat. “It’s doable,” he says. Verifact says that it is currently in talks with market makers about providing liquidity. Right now, the project is so small that it is being bootstrapped by Positron Capital Management. There are a number of ongoing lawsuits in the US over whether prediction markets should be considered financial instruments or gambling, but it’s hard to discern how Verifact would factor into that debate because of its rather odd business model. For the time being, the company is only offering its markets to people outside of the United States as it looks for the most viable legal path forward domestically, as it is not a licensed exchange in the US. But Wokwicz claims he purchased a regulated financial exchange in the last year and intends to roll Verifact into it when he can.

events.title: Oil prices would have hit $200 a barrel if not for East-West pipeline, Aramco chief says
events.summary: Brent crude prices would have reached up to $200 per barrel if Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline did not exist, the chief executive of Saudi Aramco said. The company ​can ⁠make its maximum ⁠sustainable production ​capacity of ⁠12 million barrels per day available ⁠within days, ​Amin Nasser ​told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday. “Our system is intact,” Mr Nasser said. Aramco has ‌the ⁠strategic ​reserves and ​flexibility ‌to ⁠isolate or shift output ⁠as required, he added. Brent crude, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, has been trading around $100 a barrel over the past month, even as more tankers are transiting the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has been playing a vital role as Aramco over the past month boosted crude shipments from its main export terminal at Ras Tanura. The company reacted quickly to a temporary halt to its main cross-country pipeline after an attack last month. Aramco has since brought flows on the East-West pipeline back to about 80 per cent of capacity, meaning it also has more oil to ship from the Red Sea. Aramco has ensured its oil supplies proved resilient throughout the conflict by relying on international storage and working to quickly repair damaged infrastructure, Mr Nasser said. He did not mention reports of recent attacks on the kingdom in his speech. Aramco is looking for alternative crude export routes and additional international storage facilities to avoid relying too much on any single method of reaching global buyers, he added. 'Scarily thin' reserves However, the oil stockpiles that cushion the world from supply shocks have become “scarily thin”, putting markets at risk of worsening unless the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens, Mr Nasser said. He was speaking only days after governments in the world’s biggest economies announced plans to release as much as 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks to ease rising fuel costs. “Until Hormuz fully reopens and confidence returns, the crude reality is that pressure at both ends of the barrel will intensify,” he said. “While the squeeze on crude is serious, refined fuel prices have risen even more sharply.” Releasing stockpiles will buy economies some time but will not fix the imbalance between supply and demand, Mr Nasser said. Even after the vital shipping chokepoint at Hormuz reopens, it may take as long as two years for energy-consuming countries to replenish their stockpiles, he said. Gulf producers are working to step up production and exports and have succeeded in boosting crude flows to near prewar levels. The higher flows have provided scant relief for oil markets, which are still pricing in security risks to supply in the Gulf and Red Sea. With inputs from Bloomberg and Reuters
