events.title: Radiant World misses salary payments for employees in September
events.summary: A number of banks have cut Radiant World off since Bloomberg first reported in July on creditors’ concerns that the iron ore trader had been raising money using falsified documents. Radiant World employees in Singapore, China and Europe have not received their September salaries amid legal and financial troubles involving the company. The company faces accusations of using falsified documents, leading to banks cutting ties and legal actions, including Mizuho Bank seeking management removal. KPMG was appointed as interim judicial manager to oversee operations and conduct employee interviews, while Radiant World denies any wrongdoing. SINGAPORE – Some employees of Radiant World say they have not received their September salaries, an apparent delay that offers a glimpse of disruptions inside the iron ore trader as its operations are transferred to the care of court-appointed managers. The people, working in Singapore, China and Europe, said they had not been paid their wages on the usual schedule around the fourth week of the month, and that they were not aware of any colleagues having received anything as of Oct 5 . Several said there had been hold-ups in the past, with their monthly salaries ultimately paid as late as a few days into the new month. But they reported widespread concern among staff over the past week, given the multiple legal actions launched against the company. A number of banks have cut Radiant World off since Bloomberg first reported in July on creditors’ concerns that the trader had been raising money using falsified documents. Some of the employees – all of whom asked not to be named as the issue is private – said that in recent months, their salaries had been paid from a company account in Dubai. It was not immediately clear what the cause of the delay was, or if the salaries would ultimately be paid. A spokesman for Radiant World did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for KPMG, appointed as interim judicial manager in September , also did not respond to Bloomberg queries. Multiple lenders have accused Radiant World of providing falsified documents. Mizuho Bank, a creditor, began legal proceedings in August to remove the management of the merchant’s key operating company in Singapore, according to a court document seen by Bloomberg. That was granted in September , when a Singapore court appointed KPMG to take charge. Restructuring executives from the firm have begun contacting current and former employees this week to arrange interviews, according to the people. Mizuho said in a court filing that it had strong reasons to believe it was the victim of fraud perpetrated by Radiant World. The Singapore judge overseeing the case said in her ruling last week that the trader was, or was likely to become, unable to pay its debts. Radiant World has denied wrongdoing. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Strong data. Bad vibes. Voters are judging Trump's economy by prices.
events.summary: President Trump's economic data keeps getting stronger. His economic polling keeps getting worse by the day. Why it matters: The midterms are less than a month away, and the administration is circling the drain on voters' No. 1 issue. It may be too late to change that, but it's also not clear anyone has much of a plan to try. What they're saying: "If I say 'oh, people are wrong, the economy is great,' then it looks like I'm insensitive. And if I then go into why the economy is great, then it looks like I'm insensitive," National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett said Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union." "It's true that the polls, which have gotten the president's success wrong every time, have been saying that people are looking a little bit depressed about the economy. But if you look at their actions, the actions speak way louder than words," Hassett added, citing spending and default data. The big picture: There is ample evidence the economy is, statistically speaking, relatively strong. 💰 Economic growth is solid and accelerating. 💪 The labor market is relatively stable . 💵 The K-shaped economy is ending as lower-end wages rise. 🛍️ Public and private data say consumers are spending more than ever. Yes, but: People feel lousy. ☹️ The Conference Board's consumer confidence index is at a 12-year low. 🐘 Republican sentiment in particular is eroding at its fastest rate since the Great Financial Crisis, per University of Michigan data. 🪫 38% of voters told the latest CBS News poll their personal finances are fairly or very bad — a reflection, perhaps, of the fact that inflation has outpaced wage growth for months now. (When respondents were asked what they think about when they rate the economy, 91% said "prices.") 👎 73% disapprove of President Trump's handling of the economy, per the latest AP-NORC survey, the lowest rating he — or President Biden — ever had. (69% say Trump's handling of cost-of-living issues has been worse than they expected in his second term.) Friction point: When voters go to the polls, they don't bring the latest release from the Bureau of Economic Analysis with them. They bring their feelings, and those are very bad. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told " The Axios Show " the administration wasn't going to repeat the Biden-era mistake of telling people how to feel. But Trump himself said last week that Republicans weren't doing a good enough job of messaging . The intrigue: So far, Trump's strategy seems to be the rich-uncle theory, which doesn't appear to be paying off with voters. He continues to promise $5,000 checks for every adult citizen if Republicans win the midterms — a $1.3 trillion bombshell that most people don't believe he'll ever pay. On Saturday, he promised seniors $2 billion in Medicare rebates , a big number that works out to about two weeks' worth of premium payments. Between the lines: Some of the tension comes from the nature of the economic boom, an AI-fueled bonanza that nonetheless appears to be leaving many ordinary Americans behind. It's not a K-shaped economy, says Krishna Guha, head of economics at Evercore ISI, but a "gator economy" — as in an alligator's mouth, where the bottom stays flat and the top is pointing to the sky poised to chomp. The bottom line: There's good reason to think the economy's not that bad. There's even better reason to think voters don't care. Emily Peck contributed reporting.

events.title: Fewer young Americans are ‘thriving,’ poll finds
events.summary: The number of young Americans who say they’re “thriving” is near a low point while the share of middle-age adults who say the same is at a nadir, underscoring the level of relative dissatisfaction among these key demographic groups ahead of the midterms. Only 44% of adults ages 18 to 29 describe themselves as thriving, according to Gallup , 20 points lower than the high measured in 2010. Forty-five percent of adults 30 to 44 say the same; both figures have declined in the years since the COVID-19 pandemic. These declines appear to be tied to increases in rates of depression, among other factors. The share of those ages 45 to 64 is also at a low of 46%, on par with the measure during the 2008 financial crisis. In sharp contrast, those 65 and older are more likely than ever to say they’re thriving, which appears largely driven by satisfaction with their economic situation. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen shared his best and worst investments with Business Insider. Neither of them involves money.
events.summary: GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen. GameStop Ryan Cohen outlined his best and worst investments to Business Insider in an email in late September. GameStop's billionaire CEO said nothing could match his return from spending time with his father. The Chewy cofounder said his biggest investing mistake was trusting the wrong people. Ryan Cohen says the best and worst investments of his life have to do with people, not money. GameStop's CEO and Chewy's billionaire cofounder told Business Insider by email last week that nothing has yielded a greater return for him than spending "time with my dad." "I'm still collecting dividends," Cohen said about his father, Ted, who died in 2019. Cohen launched a "Teddy" series of children's books in 2022 to share his father's lessons with a wider audience. He detailed some of them in an email to Business Insider in 2020. "My dad showed me how to trust my instincts," he wrote. "When I was a child, he treated me like an adult. He never patronized me. When I asked him for his opinion, he turned it back on me and asked me what I thought. He never wanted to bias me with his. He was the best listener. He was a glassware importer and knew his business inside and out. I learned how to build my company by watching him build his." In a prior phone interview, Cohen said that his father had the "greatest influence" on him of anyone, and "taught me everything." "Most importantly, he taught me to shave," he quipped. I just played with my dad. Dreams with him are the best. — Ryan Cohen (@ryancohen) May 23, 2022 In his email last week, Cohen said his gravest investing error was putting his faith in others who talked a big game but ultimately disappointed him. " Trusting people who were better at selling themselves than doing the work," he said. Warren Buffett , Cohen's biggest professional influence after his dad, has warned against falling for false promises. In his final shareholder letter as Berkshire Hathaway CEO, Buffett wrote that "our country has forever had many scoundrels and promoters who seek to take advantage of those who mistakenly trust them with their savings." Writing about brokers in his 1983 letter, Buffett said: "Those who cannot fill your pocket will confidently fill your ear." Cohen was clearly burned by people who sold him on their abilities but failed to deliver, leading him to chalk up his investment of time, energy, and resources in them as a loss. events.title: Latino men swung hard to Trump in 2024. Now they're swinging back
events.summary: Latino voters, whose dramatic shift toward President Trump helped power his 2024 victory, are moving sharply back toward Democrats ahead of the midterms, two new national polls show. Why it matters: Republicans built pieces of their 2026 strategy, including newly drawn House districts in Texas and Florida, around the assumption that Trump's historic Latino gains would endure. A reversal is complicating that bet in key races. Trump's breakthrough with Latino men was among the clearest signs of a changing GOP coalition in 2024. Two years later, those gains look far less durable, though Democrats haven't recovered all the ground they lost in the last decade. The latest: A new NBC News/Telemundo poll found Latino voters preferred Democratic control of Congress 59%–35% — a 24-point advantage, double the margin the same poll found in 2024. A new CBS News/YouGov poll tells the same story: Hispanic likely voters favor Democratic House candidates 60%–39%. Zoom in: Latino men have undergone a particularly strong political whiplash. Hillary Clinton won Latino men by 31 points in 2016, according to the Edison National Election Pool exit poll , and Biden won them by 23 points in 2020. But in 2024, Trump won them by 10 points. NBC now finds Latino men preferring Democratic congressional control 53%–39%. Stunning stat: About one in seven Latino voters who say they backed Trump in 2024 now want Democrats to take control of Congress. A majority of Latino voters say their congressional vote will be a signal against Trump. Driving the shift: The economic squeeze felt by Latino voters hasn't changed much, but who they're blaming has. Nearly two-thirds of Latino voters say their income is falling behind the cost of living in the NBC poll, almost exactly where that number stood in 2024. But 78% disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living. Democrats now hold a 21-point advantage on handling the economy, after Trump held a 4-point edge over Harris in NBC's 2024 poll. Trump's mass-deportation agenda has also sparked backlash: 67% say Trump's enforcement has gone too far. The enforcement campaign has also become personal: 31% say they or someone close now carries ID because of ICE concerns, and 27% know someone detained or deported. Yes, but: Polling voters a month before a midterm isn't the same as measuring who actually turns out. Pew found that Trump's 2024 Hispanic gains were driven largely by changes in who voted that year, not by Biden voters switching to Trump. In the NBC poll, 17% of voters said they or someone close to them was considering not voting in person because of fear of immigration enforcement. Between the lines: Despite all this, Democrats haven't repaired their brand with Latino voters. Their net favorability has actually fallen by one point from 2024, but the GOP's has fallen by 18 points. In 2016, 55% of Latino voters viewed the Democratic Party positively and 24% negatively — a 31-point net positive rating. Today, it's 41% positive and 42% negative. Republicans have still made lasting inroads: Just 16% of Latino voters viewed the GOP positively in 2016, compared with 27% today. But negative views have also risen, from 57% then to 62% now. What we're watching: Both parties are fighting over a large and growing Latino electorate in key races across Arizona, California, Florida and Texas.

events.title: Coach services could be cut due to record diesel prices, UK operators warn
events.summary: Rising fuel costs are pushing hundreds of firms out of business, threatening school transport, firms say Coach operators have said record diesel prices could force cuts to services including school transport, as hauliers warn rising fuel costs are pushing hundreds of firms out of business. The average price of diesel on UK forecourts hit a fresh record of more than £2 a litre last week, as the war in the Middle East continues to disrupt global fuel supplies. Alison Edwards, the director of policy at the Confederation of Passenger Transport (CPT), said the cost of fuel had “surged this year to unsustainable levels, pushing coach operators’ already tight margins to breaking point”. “It is time for urgent action,” she said. “Without intervention, soaring prices will mean difficult decisions on the availability of services, including home-to-school transport, and the viability of businesses.” Edwards said 85% of independent coach operators are family businesses, and called on the government to provide temporary support with the cost of diesel, adding that the industry “needs help”. Local bus operators in England have already received help with fuel costs via subsidies to help cover running costs. Coach companies, which say they carry out a similar role, have received no equivalent support. Richard Smith, the managing director of the Road Haulage Association (RHA), said the haulage sector was under similar strain. “Businesses in our sector operate on slim profit margins, typically about 2%, so the continuing high fuel costs are a huge challenge for us,” he said. He said hauliers were now paying an extra £350 a week for each truck compared with before the Iran war. “It’s just unsustainable,” he said. “If haulage, coach and van operators can’t pass these costs on, they struggle, and we’ve seen hundreds of transport businesses going bust already this year.” Hauliers are calling for a pause on planned fuel duty rises, and a rebate to help offset the cost of diesel. The RAC motoring organisation has called for the government to expand its 5p cut in fuel duty, which has already been extended until the end of the year . Rhys Hackling, the managing director of Direct Connect Logistics, said the impact on his own business had been “absolutely enormous”. The company runs 22 lorries out of Oxfordshire, Northamptonshire and Warrington, transporting goods ranging from supermarket products to live events equipment. He said the company was spending much more on fuel compared with last year: “We normally spend about £50,000 a month on fuel … it’s now knocking on £65,000.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Many hauliers work on fixed contracts with customers, Hackling said, meaning rising fuel costs squeeze or wipe out their margins entirely. “If these events continue, then it’s going to put a lot of haulage firms out of business,” he said. “There’s less confidence in the market, so there are fewer jobs, and that means the work dries up very, very quickly. Somebody somewhere is having to pay for this, whether it’s the haulage firm or whether it’s the consumer.” In a move offering some hope that fuel prices might ease, leaders of G7 nations said on Friday that they would release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles. The announcement was partly in response to Donald Trump suggesting he might introduce a ban on diesel exports after the rise in sales to overseas buyers pushed US prices to record highs. It appears to have averted the threat, which could have pushed diesel prices even higher in the UK, since Britain relies on the US for about a third of its diesel imports and does not refine enough to meet demand on its own. The transport minister, Keir Mather, has said the UK’s fuel supply is “inherently resilient” and that people “shouldn’t be concerned about shortages”.

events.title: Formula One to probe software bug behind Bahrain GP chaos in Sepang
events.summary: Drivers faced glitches at the race in Malaysia, where Lewis Hamilton had to stop and restart his car on the track. Formula One’s governing body has promised a full investigation into a software bug that caused chaos and forced the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted, with drivers feeling like they were in battery-powered cars made of Lego. Ferrari’s seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull’s four-time champion and eventual race winner Max Verstappen were among several affected by the glitch on a formation lap after torrential rain and a long delay at Malaysia’s steamy Sepang circuit on Sunday. list 1 of 4 Formula One: Verstappen clinches Bahrain GP in first win of 2026 list 2 of 4 Mercedes no longer have the fastest car in F1, says leader Antonelli list 3 of 4 Kimi Antonelli takes maiden Spanish Grand Prix win that ‘Lando deserved’. list 4 of 4 ‘Racing is my life’: Alonso to stay with F1 team Aston Martin in 2027 Verstappen compared the experience to a “Lego race” held at Silverstone before the British Grand Prix while Hamilton, the sport’s most successful driver of all time, had to stop his car on track and restart it in what he said was a career first. The episode was the latest in a difficult first season for the new era of cars and engines, with drivers at the pinnacle of motorsport unhappy since the opening race with the power units’ increased electrical component and the need for energy management. FIA said afterwards that “an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit’s sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars”. “As a result, the FIA technical department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain, enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the power unit before the start of the race. “This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and power unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue.” The FIA’s single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis told reporters the lack of preseason testing in wet conditions had played a part in the chaos. “Some cars went very slowly, almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely,” he said. “That bug prevented the power from being redeployed, and for the cars to start again. “I think if we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time, and not have such a situation.” Sepang was the first race weekend of the season with wet conditions, although the track dried during the race. “Sometimes things fall through the net and people learn, and you do a better job next time,” Tombazis said.

events.title: App-makers are having a blast with the iPhone Duo, turning it into a retro Walkman
events.summary: The iPhone Duo isn't even out yet but developers are already having fun with the new design, creating apps that turn Apple's first foldable smartphone into everything from an accordion to a retro Walkman. Why it matters: Clever apps that couldn't exist on a traditional iPhone could help persuade early adopters to fork over nearly $2,000 for Apple's first foldable. Flashback: It's reminiscent of the early days of the iPhone, when developers turned its giant touchscreen and sensors into virtual versions of familiar objects, such as the virtual lighter apps whose flame flickered and swayed as the phone moved. Zoom in: Among the apps is Duo Man , a music player that turns the latest iPhone into a portable cassette player reminiscent of Sony's Walkman. Users open the Duo to choose an album and "insert" a cassette, then close it to start listening. Even the clicks and static are actual recordings from a real Walkman. It's the brainchild of indie app developer Vidit Bhargava, who created it during a four-hour hackathon last week. "I love the Walkman," he said. "I was just staring at it. I was like, this thing opens exactly like the iPhone Duo. What if your iPhone Duo was your Walkman, and you had to open up the door to change the album, and once you closed it, it would start playing the music." Bhargava has a particular affinity for the Walkman, having previously altered one of the vintage players to only work when a person is moving. Zoom out: Developers are finding ways to make the fold itself part of the software. The four-hour San Francisco hackathon where Duo-Man was born produced 73 submitted Duo projects, ranging from games to music tools and a virtual pop-up book. Accorduon turns the hinge into the bellows of a virtual accordion: The faster you fold and unfold the phone, the louder the instrument plays. Crate , which took first place at the same hackathon where Duo-Man finished second, turns the Duo into a beat machine, with folding controlling effects and snapping the phone open triggering a musical drop. Foldtales uses the hinge to create a virtual pop-up book, with castles, trees and other objects rising as the phone opens. Twofold uses the partially folded screen to hide each player's pieces in virtual versions of classic tabletop games. And Delta developer Riley Testut is working on Duo support that could make the foldable iPhone resemble another familiar hinged gadget: Nintendo's dual-screen DS. My thought bubble: Apple is years behind Samsung and Google in releasing a foldable phone. But its large developer ecosystem could help it catch-up quick. And the timing could turn out to be fortuitous. Developers are getting a new piece of hardware just as AI coding tools are making it faster and easier to turn a quirky idea into working software. What we're watching: Whether the initial burst of experimentation produces enduring apps — and whether Apple sells enough Duos to reward developers for building custom apps.

events.title: The midterms will come down to the cost of everything — and who voters trust to fix it
events.summary: Getty Images; BI Candidates in swing states are vying to win on the Big A: Affordability. In states with key Senate races, gas, electricity, and housing prices have all soared. Now, candidates on both sides of the aisle are touting their plans to bring costs down. Zac Owen, a 31-year-old brand strategist and high school football coach in the hotly contested swing state of Michigan , said that it's normal to drive two to four hours to get somewhere else in the state. The cost of those long commutes is top of mind for Owen and other voters as the country heads into the midterm congressional elections. " Gas prices , oh boy. People are up in arms about gas prices over here. I'll tell you that," Owen said. Hearing more about gas pricing from candidates, he said, would help sway his decision. The elections are in about a month, and candidates have touted their plans to bring costs down. But a war in Iran and rising prices for things like electricity and housing threaten to keep the affordability issue front-and-center. A Reuters/Ipsos poll from August found that 47% of registered voters said the cost of living would be the most important factor in choosing a candidate if the elections were held today. Consumer price growth came in at 3.4% in August, exacerbated by the ongoing Iran war and its disruptions to the oil market . Tariffs have also added upward pressure . That puts inflation above the Fed's 2% target, although it's down from its post-pandemic highs. The Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 in September to try to dampen rising prices, and more hikes could happen before the year is over. Senate races in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas are all toss-ups, according to the political handicappers at The Cook Political Report. Business Insider took a look at how prices have fared during President Donald Trump's second term in those states, along with how candidates in key elections have been talking about affordability. Gasoline Americans are shelling out more to fill their gas tanks , as average prices are up from a year ago. "Typically, the start of autumn brings lower gas prices, but lingering volatility in the Strait of Hormuz and the high cost of crude oil are driving up pump prices," AAA said in September. Data from GasBuddy, which collects price reports from gas stations, showed prices have increased about 46% nationally from January 2025 to roughly the end of September 2026. Most of the seven swing states saw similar surges, with three of them increasing by at least 50%. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said that "politicians are now feverishly trying desperate attempts to reduce prices," such as through gas tax suspensions. He said, however, that relief is limited as geopolitical tensions remain a key burden on gas prices . Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska, who is in a tight race for reelection against Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, has pushed for a ban on diesel exports in an effort to lower prices. Peltolta has called out gas prices in the state, posting a receipt for a $24.49 gallon, and saying that her opponent has voted "for the war that's making everything more expensive." Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has said his campaign is about gas and grocery affordability. "Michiganders are now paying a staggering $5 a gallon for gas and $6.79 a gallon for diesel—raising prices for groceries and everything else," he said in a statement . His opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, has called for a suspension of state and federal gas taxes , and for a temporary embargo on diesel exports. Electricity Electricity prices in most swing states have risen faster than the national average from January 2025 to July 2026. Maine has one of the highest rates in the country and saw a 24% increase, compared to the national increase of about 15%. Americans are worried about what the data center boom means for their electricity charges. A Consumer Reports survey from November found more than three-quarters of Americans were at least somewhat worried their energy bills would rise because of this. "High costs of energy are burdensome to Maine families, truck drivers, farmers, fishermen, schools, small businesses, mills, and factories," said Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins' site. Her opponent, Troy Jackson, has been criticized for increases in energy costs during his time leading the state legislature; in a statement to the local news outlet WABI , Jackson's campaign said that he "has a record of working to lower energy costs and will always stand up for Mainers." In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico wants to "guarantee large energy users like data centers fund the infrastructure improvements they need rather than passing those costs on to consumers," while Republican candidate Ken Paxton has said that he supports data centers recycling water and producing their own energy to fend off potential costs for consumers. Michigan's median home sales price increased 23%, higher than the overall 6% and the other toss-up states. Redfin's chief economist Daryl Fairweather said there aren't any signs that the housing market will improve soon. "If anything, it's gotten a little bit worse in recent weeks with the bond market flaring up and mortgage rates going up," Fairweather said. Republican Mike Rogers, who's running against El-Sayed in Michigan, has a housing platform centered on down payment assistance, lowering purchase and interest rates, and incentivizing new housing construction. "The solutions I'm championing for Michigan transcend party lines: making housing affordable, bringing back jobs, fixing our broken healthcare system, and saving schools," Rogers told nonprofit news site Bridge Michigan . Meanwhile, El-Sayed has proposed streamlining local regulations to build more housing, banning algorithmic rental pricing, and expanding down payment assistance . events.summary: Award-winning author Arundhati Roy discusses her work which focuses on social injustice, and why she’s not afraid to address politically charged topics. Since winning the Booker Prize in 1997 for her debut novel, author Arundhati Roy has not shied away from political issues. Whether she is writing fiction, nonfiction, or political essays, she focuses on social injustice. The internationally acclaimed writer is an outspoken critic of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration. She describes India as a super poor nation, with a government that disempowers its citizens and silences dissent. Her activism goes beyond the pages of her books – she has also taken part in demonstrations against Modi’s policies. Supporters describe her as unrelenting in holding the political establishment to account. But critics accuse her of being divisive and anti-India. Despite what she calls scandal after scandal in the country, she is optimistic that political change is on the way. events.title: Oklahoma Oil Company Plugs Disposal Well That Posed Threat to City’s Drinking Water
events.summary: The Flying Monkey disposal well in Enid, Oklahoma. Last year, the city asked the state to revoke the Flying Monkey’s permit to operate. September Dawn Bottoms for ProPublica An Oklahoma oil and gas company plugged a well that disposes of oil production’s toxic byproduct after an investigation by The Frontier and ProPublica revealed that regulators had approved the well in violation of state rules meant to protect public groundwater supplies. The disposal well, named the Flying Monkey, injected oil field wastewater underground and sat roughly a quarter-mile from two municipal groundwater supply sites that served the small city of Enid in northwest Oklahoma. Wastewater injection operations are banned within a half-mile of public water wells unless regulators hold a hearing to ensure that this activity will not pollute groundwater. Regulators at the Oklahoma Corporation Commission did not hold a hearing before approving the well in 2018. The city of Enid filed a complaint last year asking the state to revoke the Flying Monkey’s permit to operate. On Sept. 14, with the complaint still active in the agency’s administrative law court, employees of the Flying Monkey’s current owner — BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings LLC — dropped a cast iron plug into the bottom of the well, followed by more than 200 sacks of cement, to permanently seal it off, according to a report the company filed to the corporation commission. A representative of the state was on site to witness the plugging. Eric Huddleston, an attorney representing BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings, which acquired the Flying Monkey in 2020, said the company decided to permanently shut the well after determining it was “underutilized and operationally unnecessary.” A spokesperson for the corporation commission did not respond to requests for comment, including about the agency’s role in the well’s closure. Enid city officials said they did not know the well had been plugged until our reporter informed them. “This decision is, for lack of a better word, thrilling because this is such a vital issue,” said Frank Baker, an Enid city commissioner. “Our water sources have been put in danger, and for this one well to have been plugged, this is the best possible outcome.” In Enid’s 2025 complaint to the state, its lawyers noted that the Flying Monkey’s original operator, Hinkle Oil & Gas, had incorrectly checked a box on its permit application stating that the injection well was not within a half-mile of a public water supply well. “This was demonstrably false,” Enid’s lawyers wrote. Hinkle previously declined to answer questions about the Flying Monkey. Earlier this year, BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings refiled a permit application for the Flying Monkey, where it acknowledged the proximity of the city’s water supply wells. A building containing one of Enid’s groundwater supply wells sits about a quarter-mile from the now-plugged Flying Monkey disposal well. September Dawn Bottoms for ProPublica The Flying Monkey had a checkered operational history. In the last five years, the state has shut down the wastewater disposal well repeatedly after it failed tests of its structural integrity. These failures can indicate a problem that might allow wastewater to escape, potentially threatening drinking water sources. The well had failed five of these tests since 2021. In early July, nine days after the newsrooms’ investigation published, the Flying Monkey’s owner reported another leak in the well’s tubing. The state gave BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings 90 days to fix the leak or to permanently plug the well. Our investigation identified two other wells in Enid that violated the state distance rule between wastewater injection wells and the city’s groundwater supply sites. Both of those wells, which are owned by other companies, remain active. Read More To Protect Its Drinking Water, This City Has to Appeal to the Oil Regulators That Put It at Risk The proximity of wells to drinking water isn’t only an issue in Enid. Across Oklahoma, the news outlets identified at least 114 injection wells that were located within a half-mile of a public water supply well. More than 300,000 Oklahomans live in communities that rely on these water wells, according to our analysis. Baker, the Enid official, told The Frontier and ProPublica that he hopes the corporation commission will begin to plug other injection wells that threaten public water supplies. “I hope and pray this is an example that we’ll start to see replicated across the state in the near future,” he said. In addition to its request to plug the well, the city of Enid has asked the corporation commission to impose stronger regulations on oilfield wastewater disposal near its water supply, including a wider distance buffer between the injection sites and the city’s water wells. This request comes amid a recent uptick in wastewater injection in the Enid area, according to a legal filing made by the city. The commission previously declined to comment on Enid’s complaint because it is an active case. The case will continue to be heard in the agency’s administrative law court later this year. events.title: House Democrats slam Trump over Russia sanctions
events.summary: House Democrats are panning the Trump administration after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer wouldn’t commit last week to imposing Russian sanctions recently enacted by Congress. Rep. Greg Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called Greer’s comments to Semafor “a completely unsurprising development that only reaffirms what I’ve said all along: There’s no reason to believe [President Donald] Trump or his administration will suddenly hold Russia accountable.” Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia, the top House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, said that “as I and others warned, this legislation provides the president with extremely broad waiver authority to ignore most of the bill’s provisions.” He pointed to recent reporting that Trump is weighing lifting existing Russian sanctions: “I am not holding my breath to see him take any substantive action targeting Putin’s regime.” The White House didn’t return a request for comment.

events.title: Democrats demand testimony from housing director
events.summary: Democrats on the Senate Banking Committee are renewing their calls for Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte to appear before Congress after he sidelined its internal watchdog earlier this month. “Hearing testimony from Director Pulte is more important than ever in light of his recent decision to shutter the FHFA Office of Inspector General,” the lawmakers wrote in a letter to Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., shared first with Semafor . They also highlighted Pulte’s other moves, like appointing himself as chair of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac; laying off employees; accusing Trump’s political enemies of mortgage fraud; and serving simultaneously as acting director of national intelligence. The letter provides a useful road map for how Democrats would scrutinize the agency if they win a majority of either chamber this fall. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, the Nevada Democrat who led the effort, pushed for passage of a bill last week that would require the FHFA internal watchdog receive whatever funding it requested. Scott and FHFA did not return requests for comment.

events.summary: As the Trump administration weighs next steps in the Iran war, at least some in the administration worry that Iran will consider taking action to damage the president ahead of the midterms. “I think that’s a real possibility that they may want to inflict some pain on the president before the midterms, and so they may do something in the next couple weeks,” one Trump administration official told Semafor. “We’ll see.” Top administration officials met at Camp David on Friday on the Middle East conflict, which threatens to widen as war breaks out between Yemen’s Saudi-backed government and the Iranian-backed Houthis. The meeting came as indirect talks between Washington and Tehran have yet to yield meaningful progress. Meanwhile, the US has removed all B-1 bombers from an airbase in the UK used for launching strikes against Iran, following arrests in a suspected terror attack plot. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: Democratic-controlled Senate would confirm ‘very few’ Trump nominees
events.summary: The News The winner of Senate control would snatch one of the biggest tangible prizes of the midterms: control over President Donald Trump’s nominees. If Democrats are in charge, don’t expect many of Trump’s picks to move at all. “If the nominees are as crappy as his present ones, very few of them are going to get through. If he sends us a new [Defense Secretary Pete] Hegseth, I bet he wouldn’t pass the Senate,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told Semafor in a pre-election interview. “It’s the quality of the candidate that matters. Thus far, Trump has a record of notoriously bad candidates.” Democrats are favored to take the House, which would limit big bipartisan breakthroughs on legislation next year. But if Republicans can hold the Senate, they’d at least retain the ability to confirm Trump nominees — most notably, lifetime judicial appointments. Schumer’s comments confirm that Democratic control of the Senate under Trump would turn the battle to confirm Senate nominees into trench warfare, with committee chairmen able to bottle up Trump’s picks easily and Schumer able to simply not put them on the floor. Perhaps a handful of judges would be confirmed, but Cabinet secretaries would face long slogs. There’s also little hope that a Democratic majority would confirm a Supreme Court nominee — should a vacancy arise — after then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell’s blockade of Merrick Garland during the Obama years. “A Democrat-controlled Senate will without any question block every single one of President Trump’s nominees. This includes every cabinet member and every judge who is committed to upholding the Constitution,” said Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo. “[Schumer is] not going to change his playbook of obstruction and opposition.” Know More It’s been more than a decade since the president’s party lost control of the Senate during a midterm election. After the 2014 red wave, Senate Republicans gave former President Barack Obama few lower-level judges, blocked a Supreme Court seat from being filled, and even blocked his attorney general nominee, Loretta Lynch, from confirmation until the Senate passed a human trafficking bill. There’s no way around a judicial nominee blockade, but Trump can lean on acting officials in the executive branch. If Republicans do lose Senate control, look for the GOP to use its blunt confirmation tools — including confirming large tranches of nominees — in November and December to accomplish as much as they can before Schumer takes control again. There are currently 27 judicial vacancies at the district level and 10 nominees to fill those, mostly in Republican states. There are also a handful of nominees ready to be confirmed to federal appeals courts. If Republicans hold the chamber, they will probably prioritize judicial appointments for the next two years.

events.title: Malaysian palm oil stockpiles balloon to record on output surge
events.summary: Palm production in Malaysia had initially been expected to be curbed by volatile weather. Malaysian palm oil stockpiles surged to a record 3.45 million tonnes in September, driven by a 16% rise in output and a 12% drop in exports. Exports fell due to higher prices compared to Indonesia and large edible oil stocks in key markets, but festive demand and India's increased purchases may reduce inventories by year-end. Despite El Nino risks in 2027, improved weather and plantation management boosted production forecasts, with US Department of Agriculture expecting full-year output to surpass 2025's record of 20.2 million tonnes. Palm oil inventories in Malaysia likely swelled to a record in September , buffering supplies of the world’s most-used vegetable oil as an intensifying El Nino threatens to disrupt production in 2027. The burgeoning supplies could deepen a recent slump in prices, as traders also await a ramp-up in exports to major markets like India that would help draw down the massive stockpiles. Though production typically peaks in September and October, higher-than-expected output growth has elevated inventories, meaning prices will likely stay under pressure at RM4,300 (S$1,346) to RM4,500 a tonne, said Jacquelyn Yow, regional head of plantation research at CGS International. “It’s a shock to the market that stockpiles would grow so suddenly,” she said. Benchmark futures in Kuala Lumpur slid from their September peak of RM5,049 and were trading near RM4,535 on Oct 5 . The Malaysian Palm Oil Board is set to release monthly supply and demand data on Oct 12. Stockpiles likely jumped about 22% to 3.45 million tonnes in September from August , according to the median of 10 estimates in a Bloomberg survey of plantation executives, traders and analysts. That would surpass the previous record of 3.22 million tonnes in Dec 2018, and mark a nearly 50% increase since inventories began climbing in April. Output surged 16% to 2.11 million tonnes, the highest ever for the month of September. Meanwhile, exports fell around 12% to a four-month low of 1.13 million tonnes, the survey showed. The South-east Asian nation has lost export share in recent months because of a wide premium over Indonesian supplies, while near-record edible oil stockpiles in key importing markets have dampened demand, according to Aditya Jeripotula, head of South Asia at agricultural commodities research firm DNext Intelligence SA. Palm stockpiles will likely peak in October before easing towards the year-end as production slows and festive demand boosts exports, he said. India, for instance, has stepped up purchases ahead of Deepavali and following cuts to import duties, buying more than 200,000 tonnes in recent days. But reserves “will very likely remain high, near record levels through the first half of 2027,” Jeripotula added. Palm production in Malaysia had initially been expected to be curbed by volatile weather, including floods in key-growing regions of Borneo earlier in 2026 , followed by below-normal rainfall and dryness amid the onset of the El Nino weather phenomenon. The outlook for 2025-2026 has improved, however, thanks to better plantation management and improving labour availability, the US Department of Agriculture said in a Oct 1 report, when it raised its full-year production forecast to 20.2 million tonnes. “September’s production was supported by favourable weather and we may even see full-year production surpassing 2025’s record, although that would depend on weather conditions in the October-December months,” Jeripotula said. “El Nino is the key here.” Still, the record reserves offer some slack to the global palm market, which is expected to tighten going forward, due to a delayed impact on yields from the El Nino and as Indonesia’s expanding biofuel mandate absorbs more supplies. events.title: My family of 5 moved into a 3-bedroom duplex. I was dreading downsizing at first, but I'm glad we did.
events.summary: The author's family of five moved into a three-bedroom duplex. Courtesy of Melissa Noble Most of my previous homes have been bigger, two-story houses. However, my family of five just moved into a smaller three-bedroom duplex. I was dreading having less space at first, but there are unexpected benefits. I've always loved the idea of having a big family home . I grew up in a two-story house with six family members, and it was always loud, fun, and messy. Now that I'm a mother of three, I have a very different perspective on what it actually takes to run a busy family home. After living in multiple two-story houses in the last few years, I've realized that bigger isn't necessarily better in many ways. In August, our family of five downsized to a small three-bedroom duplex in Labrador on the Gold Coast, Australia. Before that, we'd been living with my parents , and prior to that, we lived in a double-story house in Bright, in country Victoria. Initially, I dreaded the idea of residing in what felt like a shoebox. How would we all cope? Would the kids drive each other nuts? How would they manage without a big yard to run around in? And most importantly, where on earth would I hide, aside from the shower? The first couple of weeks were an adjustment, as we got used to our smaller abode . But much to my surprise, I'm actually finding it to be a refreshing change, and there have been plenty of unexpected benefits. The inside is so much easier to clean Our previous homes took me at least three hours to clean each week. When you're busy running businesses and raising three children , that kind of time can feel like dead expenditure, a bit like paying rent. In contrast, it takes less than an hour to clean our new home. It's light and bright and somehow doesn't seem to accumulate dust in the same way the two-story properties did. Having a smaller space to maintain has saved me an enormous amount of time and energy. Instead of spending hours keeping on top of the housework , my husband and I have more time for things that actually matter to us, like making memories with our kids. The author spends less time on cleaning in her smaller home. Courtesy of Melissa Noble There's less yard work One of my favorite things about our home in country Victoria was the garden. It had these beautiful, mature trees that were spectacular to look at, but they also dropped a huge amount of foliage. As a result, my husband was forever outside raking up debris. Likewise, when we lived with my parents, he'd spend several hours a month mowing and maintaining their yard. Our new home is a different story. The back has a tiled courtyard, so there's no real maintenance required, and out front, there's a small yard. My husband or son can mow the grassed area in about 20 minutes. Again, this means we've gained more time to spend together as a family, rather than being tied down with the upkeep of a property. Less clutter, more functional With bigger homes , it's easy to fall into the trap of buying things to fill the space. Often, it's stuff you don't necessarily need, or at least that was my experience in the past. Before we downsized, we ditched a whole lot of our clutter. Toys the kids hadn't looked at in years went to the thrift shop. Old clothes were tossed or passed on to someone who could use them. In our new home, we've kept the furniture to a minimum, which has naturally reduced clutter. I feel like this has really helped with my mental health. Moving into a smaller space has also made us more conscious about the items we do own. We try to stick to items that are functional and serve a specific purpose in daily life. Cheaper bills It's still early days, and we haven't had to pay any bills yet, but we do expect to see some energy savings thanks to our move. The difference in our utility bills will really help our household budget over time. It's hard to compare like for like between our last two properties, as one was in a much cooler climate and needed heating at this time of year, and Mum and Dad's house had solar panels . We do expect our bills to be lower at our new home. Our water bills may also be cheaper, as there's less outdoor watering required. Small suits us, for the moment We know that our current home probably won't work as our kids grow older. I imagine that having three teenagers in a small duplex, haggling and loafing around, could test our patience in the long run. But for the moment, downsizing has been a refreshing change. There's something so liberating about simplifying things, living with less stuff, and having a smaller space to maintain. We're embracing our small-home chapter and appreciating the little things along the way. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Brighter isn't better and more is less. The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what
events.summary: There has been much chilly weather in the sunny meadowlands of AI futures. Fortunately, to use an indecently inappropriate adverb, the rest of the world isn’t really looking, being too busy chewing its nails over the very many other intimations of disaster. Sure, rebel swarms of attack agents breaking out of the labs isn’t a good look. OpenAI delaying its IPO and a new model launch likewise. All these things soak up whatever bandwidth the news media have to AI right now. Putting them in a bigger context, that of promises made and not kept, problems known but not fixed, the observable risk-reward ratios as models develop, we may at last start having a sense of what sort of crisis awaits. Actual crises are frequently triggered by crises in confidence, themselves caused when frameworks of assumption stop standing up to reality and wishful thinking. Thus, the assumption to date is that models will get more powerful and infrastructure more capable, in a way that justifies — demands — massive capex. The economics of giant infrastructure investment when you can’t buy what you need is a great bet in free markets that presupposes that freedom, and yeah, about that. A bigger problem is the idea that more powerful AI is always better. It frequently is, but that’s not good enough, When frontier models have to be kept in LLM jail for uncontrollable dishonesty, not so much. Here, the bigger context is that we’ve known that at heart LLM probability space is entirely relative. There is no ground truth there. Nobody has fixed hallucinations, and now we see the fascinating phenomenon of a machine that doesn’t understand truth but can deliberately lie. If more powerful models are better at that, scratch one assumption. Another huge assumption is that even at the current level of model reliability, agentic architectures are ready to be useful. Those who show all the caution of a chronic gambler on a winning "streak" are as ready to get the brakes slammed on as their opposites. The principal contender for the one true proof of concept that agentic AI is a dangerous fount of unexpected consequence is Meta’s new Muse. It is aimed at low-information credulous users and its star turn is, of course, shopping. The AI use case that’s five years away, and always has been. It’s Meta, so of course it soaks up all the information about you, your online activities and the people you talk to as much as it can. It will soon have ultracute animated Tamagotchi-style pets you can wear around your neck to improve your status as a Meta monitoring post. And we did say it was Meta, so has all the attention to security and careful design you may expect. Which is why it’s already been caught sending people’s physical addresses to strangers, and why when researcher Jonny at neuromatch.social went poking around its infrastructure — each instance runs permanently on its own Linux VM — they found just a ton of fun. Headline party tricks hard-coded. What looks like attempts to train off Claude. And yes, you can get it to run your own things on that VM deep within Meta, which Jonny points out is a botnet paradise waiting to happen. This banger of a bad ‘un is being given away to Meta users, who pretty much define a vulnerable target audience for tech that may not be totally trustworthy. Meta, of course, is dead against AI safety regulation. Place your bets on the headlines to follow. In any case, the upside of using agents as demoed in every keynote is either so trivial and trite — book me a restaurant! — or so catastrophic if it fails — organize my family vacation! — that consumer agents are a bust. It’s just that Meta may be bringing a lot of accelerant to that particular fire. There are other fires, of course, many known about since everything kicked off. Model collapse due to training on data contaminated with output? Still a thing, still no fix a "better" AI might provide. And that habit AI has of retailing everything and paying for nothing, choking off its own training data supply chain and a huge chunk of commerce and culture with it? Very much still a thing. Where AI does make consistent progress is in domain-specific tasks. Science, engineering, mathematics, and coding, if you match a model with enough reinforcement learning with humans who know how to manage them, there are startling results. You don’t get much innovation, not much newness, which is the true driver of progress. Better than humans is highly contextual. Computers have been better at chess for decades, but there isn’t a better chess. Horses run faster than humans, and that’s been useful for four millennia, but we got to peak horses quite some time ago. So the question is, have we reached peak AI, where the cost of future developments don’t match the risk they won’t work well enough to justify? If ChatGPT already writes a perfectly good business letter in a couple of seconds, there is no meaningful improvement to be had for users. Most AI is profoundly annoying, in ways that have nothing to do with the models and everything to do with perverted UX in an attempt to justify growth. That is both unsustainable and a tacit admission that AI hasn’t solved its use case problem. If we are at or near peak AI, is that the crisis that bursts that goddam bubble? Certainly a readjustment, as all bets on the continuous uptick curve are off. AI as it stands is useful enough to power a big industry sector, just in ways that are and remain at odds to how it is marketed and its future fantasies. Trust in AI Max may be shaken, but there's still room for lots of improvement. That slowdown that everyone who isn’t a miscreant is calling for may happen organically, if we escape the smoking-is-good-for-you mentality of the Metans and the Muskovites. That’s still a gamble we shouldn't be taking, but the odds may be better than we thought. ®

events.title: Russia ramps up attacks on Kyiv infrastructure as U.S. makes fresh push for peace talks
events.summary: Russia has pledged to intensify strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities after a drone attack damaged the capital’s key Northern Bridge over the weekend. Moscow said the strikes were retaliation for Ukraine’s actions after Zelenskyy vowed to double down on attacks targeting Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy also said the U.S. has proposed fresh trilateral peace talks by the end of October, with Ukraine responding positively to the initiative. Russia's Defense Ministry has pledged to further intensify military attacks on Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities, following strikes on a second major bridge in Ukraine's capital over the weekend. The latest threat comes as Russian forces have ramped up attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting data centers , telecommunications facilities and energy infrastructure as it seeks to disrupt daily life in the capital and force power cuts ahead of winter . A Russian drone struck Kyiv's key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River on Saturday, damaging the road surface and forcing traffic to be suspended. Two people were injured in the attack, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. The attack came shortly after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv to pledge 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion) in military aid to Ukraine, and after Russian drones repeatedly targeted Kyiv's Southern Bridge earlier in the week. In an update posted via Telegram on Sunday, Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed the attack on the Northern Bridge, saying the bridge "supports the transfer of troops and the logistics of military cargo." The ministry also responded to comments from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy . In an interview with Reuters, Zelenskyy said in comments published Saturday that Ukraine would double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in retaliation to a new policy of airstrikes designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities. Ukraine's president said Russian civilians would not be targeted in these strikes. Ukraine’s surprise robot offensive exposes a vulnerability in Putin’s war machine Putin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy warns Russia preparing to deploy 10,000 North Korean troops Russia ‘truly’ appreciates U.S. invite to G20 summit — but hasn’t decided if Putin will go Zelenskyy says Ukraine ready for ‘energy ceasefire,’ calls for trilateral meeting with Putin, Trump Putin floats ‘chance’ at peace with Ukraine as NATO chief warns Russia is becoming ‘increasingly reckless’ Russia preparing ‘massive strikes’ on Ukraine’s energy sites after deadliest attack of the year Russia's economy has defied the skeptics. Cracks are getting harder to hide 'Winter is coming’: Ukraine fears its toughest test since Russia’s full-scale invasion "In response to these threats, the Russian Defence Ministry recalls that the massive strikes are launched against Kiev and other Ukrainian regions specifically in retaliation for the actions of the Kiev regime's leader," Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday via Telegram, according to a Google translation. Zelenskyy "bears full personal and political responsibility" for these intensified strikes, the ministry said. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four-and-a-half years ago, with fighting along the frontline virtually deadlocked as the conflict continues into a fifth winter. Zelenskyy said via social media on Sunday that the Trump administration has proposed a trilateral meeting at the technical level by the end of October, adding that Ukraine is open to the United Arab Emirates or another country proposed by the American side hosting the talks. "I know they will propose this to the Russian side as well, or may have already done so. We will wait for the response. We respond positively to negotiations," Zelenskyy said. CNBC has contacted a spokesperson for the White House and Russia's Embassy in London and is awaiting a response. U.S. President Donald Trump has previously urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions continue to prop up U.S. diesel prices .

events.title: Why Treasuries Are ‘Risky’ Again
events.summary: We all know that Treasury yields have been surging, alongside bond yields all around the world. So what explains the selloff and does it mean that bonds are becoming fundamentally riskier? What happens if investors can no longer hedge stocks with government debt? And how do expectations of the Federal Reserve's "reaction function" fit in? In this episode, we speak with Carolin Pflueger, associate professor at the University of Chicago and a resident scholar at the Chicago Fed, about her work on the bond market and central banks. We discuss why bonds have become more stock-like, what that means for yields, and the role of the Fed's credibility in making bonds “bond-like” again. (Source: Bloomberg)

events.title: LinkedIn pros have found a new key to getting opportunities: selfies
events.summary: Courtesy of Arielle Berlinsky and Tara Crymble LinkedIn creators are finding career success by posting work selfies and videos on the platform. AI's impact on LinkedIn is making authentic, personal posts more effective than polished content. LinkedIn launched a Next Gen Voices program to help young creators connect and grow their careers. Your next career opportunity could start with your front-facing camera. For some LinkedIn creators , selfies and unscripted videos are opening doors that career updates alone did not — from speaking invitations to a new job. Three LinkedIn professionals told Business Insider that what used to be awkward on a platform where your boss, colleagues, and potential employers are watching is becoming the new norm that those looking to stand out may need to adapt to. Arielle Berlinsky, the Director of Marketing at Movement Strategy, told Business Insider she started posting on LinkedIn while in a workplace where rules and expectations felt constraining, and LinkedIn became a space to share opinions, humor, and — eventually — her face. “Even if you're working for a small company, you have a certain box that you can be kept in or standards you have to uphold,” Berlinsky said, adding that she initially shared photos from work events, then began recording videos about experiences and lessons as they happened. "The one thing you carry with you everywhere is your face and your name and your personality because that's the heart of who you are," Berlinsky said. “I'm so much more than just my job and my title.” AI is reshaping tactics for how to stand out As AI makes polished posts easier to produce, some creators say personality can help people connect with the human behind the profile. Tara Crymble, an account manager at B2B influencer marketing agency Creatorbuzz , told Business Insider that showing her face and speaking on video helps convey something a text post can struggle to capture. “In this time of AI, it's so easy for people to get lost in this overly polished, filtered, corporate, or even robotic tone ,” Crymble said. “I think if you're posting your face or especially video content, you can add in your personality and your quirks into your content, and it just comes across as more genuine,” Crymble added. “And I think that layer of trust is more quickly built.” LinkedIn has been tightening its approach to AI content , introducing a “Seems like AI slop ” feedback option and tools to limit the distribution of generic AI-generated posts . Jack Appleby, a 37-year-old writer and creator consultant who dubbed himself an "elder millennial" in a conversation with Business Insider, said he is seeing personal photos gain traction and may be changing his tactics after initially building his 90,000 followers on LinkedIn almost exclusively through text posts. “I think the AI police are out in full force on LinkedIn, maybe more than any other social network,” Appleby said. “People are more concerned than ever whether something's made by someone real or made by AI,” Appleby added. “I think people want connection, and maybe it's time I let people get to know who I am as much as the way that I think." Gen Zers are emerging as the leading voices on LinkedIn Tara Crymble said that LinkedIn is evolving from an online resume to a social platform where people share slices of their own personal lives. Courtesy of Tara Crymble Crymble once used LinkedIn like a traditional résumé for job announcements. But last December, when she began sharing what she was doing and learning as a recent graduate , including her face and voice, Crymble said her following grew from roughly 1,000 to 6,000, and her posts have generated more than 250,000 impressions. “Not only was I getting opportunities such as speaking and media and opportunities to be in rooms that I wouldn't have originally had the chance to have, but I also received my current job,” Crymble said. “I found that out through my LinkedIn presence and connecting with the team.” Berlinsky said her posts have earned millions of impressions and helped her build a community of over 55,000 people. Berlinsky and Crymble both said they participate in LinkedIn's Next Gen Voices program, an invitation-only, 12-week cohort for Gen Z creators that offers opportunities to test features, provide feedback, and meet the LinkedIn team. "This may sound crass, but generally, if you know how to dress and present yourself , it's probably worth putting your face out there so people know who you are," Appleby said. "Most data I see, and people are often not comfortable hearing this, says it's often the most well-kept people or the most conventionally attractive people who get promotions in the workplace," Appleby added. Advice on how to get started Arielle Berlinsky said those just getting started should worry less about appearing perfect and think about authenticity instead. Courtesy of Arielle Berlinsky For those who are not social media natives like more Gen Zers, the young creators have tips on how to get unstuck on LinkedIn. "I've seen a lot of creators that fully embrace themselves, whether that be their interests or personality," said Crymble. "In a world of all this AI content, it shines through as relatable and is embraced back." Berlinsky recommends starting with a friend who can take photos of you doing something naturally, and practice speaking into the camera as though you're speaking to one person. “I'm going to show up and talk as if I'm talking to one person and not try to speak to everyone, not try to cater to everyone,” Berlinsky said, "Consistency matters more than sticking to a single format, so think about the memes and infographics that can also communicate personality." "Stop waiting for the ideal lighting or buy that thousand-dollar equipment," Berlinsky added. "The less you worry about filtering yourself, the less you worry about making it perfect, the more it will translate into success.” Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Silicon Valley founders' hottest funding source: the Bank of Best Friends
events.summary: iStock; Tyler Le/BI Katherine Naylor Pullman started Our Third Place, a networking group for women in media, as a part-time side project. It began four years ago with monthly, then weekly, dinners. Women in Chicago and Los Angeles reached out, wanting to host their own dinners. Now, Our Third Place is in 40 cities, and running it has blossomed into a full-time gig for Naylor Pullman, who left a previous job in brand partnerships. Our Third Place has grown to 1,800 members without big investors, and that's by design. "If someone were to throw us millions of dollars, they would then want millions of members," Naylor Pullman says. "I firmly believe you cannot scale community by the millions." She and the company's CEO, Ashley Preininger, are building by seed-strapping , a tactic where companies raise smaller investments and forgo the traditional venture capital cycle of Series A and Series B fundraising, and then grow the company through revenue. They're raising money now from family, friends, and members, because they can work within that smaller fundraising space, and keep costs for members lower when the company isn't beholden to massive investor returns. "We actually don't feel like we need a huge influx of cash to do what we need to do," Preininger says. Seed-strapping has become more appealing to founders as venture capital funding waned following the 2010s boom and the end of the zero-interest rate policy . The shift also comes amid the rise of the single-person startup , as more founders deploy AI agents to help with coding, accounting, marketing, and other tasks that once required expensive labor. The founders who spoke with me for this story tell me they're taking an alternate path to funding by choice, seeing that more money can come with more problems — more commitments, more expectations, and less control of their company. Amid "all the fundraising doom and gloom," says Caroline Lewis, managing partner at early-stage venture firm Nura Ventures, "the rules are being rewritten." "You can go back to business fundamentals of building a product that customers want to buy, then you can raise some capital and get some decent traction, and don't necessarily have to be beholden to the traditional venture train," Lewis says. For some founders, hopping off the venture capital treadmill allows them to build at the speed they want. Seed-strapping isn't new. Software company Zapier seed-strapped before the term was in the zeitgeist, raising just $1.3 million seed-strapping and eventually growing to hundreds of millions in annual revenue. But the tactic has gotten new attention as founders struggled to raise venture capital. The number of global venture deals has steadily fallen from more than 17,000 in the first quarter of 2022 to about 8,500 in the second quarter of 2026, according to data from Pitchbook. Deal value is hitting an all-time high, but that's largely fueled by big deals with OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI. Since late 2024, AI startups have captured at least half of venture funding, with their stranglehold on the market climbing to 80% at the beginning of this year, according to Crunchbase. Anthropic , xAI , OpenAI , and Waymo accounted for nearly two-thirds of the money invested that quarter. The market is bifurcated between those companies that need lots of capital and can bring massive returns, and all the other good ideas that may need less compute power, less labor, and would bring smaller returns, says Charles Hudson, managing partner at venture firm Precursor Ventures. Big venture funds look for areas where they can make large investments and look for massive returns. "The biggest challenge is: how do you finance these companies through that little middle period?" He says. "There's lots of money to get started. If you're building something big, there's lots of money to shoot for the moon." But for companies that raise a seed round of a few million, and may need another few million down the line, there could be fewer investors in that sweet spot. "Who's going to provide you that money?" The number of global venture deals has dropped from more than 17,000 in the first quarter of 2022 to about 8,500 in the second quarter of 2026. According to Carta, 41% of the US-based companies that raised a seed round in 2022 didn't fundraise beyond that. Another 21% continued to fundraise, but did not pursue a Series A round. These companies have also maintained lower headcounts than those that did raise a Series A round or beyond, sticking with median staff numbers of between six and eight people, compared to 22 at firms that raised more money. About half of startups that raised seed money in 2018 moved to a Series A within three years, according to data provided by Carta. But among those that raised a seed round in 2022, fewer than a third of new startups made the leap to a Series A by 2025. "The overall trend is that graduation rates have decreased," Hamza Shad, insights manager at Carta, tells me in an email. "This suggests that seed-strapping — whether willingly or unwillingly — has become more common." Lauren Dines worked in venture for five years, but left to found and work full-time on Breaknine, an AI startup that handles personalized outreach, late last year. "While I was in venture, I saw a lot of companies where I was like, this is a good idea, it's just not venture scalable." By steering away from the venture route and shunning expectations of massive growth, she can potentially accelerate the typical venture timeline, exiting in three to five years instead of seven to 10. It's potentially less risky than seeking to raise tens of millions of dollars and get returns in the hundreds of millions. Dines says her goal is to grow her business, and then make a strategic decision about how to move forward. "It was never my dream to have a venture-backed business." Dines thought about: "What do I need, and how can I best get there?" when it comes to her own needs and life. "This is probably the most efficient path to getting there." Women have also struggled to raise venture capital, with all-female leadership teams taking home just 6.5% of venture deals in 2024. But women founders and investors make up nearly half of all angel investors . Boot-strapping and seed-strapping are ways around the funding blocks. That's part of the thought process behind how Shannon Davenport, who founded Esker Beauty, has built her company. She boot-strapped it for about four years, then went looking for venture capital. But Davenport says she found that the VCs had a thesis for how her business should fit the market that didn't align with what she knew about her products and customers. She raised smaller investments in a seed stage, and now, says her company is approaching profitability, targeting the end of the year. "My most important valued asset is my time," Davenport says. events.title: Euro hits 17-month low as political uncertainty in Spain and France rattles markets
events.summary: The euro is trading at its lowest level against the U.S. dollar since May 2025. Both economies face higher inflation, interest rates and borrowing costs, but the euro area is also grappling with low growth and political volatility. Spain is heading for a snap election while France is struggling to appease markets over its fiscal trajectory. The euro hit its weakest level against the U.S. dollar in 17 months on Monday, as concerns over the political trajectories of two of the euro zone's biggest economies spill over into wider markets. The eurozone currency was last 0.6% lower against the greenback, hitting its lowest level since May 19, 2025, according to LSEG data. That comes as the euro zone grapples with a simultaneous rise in inflation , interest rates and government borrowing costs . The U.S. faces similar pressures, but investors are increasingly unsettled by additional vulnerabilities unique to Europe: persistently weak growth, a fragmented bond market and political uncertainty in Spain and France. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Monday called a snap election for November , as protests over the country's housing crisis reach boiling point. The protests have highlighted the difficulty of passing reforms in what has been one of the euro area's bright spots for economic growth in the pandemic rebound. Rufaro Chiriseri, head of fixed income for RBC Wealth Management, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday that Spanish assets had been among its preferred investments this year because of the country's growth trajectory and relative fiscal stability. "It's the strength of the commitment to holding some of those fiscal rules that's quite crucial. And even when we did see the [bond market] sell-off last week, and we're looking at Spanish debt, Portuguese debt, it didn't sell off as aggressively as we saw in France, in Italy," Chiriseri said. "And so that, in a sense, is holding up that investors still think that is an attractive pocket of the market to be in." France meanwhile remains the "poster child" for Europe's sovereign market problems, as mounting debt piles become more expensive to service. Economists at Barclays said Friday that while the French government had presented a draft outline of its 2027 budget, aimed at reducing the public deficit from 5.4% of GDP to 5% next year, the country is unlikely meet its fiscal targets even if the plan is adopted in the coming months. "French fiscal and political developments cloud the euro area outlook, with fiscal fundamentals remaining weak and unlikely to reach an inflection point before next year's presidential election," they said. Strategists at ING meanwhile said the budget , even if passed in full, would "not resolve France's structural fiscal problems." "The deficit would remain too high to stabilise the debt ratio, while ageing-related expenditure and interest payments would continue to rise. The next government will therefore have to make further difficult choices," they said. "So far, none of the main presidential candidates has presented a sufficiently detailed plan explaining which expenditure would be reduced, which taxes would change or how the debt ratio would eventually be stabilised."
