events.title: People really hate AI, so why can’t they get enough?
events.summary: Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.” “I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied. It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype , steered by zealots , inescapable . The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now. On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast. According to the Pew Research Center, more adults in the US think AI will have a negative impact on them personally, and on society in general, than expect a positive one. The pessimism is strongest among the young. More than half of people worldwide say that AI products and services make them nervous, according to a report from Stanford University . In a Gallup poll in May, 71% of US adults said they would oppose construction of a new AI data center in their area, far more than the 53% who said they would oppose a new nuclear power plant. And in an NBC poll in March, AI was less popular than ICE. Yet the number of people using AI is still skyrocketing. ChatGPT hit a billion monthly users in May, according to the market analysis firm Sensor Tower. Google DeepMind’s Gemini is close behind, logging 950 million users in July. According to Pew, half of US adults now say they use a chatbot , more than twice the number who said they did in 2023. One in four people say they do so every day. And it’s a global habit: More than a third of adults across all 38 OECD countries (a group of the world’s wealthiest democracies) report having used generative AI tools in the last three months . All these surveys paint a picture of two contradictory truths: A lot of people really do not like AI and a lot of people cannot get enough of it. What’s going on? It’s possible that these are two distinct groups, but I doubt it. The numbers don’t add up unless the Venn diagram is on its way to being a circle. It’s also possible that the more people use AI, the more negative their opinions about it will be. There’s at least a correlation to back this up : The Global North, where adoption is highest, skews pessimistic. In the Global South, where adoption levels are lower, people are more optimistic. But here’s what I really think is going on: When people say they hate AI it’s not the technology they dislike but, rather, the relentless drive of the companies behind it to push the tech upon us in as many ways as possible . They’re telling us to brace for the biggest social and economic upheaval in generations. How do they expect people to feel? In many ways, we’ve been here before. We saw a similar dynamic play out with social media over the last 20 years. Billions flocked to Facebook and Twitter despite mounting techlash against the companies that ran those services. Ditto for Google search. With social media there wasn’t much anyone could do. Quitting a platform meant losing all your content and connections, giving you the choice to suck it up or start over. But with AI there’s still a chance for people to have some sway. There’s certainly more political appetite for regulation this time around. All 50 US states have either passed or proposed laws governing the development and deployment of AI , creating a patchwork of more than 2,100 bills across the country—a tenfold increase in three years. And with a number of top-class open-source alternatives to Google and OpenAI and Anthropic already on the market, there’s also (for now, at least) the potential for more consumer choice and the market pressure that goes with it.  I don’t want to be naïve. Trillion-dollar companies are hard to move. But what comes next is not as inevitable as those companies often imply. When I asked the Springboards CEO why his firm was developing a new model if he didn’t really like AI, he told me there was no walking back from LLMs—but you could still make them do something different.  Here’s hoping we see a lot more of something different: Clarity about what AI can and cannot do and, crucially, a technology that’s not sold as if it’s about to take over the world.

events.title: Non-oil sectors in UAE and Saudi Arabia maintain strong growth trajectory despite Iran war
events.summary: The non-oil private sectors of the UAE and Saudi Arabia maintained their expansion trajectory in September, as the Arab world’s two largest economies shook off the effects of the Iran war . The seasonally adjusted Riyad Bank purchasing managers’ index – a benchmark gauge of the kingdom’s non-oil economy – rose to 55.3 in September, from 53.8 in August, well above the neutral 50 mark that separates growth from contraction. The rate of improvement in the non-oil sector business activity last month was the strongest since February and marked the sixth consecutive month of improvements in business conditions. The acceleration last month was largely driven by a marked rise in new order growth, although it masked the softening in the rate of output growth. New orders hit levels closer to the index’s long-run average, suggesting that demand in the kingdom has recovered well after a slowdown in the middle of 2026. Businesses surveyed also referred to gradual improvements in the market that led to increased client numbers and higher spending. “The acceleration was primarily demand-led. New orders increased at their fastest pace since February,” said Naif Alghaith, chief economist at Riyad Bank. The September reading of the PMI index was broadly consistent with the “wider picture of the Saudi economy”, which was driven by domestic consumption, investment activity, government and PIF-related projects. “The strong improvement in new orders provides a positive forward-looking signal for activity in the coming months,” Mr Alghaith said. While the recovery was predominantly driven by the domestic market in September, new orders from foreign customers have now dropped for seven months running. Companies surveyed pointed to the effects of supply chain disruption amid the regional conflict that in some cases led to shipping delays. Gulf states including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, Opec’s biggest oil producer, have faced attacks during the war, which is now in its seventh month. The tourism and leisure, retail, aviation and properties sectors across the Gulf took a hit as Iran attacked civilian infrastructure and regional energy installations during the early days of the conflict. Gulf economies have bounced back gradually, although Iran continues to attack commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, while Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports are under a "maritime blockade" from Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthi rebels. Demand drives UAE Demand conditions in the UAE non-oil private sector also continued to improve markedly in September, boosting pricing power and enabling companies to raise their selling prices at the fastest pace in more than 15 years in response to higher input costs. Meanwhile, business activity increased rapidly and higher output requirements encouraged companies to expand both purchasing activity and employment, with staffing numbers rising modestly last month. The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UAE Purchasing Managers' Index in September remained stable at 55.3 recorded in August, well above the 50 mark that indicates growth in economic activity. The latest PMI reading is “another indication that the non-oil economy has moved past the midyear slowdown linked to the Middle East conflict”, said David Owen, principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. “Businesses saw customer demand improve, not just in local markets but abroad as well, with new export business rising at the strongest rate in nearly two years,” he added. The improvement in the UAE’s business conditions was mainly driven by a “rapid monthly rise in output”, with the fastest rate of growth since February, before the outbreak of the war. Stronger demand conditions also supported a marked increase in new orders, although the pace of expansion eased from the seven-month high posted in August. The overall new order numbers were also supported by an increase in new business from abroad, which expanded for the third consecutive month and at the sharpest pace since November 2024, PMI data showed. However, as the demand strengthened, companies raised their output prices at the steepest rate since May 2011, which was among the fastest since the survey began. "While the economic picture looks more robust now, selling charges also rose markedly, suggesting that firms are taking the opportunity to boost their margins following a period of strong input cost pressures,” Mr Owen said. “With oil markets remaining volatile, and shipping routes still constrained, input costs and selling charges may remain elevated." Dubai momentum Non-oil private sector business activity in Dubai, one of the biggest business and tourism centres in the Middle East, also maintained a sharp growth trajectory. The Dubai PMI posted 54.5 in September, up from 54.1 in August, signalling a “solid improvement”, as the pace of growth was fastest in 2026 so far. The boost to Dubai’s non-oil economic activity was largely driven a "sharp and accelerated increase in output”, the fastest so far this year. New orders also rose markedly, supported by the strongest expansion in new business from abroad for two years, the PMI survey data showed. Although employment in the emirate increased in September, the backlog of work still increased at a sharp pace. “The rate of output price inflation quickened to the fastest since January 2014 as companies passed on higher input costs to customers,” the survey found.

events.title: HKTDC’s Belt and Road Summit drives momentum
events.summary: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] The 11th Belt and Road Summit, which took place in Wan Chai on 9-10 September, brought together more than 6,200 top officials, business leaders and senior professionals from 70-plus B&R countries and regions to explore opportunities for further cooperation and partnerships. Co-organised by the HKSAR Government and the Hong Kong Trade Development Council (HKTDC), the signature event gave attendees the chance to promote cross-regional trade and industry collaboration, as well as to accelerate new initiatives and achieve concrete outcomes. Underlining these intentions, the Summit’s broad theme this year was “Advancing High-Quality Development‧Embarking on a New Journey”. Significant results were achieved not just in showcasing over 300 investment projects, arranging more than 800 meetings between potential dealmakers, and facilitating the signing of more than 60 memoranda of understanding (MOUs) and other agreements. Equally notable was the diversity of sectors involved, ranging from finance and professional services to manufacturing and construction; the presence of organisations from the ASEAN bloc, Central Asia and the Middle East, and the interest shown in what Hong Kong can offer nowadays as both a “super connector” and a “super value-adder”. The two-day agenda featured a series of keynote addresses from high-profile speakers plus plenary sessions and informative panel discussions. This allowed participants to share their expertise on policy issues, navigating risk, and creating opportunities for enterprises to expand into international markets at a time of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical uncertainties. There was also an emphasis on innovation, enhancing trade and investment resilience, and helping to transform initial connections into tangible results and lasting ties. For instance, in his opening remarks, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu noted the importance of a proactive approach to advancing regional exchanges and opening new markets. The former highlighted the immense possibilities in trade, transport, industry, technology, capital investment and human resources that came with reviving the ancient Silk Road in a modern format and establishing comprehensive strategic links. Cosse said it made sense then because the B&R pillars of infrastructure, connectivity, trade facilitation and financial integration aligned with Uruguay’s long-term belief in multilateral cooperation and free trade. And today that commitment to enhancing capital flows and developing joint projects with Hong Kong and other partners in Asia remains as strong as ever. Besides formal plenary sessions and high-powered debates, this year’s Summit also introduced new thematic zones to spotlight Hong Kong’s ability to support the practical needs of enterprises in different sectors. For instance, the “GoGlobal Connect Zone” showed how the city’s professional services expertise has helped Chinese Mainland companies plan for expansion and connect with international markets. There were also roundtable discussions and a one-stop exchange and matchmaking platform to assist with answers and general advice. Separately, the Central Asia Zone featured eight exhibitors from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, showcasing the rapid development and investment opportunities in Central Asia. And the Middle East Zone gave attendees a much fuller understanding of the potential for business and investment in the six countries, covering Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and UAE. Saleumxay Kommasith, the Deputy Prime Minister of Laos, used his special address to illustrate Belt and Road cooperation in practice. He highlighted the impact of the Laos-China Railway, which opened in 2021. Since then, it has carried more than 70 million passengers and transported over 90 million metric tonnes of freight.

events.title: WA premier backflips on desalination plant amid $543m pipeline upgrade
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts $543m Goldfields water pipeline upgrade begins as premier backflips on desalination plant Premier Roger Cook and Kalgoorlie-Boulder Mayor Glenn Wilson at the Mt Charlotte water reservoir. ( ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas ) Work has begun on a long-awaited $543 million upgrade to Western Australia's historic Goldfields water pipeline. The upgrades are designed to increase the pipeline's capacity by about 10 per cent and are due to be completed by the end of 2027. Early stage work is also progressing on plans for a proposed desalination plant at Esperance, which could potentially provide additional water capacity for the Goldfields. The West Australian government is weighing up plans for another desalination plant on the south coast as work on a $543 million upgrade to the historic Goldfields water pipeline ramps up. Speaking at Kalgoorlie's Mt Charlotte Reservoir, where water from the Golden Pipeline first flowed in 1903, Premier Roger Cook said the upgrades would "futureproof" the Goldfields and Wheatbelt regions for generations. Mr Cook also conceded decades-old proposals for a desalination plant at Esperance, 700km south-east of Perth, could form part of plans to secure the water supply for WA's inland communities. It is a significant backflip for the government, which strongly criticised the WA Nationals for pushing the proposal during last year's state election. Water rushes into the Mt Charlotte reservoir at Kalgoorlie on January 24, 1903 after travelling along the 566km-long Golden Pipeline. ( Supplied: State Library of WA ) "We looked very closely at the idea of a desal plant at Esperance and then piping it up to Kalgoorlie," Mr Cook said. "It was decided, through engineering design, that we were better off increasing the capacity of the Goldfields pipeline rather than building a whole new pipeline up from Esperance. "I think we will need a desalination plant at Esperance. We will need desalination plants the length and breadth of this state, both as part of a growing economy and drying planet, so that's going to be an important piece of work. "Whether you ultimately see a desalination plant in Esperance feeding the Goldfields region more generally or simply meeting the needs of the growing Esperance community, I think you will need desal there." The Goldfields water supply scheme took five years to build during WA's 1890s gold rush. ( ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas ) During last year's election the WA Nationals promised to put $100 million towards an Esperance desalination plant to pipe water to Kalgoorlie-Boulder. But Labor's then-water minister Simone McGurk dismissed the proposal as "unviable" and a "thought bubble". On Monday, Water Minister Daniel Pastorelli confirmed the government utility Water Corporation was in the early stages of planning for a desalination project at Esperance. Construction is also progressing on two significant desalination plants in WA: the $2.8 billion Alkimos plant near Perth and the $1.1 billion Dampier plant in the Pilbara . There are also plans for another plant at Albany in the Great Southern. Roger Cook speaking to media in Kalgoorlie-Boulder on Monday, October 5. ( ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas ) The premier's comments about water security come after two key contracts, worth $170 million, were awarded in July to upgrade the capacity of the historic Goldfields Water Supply Scheme. The 566km-long pipeline was commissioned 123 years ago and supplies drinking water to more than 100,000 people across the Wheatbelt and Goldfields. Mr Pastorelli said work on the pipeline upgrades are now underway, with about 44.5km of pipeline to be replaced through the Wheatbelt shires of Merredin, Westonia and Yilgarn. It is expected to increase the pipeline's daily capacity by 7.2 million litres, or about 10 per cent, by the end of 2027. Mr Pastorelli said demand for water in the Goldfields had increased by 16 per cent since 2021, driven by the booming resources sector, and that the upgrades should satisfy existing demand "for some time" based on current projections. "This infrastructure will last … the pipes are being manufactured locally and will last for up to 150 years," he said. Mr Pastorelli said the government expected to award tenders in coming months for subsequent works at Binduli Reservoir near Kalgoorlie-Boulder, which would double its capacity from 400 to 800 million litres. Roger Cook with Kalgoorlie MLA Ali Kent and Daniel Pastorelli at Mt Charlotte water reservoir. ( ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas ) Kalgoorlie-Boulder Mayor Glenn Wilson welcomed the investment in the pipeline.

events.title: The Agentic AI Super Cycle
events.summary: The biggest technology revolutions of the past were driven by steam engines in the 1700s, railroads in the 1800s, electricity, cars, phones, planes, computers, and the internet in the 1900s. Now we are at the dawn of the Agentic AI revolution, which will be the biggest of them all. A few years ago, Goldman Sachs predicted Generative AI would increase global GDP by about 7% over 10 years. McKinsey had a roughly similar projection. Today, more than half of USA GDP growth is due to AI infrastructure investment. Agentic AI is much more powerful and more economically impactful than generative AI (and any previous industrial revolution) and requires much more compute investment for broad adoption. More than half of GDP in advanced economies is labor, with more than half of that labor being cognitive work that can be made much more productive with agentic AI. So far, coding is the early adopter, with most coders now using agentic AI to generate and validate most code. That makes the coder more of an architect and manager. What’s astounding is that this happened in less than 2 years. Frontier models are now used extensively to generate code for the next frontier model. But how quickly will other fields extensively adopt Agentic AI, and will supply chain constraints be overcome to meet the demand? Recently, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, called for a pacing of the development of frontier models to ensure everyone is building in the right controls and safeguards. AI leaders agree these controls are important. “We’ll make AI that is incredibly safe,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO. Any pacing of model development won’t slow the pace of investment. Dario noted safeguards will involve more training. Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, noted on CNBC recently, “even if we stop today, the amount of intelligence that’s available in the world is massive,” and “there is so much opportunity to drive growth with good ROI (return on investment.)” Data center AI CapEx (capital expenditure) will reach ~$1 trillion this year, and is projected to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030 (Source: Jensen Huang, Goldman Sachs Technology Conference). By comparison, world GDP is expected to be $123 trillion this year. AI is expected to go from ~1% to ~3%. Of the world’s top 10 highest market capitalization companies, 8 are major AI players: Nvidia, Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, TSMC, SpaceX, Meta, Broadcom. Collectively they make up almost 20% of the total market cap of the world’s publicly traded companies. Only a couple of these AI companies were in the top 10 a decade ago. Anthropic is expected to join the top 10 market capitalization club later this year. Massive companies like Nvidia are projecting 70% growth in revenues next year at huge scale. It’s natural to think this can’t keep going. But maybe it can. The key factors are: If agentic AI has high ROI; If it has a huge TAM (Total Adressable Market), and If it continues to become more powerful and less costly for years to come. If all those conditions are met, then we are in the biggest supercycle of our lives — and of history. The AI leader companies will get much bigger along with the US and world economies. There will be losers, there will be pauses/plateaus/consolidation, but this is a 10+ year super 2 cycle. Data center AI investment offers very attractive ROI The hyperscalers, Anthropic, and OpenAI are ramping AI CapEx because they see rapid demand growth, strong ROI, and because they don’t want to fall behind competition. This is a gold rush. Morgan Stanley in July concluded the major hyperscalers had paths to 25% to 50% ROIC (return on invested capital) for GenAI. These are very attractive returns. Dave Patterson, distinguished engineer and fellow at Google, said at the recent AI Infra Summit that Google recovers its cash outlay for a TPU in 1 year, and in 2 years for its custom Axion CPU. At Goldman Sachs Tech Conference, Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, said TPUs paid back twice as fast as GPUs, so even GPUs recover their investment in 2 years. This is a fantastic ROI, although he might be leaving out land and building costs. The reason this isn’t increasing near-term profits already is because Google keeps increasing CapEx spend faster than revenue growth. Amazon senior vice president Peter DeSantis talked at AI Infra Summit about how the company builds the data center and the racks in parallel with building the Trainiums. This accelerates cash recovery, enabling Trainium shipments from the end of the production line to the data center to be in operation (and making money) in a couple months. He contrasted this to most companies that build the chips, then the trays, then the racks, then the rows, then install. That keeps cash tied up much longer before revenue generation. New Street forecasts that hyperscaler negative cash flow will bottom in 2028 at 20% of revenues, but then rapidly turns to a positive free cash flow of 10% of revenues by 2030. AI cloud revenue grows almost 10× from 2026 to 2030! And AI cloud revenue by 2030 exceeds non-AI. TSMC builds >90% of all AI compute devices (GPUs and custom XPUs like TPU and Trainium). TSMC is an extremely well-run company that does its homework thoroughly. At the recent Goldman Sachs Technology Conference, TSMC’s CFO said the foundry thinks we are still in the very early stage of a megatrend. Token costs are dropping fast using advanced processes and packaging, but this leads to increased demand for AI compute. TSMC is building numerous huge fabs and advanced packaging factories to try to keep up. We need a LOT more AI compute at much lower $/token At the Goldman Sachs Tech Conference, Jeetu Patel, Cisco’s president and chief product officer, said that agent consumption of tokens now exceeds consumption of tokens by humans using GenAI, and <2% of humans are now using agents in a power user capacity. So the half of today’s tokens that are agentic could grow 50× when 100% of humans use agents in a power user capacity. And that’s for today’s models. Future models will grow exponentially in compute requirement, but costs are coming down exponentially at the same time. Figure 1: Agentic token consumption has soared to >50% of total demand. Source: Cisco Goldman Sachs in May projected token consumption will grow 40× from mid 2026 to mid 2030. At the AI Infrastructure Summit, Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale/HPC computing, showed how Agentic AI is 100× more compute-intensive than chat – and this is with just four agents. Figure 2: Agentic AI requires 100× more AI compute than chat. Source: Nvidia, AI Infra Summit At AI Infra Summit last month, Pat Gelsinger, general partner at Playground Global, explained we need a 10,000× improvement across the AI infrastructure stack. events.title: Extreme Environments Push Chips To Their Breaking Point
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Orbital data centers, military/aerospace vehicles, HPC experiments, quantum, and advanced manufacturing equipment are all putting pressure on chips to withstand extreme environments. Conditions include any combination of thermal and mechanical shock, radiation, high speeds, noise, vibration, pressure, and humidity. Advanced 4D modeling, simulation, AI/LLM-based design exploration, and physical lab tools are all needed to ensure complex chips and systems can survive. Chips that were once qualified against a limited set of operating conditions are now being designed for environments where multiple stresses hit at once. Radiation, thermal shock, vibration, pressure, noise, and cryogenic temperatures are colliding in applications ranging from orbital data centers and defense systems to particle physics, quantum computing, and advanced manufacturing. That is changing how chips are designed and qualified. AI-enabled design tools, machine learning, and language models can explore more design options earlier, but virtual models still have to be checked against physical behavior. For extreme-environment electronics, the challenge is not just predicting failure modes, but reproducing enough of the real operating environment to trust the prediction. Space is becoming one of the clearest pressure points. The growth of satellite constellations, orbital data centers, space probes, surface explorers, and military space systems is increasing demand for radiation-hardened designs, including at newer process nodes where performance and power benefits must be balanced against survivability. That demand is already showing up in the design ecosystem. “We have seen a major uptick in activity for rad-hard fab processes, particularly in the new process nodes to support orbital data centers,” said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management at Synopsys . “A lot of this is owing to the Golden Dome (multi-layered U.S. missile defense initiative). The next frontier for the next battlefield is space, and so you’re seeing the investment now accelerate, and we’re going to see a lot more rad-hard designs added.” Beyond national security, governments and nations are competing for global leadership in emerging technologies. For example, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) is working with Morgan State University, Northrop Grumman, and Project Omega on the DARPA-funded Rads to Watts program, which aims to convert Cold War-era radioactive decay into high-density nuclear micro-power radiovoltaic systems for extreme environments, including space, remote sensing, undersea infrastructure, and defense applications. [1] Radioisotopes such as Strontium-90 will be converted directly into electricity to operate for decades without refueling or battery replacement. Researchers achieve this by combining ultra-thin semiconductor layers with high-energy, beta-emitting isotopes. Simulation, characterization, and survivability analysis are essential to ensure these systems can operate in harsh environments. Meanwhile, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory is working with Siemens on a project titled Accelerating eXtreme Environment Specs-to-Silicon (AXESS) that uses LLMs and smaller surrogate models to speed up design exploration, then integrate and co-optimize all stages of chip development for quantum computing, fusion energy, and particle physics. [2] Fig. 1: A Fermilab engineer holds a custom circuit board designed to measure chip performance in cryogenic environments. Source : JJ Starr/Fermilab Each extreme-environment application presents a unique set of physical stressors that the hardware device must account for. “Particle accelerators and research accelerators are a particularly challenging environment because the doses are ridiculously high, and you need the equipment to do its thing while it’s getting damaged by the radiation,” said Hugh Barnaby, leader of extreme environment reliability in the U.S. Department of Defense’s ME Commons SWAP Hub at Arizona State University. “That extends to the medical equipment that’s used in proton therapies for cancer, which uses high-energy electrons. And in semiconductor manufacturing, lithography causes radiation damage. They’re using X-rays now for some of the really advanced technology, like backside power delivery. They have the power distribution on the backside of the chip. They used to use a wafer-analysis technique called LADA (laser-assisted device alteration), but now they can’t because the power is on the backside. They can’t use the lights. So they’re considering X-ray-assisted device alteration lasers (ZADA). The problem is, they’re worried about the X-rays causing damage to the material.” Barnaby and one of his students, Jereme Neuendank, found that strange things happen to semiconductors at very low temperatures. [3] “If you combine that with radiation, it gets even weirder,” said Barnaby. ” We had some good theories with models backing them up, and we’re still doing a lot of work in that area.” Lab tools are evolving to study the effects of multiple stressors at once. ASU researchers developed the Rigel DSTAT, which has three rods collectively containing 9,000 Curies (Ci) of radioactive material to simulate the radiation environments found in space and nuclear applications. It also contains a tiny cryostat, which enables devices to be exposed to really saturated, extremely cold temperatures by evacuating a chamber and then filling it with either liquid nitrogen or argon, whose temperatures are about the same. “Then we can do radiation testing at liquid nitrogen, which is 77 Kelvin,” said Barnaby. Fig. 2: This illustrated setup shows how ASU’s extreme environments lab would test radiation and extreme cold together to mimic space. Illustration by Sophia Franz. Source : ASU The tool was ideal for a company designing readout ICs for satellites that would need to withstand cold, radiation, ionizing-dose threats, and low-frequency noise. In particular, random telegraph noise has emerged as one of the biggest reliability problems today, especially in analog/mixed-signal electronics. And that noise problem is exacerbated in the cold. “You want the cold to reduce the noise that comes off of the diodes that are creating the currents, the light detectors,” Barnaby noted. “They like the cold there. But when you’re doing the CMOS, to do the readout of those signals, the random telegraph noise signal does not, at best, improve with cold temperature. We’re still studying that physics.” The applications for these kinds of lab tools are growing. “We have talked to people about doing research in thermal energy exploration,” he explained. “We’ve also been getting into advanced packaging, which means extending into a pretty wide array of reliability issues such as pressure, humidity, high tempe

events.title: South Korean banks on high alert after wave of cyberattacks
events.summary: Shinhan Bank and Yegaram Savings Bank reported the largest breaches, affecting about 25,000 and 40,000 people, respectively. A wave of cyberattacks exposed personal data at seven South Korean financial firms, with suspicions of a single attacker using AI to breach security systems. Authorities ordered emergency security measures, including blocking external access and conducting thorough investigations into the breaches and AI-based attack methods. Concerns arose over banks' cybersecurity spending levels, prompting regulators to focus on overall security frameworks and vulnerabilities rather than just budgets. SEOUL – A wave of cyberattacks has exposed personal data at seven South Korean financial firms, prompting emergency security measures as regulators investigate whether a single attacker used artificial intelligence to breach their defences. Shinhan Bank and Yegaram Savings Bank reported the largest breaches, affecting about 25,000 and 40,000 people, respectively. The authorities found the same attacker’s internet protocol address across all seven affected firms, raising suspicions of a coordinated campaign. The Financial Services Commission (FSC) convened an emergency meeting with financial industry leaders on Oct 4 and ordered firms to block external access to systems unless essential for business operations. “We cannot rule out the possibility of attacks using AI,” FSC chairman Lee Eok-won said, urging the sector to maintain the highest level of vigilance. Lee said there were no signs that information directly usable for payments or other crimes had been leaked, but warned that the exposed data could facilitate voice phishing and fraudulent text messages. The breaches first came to light on Sept 30 at Shinhan Bank, where leaked loan application data included names, phone numbers, annual income and calculated borrowing limits. KB Kookmin Bank suffered similar breaches affecting 153 individuals, while Hana Bank reported 89 cases. Woori Bank and NH NongHyup Bank detected attempted intrusions but successfully blocked them, with no data breaches reported. Regional banks and non-bank financial institutions were also affected, including BNK Busan Bank, where 11 outsourced workers were impacted; Yegaram Savings Bank, which reported 40,000 cases; Welcome Savings Bank, with 2,200 cases; and Hyundai Capital, where 146 individuals were affected. With the same attacker’s IP address found across all seven affected financial companies, the authorities suspect that a single attacker used an AI-powered tool to launch simultaneous intrusion attempts. Other traces indicate that Artex, a Chinese-developed AI-based penetration-testing platform, was used. The tool is designed to identify security vulnerabilities and select its next intrusion method based on the results of previous attacks. To circumvent the tightly secured core systems of banks, the hacker instead targeted less-protected non-core systems, such as sales support platforms. Financial regulators plan to overhaul the sector’s security framework in response to the incident, to strengthen defences against evolving cyber threats. The authorities have ordered financial institutions to block external access unless it is essential for business operations. President Lee Jae Myung on Oct 4 called for a thorough investigation into a series of hacking attacks. “Lee instructed authorities to take the matter seriously, conduct a thorough investigation and spare no effort in coming up with measures to address the issue,” presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said in a press release. Damage varies by cybersecurity spending The string of security breaches has raised questions over whether commercial banks, which are reporting record profits, are spending enough on cybersecurity. While Shinhan Bank suffered the most significant breach among the top four commercial banks in the recent cyberattacks, its relatively low level of cybersecurity spending has come under scrutiny. Shinhan Bank’s information security budget stood at 40.59 billion won (S$38.7 million) in 2026, the lowest among the top four commercial banks here. KB Kookmin Bank had the largest budget at 86.07 billion won, followed by Hana Bank at 63.63 billion won and Woori Bank at 61.56 billion won. In 2025, Shinhan ranked second-lowest among the four top commercial banks in information security spending, with 36.9 billion won, ahead of only Woori Bank’s 36.4 billion won. Given the difference in scale between the banks, however, Shinhan’s spending could be considered relatively lower. Regulators say differences in the damage cannot be explained simply by how much each bank spends on cybersecurity. Instead, they are focusing on how effectively each bank’s overall security framework addressed vulnerabilities in individual business systems.

events.title: Trump proposal could make it easier to suspend or expel Head Start students
events.summary: The Trump administration has proposed changes to Head Start regulations that would remove rules against suspending and expelling preschoolers It was sometime around Xavier Rogers' second birthday that his mom and Early Head Start teachers noticed a shift in his demeanor. Xavier, usually a happy baby, now mostly wanted to play alone and would sometimes bite and hit other kids in his class. Instead of removing Xavier from his class, his Chicago-area preschool gave the family extra support from a social-emotional and mental healthcare team. “With these supports in place, I feel like he has grown tremendously,” said Xavier's mom, Joanna Isitt, a Head Start teacher herself. Now 4, “he’s become much, much more aware of himself and how he feels and how others may feel.” He's less likely to resort to negative behaviors, and he even encourages her to join him in breathing exercises, saying, “OK, Mama, smell the flowers, blow the candles.” The protections and support Isitt and her son received are part of longstanding Head Start regulations, but they could soon disappear under the Trump administration’s proposed rule change for the 61-year-old early childhood education program. The proposal would eliminate federal guidelines that keep kids who exhibit behaviors like Xavier’s from being removed from Head Start programs. Instead of receiving the help he needed to self-regulate, the little boy could have been told to leave, and his mother could have been left scrambling for alternative care. AP has partnered with The 74 , an education-focused nonprofit news outlet, to cover the impact of the Trump administration's proposed changes to Head Start. The family lives in Illinois, which has its own regulations against imposing exclusionary discipline such as suspensions and expulsions on preschoolers. But some other states, such as South Carolina and Florida, do not. The updated Head Start rules would ask providers to make their own discipline policies by following state and local licensing requirements. Advocates and experts fear Head Start students and families in these places could experience a more punitive reality if the proposed changes take effect. Suspensions and expulsions are associated with negative outcomes, including lower educational achievement, decreased likelihood of graduating high school and depression. “If the state of Florida doesn’t have standards related to suspension and expulsion, and that’s what the administration wants us to go by … I think as a country we should all be very concerned that we’re taking our most vulnerable children and families and potentially putting them in an environment where they’re going to have no protections,” said Wanda Minick, executive director of the Florida Head Start Association. Only 14 states and Washington, D.C., have laws or policies that align with Head Start’s rules around exclusionary discipline, according to a recent analysis by the Children’s Equity Project at Arizona State University. Of those, researchers said, only around half the laws appear to apply to all children under 5, the population served by Head Start. And in only one, Minnesota, do the regulations explicitly include Head Start programs. That means that in 70% of states, Head Start students would be left with fewer guardrails should the rule change pass. Many of the states with flexible rules or no laws end up removing the most preschoolers from their classrooms, while states with tighter regulations suspend far fewer, according to an analysis of 2023-24 federal data by The 74 and The Associated Press. The data captures suspensions for pre-kindergartners who are enrolled in public school districts. South Carolina reported suspending 604 public preschoolers a total of 1,181 times that year, while Minnesota reported zero students suspended. Florida reported expelling 466 public preschoolers, more than any other state. Ultimately, the data shows, some Head Start students would remain shielded from expulsion and suspension, but some would not — simply depending on where they live. The public may comment on the rule change through Oct. 6. Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials US Marine arrested on suspicion of murder after 'brutal and heinous' death in Japan District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' The Trump administration is attempting to roll back these discipline safeguards along with many of the tools that prevent behaviors from escalating in the first place, advocates said. These include lower adult-to-child ratios, a required number of monthly mental health consultations, timely developmental screenings and staff breaks. In this environment, “if they were to make it permissible to either reject kids or throw them out, I think a lot of teachers would, because they’re just feeling so much strain,” said Joel Ryan, executive director of the Washington State Association of Head Start.

events.title: Lao man deported by the US to Eswatini is released after more than a year in prison
events.summary: A Lao man deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has been released after more than a year in prison CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- A Laotian citizen deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration's immigration crackdown was released from a maximum-security prison in the African nation on Sunday after being held there for more than a year, his lawyer said. Phone Chomsavanh was among five immigrants deported to Eswatini — where he has no ties — in July 2025 in the early days of the Trump administration's secretive and highly contentious third-country deportation program. Chomsavanh's U.S.-based lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said in a statement announcing his release that he had only been informed that he was being deported to Eswatini shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him and other deportees landed there more than 14 months ago. Chomsavanh was now being deported to Laos, Nguyen said. Chomsavanh and the four other immigrants he was deported to Eswatini with were convicted of serious crimes in the U.S., but had served their sentences by the time they were sent to the Matsapha Correctional Complex near Eswatini's administrative capital, Mbabane. “He had already served his time. Instead they put him on a plane without telling him where it was headed and left him in a prison in a country he had never heard of, where nobody ever accused him of anything," Nguyen said. “He sat there for more than a year. No notice, no hearing, no chance to object. That is not due process by any definition.” He said in separate messages to The Associated Press that Chomsavanh had left Eswatini and landed in Johannesburg en route to Laos. An Eswatini government spokesperson didn’t immediately acknowledge Chomsavanh’s release. Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand after his parents fled Laos, and his family moved to the United States when he was 7, his lawyer said. Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported from the United States to African countries that aren't their home nations since the third-country program began last year, according to advocacy groups Human Rights First and Refugees International, which have been monitoring the deportations. Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the U.S., some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. Eswatini, which is Africa's last absolute monarchy and is ruled by a king, was paid $5.1 million by the Trump administration to take deportees, according to the agreement between the countries. Eswatini has received around 30 deportees so far. Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials US Marine arrested on suspicion of murder after 'brutal and heinous' death in Japan District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' The program, which results in immigrants being held in countries they have no ties to and where they haven't been charged with any crime, has been fiercely criticized by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the U.S. and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent. The Trump administration has defended the policy as a way to quickly remove immigrants who have final deportation orders from the U.S. when their home countries might not immediately take them back. Last month, a U.S. appeals court upheld a judge's ruling to halt the program, because it didn’t give immigrants facing removal from the U.S. time to challenge their deportation to a third country if they fear persecution or torture there. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last week to temporarily allow U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to continue swiftly removing immigrants to third countries, though it will hear arguments in the case in December. The program has largely been carried out in secrecy, with little transparency over how many immigrants have been deported to third countries, and where and in what conditions they are being held. events.title: Holiday cottage company insisted on a death certificate to amend our break
events.summary: Sykes Holiday Cottages showed no empathy and insisted on paperwork we didn’t have so soon after my husband’s death W e booked a break with Sykes Holiday Cottages for 11 of us to celebrate my mum’s 80th birthday last February. The cost was £2,400, paid for by my 87-year-old dad, but it was my husband who made the booking. In January, my husband was diagnosed with aggressive lymphoma, and he died 10 days before the trip. My parents and some other members of the party still planned to take the holiday, and my dad informed Sykes of the death, since my husband was their point of contact. Sykes declared that the booking could not be honoured in my late husband’s name and that they would need a copy of his death certificate to move it into my name. We did not have one since an inquest into the death had been ordered. Sykes said a copy of my marriage certificate would suffice. I submitted this, only to be told that “an official document recognised by the state that confirms the passing of the deceased” was required. We provided a screenshot of the inquest listing from the coroner’s court website but were advised that this was not sufficient evidence. My GP wrote a letter confirming the death, but Sykes did not reply, and by then we were all too distressed to continue. Later, Sykes sent numerous emails to my late husband’s email address asking whether he had enjoyed the stay. We never received a refund, and I have not felt emotionally strong enough to do anything further before now. I could hardly believe what I was reading as I trawled through Sykes’s correspondence. Its response, on being informed of your husband’s untimely death, was to send him an email asking for information. When Sykes received the requested marriage certificate, the company simultaneously stated in an email that this provided sufficient proof for the booking to be transferred to your name, and that the booking could not be transferred without an official confirmation of death. The GP letter confirming the death merely elicited an email saying Sykes would be in touch. By then, the trip was two days away. Sykes still did not amend the booking name, nor did it acknowledge the link to the coroner’s inquest listing. The next you heard from them was the first of several emails addressed to your late husband hoping that he had enjoyed the holiday. When you asked them to stop using his email address, Sykes apologised for the “inconvenience”. Four days later, when you had to complain about another such email to him, you were told unapologetically that feedback forms are sent automatically. By then, Sykes had been informed multiple times over a fortnight that your husband had died. Sykes, I discover, does not have an official bereavement policy which, given the size of the business, is poor enough. But empathy does not require an official mandate and you received none. Its onerous name change requirements are more suitable for a visa application than checking into a Cumbrian cottage. It refunded the £2,400 pronto when I got in touch and added £150 in “goodwill”. I think that’s a paltry sum for the distress it caused, but you have accepted it so you can put the ordeal behind you. A spokesperson said: “We have contacted the family directly to apologise and resolve the matter, and are reviewing our processes to ensure situations like this are always handled with the care and sensitivity they deserve.” Hats off to first-class customer service Our spirits need some good news, so here are some tales of how customer service ought to be. “We bought a secondhand Scandibørn bed from a third-party seller and found four screws were missing,” writes CC . “They were so specialist that no shop even knew what they were called. We contacted Scandibørn with low expectations of help, but they immediately offered to send us the missing screws for free. Exemplary customer service, which has earned a customer for life.” MS , meanwhile, raises his revamped hat to Tilley. “Thirty years ago I bought a Tilley hat, which became a constant companion on walks and holidays. It was beginning to show its age and, since the label promised a lifetime guarantee, I contacted Tilley. I was asked to submit photographs and was promptly invited to choose from three designs. The replacement was dispatched within days, with a handling charge of £20. Sadly, this one will outlast me.” We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. events.title: Saudi Aramco cuts Asia crude prices to six-year low amid recovery as oil flows rebound
events.summary: Saudi Aramco has cut prices for its flagship crude grade sold to Asian buyers to a six-year low, as the world’s largest oil exporter competes for market share amid a recovery in oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The state-owned Saudi oil company will sell Arab Light crude to Asian customers at a discount of $5 a barrel below the regional benchmark for November, widening the discount from $2 a barrel in October, according to a Bloomberg survey. Traders and refiners polled by Bloomberg had expected Aramco to raise prices by $5 a barrel for November. The price reduction signals that Saudi Arabia may be seeking to boost sales to Asia as oil flows from the Middle East recover after months of disruption linked to the Iran war. Aramco raised its November crude prices for Europe by $3 a barrel, while leaving prices for the US unchanged from October, Bloomberg reported. Although attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue, the volume of oil passing through the waterway has increased over the past few months. Saudi Arabia sold almost 100 million barrels of oil to Asian buyers in mid-September, helping to avert a looming supply crunch. The kingdom has also restored much of the crude flow through its East-West pipeline after suffering damage in an attack. The recovery has helped increase oil exports from the Middle East, with JPMorgan estimating last week that shipments had reached 98 per cent of prewar levels, Bloomberg reported. The pipeline allows Saudi Arabia to transport crude from its eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, providing an alternative export route that bypasses the strait. Aramco’s official selling prices apply to crude supplied under long-term contracts to refiners, who would typically collect their shipments from Ras Tanura on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast. Ras Tanura hosts one of the world’s largest oil export terminals and a major refining facility. The port handles a significant share of Saudi crude exports, with cargoes typically heading to markets in Europe and Asia, including China, Japan and South Korea. But continued risks to shipping through the strait have prompted many customers to avoid the route. Aramco has asked Asian refiners to submit nominations for the volumes they intend to collect in November from ports inside the Arabian Gulf, as well as from Yanbu on the Red Sea and Sidi Kerir on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, Bloomberg reported.

events.title: Singapore’s retail sales up 0.7% in August, led by cosmetics and telecom equipment sectors
events.summary: Takings at the till rose 0.7% year on year in August, following July’s 1.3% increase, according to data from the Singapore Department of Statistics. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s retail sales inched up 0.7% year on year in August 2026, following July’s 1.3% growth, according to data from the Singapore Department of Statistics (SingStat). In a release on Oct 5, SingStat said retail sales excluding motor vehicles, parts and accessories rose 1.6% year on year, compared with 1.3% growth in July. On a month-on-month and seasonally adjusted basis, retail sales fell 1% in August. Excluding motor vehicles, parts and accessories, sales rose 0.6%. Total retail sales were estimated at $4.5 billion in August, with online transactions accounting for 15.7% of the total, up from 15.2% in July. Within the retail trade sector, the majority of industries recorded year-on-year growth in sales in August. Cosmetics, toiletries and medical goods saw the strongest year-on-year growth, with sales going up by 11.2%, partly driven by higher sales of cosmetics and toiletries. This was closely followed by the computer and telecommunications equipment industry, where sales grew by 10.7%, driven by higher mobile phone sales . Other industries that recorded year-on-year increases include recreational goods, where sales rose 4.3% and petrol service stations, where sales climbed 3.2%. In contrast, motor vehicles, parts and accessories recorded a year-on-year decline in sales of 4.6%, while retailers of watches and jewellery saw a dip in sales of 2.7% in August. The Singapore economy is running hot on the artificial intelligence boom, but consumer spending and the job market appear to be cooling, said Maybank economist Chua Hak Bin. Consumers may be turning more cautious on the back of a softer job market, the pullback in global stock markets and the uncertain outlook, he said. The SingStat data also showed that food and beverage services sales fell by 1.6% year on year in August, extending July’s 1.9% decline. The total F&B sales were estimated at $1.7 billion, with online transactions accounting for 20.6% of the total, down from 20.9% in July. Within the F&B services sector, cafes saw the biggest drop in year-on-year sales of 5.3%, while foodcourts and other eating places recorded year-on-year fall in sales of 4.8% in August. Restaurant sales also decreased by 2.1%. In contrast, sales at fast-food outlets rose by 7.8%, while those of food caterers increased by 2.9%. Retail sales should be supported in the coming months by still stable, albeit mixed, labour market conditions; higher tourist spending associated with large-scale events such as the Formula 1 Grand Prix and major concerts; and ongoing government support measures, said DBS Bank senior economist Chua Han Teng. “While inflation is not accelerating, it has been rising and is likely to somewhat erode consumers’ purchasing power, which could prompt households to exercise greater prudence in their spending and, in turn, limit the pace of retail sales activity,” he added. Selena Ling, chief economist and head of OCBC Group Research, said the outlook is hazy, as the anticipated impact on outdoor activities – including leisure, sports and F&B – is likely negative in the near term. “While we do have the Singapore International Energy Week and F1 in October, the question remains how prolonged the haze situation is going to be. On the flip side, sales of air purifiers and masks should improve,” she added.

events.title: Ben Affleck says he had a ‘heart attack’ when he first saw what AI could do — then he used it in his movie
events.summary: Ben Affleck said his company's AI tools are designed to support, not replace, people working in film. Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images Ben Affleck said his first close look at AI gave him a "heart attack." He then built a company that spent eight months shooting footage to train AI tools for film crews. Affleck said he used AI on his upcoming film, "Animals," but won't say exactly how. Ben Affleck said he wants AI to support filmmakers and artists in the creative process. Speaking at the Bloomberg Screentime event in Los Angeles over the weekend, Affleck said his company's AI tools are meant to help creatives work more efficiently, not make them obsolete. Affleck said his interest in AI grew after he started a visual-effects company, and he was able to use his celebrity status to get a closer look at the early work coming out of Google and OpenAI. "At first, I kind of had a heart attack. I called Matt Damon , and I was like, dude, we have to do as many movies in the next few years because we're finished," Affleck said. He said he began wondering how AI could be used "in an ethical way" to help people make movies without shutting others out. His solution, he said, was to create his own dataset so the technology could work "hand in glove" with artists. So, Affleck said he "raised the money" and spent eight months shooting a large collection of footage, which he used to further train existing AI models for specific filmmaking tasks. He said AI models first learn basic concepts, such as colors, from huge amounts of footage. But to understand the finer points of filmmaking, the models need more professionally shot material. "In order to obtain that information, I was concerned that most of the models being used had been trained on my peers' — people I know — work and I was uncomfortable with that," Affleck said. "I thought, that's not really a viable business." Instead, Affleck said, his company takes open models built on publicly available footage and trains them for cinematic work. Filmmakers can then further train the tools on their own productions as they work, retaining the proprietary nature of their footage and the learning that comes from it, he said. Affleck added that the AI is not meant to "replace people" nor "eliminate" them. "I don't believe that there will ever be 'Just type it in and make a movie that people want to see,'" Affleck said. "But the whole effort behind it was to do something ethical, to do something that did not displace people, but that allowed people in this economy and this world to benefit from this technology." In July, Netflix paid $587 million for Affleck's company, InterPositive. Affleck said he also used the AI tool "for lots of things" on his upcoming film, "Animals," mostly during post-production, though he declined to say exactly how. "Animals" is set to be released on Netflix on October 9. "I'm a little bit hesitant to point out what they are or even talk about it because, like, in my business, we're trying to foster the illusion of reality, right?" Affleck said, comparing it to a magician explaining how a trick works. AI remains deeply divisive in Hollywood. Some figures, including James Cameron and Martin Scorsese, have supported its use as a creative tool, while others, such as Guillermo del Toro and Christopher Nolan, have questioned its potential impact on jobs and artistic control. events.title: SGX and partners roll out youth stock programme to lower barriers and equip young investors
events.summary: The Youth Stock Ambassadors Programme will give selected young investors capital market education, practical exposure and opportunities to engage with the ecosystem. SINGAPORE – An initiative was launched on Oct 5 to get more young investors interested in the Singapore stock market. Called the Youth Stock Ambassadors Programme, the scheme will give selected young investors capital market education, practical exposure and opportunities to engage with the ecosystem. It was launched by the Singapore Exchange (SGX), Securities Association of Singapore and Securities Investors Association (Singapore), or SIAS. It comes as the SGX kicked off its scheme on Oct 5 to make investing in higher-priced stocks more affordable for investors, with the reduction of board lot sizes for an initial 11 selected stocks. The three organisations said in a statement: “Together, these initiatives lower the barriers to entry for investing, arm younger investors with more information on the Singapore stock market, and provide them with the opportunity to access higher-value Singapore stocks with smaller amounts of initial capital.” The new programme will be a youth-led platform that is open to students in tertiary institutions. The students should have an interest in capital markets and investing. The Securities Association of Singapore and SIAS will start by engaging the SIAS Youth Chapter to gather feedback and create the programme together. Young investors who are selected as Youth Stock Ambassadors will receive capital market education and training, opportunities to engage with listed companies, as well as internships and mentorship. These young investors will also develop analytical, research and content creation skills. “The programme aims to build a community of informed investors who can help inspire and support the next generation on their investment journeys,” the three organisations said. Members of the Securities Association of Singapore will also work closely with SIAS to increase overall engagement with young investors, not just through the new programme. Securities Association of Singapore chairman Wilson He said: “The reduction in board lot sizes is a positive step towards making Singapore equities more accessible, but it is only part of the equation. “It must be complemented by investor education, access to quality research, mentorship, internship opportunities and practical market exposure.” He added that the new scheme aims to empower young investors with the knowledge, confidence and support needed to become informed, long-term participants in Singapore’s capital markets. He noted that the association’s member brokerages are also committed to supporting the reduced board lot roll-out through their own investor education and outreach initiatives. SGX group head of global financial markets Ng Yao Loong said that building the next generation of investors goes beyond making Singapore equities more accessible. “The Youth Stock Ambassadors Programme provides opportunities for young investors to engage with listed companies and market practitioners, helping them build informed investing habits and a longer-term perspective,” he added. Meanwhile, SIAS vice-president Ang Hao Yao noted that an issue among young investors is that they may be overwhelmed by the amount of available information. They also need to build a strong foundation in investment principles and knowledge. “For many, the amount needed to get started on investing in Singapore stocks can be a real barrier. With the launch of reduced board lot sizes, it lowers the entry point by making the Singapore market more approachable and creates an opportunity to build sound investing habits earlier,” he said. Tay Jingxuan, an executive committee member at the Singapore Institute of Technology’s Investment and Commerce Club, said that the lot size reduction is a timely opportunity for students and young adults to begin their investment journey early. “While many young individuals recognise the importance of early investing, capital constraints often pose a significant barrier,” she added. “For many students, setting aside a few thousand dollars to start building positions in blue-chip stocks can be difficult, given our limited savings and inconsistent part-time income.” She said that the board lot size reduction means that young investors may feel less intimidated when they want to invest , as they no longer have to commit a large portion of their personal capital with limited investing experience . Phoon Mei Gi, president of the NTU Investment Interactive Club, also said that it gives young investors like her more flexibility. “For example, I could set aside around $150 every month to slowly build a position in a higher-priced stock that I previously did not consider because the minimum board lot was too expensive. Instead of waiting until I’ve saved up a much larger amount, I can start smaller and invest more consistently,” she said.

events.title: From hotel suites to virtual reality, museums turn to licensing deals as costs rise
events.summary: Natural History Museum and British Museum among cultural institutions leveraging collections and exhibitions They are often free to visit but museums are bolstering their finances by putting their stamp on everything from upmarket hotel suites to trendy jumpsuits and virtual reality experiences. Forget buying a T-shirt. If you can afford the “from £724” price tag, you can spend the night in the Natural History Museum family suite at the Park Plaza London Riverbank hotel, which has an interior inspired by the museum’s founder, Sir Richard Owen, complete with Tyrannosaurus rex bunk beds. Deals such as this are becoming more commonplace as cultural institutions look to leverage their renowned collections and trusted brands in the face of funding cuts and rising costs. Data shows that overall UK sales of licensed merchandise and services grew 7% to $19.2bn (£14.5bn) last year, according to the industry trade body Licensing International. A breakdown of the UK market figures shows that the “art property” category, which includes museums, grew by more than 8%, while “attractions and promotions” (which includes immersive experiences at museums and art galleries) soared by 53%. “Our licensing programme continues to grow consistently at about 15% year on year,” said Louisa Skevington, the licensing manager at the Natural History Museum, who added that “experiences” were becoming an increasingly important part of that. “It’s about finding creative ways to bring the museum and its stories to people wherever they are, while continuing to grow the reach and impact of the programme.” The Natural History Museum’s previous deals include a Farrow & Ball paint range inspired by Werner’s Nomenclature of Colours and a collection with the fashion brand Lucy & Yak featuring dinosaur-print jumpsuits and dungarees, aimed at millennials and gen Z. More recently it worked with the virtual reality experience company Sandbox on the prehistoric adventure Age of Dinosaurs. The importance of licensing means a growing number of museums, galleries and heritage organisations are exhibiting at this week’s Brand Licensing Europe conference in London. New attenders include the National Gallery, the National Trust for Scotland, the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford and Tate Enterprises. They join the British Museum , the Natural History Museum, the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Imperial War Museum. The competition is stiff, however, as the agenda includes talks on the “Bluey effect” and the new Harry Potter TV series. The huge demand for Bayeux tapestry tickets “demonstrates the appetite for major cultural moments, and the opportunity to build on that interest beyond a visit to the museum”, says Craig Bendle, the manager of product licensing at the British Museum. Indeed, the Bayeux tapestry merchandise created by its separate retail team, which includes a collaboration with the London department store Liberty, made it into Vogue . Bendle reports growing interest from brands that want to create something “genuinely distinctive”, with the museum’s collection of more than 8m objects an “extraordinary source of inspiration”, he says. The V&A is also looking for novel ways to draw on its 2.8m objects. It launched 63 product ranges in 2025, which demonstrates the “growing role licensing plays in taking the V&A beyond our museum walls”, said Jen Maude-Roxby, its head of licensing and business development. That programme includes William Morris-inspired phone cases with the tech accessories brand CASETiFY, and pictures for the art store of Samsung’s “the Frame” TV, which displays artworks when the TV is off, transforming the blank monitor into a picture.

events.title: ‘I didn’t know what to do’: collapse of providers of high-end digs leaves students in shock
events.summary: Cost of living crisis and drop in international students hits market for purpose-built accommodation “I t was dead in the middle of summer, it was a shock,” says Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan. The fourth-year game design student at Abertay University was at home with her family thousands of miles away in Thailand when she discovered the owner of her Scottish studio flat had abruptly gone bust. “I was like, my hands are tied. I’m not in the country. I don’t know what to do,” she says. Sriwiboonrattan was forced to act quickly to secure new housing for the academic year, which has just begun, paying £850 to have her possessions moved. Her sudden upheaval was emblematic of the wider crisis in student housing. While UK universities face a financial crisis , providers of accommodation are grappling with falling international student numbers , a cost of living squeeze and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties. A string of tower blocks known as purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA), targeted at more affluent students, have run into financial difficulty. It had been touted as the ultimate student living: smart city centre blocks with gyms, cinemas and rooftop terraces have sprung up across the UK. A world away from the traditional image of dirty and dingy shared digs , the flats have offered a spacious alternative for their relatively affluent residents – often international students. Now, some sit half empty, and several schemes have gone bust . Sriwiboonrattan was among nearly 70 students in Dundee who were left scrambling to find accommodation in late July after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a 116-room city centre block that had a concierge and a shared games lounge with a pool table. Despite the boom in housing developed by financial institutions in recent years, many students heading off to university this term faced a different dilemma. Rents at the tower blocks have grown much faster than maintenance loans for British students, leaving PSBAs financially out of reach. Meanwhile, the cost of living crisis has put financial pressure on students seeking university-owned or managed accommodation, while rising rents have hit those wanting to live in shared private rentals. Underlining the scale of the shortage of affordable housing, the students’ union in Bristol included an emergency support number for the housing charity Shelter in an email to new students. At PSBAs, the national average rent, excluding London, is £191 a week including bills, according to the website StuRents. At the top end, en suite rooms in Manchester command a weekly rent of £170 to £320 , whereas in London, en suite rooms are £250 to £650 a week , and studio apartments in Bloomsbury cost between £550 and £800 plus. “I wasn’t able to get into PBSA because it is very expensive in Birmingham,” says Soham Chougale, 23, a student at University College Birmingham. “I am an international student, so my working hours are capped at 20 hours [a week in term time], which means I can’t afford to live in PBSA,” says Chougale, the education officer at UCB Guild of Students . He lived in university-owned dorms for the first two years of his aviation management degree and now shares a two-bedroom privately rented flat with a friend. On campus, he paid £660 rent including bills a month during the first year, which rose by 10% in his second year; now he pays £700 rent a month, excluding bills. While living on campus “gave me the best feeling of community” and “I still have those friends that I met on the first day”, the wifi was patchy, some facilities were broken and there was a mouse infestation, he recounts. “PBSA can be quite pricey,” says Matthew Pointon, a real estate analyst at Capital Economics, but adds: “Normally professionally managed buildings are better in terms of quality.” In London, which attracts the richest students, there is still demand for upmarket accommodation, but outside the capital, there is an oversupply in some cities, such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham. This week, university staff began strikes in Dundee, Edinburgh and Nottingham over budget cuts, with the industrial action threatening to wipe out a term of teaching for many students. In Nottingham, demand has fallen from a pandemic peak of 46,295 beds in 2022-23 to 42,290 beds in 2025-26, while 7,700 more PSBA beds came on to the market, the student housing charity Unipol calculated. The number of students arriving from China has stagnated, and those from the new growth countries India, Pakistan and Nigeria are much more cost-conscious than the pre-Covid students from China , says Martin Blakey, an adviser on student living and the former chief executive of Unipol.

events.title: The 2029 tipping point: Western populations are about to start shrinking, piling pressure on public finances
events.summary: Europe's population will peak in 2029 according to forecasts, while the U.S.'s lies further ahead but is heavily dependent on immigration. Moody's says the fiscal pressures from aging emerge long before populations actually start shrinking. AI and increased productivity can only partially offset the long-term challenge of an aging workforce, Chemla said. As Western populations age, fewer workers and higher costs will strain public finances, credit rating agency Moody's has warned. Europe is at the sharp end of the demographic shift. The European Union's population is projected to peak as soon as 2029, "after which a sustained long-term decline will begin," according to the European Commission. The U.S. Census Bureau does not expect the American population to peak until 2080 under its main projection , or until 2043 under its low-immigration scenario. Excluding immigration impact, the population decline has already started. But Moody's says the fiscal pressures from aging emerge long before populations actually start shrinking. Today, G7 economies have about three working-age people for every person over 65. That ratio is expected to fall to around two by 2050, putting further pressure on growth and public finances, including healthcare systems, according to Moody's. Aging populations affect economies through slower economic growth, greater pressure on public finances from pension and care costs, changing consumer demand, and shifts in real interest rates and sovereign yields, Olivier Chemla, vice president of credit strategy and standards at Moody's, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday. In a report published last week, Moody's forecasts that the world's aging populations will have fundamental impacts on the global economy and lead to difficult policy decisions. While population growth has long been a tailwind for growth and creditworthiness, falling fertility rates and unprecedented speed of changing age structures are now changing that picture, Moody's writes. "Fewer workers will limit productive capacity, while fewer households and consumers will weaken demand. As a result, countries will have to rely more on productivity to sustain growth," the report states. "This is a partial mitigant because you can certainly replace and enhance the supply side of the economy in factories and in services, but at the same time, robots do not consume – at least not yet – and so on the demand side, you will still be having that gap, which will slow growth," he added. And it's not only Europe and the U.S., but emerging economies are aging rapidly, too. China's share of people aged 65 and over has doubled from 7% to 14% over the past two decades, with Brazil, Thailand and Turkiye on similar trajectories. These countries will face the costs of aging at much lower income levels than the advanced economies that aged before them, the report says, noting that in Europe, the same shift took several decades.
