events.title: Money stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400%
events.summary: Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and family The total amount stolen by criminals who hack into people’s emails and social media accounts and then pretend to be them has risen by more than 400% in a year, official UK data shows. In many cases, the scammers are hijacking people’s accounts in order to use their identity to sell fake event tickets – such as to sold-out gigs – to unsuspecting friends and family. The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25, according to the Report Fraud service run by the City of London police, which holds national responsibility for economic crime. However, the true total may be much higher as many scam victims do not report the crime, often because they feel embarrassed, and sometimes because the individual amount of money involved was relatively small. The Guardian previously featured the case of a music fan whose Instagram account was targeted by hackers, who used her identity to advertise tickets to an Oasis gig and stole £1,400 from her friends. She said the hackers impersonated her so well that her friends and family genuinely thought they were speaking to her. Others have been scammed by fraudulent WhatsApp and text messages in which a criminal pretends to be their child or a relative who is in an emergency situation and urgently needs cash. This has been dubbed the “Hi mum” scam . Data from Santander has shown that among customers of the bank, fraudsters pretending to be someone’s son were the most successful at extracting cash, followed by daughters. Ch Supt Amanda Wolf, head of Report Fraud operations, said: “For most people, being hacked isn’t just a cyber issue – it’s personal. It can leave victims locked out of important accounts, worried about what information has been accessed, and concerned that criminals may use their identity to target others.” She added that what starts with one compromised account “can quickly impact family, friends and colleagues as fraudsters exploit trusted relationships to commit further fraud”. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Report Fraud is launching an awareness campaign urging the public to protect their online accounts from hackers by switching to passkeys where they are available. A passkey uses an individual’s device and biometrics to authenticate them and cannot be hacked like a password.

events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Decoded by POLITICO that he does not accept "the really catastrophic risks" of AI. Heather Diehl/Getty Images OpenAI's Sam Altman diverged from Anthropic's views, saying that we should embrace AI despite risks. Altman agrees with tougher AI regulations, but advocates for a "lighter touch." He believes people will do "orders of magnitude more good stuff than bad stuff" with AI. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said there was a fundamental difference in worldview between his company and rival Anthropic on artificial intelligence regulation, arguing in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO that the technology's benefits justify accepting some risks — and that AI should remain broadly accessible to the public. "I think there's a lot of daylight," Altman told Decoded co-author and POLITICO senior tech reporter Brendan Bordelon. Asked specifically where he diverges from Anthropic and its CEO Dario Amodei, Altman said, "we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency." Anthropic has long been viewed as the strongest proponent of AI regulations within the industry, a stance that until recently was at odds with the lighter touch approach favored by OpenAI. But the policy differences between the two leading AI firms have narrowed in recent months, with OpenAI coming out in favor of tougher rules as it grapples with high-profile hacking incidents and rogue behavior by its models. Altman agreed with Amodei's call last month to slow the development of the most advanced AI models. His company has followed Anthropic in endorsing new state laws that impose stricter safety requirements than what the ChatGPT maker had previously supported — a shift from its prior state strategy . And OpenAI lobbyists recently endorsed a bipartisan House proposal that would require top AI companies to embed outside safety evaluators. Despite the convergence, Altman tried to distinguish his firm's regulatory stance from Anthropic's. "I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, 'This technology is going to get so powerful, and it's so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,'" said Altman. But he called it "a completely unacceptable tradeoff" that runs counter to the "lighter touch regulatory stance" backed by OpenAI. "I wouldn't take a trade of saying like, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no kind of like misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen," said Altman. "Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff." The OpenAI CEO later added that he does not accept "the really catastrophic risks," including the potential for "a serious loss of control to AI." The interview, appearing in Monday's debut edition of Decoded and its accompanying daily podcast, also delved into President Donald Trump's new AI accord with top tech firms and his attempted rebrand of AI to "super intelligence;" the rash of autonomous hacking incidents carried out by OpenAI models and whether the company should face legal liability; Altman's thoughts on AI industry money flowing into U.S. politics; the influence of effective altruists inside OpenAI; and his views on key political power players including French President Emmanuel Macron to California Gov. events.title: Tories to pledge to scrap Environment Agency and Natural England
events.summary: Shadow chancellor will also promise to scrap affordable homes regulations as part of strategy to refocus on growth The Conservatives will announce a bonfire of regulations including abolishing affordable homes and community funding rules as well as scrapping Natural England and the Environment Agency . The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, will say the party intends to “streamline regulations” that protect nature and oblige developers to include affordable homes and community services such as GP surgeries, to speed up infrastructure and housebuilding. The announcements on Monday are a signal that the party intends to refocus on the economy, an area where it has made relatively little progress in the polls. Tory strategists believe there is a major opening to make gains against Reform and Labour, given the limited focus on growth from Andy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, at the Labour conference last week. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch , published a new tract on Sunday called The Right Way, which she said would be the bedrock that underpinned the party’s policy development before the next election. Polls have the party still trailing third behind Labour and Reform UK. Introducing the document – inspired by Margaret Thatcher’s The Right Approach from 1976 – Badenoch said the Conservatives still expected to win the next election and needed to “hit the ground running … We will need to be ready from day one, having already shown people what kind of government we are going to be.” “Keir Starmer didn’t have a plan. That’s why he’s gone,” she said. “Andy Burnham doesn’t have one either and that is why I know the announcements he is making will all come to naught. We have to be different, different from Labour, and different from the party we were two years ago.” In a slew of announcements at the Conservative party conference on Monday, the Tories will pledge measures that they claim would cut the price of a new home by £50,0000, including scrapping net zero regulations on housebuilding, such as the Future Homes Standard, which requires all new homes in England to be zero-carbon ready. The party will promise to replace section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy that oblige developers to build a proportion of affordable housing and support school and health service demands locally. Instead, there will be a “one stop” levy on developers, Griffith will say. The party has also pledged to abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency, “moving to a more streamlined regulatory landscape to protect our environment”. Griffith will say in his first speech as shadow chancellor that the Tories would continue to back the expansion of Heathrow airport and leave the Aarhus convention, which makes it easier for community groups to oppose developments. Conservative shadow Treasury ministers will be tasked with finding new ways of simplifying tax for individuals and businesses, Griffith will say, calling the tax code “a cat’s cradle of complexity”. Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning In his speech, he will say: “No one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation. “Our task just got bigger. We face a prime minister that wants to return Britain to an imagined past. A socialist fever dream of the 1970s. Cheaper homes, lower taxes and less red tape. This will be the most ambitious deregulation project in a generation. We will be more prepared than ever before. We will set out our plans line by line. Every bill, every regulation, every chapter.” Griffith will say that the government must speed up the building of a Heathrow third runway in whatever way it can. “I refuse to accept for a single moment that the country of Brunel and Bazalgette, of the vaccine taskforce and the Mulberry harbours , has to sit around waiting until the 2040s to get a third runway built,” he will say. Burnham has recently expressed personal scepticism about the Heathrow third runway, saying he would take differing views seriously. The new shadow housing secretary, Katie Lam, will say the scrapping of housing regulations and of enforcement bodies would mean “anti-growth ideologues can never again hold our country hostage”. The party said Natural England and the Environment Agency were preventing too many homes being built and adding unnecessary costs to building. Both bodies would be scrapped, with their necessary functions brought directly into Defra.

events.title: C-Suite Member Spotlight: 140 Years of Everyday Moments
events.summary: As DFI Retail Group marks its 140th anniversary, Group Chief Executive Scott Price says the company’s future will depend on fulfilling the needs of our customers, investing in innovation and continuing to earn trust in the everyday moments that define modern retail. A morning stop for breakfast before work. A coffee picked up between meetings. A grocery stop on the way home. A stop for health and beauty products. A weekend trip to choose furniture for a growing family. A rewards offer that helps make the weekly shop go further. These are ordinary moments in Hong Kong life. Yet for DFI Retail Group, they represent the foundation of a business that has grown with the city for 140 years. Founded in Hong Kong in 1886, DFI has evolved from a local enterprise into one of Asia’s leading retail groups, serving millions of customers every week through brands spanning food, convenience, health and beauty, home furnishings and loyalty rewards. For Scott Price, Group Chief Executive of DFI Retail Group, the anniversary is not only a milestone in the company’s history. It is also a reminder of the role retailers play in daily life, often in ways that consumers rarely stop to consider. “Retail is woven into people’s lives in ways that often go unnoticed,” Price says. “It is there in the everyday decisions people make for themselves and their families. When retailers do their job well, they make life a little easier, a little healthier and a little more convenient.” DFI is marking its 140th anniversary under the theme “140 Years of Everyday Moments”, a phrase Price says reflects both the Group’s history and its continuing purpose. While anniversaries are often viewed as opportunities to look back, DFI is using the milestone to recognise the customers, team members and communities that have shaped the business, and to focus on how retail must continue adapting to changing expectations. Price explains that few industries are as closely connected to the routines of everyday life as retail. Across DFI’s portfolio, customers encounter its brands at different moments and for different needs. From supermarkets such as Market Place to Mannings and Guardian for health, wellness and self-care products, to 7-11 for a snack or collectible, and to IKEA for homewares, Price says its brands are connected by a common purpose: Serving Asia sustainably for generations with everyday moments. That role has become more important as lifestyles have changed. Consumers today are busier, more digitally connected and more discerning. They expect retailers to provide not only the right products, but also convenience, value, reliability and a seamless experience across physical and digital channels. In a city such as Hong Kong, where time, space and household budgets are constant considerations, retail is expected to work harder for customers. “Customers consistently value businesses that understand their needs and earn their trust,” Price says. “That has remained true even as the way people shop has changed dramatically.” Adapting Through Generations of Change Reflecting on DFI’s 140-year history, it has unfolded alongside Hong Kong’s transformation from a trading port into a global financial and commercial centre. During that period, the retail industry has been reshaped by urbanisation, rising living standards, changing family structures, technological innovation and the emergence of digital commerce. Shopping habits have shifted from traditional high-street transactions to omnichannel experiences, loyalty ecosystems and data-driven personalisation. For retailers, the challenge is no longer simply to operate stores. It is to understand customers across multiple touchpoints and respond quickly to changing needs. “Over more than four decades in Asia, I’ve seen enormous change in how people shop and interact with brands,” Price says. “But customers consistently value businesses that understand their needs and earn their trust.” Price explains that maintaining that trust requires continuous investment. As such, the Group is strengthening its capabilities in technology, talent, supply chain and customer engagement, while remaining focused on the fundamentals of quality, service and value. The company is also operating in a market where expectations of retailers are broadening. Customers increasingly want businesses to act responsibly, support healthier lifestyles and contribute positively to the communities in which they operate. For Price, these demands are not separate from the future of retail. They are central to it. Retailers that succeed over the long term, he believes, will be those able to combine operational excellence with a deeper understanding of people’s lives – how they shop, what they value, how they make choices and what kind of support they expect from trusted brands. In such a competitive and fast-changing sector, trust has become one of retail’s most important assets, Price says.

events.title: Residents fear there is no stopping $32b hyperscale data centre
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Western Downs residents fear being steamrolled as council assesses $32b data centre Ross Thornton says he is "mildly opposed" to the hyperscale data centre outside Dalby. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) A proposal to build a massive data centre near the Western Downs town of Dalby has locals wondering about the details of the plan. Anthropic has already signed a deal to use a portion of the site despite no approvals being issued. Some residents are petitioning against the plan, while others would like to meet and learn more. Dalby antiques dealer Ross Thornton is surrounded by history but worried about the future now that a $32 billion data centre is proposed just out of town. "People don't know enough about it," he said. Dalby is a country Queensland town 200 kilometres from Brisbane. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) The 70-year-old is calling for a public meeting amid fears residents will be steamrolled in the push to embrace the artificial intelligence boom. Anthropic has signed a deal in Australia to use the first of four buildings at the proposed hyperscale facility, well before it has received any approvals. The Queensland government confirmed it will be taking over from local governments as the "responsible assessor and coordinator" of data centre applications in a yet to be released planning framework. About 50 per cent of the Western Downs is cropping land. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Mr Thornton has lived through the rapid industrialisation of the country town before, when the coal seam gas industry swept through more than a decade ago. "It caused a boom-bust cycle and no-one wants that," he said. "[We want to know] what's the impact going to be … and any of the pros and cons relating to it." Dalby antiques dealer Ross Thornton wants a public town hall for more information on the proposed data centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) A petition to parliament opposing the Western Downs Digital Park has gained more than 21,000 signatures — more than any petition currently open in Queensland. "We know that when big business comes in, the locals don't have a say," Angela Prenzler, who has been promoting the petition, said. Angela Prenzler has lived in Dalby all her life and is concerned about the proposed data centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) The Dalby resident said she was sceptical of the developer's plans to predominantly use rain and recycled water for its operations. "We are always in drought," Ms Penzler said. She said the online petition was gaining traction, including in other country areas. "They know it could happen in their regional town too," Ms Prenzler said. Dalby businessman Doug Machin, who owns a machinery business, a café and a grocery shop in town, feels conflicted about the project. Doug Machin and his daughter at the Dalby Machinery Centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) "You never knock back development," he said, then added it would be challenging to source the suggested 1,500 jobs required to build the data centre. "If you went to most businesses and farmers, we just don't seem to be able to get the [workers]." Unlike New South Wales and Victoria, Queensland has no dedicated data centre planning pathway. The Crisafulli government said it was in the process of developing a framework that would "mirror its reforms to renewable energy development". "This will ensure a consistent and transparent framework across the state, as many councils don't include data centres in their planning schemes, which creates confusion and inconsistency," the government said in a statement. "Any deals done must be with the backing of councils and communities." The Western Downs region is known as the "energy capital" of Queensland but has historically been an agricultural area. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Western Downs Mayor Andrew Smith said he had been assured the project in his region would remain under his council's purview — but it may be out of the council's hands. Singapore-based developer Zerra DC has applied for "prescribed project" status, which means Queensland's coordinator-general could step in and fast-track approvals to prevent "unnecessary delays". "We've had good conversations with the state. We're confident in our ability to assess large scale development," he said. Chinchilla resident Shay Dougall earned her doctorate researching the impacts of the coal seam gas industrialisation of the Western Downs and says history should guide decision-making. Shay Dougall says residents deserve to have a say about what happens in their area.

events.title: Scoop: White House monitors suspected plague outbreak in Russia
events.summary: The White House is monitoring reports of a suspected plague case and related quarantines in Russia, a Trump administration official told Axios on Sunday. Driving the news: Russian health authorities have taken precautionary measures in response to the death of a woman who worked at an anti-plague research factility, but have not confirmed that she contracted plague. What they're saying: The Trump administration "is aware, monitoring the outbreak, and assessing options," the administration official said. The backstory: On Sept. 25, 28-year-old Daria Shipilova, who worked at an anti-plague research institute in Russia's Irkutsk region, broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen, local reports said. Shipilova was admitted to a hospital on Sept. 29 with symptoms of severe pneumonia and died overnight between Oct. 1 and Oct. 2. After her death, authorities imposed quarantines at several medical facilities in the region and placed nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shiplova under medical observation. Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said those being monitored showed no signs of illness and had tested negative. Russian media reports suggested Shipilova may have contracted pneumonic plague, but health authorities have not confirmed the diagnosis. Russia's public health agency said Shipilova had "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that further testing found no microorganisms linked to her work. The agency said the epidemiological situation in the region remains stable. Zoom out: Plague is a potentially life-threatening bacterial disease but can be cured with antibiotics when treated promptly, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . White House spokespeople referred questions to the State Department, which did not respond to a request for comment.

events.title: Can ‘super intelligence’ and a non-binding safety pact solve AI’s image problem?
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. President Donald Trump hosted many of the biggest names in artificial intelligence this week — in part to announce that the U.S. government isn’t calling it artificial intelligence anymore. Now it’s super intelligence. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed the motivation behind the meeting and what effect it might have on the AI industry. We were all pretty skeptical that the “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities” that the executives signed will amount to much, especially since — as Sean noted — it’s “deeply non-binding,” at least from a legal prospective. (Instead, Trump said he considers it “morally binding.”) Kirsten suggested that the meeting’s real significance may have been as “a rebranding effort around AI.” (An effort that continued this weekend with Trump’s announcement of a new Super Intelligence Force .) For her, the big message was, “AI is going to kill us, it’s scary, it is going to take jobs — but super intelligence is not.” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Anthony: Officially, by order of the president of the United States, it’s not artificial intelligence anymore, it’s super intelligence. We were talking about this last week , because this is something [Trump has] been hinting at — he doesn’t do hints, he’s been saying [it] for a while. But now it’s signed into executive order. If you’re an official U.S. representative, you are supposed to say super intelligence, not artificial intelligence. And this was also part of this broader announcement around AI safety, which I think is both interesting for this pact that was announced, but also the fact that it happened at all. It seemed to have come together fairly quickly, because just two weeks ago, a week ago, President Trump was saying, “We don’t need any of this, we need to lead in AI, we can’t constrain it in any way, we don’t need any regulation, anyone who’s saying that there’s any danger from AI is essentially a Chinese or Democratic plant.” And yet all these AI CEOs got together with him earlier this week and signed this pact. Kirsten: Leading up to that, we should say, not only was there pushback on regulation, and we can talk about whether this executive order even does any of that — I would say no, there’s a little bit of theater there — but the important and interesting thing is that just days ago, Anthropic was really in the doghouse, if you will, in terms of what was happening behind the scenes with President Trump. That all changed when [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei was invited to a 10 p.m. dinner. He had this sit-down, and then just days later, we had this luncheon, and at this luncheon, we have pretty much every tech power broker from every major tech company that exists. So Mark Zuckerberg was there, Jeff Bezos was there, Elon Musk was there, Dario of course was there, they were all there. I’m wondering if any of you watched the press conference that happened afterwards, which there’s been many, many memes about, because of the interesting, funny behavior when you bring a bunch of tech CEOs together. But I guess my bigger question for both of you is: What does this all mean? And does it mean anything? Sean: How much time do you have? First off, sure, they had dinner, Trump and Dario. If you read the Time magazine interview that Trump just did, your guess is as good as mine as to how informed he was that that dinner was even going to be happening, which is a strange reality to live in, but it’s just the one we inhabit. I will also say one other thing that makes me skeptical — surprise, surprise — of how repaired the relationship is between the administration and Anthropic, is that for as much as there are clearly people trying to put those two groups together, the Defense Department is still very adamant that Anthropic is terrible and woke and a national security risk. Emil Michael goes off on Anthropic every other day on X, it seems. I think there’s still some distance there despite Dario showing up to this thing. As far as the agreement and all of that, let’s be real, they misspelled the United States on the agreement that they all signed. It is also just deeply non-binding. I mean, it is completely voluntary. I think my favorite aspect about it was that Trump described it as quote “morally binding,” which is just a level of abstraction and terminology that I’ve never heard of before. events.title: Short-stay operators have mixed reactions to SA's register proposal
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Short-stay accommodation providers have mixed response to SA register plan Jenny Bickley says renting out her property on a short-term basis is more profitable than a traditional rental. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) South Australia is set to join New South Wales and Western Australia with a registry for short-stay accommodation. The scheme is still being shaped but the initial feedback from operators has been mixed, with some raising concerns about security and the impact on local government decisions. Public consultation closes on October 30. Accountant Jenny Bickley makes about $45,000 in profit each year from guests hiring her dual-abode property in Mount Gambier. "The Airbnb model is way better than renting," she said. While Ms Bickley is one of many South Australians who run a short-stay accommodation business, it is not exactly clear how many there actually are. Jenny Bickley says most of her guests are tourists. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) Last year, the state government wrapped up its inquiry into the sector amid nationwide concerns about the model affecting housing and rental affordability. Among the takeaways: SA lacked the data. The committee floated a registration scheme, a concept already seen in Western Australia and New South Wales. Jenny Bickley is concerned about "severe security risks" from a short-stay accommodation register. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) The Short Term Accommodation Association Australia (STAAA) backed a statewide register but wanted the approach reconsidered and warned of "unnecessary duplication". The details have not been locked in, but a discussion paper indicated councils could apply their own land-use codes and decide rates, something the STAAA was not keen on. "We need one state, one register and one consistent registration system," executive director Keiran Craig-Jones said. Ms Bickley, who fought council rate hikes in Mount Gambier, believed registration could help shake any "cowboys" operating unlawfully but echoed the STAAA's concerns. Ms Bickley said most of her booking were people visiting the town for events. Fourth generation farmer David Galpin entered the world of short-stays last year when he pitched his purpose-built paddock-view property in Penola as a luxury escape. Mr Galpin welcomed the register and believed it could inform the family's future business moves and even lead to more short-stay rentals. David Galpin says despite his research he does not have a "full picture" of the supply of short-stay accommodation. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) Ms Bickley said she understood the benefit for government decision-making, but was concerned about potential security issues. "Nobody actually knows the location [of my property] until they complete the booking," she said. Keiran Craig-Jones says legislation should be clear about exactly what information is collected and for what purpose. ( Supplied ) Mr Galpin was less concerned by the risks of a public register given his farm was "different to having a flat or something in a city or town". Ms Craig-Jones said while security was a "legitimate issue to consider", she was not aware of any increased burglary, squatting or similar offending following registers in other jurisdictions. Short-stay accommodation challenges National Shelter chief executive Jackson Hills said there were hundreds of local government areas nationwide, but about 40 or 50 faced "a much bigger challenge" around short-stay accommodation. In certain hotspots, such as Noosa in Queensland , he said policymakers may have "got the balance wrong" given shortages in the local workforce. Jackson Hills says knowing the real number of short-stay accommodation places would better inform decisions. ( Supplied ) Mr Hills said Australia would be better off understanding what the actual levels were before moving to "arbitrary policy responses". "There are local governments focusing on their local economies and that's exactly where the conversation should be," he said. Public consultation for South Australia's registry closes on October 30 at 5pm. ( ABC News: Hamed Akrami ) A small-scale banana farmer who has had his agreement to supply Coles ended due to the supermarket simplifying its supply chain says the move signals the end of small-scale farms across the country. Industry experts have claimed Coles and Woolworths are centralising their supply chains in a bid to cut costs. Some experts worry producers will become more vulnerable if supermarkets continue to do so. After 30 years of selling bananas to Coles, New South Wales farmer Amrit Singh believes the supermarket's decision to stop buying his produce signals a possible end for small, family-run farms like his. In the past two months, Coles and Woolworths confirmed they would pull various local products from their shelves, with suppliers told the decisions were due to changes to the supply chain. Amrit Singh says small-scale growers are "price takers", not price makers. ( ABC News: Samuel O'Brien ) Industry experts have said major Australian supermarkets are centralising their supply chains in a bid to cut costs, warning some producers could now be at greater risk of having their products removed from supermarket shelves. Woolworths said its supply chain network had expanded, while Coles rejected the experts' claims. An inquiry by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) into supermarkets last year found Coles and Woolworths had overwhelming power in their trade relationships with suppliers. Amrit Singh labelled Coles's decision to pull local bananas from its shelves as "anti-competitive" and said supermarkets should be encouraging diversity in growing regions. ( ABC News: Giulio Saggin ) In August, Coles confirmed it would stop selling Coffs Coast bananas, pumpkins and cucumbers in an effort to simplify its supply chain. While Tasmanians can shop at 17 Coles and 32 Woolworth supermarkets, there are no Aldi stores — and that won't be changing anytime soon, according to the company CEO. Mr Singh sold his bananas indirectly to Coles through a wholesaler, an agreement he said was worth hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. The produce is now expected to come from north Queensland, but Mr Singh believes his business is too small to compete with north Queensland's banana industry. "Freight costs [involved in] getting access to those [new] markets are going to be extremely high," he said. Mr Singh said farmers who did not sell directly to supermarkets had "no power" to negotiate trade agreements and were forced to reduce prices to support promotions and specials. Coles says keeping its supply chain efficient helps it absorb costs and reduce the impact on grocery prices. ( ABC News ) Rise in 'middlemen' leaves farmers vulnerable NSW Farmers Association principal economist Samuel Miller said supermarket giants had long been centralising their supply chains. He said one way they were doing this was through buying produce from packhouses or "middlemen" — selling on behalf of a group of growers — instead of directly from them. "When those supermarkets make a decision like consolidating their suppliers or rejecting some produce … it affects not just that supplier in the middle, but it can affect dozens, 40 or 50 other farmers down the line." Samuel Miller says supermarkets have a large share of the market, so they hold negotiating power. ( Supplied: Samuel Miller ) In a statement to the ABC, Coles said it continued to source directly from a range of Australian producers. "In fresh produce, aggregators are not new and have long played an important role in Australia," a spokesperson said. In August, Woolworths confirmed it would stop selling Tasmanian beef in stores around the country from early next year. ( ABC News: Laurissa Smith ) Queensland University of Technology retail marketing professor Gary Mortimer said meat was one of the main supply chains where processing had been centralised, citing Woolworths's decision to stop selling Tasmanian beef from early next year. Gary Mortimer says supermarkets centralising their processing can give shoppers greater product consistency. ( Supplied: Gary Mortimer ) Some suppliers said they were told this was due to rising production and shipping costs. "Over the last 10 to 15 years, what we've seen is that reduction of in-store processing back to centralised processing," Professor Mortimer said. events.title: Australia's fossil fuel expansion 'slap in the face' to Pacific nations
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Pacific leaders challenge Australia's fossil fuel expansion ahead of pre-COP31 talks in Fiji Marica and Sami have been living in a tent for five years, waiting for their village to be rebuilt. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) As she sits crossed legged on the floor inside a large tent, 66-year-old Marica Malumuca describes the place she's called home for the past five years. "When it rains heavily it feels like we're living in a balloon because we can see the parts of the tent bulging where it's filling up," she said. Ms Malumuca's village, Nabavatu, was declared unsafe in 2021 after two cyclones cracked the ground beneath it, and she was moved to a temporary settlement in Savadrua. There are 37 tents at the temporary site. Some can fit three people and others accommodate up to seven. Ms Malumuca's son, Sami Veloko, moved home from the city to look after her as they wait for Nabavatu to be rebuilt. Pacific communities are already feeling the impacts of climate change. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) "Those people who stay in these tents, they used to stay in a good house; a cement house, a wooden house of a high quality," he said. "You cannot believe — even they themselves cannot believe — that they stay in this kind of tent." Small island states are already being disproportionately affected by displacement as climate change drives more extreme weather. The United Nations warned the impacts of tropical cyclones have become more severe due to rising sea levels and an increase in heavy precipitation. More than half of Pacific Island countries' infrastructure is located in coastal areas at risk from rising seas, which happens as higher temperatures melt glaciers and ice sheets. Nabavatu is yet to be rebuilt, five years after it was damaged by cyclones. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) As world leaders prepare to descend on Mr Veloko's home country for high-level climate talks, he has a message for them. "We are getting the effect of climate change and we are the vulnerable people, the Pacific people," he said. "Because of what they have contributed to carbon dioxide, the industrialisation that they have developed in their countries, we are getting the worst of it." Climate diplomacy at heart of security strategy Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will join global leaders at the pre-COP event, which will feature preparatory talks ahead of next month's United Nations COP31 climate summit. Australia has led the charge for the lead-up talks to be held in the Pacific and is spending millions of dollars on the event as part of its broader regional security strategy to become the "partner of choice" for the Pacific islands. Anthony Albanese attended the 2026 Pacific Island Forum in early September. ( ABC News: Mark Moore ) The Albanese government has vigorously pursued a series of bilateral security deals with Pacific nations since coming to office including Vanuatu, Fiji, Tuvalu, Nauru and Papua New Guinea, with almost all of them including commitments to act on climate change. According to the Lowy Institute, Australia remains the Pacific's largest bilateral donor and biggest development partner , having spent almost $19 billion of a committed $20.6 billion. Wes Morgan, a research associate with the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at UNSW who lived and worked in the Pacific for more than a decade, said the federal government understood that to become the Pacific's partner of choice it must act on the region's key security threat. "That is why there has been the inclusion of commitments on climate change in these bilateral security arrangements, but more broadly why Australia is working with Pacific island countries to drive global action on climate change," he said. "That's why Australia had its hand up to host the UN climate talks with the Pacific." For Pacific islands like Ebeye, rising oceans caused by the continued burning of fossil fuels is a real and acute problem. ( Supplied: Hall Contracting ) But Dr Morgan said Australia remaining one of the world's largest fossil fuel exporters "flies in the face of the narrative Australia's pursuing with Pacific Island countries". "Australia's biggest contribution to the climate crisis is the export of coal and gas, so the emissions associated with Australia's exports of coal and gas more than doubled the emissions from Australia's entire domestic economy," he said. Can Australia be both a gas giant and a climate leader? Seven years after it was first mooted, the extension of Australia's biggest gas project could not have landed at a more critical juncture for the nation's climate credentials.

events.title: The Guardian view on trapped leaseholders: Labour must keep its promise to set them free | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on trapped leaseholders: Labour must keep its promise to set them free The government pledged to end an unfair system. Ministers must give homeowners power over costs, rather than another place to complain “T o the millions of leaseholders across the country, you have my word. The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,” Andy Burnham told the Labour party conference . Only a few hours earlier, his housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had announced that the government would legislate for a new independent regulator and launch a consultation to cap “rip off” administrative fees. While these are undoubtedly steps in the right direction, they are miles away from Labour’s manifesto promise to “finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end”. In its modern form , leasehold in England and Wales turns homes into income streams for freeholders. It should be abolished. There are powerful vested interests – billionaires , aristocrats and big businesses – that would oppose this move. But the system of service charges is crippling the housing market because its exorbitant cost puts off prospective buyers. The average annual service charge for a flat in England and Wales is now £2,405 , up 32.6% since 2020 and 55.6% over a decade. Owners of flats in high-rise blocks in London are paying service charges of more than £7,000 a year. Little wonder that first-time buyers are increasingly bypassing flats . The current system sees homeowners enter into long-term leases in which they must pay sums annually to freeholders. These can rise quickly to very high levels. The government proposes a £250 annual cap on ground rents for existing residential leases and limits on fees for requests such as keeping a pet. Ministers are consulting over whether residents could pay less to buy out freeholds . But there is no sign of action on annual service charges for maintenance costs determined by distant firms. Last year, 37% of flats across England and Wales had a service charge that exceeded 1% of their value – making them hard to mortgage and sell. Surely homeowners should not have to buy their freedom at an outrageous price while being charged for years by a management system they cannot realistically change? The issue of leasehold has become a campaign flashpoint in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Six out of seven homes sold in the constituency last year were sold as leasehold. The Green leader, Zack Polanski, who is standing to be the MP, has made the issue a concrete test of Labour’s credibility . The Greens have paired leasehold abolition with rent controls and affordable housing as part of their claim to end “rip-off Britain”, accusing Labour of favouring developers. Labour denies this, but ministers know that housing is a political powder keg that has already exploded in Berlin and across Spain . It is remarkable that while legislation banning new leasehold properties is expected before the next election, it is unlikely to come into force until after it. Ministers are said to be afraid of being taken to court by freeholders. But government has already won against them in the courts when defending Michael Gove’s housing bill. The question for the government is whether the proposed reforms give the owners of the existing 5m leasehold homes a credible route out of their dependency – or just regulate their continued subservience. Ministers must show how a leaseholder trapped today will in the future take back control – by obtaining the right to manage property, being able to buy the freehold or converting to commonhold. If ministers offer just another complaints mechanism, they will have broken their promise to end an injustice.

events.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility ! On an average day in San Francisco, you might see dozens (hundreds?) of Waymo robotaxis zipping around the city — and with little disruption. But, as TechCrunch has reported, there have been numerous incidents of robotaxis impeding traffic, driving into crime scenes, and interfering with first responders. And not just in the Bay Area. In some cases, companies have relied on first responders to move their robotaxis. These disruptions are occurring in the early stages of the robotaxi era. California has a new law hoping to get ahead of the problem before the next impending wave of robotaxis land. Senate Bill 1246, which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom this week, sets a series of new rules for AVs designed to improve safety and response times when they become disabled or interfere with emergency responders. The law also creates ways to hold these companies accountable if they don’t. Autonomous vehicle technology companies like Tesla , Waymo , and Zoox will have to provide first responders with local, on-the-ground support when their robotaxis cause problems and could also face penalties if a robotaxi blocks police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes. The law also says AV developers can only employ remote drivers who are based in the United States and those drivers must hold a U.S. driver’s license. They must also notify cities, towns, and other local jurisdictions about the location and status of vehicles during system-wide failures and must provide “local incident technicians” who can assist with AV accidents and obstructions. There are still some details to hammer out, which the Department of Motor Vehicles will handle since it’s the main regulator of autonomous vehicles in the state. But when this law goes into effect in July 2028, will it actually keep robotaxis out of the way of emergency responders? It likely won’t, but hopefully this law reduces the chaos and raises the accountability when something does happen. Perhaps the better question is will other states follow California’s lead or wait for the federal government to weigh in? events.title: LIM Advisors founder George Long: ‘We’ve been here 30 years. We’re going to be around’
events.summary: Thirty years of Asian alternatives, from the 1997 crash to Japan activism, a smaller firm on purpose, and a caution that no asset class is perfectly safe [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] George Long does not talk like a man selling vision. The founder, chairman and chief investment officer of LIM Advisors is understated and unshowy. After three decades running an independent firm in Hong Kong, what comes through is a temperament suited to difficult Asian markets: calm, pragmatic and focused on protecting capital when conditions turn. Long left Barclays’ Asia Pacific asset management business in late 1995 to set up LIM Advisors, one of the longest continually running alternative investment firms in Asia. The Hang Seng had fallen 31 per cent in 1994, and clients wanted a less volatile way to manage money. “A lot of my investors said, can you create a more stable way, a more diversified way, not so much dependent on the stock market.” Convertible bonds were his answer. LIM rolled out its first fund in January 1996 focused mainly on Asian convertibles. A year later the Asian financial crisis hit. Long recalls the Hang Seng falling about 25 per cent over two years, yet “we were up about 12 per cent.” “It was really tough because no one wanted to invest in Asia at that time even though the market was extremely cheap.” The SARS pandemic in 2003 arrived before the region had fully recovered. The Hong Kong market fell nearly 18 per cent and travel almost stopped. LIM later lived through the Japanese banking crisis around 1999, the 2008 global financial crisis, Covid and the latest Iran war shock. His father did not invest at the start but after about 15 years he did. “When I set up my business, my father didn’t give me money. After 15 years he said, okay, I’ll now give you money, because you’ve proved you can survive.” “Now we’re 30 years old. We proved we can survive.” Japan is an important part of the firm’s focus. Long has covered the country for four decades. LIM has maintained a research team in Tokyo since 2002. He says it “may be the second oldest hedge fund office in Japan”. Foreign interest was thin for years and has only revived over the past three years. Precious metals and mining stocks are a major bet. Long thinks they gain from persistent inflation and a weaker dollar reserve role. The portfolio also holds copper miners. He sat on Australian mining boards in the early 2000s. He also thinks Hong Kong can become a serious gold trading centre, given storage, no capital controls and the old bullion market. The latest Policy Address sets out a gold clearing system, tax concessions for commodity trading and a larger official role for bullion. China is another large bet. “The Chinese stock market is relatively inexpensive compared to, say, the US stock market. China went through a major correction and has only partially recovered. They’re still relatively good value.” Chinese convertibles remain “an interesting niche opportunity.” He also holds Hong Kong property and financial names. The first fund has evolved over three decades. Convertible-bond and other Asian arbitrage, then high-yield, largely dried up. As those trades thinned out, the portfolio was steered towards corporate events, metals and China. The fund has since been renamed the LIM Global Opportunities Fund. “It’s a broader fund now and can invest in any liquid asset anywhere based on my 40 years of experience.” Fifteen years ago capital came more from Western institutional investors. International investors, especially Americans, lost some interest in Asia. More of the money now comes from Asian family offices, foundations and funds of funds. He will not give up Hong Kong. The city, he says, is still a major international financial centre, with a good legal system, infrastructure and talent. “But sometimes the government can take a while to change things such as the taxation of funds, but they generally move in the right direction.” Tokyo is the only other Asian office. There is a small New York office. Looking out five or ten years, he sees a rougher climate. “Interest rates are going up; inflation is in the system.” He started at a major New York bank in 1982, when US rates were high. “Most people who are even in their 50s have never seen high inflation and interest rates. I’ve seen that. I also saw a lot of commodity inflation early in my career.” No asset class, he says, is perfectly safe. The dollar is no longer as dominant as it was. Gold should hold its value, even if it fluctuates, as it did recently. Japan will still matter, and so will China. “We’ve been here for 30 years,” he says. “We’re going to be around.”

events.title: Fulcrum Echo promises AI text in the style of any writer, so I tested it
events.summary: Fulcrum faces an identity crisis, even as it works on creating one by enabling anyone to imitate another person's writing style. The AI startup, founded in 2025 and previously operating at fulcrumresearch.ai, now uses fulcrum.inc and could easily be confused with one of the handful of other companies named Fulcrum or some variation of that. There's Fulcrum (withfulcrum.com), Fulcrum (fulcrumapp.com), Fulcrum AI (fulcrumai.us), Fulcrum Digital (fulcrumdigital.com), Fulcrum Labs (fulcrumlabs.ai), Fulcrum (fulcrumpro.com), Fulcrum Insurance Technology (fulcruminsure.app), and perhaps more. This Fulcrum is offering a large language model called Echo, which allows you to generate text in the style of a well-known author. Fulcrum appears to have no issue with corporate echoes. It now falls to writers to decide whether they have an issue with non-corporeal imitation. "Echo can do any writing task, from literary fiction to casual chatting, in whatever style you choose," the company says, and then launches into an exploration of how the technology works without addressing whether imitating a person's writing style poses any problems. Suggestions in the Echo Playground, for generating sample text, include Paul Christiano, Emily Dickinson, and Donald Trump. So, the full gamut of literary achievement: from AI safety expert to acclaimed 19th-century poet to the wordsmith who brought us "covfefe." But Echo will echo even the style of not-so-famous scribes, such as this reporter. So I fed the model a recent op-ed to assess its copying capabilities. The result was mixed, but better than the AI-crafted pitches that have been hitting my inbox for the past few months. I asked the model, "What do you think about the possibility that AI is conscious?" Here's part of the response, notionally written in my writing style. I suspect the debate about whether AI is conscious is less consequential than the debate about whether AI is profitable. Consciousness is a word that invites philosophical speculation and TED Talk invitations. Profitability is a word that invites shareholder lawsuits if you get it wrong. If you ask Meta's latest model whether it's conscious, it will probably say something reassuringly vague, trained as it is on the corpus of human equivocation. If you ask Mark Zuckerberg whether Meta's AI is conscious, he will probably say something about how we need to focus on the future being for everyone, because that's a question that doesn't require him to discuss the ad targeting business. The evidence for AI consciousness at the moment is about as strong as the evidence for Zuck's credibility as a futurist. Which is to say, it exists mainly in press releases and earnings calls. What's clear is that software can simulate aspects of human conversation well enough to unsettle people, and that unsettled people are a valuable audience. If you can convince users that your chatbot understands them – or might, someday – you can sell them subscriptions, or better, harvest their attention for advertisers. The style is familiar but makes a lot of choices I wouldn't have made. I wouldn't begin with "I suspect…" – commit or go home. The consciousness/profitability parallel construction is clumsy. "TED Talk invitations" bets on alliteration at the expense of coherence – "discourse" or "chatter" would work better than "invitations." I wouldn't have written "corpus of human equivocation" – a nice turn of phrase, but an unnecessary shot at training data when the point is the model's response rather than the provenance of that response. Though off-topic, Echo did a passable job of reproducing my op-ed's skepticism of Meta and its CEO. The paragraph that begins "The evidence for AI consciousness at the moment…" is succinct and sounds good. It just doesn't make much sense because there's nothing in the text that addresses Zuckerberg's predictions about the future or whether they're credible. And that's not really relevant to the prompt about AI and consciousness – a subject about which I'd be far more dismissive if opining. As AI research, Echo is an improvement on the text emitted by many AI models. But whether the beneficial uses of this technology outweigh the harms is less clear. Generative AI models that imitate artists' visual styles remain controversial and are the subject of ongoing litigation. And voice imitation has also raised questions about publicity rights and the risk of deception. Such concerns have prompted US lawmakers to propose the NO FAKES Act, which would create federal protections against certain unauthorized AI-generated replicas of a person's voice or visual likeness. If writers generally have no copyright in their writing style itself, and limited practical means to stop unwanted automated imitation of it when their published work is publicly accessible, then the surest defense against Echo may be silence.®

events.title: Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift
events.summary: Reform UK leader was interviewed for half an hour last month over money from crypto billionaire Nigel Farage has been interviewed by the standards commissioner for an investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne . The Reform UK leader spent about half an hour being questioned over the money, the Sunday Times reported. Farage maintains the gift was for his personal security. The interview conducted last month is a sign the process is nearing a conclusion, although Reform UK is not believed to have been informed that the report is finished. An MP under investigation is usually notified before the conclusion of the process. If the commissioner finds that there has been a serious breach of the rules, the matter is passed to the standards committee of MPs and lay members, which can ask for further evidence. The committee can recommend a sanction or override the report. If it suggests more than a 10-day suspension from the Commons – and parliament agrees – the Reform UK leader could find himself facing a recall petition and second byelection in his Clacton constituency. Farage has been under investigation over the gift since shortly after the Guardian revealed in May that Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024. The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter , not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament. After a slide in the polls over the summer, Reform is about to embark on a major reorganisation at its headquarters to try to revive its fortunes. Insiders said it would involve a big shake-up of staffing, in addition to the suspensions of James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, Farage’s close aide. The pair are facing an internal investigation into whether they encouraged illegal foreign donations during an undercover investigation by reporters from Verbatim. The inquiry is being carried out by lawyers who are expected to reach their conclusions soon. The matter is also the subject of a police inquiry. The party is working out how to spend £72m in donations from Harborne and another crypto billionaire, Ben Delo. The huge sums have prompted calls from political rivals for a donation cap. Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning A possible use of the money is the relaunch of a TV channel that produces Reform-related video coverage and a show fronted by Farage. Farage told the Sunday Times he thought the reaction to the donations would be “far worse” but had produced “some grudging respect – the fact that I managed to pull off a coup of that magnitude, I think people were quite impressed”. It is not clear whether the donations fall within the rules because the government is putting forward legislation to ban overseas donors from giving more than £100,000 in a calendar year – backdated to March this year. Harborne joined the UK electoral register only this summer and Delo has been largely based in Hong Kong, although on the register for some years. If the donations are ruled impermissible, Reform could have to hand them back, a prospect that is likely to lead to court action.

events.title: Yemeni and Saudi forces launch counteroffensive against the Houthis
events.summary: Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis on Sunday in an effort to win back territory from the rebel group, the head of Yemen's presidential council said in a speech. "We have exhausted all opportunities for deescalation with the Houthi militias," Rashad al-Alimi said . Why it matters: One of the key objectives of the operation is to regain control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. When the Houthis took over territory on the Red Sea coast close to the strait, it gave them — and Iran, which backs them — powerful leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy. Despite pleas from Saudi Arabia, the U.S. is not getting involved in direct combat against the Houthis for now. It is providing intelligence and targeting support, U.S. officials say. Driving the news: The counteroffensive has been planned for many weeks by Yemen's internationally recognized government and Saudi Arabia. Tens of thousands of ground troops loyal to the Yemeni government are participating. The Saudi military is mainly providing air cover for Yemeni forces and conducting airstrikes against Houthi targets. The goal is to retake the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control for several years. The Houthis continued launching missiles at Saudi targets over the weekend, including at facilities of state-owned oil giant Aramco. The intrigue: President Trump is caught between wanting to help Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, his friend and ally, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen, viewing it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said. On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the official said. A second U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now," but stressed that could change if the operation runs into problems. What to watch: On Friday, Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the conflict in Yemen, Axios first reported. It's unclear whether the meeting ended with new policy recommendations for the president regarding Yemen.

events.title: Dubai to expand CommerCity in push for digital economy growth
events.summary: Dubai CommerCity (DCC) , the free zone dedicated to digital commerce in Dubai, is launching the second phase of its expansion programme with Dh1.8 billion ($272.2 million) investment that will help the emirate grow its digital economy . The free zone is set to deliver the expansion project in phases between the first quarter of 2027 and the fourth quarter of 2028, Dubai Media Office said in a statement on Sunday. “Phase two of Dubai CommerCity comes at a time when Dubai continues to demonstrate its ability to grow and expand despite the changes and challenges facing the global economy,” Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed, Chairman of Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (Diez), said. The free zone, which is a joint venture between Diez and Wasl Group, will add a series of projects across its three districts: the Business Cluster, Logistics Cluster, and Social Cluster. On aggregate, the projects will add more than 91,000 square metres of new office space, increasing the free zone’s capacity and expanding its integrated ecosystem to serve companies operating in digital commerce and technology sectors. The push to expand the free zone builds upon Dubai CommerCity’s record demand, with occupancy reaching nearly 96 per cent across its office, logistics, and retail spaces. Investor confidence “This expansion reflects the growing investor confidence in Dubai’s economic ecosystem and its ability to attract high-quality investments while providing an advanced economic infrastructure that responds to rapid shifts in emerging sectors,” Sheikh Ahmed said. The move, he added, aligns with the Dubai Economic Agenda, D33, objectives and helps strengthen Dubai's position as a global hub for the digital economy and future commerce. Launched in January, D33 aims to double the size of Dubai’s economy , with a target of reaching Dh32 trillion by 2033 and establishing the emirate among the top three global cities. The plan envisages a programme to support 30 private companies to achieve unicorn status – worth more than $1 billion. Other business incubators will support the growth of private companies, with 400 of the most promising identified. The expansion of the Business Cluster and the Social Cluster will add 86,000 square metres of new space, which will add to options available to local, regional and global companies that are looking to become a part of the Dubai CommerCity ecosystem, the Media Office said. The Business Cluster will include additional office space across six new buildings, including shell-and-core offices, fully fitted workspaces, and flexible plug-and-play solutions. Within the Logistics Cluster, the phase two expansion will add The Hive, a 5,600 square metre facility that will provide an alternative logistics model. It will feature 181 flexible units, alongside climate-controlled fulfilment areas, as well as digitally managed loading and unloading zones, the Media Office said.

events.title: Retailers are making returns harder. A carpet seller taught me why that’s a mistake | Gene Marks
events.summary: Retailers are making returns harder. A carpet seller taught me why that’s a mistake A standard business practice offsets future costs by funding a reserve for returns – but many small businesses don’t do it I n my 30-plus years of being an accountant I have learned many business lessons from people who were much smarter than me. Jerry Crawford was one of those people. Jerry taught me about product returns. Jerry – who sadly passed away a decade ago – sold carpets wholesale from a nondescript little building in south Jersey. He employed about 50 people and counted many local and national carpet retailers as his customers. When I reviewed Jerry’s books, I noticed a large reserve for “returns”. “They’re a part of every business,” he told me. A “reserve” is something businesses create for potential future costs. Some reserve for bad debts. Others reserve for inventory that grows old and will need to be disposed of. And plenty of businesses – like Jerry’s – reserve for the potential costs that will be incurred if a customer returns their product. Returns are just a normal part of business. Plenty of small business owners like Jerry go to great lengths to make the process as easy as possible. Some big companies, such as Amazon, do the same. “There’s a cost to do this,” Jerry said. “So I make sure to build a reserve for that cost.” Makes sense. And yet, it seems that many businesses still haven’t learned this lesson. According to the Wall Street Journal , many Americans are complaining that it’s getting harder to return things. They’re seeing “surprise fees, shorter return windows and more questions about their reasons for sending products back”. Some, according to the report, are “getting warnings that they won’t get a refund on their next return”. Jerry would be shaking his head at this. To him, it wouldn’t make sense. And it doesn’t make sense to me either. Yes, there are a few bad actors that will take advantage of the practice. And yes, accepting returns adds costs for a business. But, like credit card fees, health insurance and overtime, this is a cost that can easily be recouped. All you need to do is capture those costs over a year or so, build a history, estimate what the next year’s cost will be and then factor those costs into your overhead. Your overhead is then factored into your pricing. In Jerry’s case, he reserved one half of 1% on each of his sales as a returns allowance based on his history of returns. He built up this reserve throughout the year, then charged returned products against it. A .5% reserve meant that instead of charging $1,000 for a roll of carpet, he charged $1,005. His customers didn’t notice the $5 difference. Would you? The difference is negligible. But for a business, those costs add up and, by doing this, those costs are covered. You’d think that, after thousands of years of business practice and the knowledge of some of the finest institutions, pundits, academics and experts, our business leaders today would understand this concept. So why don’t retailers realize this? It’s a mystery to me. They must see that creating obstacles and charging their customers for returns only creates animosity, ruins their loyalty and results in unfavorable press coverage. It’s shocking to me how businesses continue to make the same mistakes over and over again, despite the lessons of history. You can keep your customers happy, build loyalty and grow your business by not nickel-and-diming them. Jerry Crawford, a small business owner with a high school education who profitably sold carpets for decades, understood this.

events.title: CDL’s Lucerne Grand launch moves 61% of 570 units at average $2,480 psf
events.summary: CDL said all unit types have been well received, with two-, three- and four-bedroom premium units being the most popular. City Developments’ Lucerne Grand in Jurong sold 61% of 570 units at an average price of $2,480 psf during its launch weekend. The development is linked to Lakeside MRT, includes retail space, and is near the future Jurong Lake District business hub. Strong demand is supported by nearby schools, a large local population, and the project's appeal to Singaporean buyers upgrading from HDB flats. SINGAPORE – City Developments Limited’s (CDL) Jurong condominium project Lucerne Grand sold 61% of its 570 units at its weekend launch, according to the developer. A total of 350 units were sold as at 6pm on Oct 4 in the project that was priced on average at $2,480 per square foot (psf). Approximately 93% of the buyers are Singaporeans, while the remaining 7% are permanent residents from countries such as Malaysia, China and India. Prices at the 99-year Jurong Lakeside project started from $1.5 million for a two-bedroom unit, $2 million for a three-bedroom unit and $2.8 million for a four-bedroom unit, which PropNex CEO Kelvin Fong said was “relatively affordable”. “All unit types were well received, with two-, three- and four-bedroom premium units being the most popular,” said CDL in a news release. The development has a commercial space on the ground floor and is directly linked to Lakeside MRT, located on the East-West Line. CDL clinched the plot of land in June 2025 for $608 million, or $1,132.08 psf per plot ratio. The take-up puts Lucerne Grand within range of the five mixed-use projects launched in 2026, said Nicholas Mak, chief research officer at Mogul.sg. The launch-weekend sales of the mixed-use projects ranged from 56.9% at Newport Residences to 98.8% at Tengah Garden Residences, he noted. Analysts attributed the “healthy” take-up rates partly to the proximity to the MRT station. “The location provides residents with excellent accessibility and convenience to one of the most heavily used MRT lines,” said Mak. He noted that the recently launched Amberwood at Holland, which sold only 11% of 212 units, is about 1.5km or a 20-minute walk to its nearest MRT station. Justin Quek, deputy group CEO of Realion, said that buyers were also “enticed” by the provision of retail space within the development, boosting convenience for residents. The development’s location near the Jurong Lake District, which is envisioned to become Singapore’s largest business district outside the city centre, also provided a positive long-term backdrop, said PropNex’s Fong. CDL group CEO Sherman Kwek said: “We are encouraged by the healthy response at Lucerne Grand, which reflects home buyers’ appreciation for its distinctive combination of connectivity, convenience and nature.” Demand could have been driven by the presence of a broad range of educational institutions, said Mohan Sandrasegeran, head of research and data analytics at SRI. Mak noted that there are seven primary schools within a 2km radius of the project. Sandarasegeran also pointed out that the last private residential launch in Jurong West was in 2016. Mak added that there is a large population of some 598,160 people living in the areas surrounding Lucerne Grand, such as Jurong East, Jurong West, Clementi and Bukit Batok. “The substantial population forms a large catchment of home buyers and HDB upgraders,” he said. events.title: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma Beddington
events.summary: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? Their careers are peaking, they’re rich in money and time – and young people think they’re cool. But maybe it’s not as simple as that ‘S top sleeping on gen X.” I heard this on TikTok recently. I misinterpreted it, with a guilty start, as: “Stop sleeping, gen X,” because I am 51 (peak X), so always tired; while not sleeping at the time, I may have been resting my eyes. In fact, Joel Marlinarson, a marketing guru , was suggesting my generation have become a powerful, if underrated, force online. Aged between 46 and 61, gen Xers with proper jobs are peaking, career-wise (although it’s a different story for those out of work, as a report last month on the struggles of over-50s jobseekers made plain). We’re more likely to own homes than the following generations ; we’re emerging from the trenches of childrearing and, the argument goes, ready to indulge in some me-time. “If gen X were a country, it would be the world’s second-largest consumer market,” the World Economic Forum reported last year , with gen X women in particular influencing 70% to 80% of all consumer spending. That makes us great customers – witness the tidal wave of menopause-washed wellness guff (Which? reported last month that many pricey supplements were no better than a cheap multivitamin ) and beauty brands for people suddenly horrified by their necks . But does it give us content-creating clout? We’re supposed to be (or at least meme lore presents us as ) the forgotten generation, low-key, countercultural slackers on the sidelines in the grudge match between millennials and boomers; aspiration and self-promotion aren’t really part of our brand. Sure, kids are scrambling for Oasis tickets and rediscovering zines ; US Vogue called us “the cool ones” and the New York Times went further with “the greatest generation”. I get the argument that it’s our time to shine. But real gen Xers have a lot on their plate and it doesn’t necessarily lend itself to fun, aspirational content. Being peak career means peak responsibility: our parents are faltering (I’m writing this as my mother-in-law is moving into sheltered accommodation) and our kids are facing awful geopolitical and economic prospects that undermine their mental health and chances of independence. We’re falling apart physically: for women, the sorting hat of perimenopause doles out a set of grim symptoms, while men are wondering what will fell them next – heart, stomach, back or knees? Who wants to hear about that? And who can be arsed to make perky TikToks? I’ll tell you who: Kathryn Turner . I was introduced to Turner, M&S Food’s director of product development, by Marlinarson, for whom she is evidence that over-50s employees are “ the next biggest influencers ”. Turner, a cheery woman in smart trousers who exudes quiet competence, has worked for M&S since 1995. She launched her account in May, but her TikToks already garner up to 2m views and her nearly 250,000 fans are devoted: “Would follow that woman into war,” commented one . “Why did we give Andy Burnham the job over her,” asked another . “ I love you Kathryn turner [sic],” wrote an account claiming to be the Heartstopper actor Joe Locke . I love her, too: Turner’s calm sunniness, as she talks viewers through innovations in the picky bits space, is a balm in a fractious world. Turner isn’t Kate Moss, Miranda July or any of the other impossibly glamorous gen X figureheads – she seems like a normal, middle-aged woman who knows her stuff and does it well. I love that she’s popping up on TikTok and I get it – I’m projecting, but I bet Turner’s great in a crisis, her desk drawer and handbag well stocked with protein-rich treats, blister plasters and ibuprofen. Maybe this is our online USP. Could watching grownups quietly bossing their busy, complex lives be the next ASMR? Because, mostly, gen X aren’t the “cool ones”: they’re the knackered ones, dealing with life, death, work and frozen shoulders. I don’t know any Mosses or Chloë Sevignys, but I know lots of Turners and I, too, would follow them into war, or at least get a dopamine hit from watching them be extremely competent in short-form videos. No one would want to watch me staring at a screen then breaking to fold some pants, obviously, but I’d love to see more of my capable peers ditch the self-deprecation (very gen X) and shine online.
