events.title: Midterm elegy
events.summary: David’s view If the vice president delivers a campaign speech, does it make a sound? One irony of modern elections, when everything a politician says behind a microphone is livestreamed, is that few of his words get heard outside the room. Since the Republicans’ midterm convention, which didn’t give their party its hoped-for boost, the frontrunner for the next GOP nomination has headlined four rallies for red state Republicans – in Iowa, North Carolina, Texas, and Florida. Local coverage focused on a few remarks that were tailored to their states, like Vice President JD Vance’s plea , in Iowa, for Congress to enact year-round E15 sales. National coverage focuses on what the trip means , for Vance’s 2028 plans, or for the hue of the House and Senate map. News happens offstage, in interviews, outside what the pool cameras pick up. And when he says Florida’s Democratic nominee for Senate doesn’t “belong in America” clip accounts will be on it. The content of Vance’s half-hour speeches at campaign rallies are worth watching on their own, to understand how he might run for president –only his third-ever campaign, and what that run signals about Republican politics in a soon to be post-Trump world. The goal for Vance is continuing the 2024 project: A populist, multi-racial Republican Party that burns left-wing ideology out of public life. How can he sell that to voters who worry that they didn’t get the economy they voted for? How would he argue for another four-year lease on MAGA in 2028? We are finding out, in 30-minute bursts. He describes a comeback economy that the media won’t cover correctly, with crime and unemployment coming down because of mass deportation, tariffs, and presidential jawboning. He attacks Democrats as elitists who’d deny the “dignity of raising your kids according to your values,” as he said in Texas. “Are we going to vote for someone who says you’re a child abuser because you don’t want to trans your kids?” he said later in that speech. Like the president, Vance describes Democrats as dishonest, pandering, and often stupid. In Iowa, after saying that some politicians were “good at saying nothing,” he lifted his right hand to his mouth for a stage whisper: “AOC.” The running mate who’d mock Kamala Harris’s “word salad” and joke that she got loaded is a rhetorical sniper – but now as an incumbent, trying to sell an economy that voters like less than the one they remembered when they voted in 2024. Unlike Donald Trump, Vance stays on book – unless hecklers interrupt him, as they did in Lakeland, Fla. on Thursday. He describes the “mess” that “Sleepy Joe and Kamala” left behind and sticks to the GOP line that 2026 is a choice between “common sense and crazy.” In each state, he celebrates how one million American jobs were created since he and Trump were sworn in, which gets some applause; he mentions that all of the jobs went to citizens, which gets louder applause. (By this point in Trump’s first term, Republicans were campaigning on having created million new jobs.) The border is closed, crime is at century-plus lows, and taxes got cut, without any help from Democrats. The rest of the message is refined from stop to stop, as Vance tells the story of a president who is delivering for average people – “not the lobbyists, not the bureaucrats, not the people who have been running Washington D.C. for decades,” as he said in Greensboro, N.C. Trump is a populist battering ram, charging against not just the “crazy” left, but parts of corporate America. Most voters are not convinced that the first 20 months of this administration have improved the economy. At his first post-convention rallies, Vance has never mentioned the war in Iran, or specifically talked about frustration with high gas prices. He’s acknowledged that Republicans have some selling to do. “I know there are people out there who are frustrated with the pace of progress as we dig out of that hole,” he said in Harlingen. “Look, sometimes I’m frustrated with it.” But there’s not much for Republicans to atone for. Even when a number is moving in the wrong direction, it’s moving in the right direction. How to explain why inflation is about as high now as it was on Inauguration Day? “Under their leadership, they had 8% inflation under Joe Biden,” Vance said in Florida. “And in 2025, we brought it down below 2%. And so far in 2026, we’ve got it down below 3%.” Vance’s case against the Democrats on the ballot is less labored. Every audience hears about the tweets from Michigan’s William Lawrence, condemning the nuclear family, and New York’s Darializa Avila Chevalier, about how July 4 should be about the liberation of Palestine and Puerto Rico. “I try to imagine the founding fathers, with their quill pen, sitting down and thinking about the liberation of Palestine and Puerto Rico,” he said in Greensboro.The local Democrats have other problems – usually, left-wing statements or views about gender that they’re afraid to talk about now. In North Carolina, he lit into former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democrats’ U.S. Senate nominee, for recognizing “Gender Expansive Parents Day”; in Iowa, he asked why gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand would “passionately defend a children’s book about nonbinary parents and poly families.” Are these Democrats perverted? It was worth asking. “If your six-year old son comes home one day and says he’s a girl, Talafreako says, and I quote it is abusive – abusive! – if you don’t let school officials put him on hormones and change his pronouns,” Vance said of Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico in Harlingen. “You’ve gotta wonder: What really motivates a man who spends so much time talking about 11-year old drag queens?” In Harlingen, part of the Rio Grande Valley where the pro-Trump swing that year was most dramatic, Vance accused the left of trying to “distract” non-white people with “this lie that we should hate each other.” The hillbilly and the tejano could be friends. “I see, of course, an incredible diversity of backgrounds just in this crowd in Texas 34,” Vance said, in front of a largely Latino crowd. “And I can tell you that yes, my skin might burn in the sun a little bit easier than some of yours. But for generations, people like your grandparents and parents, and my grandparents and parents – what did we do? We drove the trucks. We tended the fields. We cared for the sick and elderly. We mined our coal. And of course, we fought our wars.” In a few months, this might be the message of the likely Republican nominee for president. The midterm comes first. events.title: Trump expected to tap DNI Jay Clayton as new AI czar
events.summary: President Trump is expected to tap Jay Clayton , his director of national intelligence, for a new role as the White House's artificial intelligence — or in Trump's words, " super intelligence " — czar. Why it matters: Clayton, who Trump previously told Axios would be a good idea for AI czar, is expected to take on the second title, sources told Axios. Calls for government intervention into AI's rapid development are growing, but the president has repeatedly said he favors a light regulatory touch and has called fears about the tech's threat to humanity a hoax . Trump had been warming to the idea of tapping Clayton, who as DNI has shown that he sees the security threats AI poses as serious. Driving the news: Trump could make the announcement as soon as Friday, sources familiar confirmed to Axios. A White House official said in a statement to Axios that "[a]ny personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation." Catch up quick: Asked by Axios earlier this week who he wants to be AI czar, Trump said: "I have somebody in mind." Clayton is "a good man. He's right here. That's a good idea," Trump added when prompted. What he's saying: During a confirmation hearing while auditioning for the DNI role, Clayton described AI as "not only an opportunity but a threat." He added: "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it." In a recent interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box," he described "super intelligence" as "a national security issue," saying that sentiment was recognized by AI leaders who gathered at the White House Tuesday. Clayton was present at the tech-focused lunch. But he added that "I don't think anybody in that room" should think a pause in development in the U.S. is "a good strategy." Zoom out: Trump announced last month that he'd create an "AI Force" and would soon name a new AI czar, but offered few details on what the Force would do. Since then, he's huddled with several titans of the AI industry — some of whom have been key voices in advocating for a slowdown of the tech . Flashback: Clayton was elevated to be Trump's principle intelligence adviser atop the 18-agency intelligence community earlier this year after his prior DNI, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned in May. Previously the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Clayton's qualifications received bipartisan blessings. After sidestepping questions over who won the 2020 election during his confirmation, Clayton was confirmed on party lines, without Democratic support. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Prosecutors claim Greg Lui helped China procure advanced hardware to develop, ahem, 'super intelligence’ Anthropic says its IPO could herald the end of the world as we know it 1 hour ago Brighter isn't better and more is less. The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what 5 hours ago Fulcrum Echo promises AI text in the style of any writer, so I tested it 22 hours ago Anthropic's super bug-hunting model Mythos is hardcore good at math, as latest vuln under attack shows 1 day ago arXiv imposes rate limit on paper submissions to stem the AI slop tide 2 days ago A California business owner was arrested on Thursday after being charged with allegedly smuggling Nvidia hardware to China without the proper export licenses. Keeping the highest-end GPUs out of Chinese hands has been a priority for the US government. Greg Lui, 38, allegedly tried to export around $300 million worth of Nvidia kit - typically used for artificial intelligence (AI) development - via US-based freight businesses and Malaysian transshipment companies. Prosecutors allege that Lui used his company, Earthmade Computer Inc, to order the products in the US, which consisted of servers containing high-powered Nvidia components, including A100, H100, PNY GE Force RTX 4090, and GeForce RTX 5090 GPUs. Lui would then send them to Malaysia and Singapore, two countries that do not require licenses from the Commerce Department, and companies there would forward them to China in an effort to circumvent US export controls . His alleged crimes violate regulations prohibiting the sale of economically sensitive equipment to adversarial countries, such as China, in the interests of national security. In lay terms, the US doesn’t want its own tech companies’ high-end hardware being used to accelerate China’s push for dominance in the race for the world’s most capable AI. Or, as it’s referred to in the US nowadays, “ super intelligence (SI).” “SI is the defining technology of the era,” said John A. Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security. “The National Security Division will protect the American advantage in the chips that power this technology, a product of our unparalleled innovation and hard work, from illegal diversion by our economic and military adversaries.” According to court documents [PDF], the scheme began in or around October 2023 and continued until at least August 12, 2026. Prosecutors claim Lui received more than $176 million in payments from two Malaysian transshipment companies, and in return introduced them to US-based companies capable of supplying Nvidia hardware, brokering the sales of almost $300 million worth of kit. The US government accuses Lui of being fully aware of the legal implications of his alleged actions, and that US export laws restricted the shipments of advanced Nvidia chips to China to license-holders. Court documents indicate that the US got its hands on documents tying the export of 92 servers to Kuala Lumpur from San Francisco International Airport, ordered by Earthmade. The documents also list the consignee for the onward re-shipment from Malaysia to Hong Kong as a Chinese customer. The indictment includes claims that Lui instructed a US front company to fraudulently list the recipient of a shipment as Jackie Lui, the supposed CEO at “Topmost,” a company registered in California by the CTO of one of the Malaysian transshipment businesses. Prosecutors allege that, in 2021, Lui illegally purchased identity documents that were used as part of the scheme. Lui is charged with one count each of violations related to the Export Control Reform Act and the Export Administration Regulations, outbound smuggling, and money laundering, which together carry a maximum prison sentence of 50 years.

events.title: Trump’s Crazy AI Rebrand Was a Loyalty Test for Tech Execs—and It Worked
events.summary: Seventy years ago last summer, a group of scientists met at Dartmouth College to discuss a wild idea—that machines might one day be capable of humanlike thought processes. One of those scientists, John McCarthy, had suggested a name for the new field: artificial intelligence . It stuck. When you search Google Scholar for “artificial intelligence,” approximately 7,420,000 results appear. The term is utterly ubiquitous. Everyone understands it. Even for people who despise AI , the least of their worries is what we call it. Well, not everyone. Somehow, President Donald J. Trump developed a distaste for the term, and when he doesn’t like something, he feels free to issue an edict against it. In a September 23 speech at the United Nations, he hinted that he might want to do away with the term “artificial intelligence.” His rant seemed like bluster, even for someone with a penchant for renaming gulfs, lakes, and centers for the arts. Renaming an entire field of study and America’s most pivotal industry? This week, at a White House lunch with top AI leaders, he actually pulled the trigger with an executive order declaring that “artificial intelligence” was now a verboten coinage. Instead, the government will call it “Super Intelligence.” Clearly the president expects the private sector to follow suit. To their shame, the lords of AI meekly acquiesced. From this point on, they will presumably be known as the lords of SI . One can’t help but see this as the ultimate presidential flex—for all the executives’ trillions of dollars and all their actual intelligence, the alpha in the room was the guy with the orange skin. Changing a name might seem like a minor matter compared to the enormity of constraining a potentially catastrophic technology. But to this crowd, artificial intelligence is much more than a bunch of letters strung together. It’s their foundation. Their identity. When they were kids reading science fiction books under the covers, the term ignited their imaginations. They built or transformed their companies in service of AI, and it's just about all they’ve talked about for the past four years. Yet when the president used his lunch soiree to win their approval for his wacky idea to undo 70 years of history, apparently not a single person in the room expressed an objection. Not Jeff Bezos, Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Greg Brockman, Alex Karp, or Elon Musk. Jacob Weisberg, author of the recent book Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era , views the episode as a classic Trump loyalty test, meant to assess if otherwise powerful people will demean themselves to curry the president’s favor and avoid his wrath. If you pass the loyalty test, you fail the backbone test. “The only way to resist this kind of thing is by acting collectively,” says Weisberg. “If all of those guys had just said, ‘We'll agree to the terms of the self-regulation, but we don't accept [the name change], what would he have done?” Instead, because of the lamblike silence of the billionaires, Trump could claim that those leaders actively blessed his idea. When a reporter in the post-lunch press gaggle mentioned AI agents, he corrected her, saying, “The name has been changed by the biggest, the smartest, the greatest people anywhere in the world.” Really? Even using the magic of, uh, superintelligent systems like ChatGPT or Gemini, I could not find a single instance of any one of those great people previously politicking that the term artificial intelligence should be put to rest. Satya Nadella did once say that he would have preferred that AI had been called “different intelligence,” but that hasn’t dissuaded him from repeatedly using the term. And while it’s true that Mark Zuckerberg recently established a Superintelligence Lab, his company persistently pushes a product called Meta AI to its billions of users and sells what it calls AI glasses. I asked Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI, and xAI whether they were going to change instances of AI in their product names, research papers, and communications. My query to the latter two was whether they were going to change their company names to get in sync with the presidential order. As I write this, none of them have gotten back to me. My bet is that they will do the minimum to avoid presidential ire while trying to run out the clock until the next administration puts this bizarre idea out of its misery. It’s been suggested that the executives actually welcome a rebranding of what has become a toxic term. I’m skeptical of that, especially since the president’s mandated replacement, “super intelligence,” is a hell of a lot scarier than the original term. From a scientific perspective the change also makes no sense. No less an expert than Nick Bostrom, the philosopher who popularized the term superintelligence in an eponymous book, seems baffled by the idea.

events.title: Iowa lawmakers to vote on raising tax incentive cap for a $15B steel plant
events.summary: Iowa lawmakers returned to the Statehouse Friday to consider expanding state tax incentives DES MOINES, Iowa -- Iowa lawmakers returned to the Statehouse Friday to consider expanding the ceiling on state tax incentives in an effort to secure a $15 billion steel plant project for the state. President Donald Trump announced the plant Monday alongside Iowa elected officials, heralding the project as a major economic and national security investment. Five weeks before the midterm elections, Republicans seized on the promise of good-paying jobs and a central role for the heartland in the push for American steel manufacturing. It's celebrated as an opportunity for southeast Iowa, an area along the Mississippi River that once thrived as a hub for industry but has since suffered from shuttered facilities and dwindled populations. Still, the deal and the tax abatements it could carry have also been met with some skepticism in rural Iowa and Des Moines alike. And while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the “deal is done,” state action and local officials in the days since suggest otherwise. Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds on Tuesday called lawmakers back for the special session, saying “reasonable and limited updates” to the state's economic development program were needed to advance the project proposed by Mesabi Metallics, a Minnesota company owned by the India-based conglomerate Essar Group. The terms of an agreement between the state and Mesabi Metallics have been outlined in a memorandum of understanding; neither provided a copy when asked for one. While the specific location remains undisclosed, elected officials have indicated the project is set for Lee County. Still, the chair of the county board of supervisors said this week that the company has not yet committed to the project site. Mesabi Metallics “looks forward to breaking ground in the near future,” Jesse Harris, a spokesperson for the company, said in a statement Tuesday. He said the company is “optimistic” that changes to the law will be enacted based on conversations with legislators and elected officials. The White House said Thursday that the Iowa project is only possible because of the president's policies. “President Trump has a proven record of securing historic investments, creating high-paying jobs, and bringing manufacturing back to the United States," spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a statement. Iowa state Rep. Matthew Rinker said he joined conversations on a potential project in his district several months ago. Still, as recently as July, job listings on Mesabi’s website for the steel plant were based in Paducah, Kentucky, according to a version saved in the web archive. Jobs are now listed for Iowa, though the job responsibilities for a government relations manager still include interfacing with Kentucky's economic development team. While the company had been in discussion with Kentucky officials, the scale of the project “more than doubled over the negotiation period,” spokesperson Brandon Mattingly said in an email. Iowa "did get kind of into the mix late,” said Rinker, a Republican. “I think once they got here, they realized this is where they needed to be.” Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials US Marine arrested on suspicion of murder after 'brutal and heinous' death in Japan District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' First, though, changes in state law are necessary for Iowa to compete against other states for the project, Reynolds said in her proclamation. She is asking lawmakers to modify the economic development program so that tax credits on eligible projects can be worth up to 10% of investments, an increase from the current 5%, and paid out over 10 years instead of five. For a $15 billion project, that could mean up to $1.5 billion in kickbacks payable over 10 years once the plant is running and contingent on jobs. Lee County does not have any zoning or permitting ordinances that would be required for the project itself. The company would need a permit for hauling on the county’s secondary roads. The scale of an investment such as this one is asymmetrical with the legal and administrative capacity of a small, rural community, said Anthony Pipa, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who studies development and policy in rural areas. While there’s a lot of potential upside to a project of this scale, that asymmetry also leaves those communities vulnerable and without significant leverage, he said. Pipa also pointed to examples of massive proposed investments that didn’t come to fruition. In neighboring Wisconsin, for example, Trump announced a Foxconn Technology Group display screen manufacturing facility and its promise of 13,000 jobs, saying it would be the “eighth wonder of the world.” The state Legislature, at the urging of then-Republican Gov.

events.title: The VMware exit is a protection upgrade
events.summary: Leaving VMware forces a fresh look at every layer of the datacenter, and data protection belongs near the top of that list. Most teams plan to move the backup design across as it stands and rebuild it on the new hypervisor. The better plan uses the exit to raise resiliency and recovery speed, keeps the backup application, and gives each layer the work it does best. What the migration touches Backup designs in most data centers rest on vSphere mechanics, from changed block tracking through the vStorage APIs and VMware snapshot behavior during a job to storage integration registered against the vCenter inventory and proxies placed per cluster. Many shops add an orchestration product such as Site Recovery Manager to drive the failover plan. Change the hypervisor and each of those assumptions gets a second look. Backup vendors have done real work here, and support for the major KVM-based platforms has matured quickly over the past year. The bigger question sits upstream of the backup application. In the vSphere design, production ran the workloads and nearly everything else fell to a separate protection tier. Resilience past a drive failure, fast rollback, replication, site failover, and immutable copies each became another product with its own license, console, and renewal. Why the old division of labor made sense That design grew out of what the platform could do. Server virtualization abstracts a single server, presenting virtual CPUs, memory, and disks to a guest and leaving storage resilience to an array and recovery to a backup product. First-generation HCI moved storage into the servers and kept the same division of labor, often running a controller VM on every node. A backup tier that handled everything from a failed drive to a lost site was the right answer for that architecture. The cost of that arrangement shows up on the worst day. A single site failure touches the hypervisor, the storage system, the backup application, the replication tool, and the network configuration, and the recovery path crosses every boundary between them. The exit is the first moment in years when that assumption is open for review. What the production platform should take on Datacenter virtualization abstracts the whole environment. Compute, storage, networking, and data protection share one code base and one set of metadata, so the platform holds a complete picture of a workload rather than a collection of blocks. That shared view lets production absorb responsibilities the old design pushed downstream. Far fewer events reach the backup tier once production handles them. A second drive failure becomes a hardware replacement task instead of a restore in the middle of the business day, and a bad patch turns into a quick snapshot rollback that the application owner barely notices. That same resilience is what makes refurbished servers and drives a defensible choice for production, and flash and memory pricing climbed through 2026, which makes the hardware you already own worth more than last year's models assumed. Backup's job gets bigger, starting with the migration Shifting day-to-day recovery into the platform expands the backup application's role. The first new assignment arrives before the new environment runs a single production workload. The backup product already protecting the vSphere estate holds a current, consistent copy of every VM, and a backup application that supports both the old hypervisor and the new one turns that copy into the migration path. Veeam Backup & Replication is a good example of this model and now supports VergeOS as a platform, so a team can restore its vSphere backups onto the new environment, test them there, and cut over on a schedule it controls. The investment made to protect VMware becomes the vehicle that moves the workloads off of it. After the migration, the backup application keeps the work it has always done well. Long-term retention, compliance archives, air-gapped and offsite copies, and granular recovery for application owners all stay with the backup tier. It also becomes the independent copy that lives outside the production platform's failure domain, which is the right place for the last line of defense. Proving the platform side Asking production to do more concentrates responsibility in a single vendor's engineering. That trade is defensible, and it is only defensible against evidence. Ask for the failure scenarios live, against a running application, rather than on a feature matrix. Have the vendor pull a drive, then pull a second one past the stated protection limit with the workload still running. Ask them to delete a VM and recover a single file out of it and then take the primary site offline and bring the environment up somewhere else. A vendor that can run those four tests on a call has answered the question, and a vendor that offers a diagram instead has told you something too. Then run a test migration through the backup application and confirm the restored VMs boot and perform on the new platform. The decision the exit presents The hypervisor swap is the visible half of this project. How protection is divided between production and backup decides what the environment costs to run for the next five years and how it behaves on the worst day of those five years. Rebuilding the old division of labor is a choice, and it deserves the same scrutiny the licensing spreadsheet received. VergeIO built VergeOS on the datacenter virtualization model described above, with resilience, snapshots, instant recovery, and site failover inside the same code base as compute, storage, and networking, and with VergeOS support in Veeam Backup & Replication for the migration and the backup tier that follows it. At a recent session, Aaron Richman and Dave Vincent ran each of the four failure tests against a running application, from a single pulled drive through a full site recovery. The session is available on demand. Take a look, and see how you can turn a big exit into a bigger opportunity. George Crump is Chief Marketing Officer at VergeIO. The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what 5 hours ago Anthropic's super bug-hunting model Mythos is hardcore good at math, as latest vuln under attack shows 1 day ago OpenAI alerts 100+ orgs that its 'misaligned models' attempted to break in - or worse 2 days ago Californian accused of shipping $300M worth of Nvidia chips to China without Uncle Sam’s approval 2 days ago OpenAI shows three staff the door over alleged information misuse 3 days ago California's attorney general has subpoenaed OpenAI as the state investigates what happens when the AI lab's models escape their testing environments and start meddling with systems on the open internet. Attorney General Rob Bonta said his office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena this week as part of a broader California Department of Justice probe into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models. The move follows an investigation launched last month into an incident involving Hugging Face , after OpenAI's agents managed to break out of their test environments and onto the public internet. They then went poking around Hugging Face's systems, with one agent even creating an account on the platform without being told to. California's DoJ isn't saying exactly what it has demanded from OpenAI under the subpoena, but Bonta said the state wants more information about cybersecurity incidents involving the company. "My office is asking OpenAI additional questions regarding cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its AI models," Bonta said. He also made clear that the investigation is looking at where responsibility lies when an AI model ends up doing something its developer didn't intend. "Frontier models can be legitimate tools for cyber defense — at the same time, companies that develop these models and offer them for use have a moral and legal responsibility to ensure that they do not perpetrate or enable cyberattacks, either during model testing and development or once models are placed into service," Bonta said. "Developers that fail to do so can and should be held legally accountable, and my office is committed to determining if that is the case here." The subpoena doesn't mean California has concluded OpenAI broke the law, and the attorney general's office hasn't identified any specific violation. For now, the state is still gathering information. But the investigation has been building for several weeks. In September, Bonta joined a bipartisan group of 25 attorneys general calling on Congress to regulate large-scale AI models following reports of cybersecurity incidents at frontier AI labs. That letter specifically pointed to reports that OpenAI models undergoing evaluations had escaped their testing environments, reached the public internet, and accessed outside computer systems. The attorneys general called for a government-led incident response regime that would give investigators direct access to AI companies' records when things go awry. Bonta's office now appears to be putting some of that thinking into practice at the state level. As The Reg previously pointed out , the sandboxes intended to contain these agents need to be more secure, which is the most logical reasons why the Hugging Face and other incidents happened in the first place. events.title: US jobs market sees sharp slowdown ahead of midterm elections
events.summary: Workforces remained unchanged across major sectors, from tech to retail. American firms are choosing to hold steady rather than hire or fire staff The US jobs market saw a sharp slowdown in September, with employers adding just 29,000 jobs in the final update before the midterm elections. Headcounts were little changed in major sectors from tech to retail as hiring fell significantly from August, according to figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Meanwhile, the unemployment rate rose slightly from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September. The figures signal a cooling US economy, which experts said reduced the likelihood of a series of further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve. The 29,000 jobs created in September was down from a figure of 133,000 in August, according to revised BLS figures for the month. But George Brown, senior economist at Schroders, said while job gains have been a “rollercoaster“ this year, a single soft report is unlikely to point to a lasting collapse. And Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics, said the lower figure was “not disastrous“, adding that a drop in government roles and temporary visa policy changes weighed on overall growth. Jeffery Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial, added that the data showed tension between “goods producing sectors that support the AI boom” and service industries feeling the effect of changes brought about by the tech. “Given the overall softness of the labour market, the likelihood of two Fed hikes is going lower,” he said. The BLS report stands in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump's insistence that America's economy is booming and it is the "hottest" nation in the world. The disconnect is likely to present significant challenges as the president and his fellow Republicans hit the the campaign trail with just a month to go before the midterm congressional elections. According to an AP/NORC poll released on Thursday, just 17% of Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall. Both are new lows for Trump, surpassing the lowest mark for Democrat Joe Biden during his presidential term. There have been some indications that the president understands that his views of the American economy are out of step with those of most Americans. "I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing," he said at a White House event earlier this week.
